According to tradition, Adi Shankaracharya found a black stone image of Badrinarayan, made of shaligram stone, in the Alaknanda and first enshrined it in a cave near the Tapt Kund hot springs. In the sixteenth century the King of Garhwal moved the image to the present temple. The temple is about 15 metres tall, with a small cupola under a gilt roof, and a stone facade with arched windows that resembles a Buddhist vihara. Earthquakes and avalanches have repeatedly destroyed it.

In earlier times pilgrims walked hundreds of miles to reach it. As late as the First World War the settlement consisted only of some twenty huts for the temple's staff, though the site drew thousands of visitors each year and up to 50,000 at the festivals held every twelve years.

The Bhagavata Purana says that Vishnu, in his form as the sages Nara and Narayana, has practised austerity at Badrikashram since time immemorial. Another story holds that the area was full of badari, a wild berry, and that Lakshmi took the form of a badari tree to shade Vishnu as he meditated. The Pandavas are said to have passed through Badrinath and Mana, 4 kilometres to the north, on their way to heaven, and a cave at Mana is where Vyasa is said to have written the Mahabharata.

Jains also hold the place sacred, holding that many Jain monks attained liberation by austerity there. The Ganges is said to have been divided into two channels when it came to earth, with the Alaknanda as one of them.
baghdad: Baghdad stands on a vast, almost entirely flat and low-lying plain bisected by the Tigris, formed by the periodic flooding of the river. The river divides the city into an eastern half, Risafa, and a western half, Karkh. The Diyala river, a tributary of the Tigris, flows south-east of the city and borders its eastern suburbs.

After the fall of the Umayyads the victorious Abbasids sought a new capital. On 30 July 762 the Caliph al-Mansur commissioned the construction of Baghdad, guided by the Iranian Barmakids, believing the site ideal for ruling the Islamic Empire. He hired two designers, Naubakht, a Zoroastrian, and Mashallah, a Jew from Khorasan, who chose an auspicious founding date under the sign of Leo. The historian al-Tabari recorded a prophecy of Christian monks about a leader named Miklas who would build a great city there, and al-Mansur, once called Miklas, saw it as a good omen.

Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and an intellectual and cultural centre, with institutions such as the House of Wisdom and a multi-ethnic, multi-religious population. For much of the Abbasid era, the Islamic Golden Age, it was one of the largest cities in the world, and its population peaked at more than a million. The Round City, its original core, ceased to exist as a result of the Mongol siege. The Mongol Empire largely destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and a long decline followed, marked by frequent plagues and shifts of power between successive empires.

Later Baghdad was the administrative centre of Ottoman Iraq, with authority over the provinces of Basra, Mosul and Shahrizor. During the First World War it was made the capital of Mandatory Iraq. After Iraq was recognised as an independent monarchy in 1932 the city gradually regained some of its prominence as a centre of Arab culture. It suffered severe damage in the Iraq War, which began with the invasion of 2003, and lost much cultural heritage and many historical artifacts.

Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq and its seat of government, on the banks of the Tigris. Its estimated population is 8 million. Historic mosques, churches, mandis and synagogues reflect its diversity, and the Masjid al-Kadhimayn, the Buratha Mosque, the Shrine of Abdul-Qadir Gilani and the Abu Hanifa Mosque are visited by millions each year. The University of Baghdad is the largest university in Iraq, and the city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Literature in December 2015.
baghdad-pact: The Central Treaty Organization, also called the Baghdad Pact and at first the Middle East Treaty Organization, was a Cold War military alliance formed on 24 February 1955 by Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and the United Kingdom. It was modelled on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and committed its members to mutual cooperation and protection and to non-intervention in each other's affairs. Its aim was to contain the Soviet Union by a line of strong states along its south-western frontier, which gave it the name Northern Tier. American pressure and promises of aid were key in the negotiations, but the United States could not at first take part.

Unlike NATO, the pact had no unified military command, and few American or British bases were established in member countries. The United States did have communications and intelligence facilities in Iran and flew U-2 flights over the Soviet Union from bases in Pakistan. The headquarters were in Baghdad from 1955 to 1958 and then in Ankara until 1979. In 1958 the United States joined the military committee.

Turkey had signed a Pact of Mutual Cooperation with Pakistan in February 1954. A secretary general served renewable three-year terms. The organisation also sponsored research and cultural bodies such as the CENTO Institute of Nuclear Science, which moved from Baghdad to Tehran in 1958, and a railway from Lake Van in Turkey to Sharafkhaneh in Iran, funded largely by the United Kingdom.

On 14 July 1958 the Iraqi monarchy was overthrown in a military coup, and the new government under Abd al-Karim Qasim withdrew Iraq from the pact, which formally ended on 24 March 1959, and adopted a non-aligned stance. The organisation then took the name CENTO. In the 1960s it declined to become involved in the Arab-Israeli conflict or the Indo-Pakistani wars: Pakistan's requests for help in 1965 and 1971 were rejected on the ground that the alliance aimed to contain the Soviet Union, not India.

After the Turkish invasion of Cyprus in 1974 the United Kingdom withdrew the forces earmarked for the alliance, and the United States Congress halted military aid to Turkey. Iran withdrew on 11 March 1979 and Pakistan the next day, and on 16 March 1979 the organisation was formally dissolved. Later defence agreements between the United States or the United Kingdom and regional states were made bilaterally.
bagram: Bagram lies about 60 kilometres north of Kabul in Parwan Province, at the junction of the Ghorband and Panjshir valleys, near Charikar. The location made it a key passage from ancient India along the Silk Road. One route led west through the mountains towards Bamiyan, and another north over the Kushan Pass to the Baghlan Valley, the Kushan site of Surkh Kotal and the commercial centre of Balkh.

The ancient city of Kapisi is identified with the site. Ancient Buddhist and Hindu sculptures suggest that it was first ruled by Indic people who migrated to or mixed with Iranian populations, among them Kambojas from Bactria. In 305 BCE Seleucus I, after a brief conflict with the Mauryan founder Chandragupta Maurya, ceded Gandhara, Arachosia and lands south of Bagram to the Mauryans. During about 120 years of Mauryan rule in southern Afghanistan Buddhism was introduced and became a major religion beside Zoroastrianism and local beliefs. Mauryan punch-marked coins found at Begram point to early trade or administrative presence.

In the first century CE Bagram was the capital of the Kushan Empire. The Bagram treasure indicates intense commercial exchange between the cultural centres of the classical world, with the Kushan Empire at the junction of land and sea trade between east and west. The Begram ivories and other pieces are purely Hellenistic, Roman, Chinese or Indian, with little of the mixing seen in Greco-Buddhist art.

The Islamic conquest of the region began in the seventh century, but conversion was not complete until Ghaznavid rule. The modern town is believed to have been founded by Babur on the ancient site. In the Baburnama he describes a visit in 1519, dwelling on the colony of Hindu ascetics at Gurh Kattri that fascinated him.
A runway was built at Bagram in 1976, and from 1979 to 1989 it was a Soviet air base. It later served as a major base for US forces in Afghanistan, which left it in July 2021.
bagrat-iii-of-georgia: Bagrat was the only known son of King Gurgen of Iberia and Gurandukht, daughter of King George II of Abkhazia. As a child he was adopted and named heir by his father's cousin David III Kuropalates, ruler of Upper Tao, who raised and educated him. In 976 David defeated Kvirike II of Kakheti and expelled the Kakhetians from Iberia, and installed Bagrat as ruler under his father's regency. Two years later, nobles allied with the new prince of Kakheti seized the fortress of Uplistsikhe and took Bagrat and his parents hostage, until David III negotiated their release.

Meanwhile Abkhazia, under the blind King Theodosius III, a maternal uncle of Bagrat, was weakened by conflict with its nobles. The eristavi Ioane Marushisdze, who had installed Bagrat in Iberia, helped to raise him to the Abkhazian crown, generally dated to 978, though some sources give two years later.

Bagrat then had to put down a revolt in Kartli, where his mother Gurandukht, the regent, had tried to assert independence. He defeated the rebels at Moghri, took Uplistsikhe from her and put her under supervision. A later quarrel with the duke Rati, son of Liparit, ended in the king besieging Kldekari. Rati was pardoned and made duke of Argveti.

When David III died on 31 March 1000, possibly murdered, Emperor Basil II claimed Tao, which David had been compelled to bequeath to Byzantium, and took it within months. He gave Bagrat's father Gurgen the title of magistros and Bagrat that of Kouropalates. In 1008 Bagrat inherited the title King of the Georgians from his father, along with the duchy of Lower Tao and Javakheti. He invaded Kakheti and Hereti and had completed the conquest of Kakheti by 1010.

He took the title King of the Abkhazians, Kartvelians, Rans and Kakhs. In 1012 he allied with the Armenian king Gagik I and marched on Ganja, took Shamkor, and made the emir Fadl his vassal, bound to pay tribute. He also defeated the Klarjeti princes Sumbat and Gurgen.

Bagrat spent the winter of 1013–1014 at Panaskerti in Tao and died there on 7 May 1014 after a reign of thirty-six years. He was buried that year in Bedia Cathedral, which he had completed in 999. He founded the office of Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia and began the Bagrati Cathedral at Kutaisi, completed in 1003. His wife Martha bore him George I, who succeeded him.

Most historians regard him as the first monarch of a unified Kingdom of Georgia, excluding the early Iberian ruler Pharnavaz I. Ten later Georgian monarchs took his name. The Georgian Orthodox Church canonised him on 22 December 2016.
bagrati-cathedral: The Cathedral of the Dormition, known as the Kutaisi Cathedral and more often as Bagrati Cathedral, stands on Ukimerioni Hill in the centre of Kutaisi, in the Imereti region of Georgia. It was built in the early years of the eleventh century during the reign of King Bagrat III, from whom it takes its name, meaning Bagrat's cathedral. An inscription on the north wall states that the floor was laid in the year 223 of the chronicon, that is, 1003.

The cathedral is dedicated to the Dormition of the Mother of God, and its main feast day is Mariamoba. It is described as a masterpiece of medieval Georgian architecture, and William Lethaby called it the finest of Georgian monuments. King George I of Georgia is buried there.

In 1692 the cathedral was devastated during the Ottoman invasion of the Kingdom of Imereti. The cupola and the ceiling collapsed, and it suffered heavy damage over the following centuries. Conservation, restoration and archaeological work began in the 1950s under the Georgian architect Vakhtang Tsintsadze. His restoration was carried out in six stages and continued through 1994. In that year the cathedral was included in UNESCO's World Heritage list together with the Gelati Monastery as a single entity. In 2001 ownership passed from the Georgian state to the Georgian Orthodox Church, and it is the cathedral seat of the Metropolitan of Kutaisi, with a monastery on the grounds and regular services.

Further works to reconstruct the building ended in 2012 and were controversial. In 2010 UNESCO placed the cathedral on its list of World Heritage in Danger, fearing for the structural integrity and authenticity of the site, and in 2017 it removed Bagrati Cathedral from the World Heritage list, while Gelati Monastery kept its status. The cathedral remains a symbol of the city of Kutaisi and one of its main tourist attractions.
bagrationi-dynasty: The origins of the Bagrationi are disputed. Georgian scholars argue they were of Georgian origin, while Armenian and Western scholars see them as a branch of the Armenian Bagratuni dynasty. A tradition first recorded by the 11th-century chronicler Sumbat Davitis-Dze held that the family descended from the biblical King David and came from Israel around 530. Modern scholarship has discounted this. Cyril Toumanoff concluded that the Georgian line began with Adarnase, who passed to Kartli after a failed rising against Arab rule in 775, and whose son Ashot I acquired the principality of Iberia in 813. The legend of Davidic descent later helped maintain the dynasty's legitimacy.

The sons and grandsons of Ashot I founded three branches, Kartli, Tao and Klarjeti, which fought each other and their neighbours. The Kartli line prevailed, and in 888 Adarnase I restored the Iberian royal authority that had lain dormant since 580. Bagrat III consolidated his inheritance in Tao-Klarjeti and Abkhazia with the help of his foster-father David III of Tao. The united monarchy flourished under David IV the Builder (1089–1125), who finished the unification by retaking Tbilisi in 1122, and under his great-granddaughter Tamar the Great (1184–1213). When the male line ended with George III, the dynasty continued through Tamar's marriage to David Soslan, an Alan prince of reputed Bagratid descent.

The Khwarezmians in 1225 and the Mongols in 1236 ended the golden age. Timur's eight invasions between 1386 and 1403 dealt a heavy blow, and by 1490/91 the kingdom had split into three: Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti, each under a branch of the family. For three centuries they lived under Ottoman and Persian overlordship, and many converted to Islam to be invested by their suzerains.

After the death of Erekle II in 1798 and of his son George XII, Emperor Paul I of Russia declared Kartli-Kakheti annexed on 18 December 1800, and Alexander I formally deposed the dynasty on 12 September 1801. Solomon II of Imereti was dethroned by Russian forces on 20 February 1810 and died in exile in Trabzon in 1815. Most Bagrationi princes who resisted were arrested and deported.

In the Russian Empire the family became prominent aristocrats, among them Prince Pyotr Bagration, a general and hero of the war of 1812. The dynasty remained a Russian noble family until the February Revolution of 1917. After Soviet rule was established in 1921 some members lost property, others moved to Western Europe, and some returned after Georgia regained independence in 1991.
bahadur-shah-ii: Bahadur Shah Zafar, born on 24 October 1775, was the second son of Akbar II and succeeded him in 1837. By then the Mughal Empire had been reduced to the city of Delhi and the territory around it as far as Palam. The East India Company was the dominant power in India, provided the emperor with a pension, and collected taxes in Delhi and maintained a military force there. Zafar had no interest in statecraft or imperial ambition.

He was a noted Urdu poet and wrote many ghazals. His court was home to Mirza Ghalib, Daagh Dehlvi, Momin Khan Momin and Mohammad Ibrahim Zauq, who was also his mentor. He was a devout Sufi, and in one of his verses he stated that Hinduism and Islam share the same essence.

When sepoys of the rebellion reached Delhi in May 1857, Zafar asked why they had come, since he had no means to maintain them. He yielded to their demands when told that they could not defeat the Company without him. On 16 May sepoys and palace servants killed fifty-two Europeans held prisoner in the palace, despite his protests. It was later believed that he was not directly responsible but might have prevented the killings.

As the siege of Delhi turned against the rebels, Zafar took refuge at Humayun's Tomb. Company forces under Major William Hodson captured him on 20 September 1857. The next day Hodson shot his sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and his grandson Mirza Abu Bakht.

Zafar's trial in the Red Fort in 1858 lasted 21 days. He was charged with aiding the mutinies, encouraging war against the British Government, assuming the sovereignty of Hindostan, and being accessory to the murder of Christians. In his defence he stated that he was helpless before the will of the sepoys. Because of Hodson's guarantee on his surrender, he was exiled to Rangoon rather than sentenced to death.

He died on 7 November 1862 at the age of 87 and was buried that afternoon near the Shwedagon Pagoda. His exile ended the nearly 500-year Timurid line, and he is seen as a hero of the rebellion of 1857.
bahadur-shah-of-gujarat: Born Bahadur Khan into the Muzaffarid dynasty, he was the son of Prince Khalil Khan, who became sultan in 1511 as Muzaffar Shah II, and of Rani Lakshmi Bai, daughter of a Gohel Rajput. His grandfather, Sultan Mahmud Begada, kept him at court. When his elder brother Sikandar Shah was named heir, Bahadur Khan feared for his life and fled, first to Chittor and then to Ibrahim Lodi; he was present at the Battle of Panipat without taking part in the fighting.

Muzaffar Shah II died in 1526. Sikandar Shah was murdered after a few weeks on the instructions of his slave Imad-ul-Mulk Khush Kadam, who put an infant brother on the throne as Mahmud Shah II. Bahadur Khan returned, the nobles joined him, and he marched on Champaner, executed Imad-ul-Mulk and had the child poisoned.

Bahadur Shah campaigned in the Deccan in 1528 and 1529, taking the fort of Ahmednagar and forcing the rulers of Ahmadnagar and Berar to sign a humiliating treaty. The fortress of Mandu fell on 28 March 1531, when Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Malwa and his seven sons were captured; they were later put to death by their guards during a rescue attempt. In 1532 he raised a siege of Chittor in return for an enormous ransom. Until his defeat by Humayun the power of Gujarat was at its height, with the rulers of Ahmednagar and Burhanpur acknowledging him as overlord.

The quarrel with Humayun began because Bahadur Shah had sheltered the Mughal prince Muhammad Zaman Mirza. The rout near Mandasur is usually explained by the treachery of Rumi Khan, the Turkish head of the Gujarat artillery. Bahadur Shah fled to Mandu, Champaner and finally Diu. When Humayun left to face the revolt of Sher Shah Suri, the country rose, and Bahadur Shah defeated the Mughals at Kanij and expelled them from Gujarat.

The Treaty of Bassein was signed on 23 December 1534 aboard the galleon St. Mattheus. Having recovered his kingdom, Bahadur Shah regretted the alliance. In February 1537 he visited the Portuguese viceroy's ship off Diu and was attacked and killed on his way back, on 13 February; his body was thrown into the sea. According to the Mirat-i-Sikandari, the viceroy had intercepted his message inviting the Deccan sultans to ally against the Portuguese. He left no son, and after his chosen heir, his nephew Miran Muhammad Shah of Khandesh, died on the way to Gujarat, the nobles chose Mahmud Shah III, son of his brother Latif Khan.
bahia: Bahia lies in the Northeast Region of Brazil, bordered on the east by the Atlantic Ocean, which gives it the longest coastline of any Brazilian state, 1,103 km. Salvador stands on a spit of land that separates the Bay of All Saints, the largest bay on the Brazilian coast, from the Atlantic. The state has three main regions: the Atlantic Forest and the maritime Recôncavo around the bay, a centre of sugar and tobacco cultivation; the Chapada Diamantina, a mountainous plateau; and the dry sertão of the far interior. Under the Brazilian Empire its borders were the Rio Real in the north and the Jequitinhonha in the south, but some neighbouring states were later formed from it.

Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted Monte Pascoal and landed at what is now Porto Seguro on the southern coast in 1500, claiming the territory for Portugal. In 1549 Portugal established the city of Salvador on a hill facing the Bay of All Saints. The city and its captaincy served as an administrative capital of Portugal's American colonies until 1763 and remained the religious capital of the Brazilian Catholic hierarchy, its archbishop serving as national primate until 1907. Bahia's captaincy was the first to fail, its lands reverting to the Portuguese crown in 1549. While Portugal was united with Spain the Dutch West India companies tried to conquer Bahia without success, and Dutch Brazil was restricted to the area from Pernambuco northward.

Bahia was once a stronghold of supporters of direct rule of Brazil by the Portuguese monarchy and was dominated by agricultural, slaving and ranching interests. It was the chief centre of the early Brazilian slave trade. A slave rebellion known as the Revolt of the Tailors took place in 1798. Salvador holds the country's oldest cathedral and its first medical college, founded in 1810. In the 19th century the Bahian abolitionist poet Castro Alves, from Cachoeira, wrote the poem Navio negreiro about slavery, regarded as a central anti-slavery text.

Because of its place in the slave trade, Bahia is considered to have the most distinctive African imprint in Brazil. This includes the Yoruba-derived religion of Candomblé, capoeira, African-derived music such as samba-de-roda, and a cuisine with strong links to West Africa, mainly in Salvador. In the interior the vaqueiro culture of cattle farmers dates from the 1550s. Bahia is the fourth most populous Brazilian state, with a population of over 14 million, and Salvador, its capital, includes a World Heritage Site in the Pelourinho. Once a year the capital moves to Cachoeira, in recognition of that city's part in the struggle for Brazilian independence.
bahrain: Bahrain is a generally flat and arid archipelago in the Persian Gulf, lying between Qatar and the northeastern coast of Saudi Arabia. A low desert plain rises gently to a low central escarpment, whose highest point is the 134 metre Mountain of Smoke (Jabal ad Dukhan). About 92 per cent of the country is desert, with periodic droughts and dust storms. Land reclamation has enlarged the area from 665 to 780 square kilometres, and by August 2008 the number of islands and island groups had risen from 33 to 84.

The name Bahrain is the dual form of the Arabic word bahr, 'sea', so al-Bahrayn originally means 'the two seas'. Which two seas is disputed: the bay east and west of the island, the seas north and south of it, and the salt and fresh water above and below the ground have all been proposed. The term appears five times in the Quran but does not refer to the modern island, which the Arabs originally called Awal. Until the late Middle Ages 'Bahrain' meant a region of Eastern Arabia stretching from Basra in Iraq to the Strait of Hormuz.

Bahrain was home to Dilmun, a Bronze Age trade centre linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, and was later ruled by the Sumerians and Babylonians. From the 6th to the 3rd century BCE it was part of the Achaemenid Empire. By about 250 BCE Parthia had brought the Persian Gulf under its control, and it established garrisons along the southern coast of the Gulf to control trade routes.

The ancient Greeks called the island Tylos and knew it as a centre of pearl trading. The admiral Nearchus, serving under Alexander the Great, is believed to have been the first of Alexander's commanders to visit it. He recorded large plantations of cotton trees on Tylos, from which cloth called sindones was made. Bahrain became part of the Hellenised world: the language of the upper classes was Greek, with Aramaic in everyday use, and local coinage shows a seated Zeus, who may have been worshipped there as a form of the Arabian sun-god Shams.

Bahrain is a kingdom, a semi-constitutional monarchy since 2002, with a bicameral National Assembly. Its capital and largest city is Manama. The King Fahd Causeway, completed in December 1986, links it with the Saudi Arabian mainland. It has been ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783 and became independent from the United Kingdom in 1971.
bahram-chobin: Bahram was a member of the House of Mihran, one of the seven Great Houses of Iran, a family of Parthian origin centred on Ray. His father, Bahram Gushnasp, fought the Byzantines and campaigned in Yemen under Khosrow I, and his grandfather Gurgin Milad was marzban of Armenia from 572 to 574. His nickname Chobin, 'wooden shaft' or 'javelin-like', referred to his tall, slender build; his epithet Mihrbandak means servant of Mithra. Parvaneh Pourshariati argues that he was probably a worshipper of Mithra, since both Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and Sebeos record him as one.

Bahram began as marzban of Ray, took part in the capture of the Byzantine stronghold of Dara, and became army chief (spahbed) of the north. In 588 the Turkic khagan Bagha Qaghan and his Hephthalite subjects invaded the Sasanian lands south of the Oxus and took Balkh, Talaqan, Badghis and Herat. Bahram, given the governorship of Khorasan and a reported 12,000 hand-picked horsemen, ambushed them at Hyrcanian rock in April 588 and again in 589, retook Balkh, crossed the Oxus and personally killed Bagha Qaghan with an arrow. His victory reached as far as Baykand, near Bukhara.

The shah Hormizd IV, already distrustful, removed him from office and humiliated him; sources differ on the reason, and the Sasanian court was suspicious of his rising fame. Bahram rebelled, the first time a Parthian dynast had challenged the Sasanian family's legitimacy. Before he reached Ctesiphon, Hormizd was blinded and killed in a palace coup that put his son Khosrow II on the throne. Bahram defeated Khosrow's men at the Nahrawan Canal and took Ctesiphon, and in the summer of 590 declared himself king of kings, claiming to restore the Arsacids.

Many hailed Bahram as the promised saviour of Zoroastrian apocalyptic belief, but nobles and priests largely sided with Khosrow II, who gained Byzantine help from the emperor Maurice. In 591 Khosrow and the Byzantine armies invaded Mesopotamia, and Bahram was defeated at the Battle of Blarathon. He fled east with 4,000 men to the Turkic khagan, probably Birmudha, whom he had once captured, and served him until Khosrow had him assassinated through bribes to the Turkic royal family.

His son Noshrad was the ancestor of the Samanids, who stressed their descent from him. Bahram's life is told in the Pahlavi romance Bahrām Chōbīn Nāma, and the Shahnameh chapters on Hormizd IV and Khosrow II are almost as much about him. Among Iranian nationalists he remained popular after the Arab conquest.
bahram-v: Bahram was born around 400, the son of the Sasanian shah Yazdegerd I. As a boy he was sent to the Lakhmid court at al-Hira, where the king al-Nu'man I provided teachers from the Sasanian court to instruct him in law, archery and horsemanship. When Yazdegerd I was murdered in 420, the nobles and priests elected Khosrow, a son of Bahram IV, as shah.

Bahram refused this and asked for help from the Lakhmid king al-Mundhir I, who gave him an army. According to a long-standing legend in the Shahnameh, he proposed that the royal crown and robes be placed between two lions and that whoever retrieved them should be shah. Khosrow withdrew and Bahram won the throne. Distrusting the nobles, he turned to the Zoroastrian priesthood and was the first Sasanian shah crowned by a chief priest.

He began his reign with a persecution of the Christians. Refugees fled to Roman territory, and when the Sasanians asked for their return Theodosius II declared war instead. In 421 the Roman general Ardaburius entered Armenia and defeated the Iranian general Narses, then besieged Nisibis but withdrew when Bahram advanced. The peace of 422 restored the earlier position, with both sides agreeing to guarantee freedom of religion in their territories.

While Bahram was occupied in the west, the Kidarites crossed the Oxus, took the rich city of Marw and reached as far as Ray. After the peace with Rome Bahram marched to Merv, where his forces routed the Kidarites and killed their king. The war ended in 427. He set up a pillar at the Oxus to mark it as his eastern frontier, and the Sogdian city of Bukhara later struck coins with his image. Armenia became a frontier province governed by a marzban.

Bahram died in 438 and his manner of death is unclear. Ferdowsi says he died in his sleep, while Nizami and Amir Khusrau say he vanished in a cave while chasing an onager. His son Yazdegerd II succeeded him. He is remembered for cancelling taxes and debts at celebrations, for encouraging musicians, and for his love of hunting, which gave him the epithet Gur, 'onager'. Nizami's romance Haft Peykar, of 1197, tells of the seven princesses who became his wives.
baikonur-cosmodrome: The cosmodrome lies on the Kazakh Steppe about 90 metres above sea level, 200 kilometres east of the Aral Sea and 33 kilometres north of the Syr Darya, close to Töretam, a station on the Trans-Aral Railway. It is the largest operational space launch facility in terms of area. The site was chosen by a commission led by General Vasily Voznyuk, influenced by Sergey Korolyov, chief designer of the R-7 missile. It had to be surrounded by plains, because the rocket's radio control system needed uninterrupted signals from ground stations hundreds of kilometres away, and the trajectory had to lie away from populated areas. A site nearer the equator is also an advantage. The commission chose Tyuratam, a village in the heart of the steppe.

The Soviet government issued the decree for Scientific Research Test Range No. 5 on 12 February 1955, and the range was founded on 2 June 1955 as a test centre for the R-7 Semyorka, the first intercontinental ballistic missile. It was soon expanded with launch facilities for space flights. The cost of the launch facilities and of several hundred kilometres of new road and railway made it one of the most costly infrastructure projects of the Soviet Union. A supporting town was built for the workers and became the city of Leninsk in 1966.

An American U-2 reconnaissance plane first photographed the range on 5 August 1957. Until 1991 its primary purpose was to test liquid-fuelled ballistic missiles, and it remained under the control of the Ministry of Defense until the second half of the 1990s.

Many historic flights began here: Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, Luna 1, the first spacecraft to pass close to the Moon, on 2 January 1959, Yuri Gagarin's flight on 12 April 1961 and Valentina Tereshkova's in 1963. In 1960 a prototype R-16 missile exploded before launch and killed over 100 people.

Most sources say the name Baikonur was chosen about 1961 to mislead the Western Bloc towards a mining town some 320 kilometres to the northeast; NASA's history says it was the name of the Tyuratam region. Leninsk was renamed Baikonur on 20 December 1995.

Russia has retained control of the facility since the Soviet Union ended, first through the Commonwealth of Independent States, and in 2005 ratified an agreement with Kazakhstan to lease it until 2050. All Russian crewed spaceflights are launched from Baikonur, which has supported the Soyuz, Proton, Tsyklon, Dnepr, Zenit and Buran rockets. Its internal railway, of 1,520 mm gauge, is the largest industrial railway in the world. A museum beside the cottages once used by Korolyov and Gagarin holds space artefacts, and a test article of the Buran programme stands at its entrance.
baja-california: The Baja California peninsula is divided between two Mexican states, and the northern one, Baja California, takes in the half of the peninsula north of the 28th parallel and the oceanic Guadalupe Island. It has an area of 70,113 square kilometres. Its backbone is the Sierra de Baja California, where Picacho del Diablo, the highest point of the peninsula, stands. The mountains divide the weather: the north-west is semi-dry and Mediterranean, the Valle de Guadalupe produces wine, and to the east the Sonoran Desert dominates, while the south gives way to the Vizcaíno Desert.

The first people reached the peninsula at least 11,000 years ago. Cochimí hunter-gatherers lived in the centre, and groups of the Yuman language family, among them the Kiliwa, Paipai, Kumeyaay, Cocopa and Quechan, lived in the north; the Cocopa and Quechan farmed the floodplain of the lower Colorado River. Francisco de Ulloa reached the coast in 1539.

After the Jesuits founded the mission at Loreto in 1697, they extended their missions northward, until their expulsion in 1768. Franciscan administration followed briefly, and in 1773 the Dominicans took over, founding a chain of missions from El Rosario in 1774 to Descanso in 1817. In 1804 the Spanish crown divided California into Alta and Baja California along the line between the Franciscan and Dominican missions. Mexico mandated the secularisation of the missions in 1833.

After the Mexican–American War ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Alta California passed to the United States, while the area of Tijuana, Mexicali and Tecate stayed Mexican. In 1853 the mercenary William Walker captured La Paz and declared himself president of the Republic of Baja California; the Mexican government forced his retreat after several months.

In 1905 the Magonista revolution, an anarchist movement based on the writings of Ricardo Flores Magón and Enrique Flores Magón, began, and in 1911 the Mexican Liberal Party captured Mexicali and Tijuana before surrendering to federal forces. The peninsula was divided into northern and southern territories in 1931. The northern territory became the 29th Mexican state in 1952, and the southern became Baja California Sur in 1974.

The state has an estimated 3,769,020 inhabitants, more than three quarters of it in Mexicali, the capital, Ensenada and Tijuana, the largest city. It borders the United States to the north and Sonora across the northern Gulf of California.
baji-rao-i: Baji Rao, born Visaji on 18 August 1700, belonged to the Bhat family of Sinnar, near Nashik. His father, Balaji Vishwanath, was Peshwa to Shahu I. He learned reading, writing and Sanskrit, but showed a passion for soldiering early and often accompanied his father on campaign, including the expedition to Delhi in 1719. He came away convinced that the Mughal Empire was disintegrating and could not resist Maratha expansion northward. When Balaji Vishwanath died in 1720, Shahu appointed the 20-year-old Baji Rao Peshwa despite the opposition of other chieftains.

Baji Rao persuaded Shahu that the Marathas must go on the offensive, and reportedly said that if the withering tree were struck at the trunk its branches would fall of themselves. He promoted young commanders who were not from hereditary Deccan families, among them Malhar Rao Holkar, Ranoji Shinde and the Pawar brothers. His main rival in the Deccan was Asaf Jah I, the Nizam of Hyderabad, who contested the Maratha right to collect chauth. In the Palkhed campaign of 1727–28 Baji Rao outmanoeuvred the Nizam with a purely mounted army that carried no artillery or baggage and lived off the country. Bernard Montgomery called it a masterpiece of strategic mobility.

In March 1729 he marched into Bundelkhand with 25,000 horsemen to relieve the rebel Chhatrasal, besieged by a Mughal force under Muhammad Khan Bangash. Chhatrasal granted him a large jagir, gave him his daughter Mastani, and before he died in December 1731 ceded a third of his territory to the Marathas. In Gujarat, Baji Rao's brother Chimaji Appa won the right to collect chauth in 1730, which provoked Trimbak Rao Dabhade into rebellion. He was defeated at Dabhoi in 1731. In Konkan, Baji Rao fought the Siddis of Janjira, and he campaigned against the Portuguese.

In 1737 he marched on Delhi, and later that year he faced a large Mughal army reinforced with artillery near Bhopal, where the Nizam sheltered. By the agreement at Doraha on 7 January 1738, Malwa was ceded to the Marathas and the Mughals promised reparations.

Exhausted by constant campaigning, Baji Rao fell ill on 23 April 1740 and died on 28 April, the night of a Sunday. He was cremated the same day on the bank of the Narmada, where a memorial stands. His eldest son by his first wife Kashibai, Balaji Bajirao, known as Nanasaheb, succeeded him as Peshwa. His son by Mastani was Shamsher Bahadur, whom Kashibai raised after both parents died in 1740. Shamsher died of wounds after the Third Battle of Panipat. By Baji Rao's death the Maratha Empire had reached its largest extent to that time.
bakelite: The reaction between phenol and an aldehyde was first reported in 1872 by Adolf von Baeyer, but its commercial use was not considered then. Leo Baekeland was already wealthy after selling the rights to his Velox photographic paper to Eastman Kodak in 1899, when he began to study phenol and formaldehyde in his home laboratory. His first aim was to find a substitute for shellac, a material in limited supply because it is made from the secretion of lac insects. He produced a soluble phenol-formaldehyde shellac called Novolak, which was not a market success. By controlling pressure and temperature he then produced a hard, mouldable material that he named Bakelite, after himself and the heat curing it needed.

Bakelite is a thermosetting phenol formaldehyde resin, formed by a condensation reaction of phenol with formaldehyde. At ordinary pressure the mixture foams violently and the cooled material is porous and breakable. Baekeland's innovation was to heat the product under pressure at about 150 degrees in an egg-shaped vessel he called a Bakelizer, which suppressed the foaming and gave a substance that is extremely hard and both infusible and insoluble. Moulded Bakelite used wood flour or asbestos fibre as a filler. Millions of parts could be made quickly and cheaply, and objects needed little finishing.

Baekeland's patent was filed on 13 July 1907 and granted on 7 December 1909, and he announced the invention to the American Chemical Society on 5 February 1909. In the summer of 1909 he licensed the continental European rights to Rütger AG, whose subsidiary Bakelite AG was the first to make it on an industrial scale. In 1922, after patent litigation that favoured Baekeland, the Bakelite Corporation was formed by a merger of three companies, and it marketed the material as the material of a thousand uses.

When Baekeland's heat and pressure patents expired in 1927, competitors appeared. Because moulded Bakelite incorporated fillers, it was usually made in dark colours, while the Catalin company made jewellery in fifteen new colours using another process. Old Bakelite objects are now collected.
bakhchysarai: Bakhchysarai lies in a narrow valley of the Çürük Suv river, about 30 kilometres south-west of Simferopol. The name comes from the Persian bāghche-sarāy, "Garden Palace"; in Crimean Tatar bağça means garden and saray palace. The earliest known man-made objects in the valley date from the Mesolithic period, and settlements have existed there since Late Antiquity. The fortress of Qırq Yer, now Çufut Qale, Salaçıq and Eski Yurt were built before the town itself and have since been absorbed into its urban area.

Bakhchysarai first appears in documents in 1502. In 1532 Sahib I Giray, Khan of Crimea from 1532 to 1551, established his residence there, and from then it was the capital of the Crimean Khanate and the centre of the political and cultural life of the Crimean Tatars. Cossacks sacked the town in 1675 during Ivan Sirko's Crimean campaign, and it was burned in 1736 during the Russo-Turkish War of 1735 to 1739. After the Russian Empire annexed the Khanate in 1783 it became an ordinary town without administrative importance, but it stayed a cultural centre of the Crimean Tatars for several decades, helped by Ismail Gaspirali, who founded the newspaper Terciman there in 1883.

During the Crimean War the town served as a hospital for wounded Russian soldiers. The Battle of the Alma was fought not far away in 1854, but Turkish and allied forces never took the town, since their main objective was Sevastopol. In 1930 it had 10,450 inhabitants, 7,420 of them Crimean Tatars. On 18 May 1944 the Sürgün, the deportation of the Crimean Tatars, prompted by accusations of collaboration with the Axis occupiers, emptied the city of them. They could not return until 1989, when Soviet policies relaxed.

The main landmark is the Hansaray, or Khan's Palace, the only surviving palace of the Crimean khans, which is open as a museum. Other sites in or near the town include the Zincirli Madrasa, the Orta Cami and Tahtali-Jami mosques, the Cave Monastery, Chufut-Kale and Tepe-Kermen. Russian readers know the town from Alexander Pushkin's poem The Fountain of Bakhchysarai (1822), and Adam Mickiewicz devoted some of the best of his Crimean Sonnets (1825) to its landmarks.
bakhchysarai-palace: The Khan's Palace, in Crimean Tatar Hansaray, is in the town of Bakhchysarai in Crimea. The Crimean Khan dynasty commissioned both the town and the palace and moved their capital there from Salaçıq in the first half of the 16th century. The palace's complex design and its minarets were constructed in that century by Ottoman, Persian and Italian architects. It became the home of a succession of Crimean khans. Some buildings now in the palace were added later, while some of the original ones did not survive past the 18th century.

The walled enclosure contains a mosque, a harem, a cemetery, living quarters and gardens. Its interior has been decorated to look lived in and reflects the traditional 16th-century Crimean Tatar style. The Big Khan Mosque, built in 1532 by Sahib I Giray, is one of the largest mosques in Crimea. It has a three-aisle square prayer hall and two octagonal minarets twenty-eight metres high. A fire damaged it in 1736 during the Russo-Turkish War, and it was restored under Khan Selâmet II Giray.

The Small Khan Mosque, in the main building, was designed for the Khan's family and important dignitaries. Its mihrab has an upper part cut with seven ornamented belts, symbolising the seven levels of heaven, and above it a stained glass window shows the seal of Suleiman.

A small fountain in one courtyard moved the Russian writer Alexander Pushkin so much that he wrote the long narrative poem The Fountain of Bakhchisaray. By the story told of it, one of the last Crimean khans, Qırım Giray, fell in love with a Polish girl named Maria in his harem, and after her early death he is said to have wept and commissioned a marble fountain so that the rock would weep like him forever. It was moved to the Ambassadors' courtyard after Catherine II ordered the annexation of Crimea. Pushkin's verses are credited in part with ensuring the palace's survival. It was added to UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage Sites in 2003.
baku-tbilisi-ceyhan-pipeline: The Caspian Sea lies above one of the largest collections of oil and gas fields, but being landlocked it makes the export of oil to Western markets difficult. In Soviet times every transport route from the region ran through Russia. After the Soviet collapse, producers sought new routes. Russia first insisted that a new pipeline cross its territory and then declined to take part.

In the spring of 1992 the Turkish prime minister Süleyman Demirel proposed a route through Turkey, and Azerbaijan and Turkey signed the first document on the project on 9 March 1993. A route through Armenia was politically impossible because of the unresolved war over Nagorno-Karabakh, which left the longer and costlier route through Georgia. The Ankara Declaration of 29 October 1998 gave the project momentum, and Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey signed an intergovernmental agreement on 18 November 1999 in Istanbul.

The pipeline is 1,768 km long and runs from the Sangachal Terminal near Baku to the Ceyhan Marine Terminal on the south-eastern Mediterranean coast of Turkey. Of its length, 443 km lie in Azerbaijan, 249 km in Georgia and 1,076 km in Turkey. It crosses mountain ranges at up to 2,830 m and passes under or over 3,000 roads, railways and utility lines and 1,500 watercourses. It is buried at least a metre deep and measures 1,070 mm in diameter for most of its length, narrowing to 865 mm near Ceyhan. Eight pump stations push the oil at about two metres a second, and at normal capacity it carries one million barrels a day.

It takes oil chiefly from the Azeri-Chirag-Guneshli field in the Caspian Sea. Kazakh oil has also reached it by tanker across the Caspian. The line cost US$3.9 billion, of which 70 per cent came from third parties including the International Finance Corporation and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

BTC Co. was established in London on 1 August 2002, with BP managing the consortium. Construction began in April 2003. The pipeline was inaugurated at the Sangachal Terminal on 25 May 2005, and the first oil reached Ceyhan on 28 May 2006. Archaeological surveys sponsored by BP began in 2000, and construction uncovered cultural artefacts, leading to coordinated research at sites in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey.

The pipeline drew criticism for its environmental risks, notably its route through the watershed of the Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park in Georgia, and for the bypassing of Armenia. Its supporters in Georgia saw it as a guarantee of the country's independence and security. It removed about 350 tanker cargoes a year from the Bosphorus and Dardanelles.
bal-gangadhar-tilak: Tilak was born Keshav Gangadhar Tilak on 23 July 1856 in a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family in Ratnagiri; the family moved to Poona in 1867. His father, a schoolteacher and Sanskrit scholar, died when Tilak was sixteen. Tilak took a degree in mathematics at the Deccan College in 1877 and a law degree in 1879. In 1880 he co-founded the New English school, and in 1884 the Deccan Education Society, which set up Fergusson College in 1885, where he taught mathematics. He left the society in 1890 for more openly political work. He had started the weeklies Kesari, in Marathi, and Mahratta, in English, in 1880 to 1881.

Tilak joined the Indian National Congress in 1890 and opposed its moderate approach to self-rule. Measures against the plague in Pune in 1897 caused widespread resentment, and Tilak published inflammatory articles in Kesari and Mahratta. After two British officers were shot by the Chapekar brothers he was charged and sentenced to 18 months in prison. He took up the slogan Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it. After the Partition of Bengal he promoted the Swadeshi and boycott movements. At the Surat session of 1907 Congress split into a radical faction led by Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, and a moderate one.

In 1908 he was convicted of sedition over articles in Kesari and sentenced to six years in Mandalay, where he was held until 16 June 1914. He rejoined Congress at the Lucknow pact of 1916 and helped found the All India Home Rule League, whose membership grew from 1400 in April 1916 to about 32,000 in 1917. He also turned the household worship of Ganesha into a public festival in 1894 and began celebrations of Shivaji's birthday in 1895, though these celebrations also contributed to religious tensions. He died on 1 August 1920.

In prison at Mandalay he wrote the Gita Rahasya, interpreting the Bhagavad Gita as justifying activism, which he called karma-yoga, against the dominant renunciate readings. Tilak supported self-rule without a complete break with the British Empire. He opposed the age of consent bill and the first girls' high school in Pune, and he refused to sign a petition against untouchability in 1918. He also wrote The Arctic Home in the Vedas, arguing that the Vedas were composed in the Arctic.
balaklava: Balaklava is a settlement on the Crimean Peninsula, now part of the city of Sevastopol and the administrative centre of Balaklavsky District. It lies at the entrance to the Balaklava Inlet, above which stand the ruins of a Genoese fortress on a clifftop. It is known in Ukrainian and Russian as Балаклава, in Crimean Tatar as Balıqlava and in Greek as Σύμβολον.

Ancient Greeks founded a settlement on the site under the name Symbolon, and it was an important commercial city for them. In the Middle Ages it was controlled by the Byzantine Empire, who called it Yamboli, and then by the Genoese, who conquered it in 1365 and named it Cembalo. The Genoese built a large trading empire across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, buying slaves in Eastern Europe and shipping them to Egypt through Crimea, a lucrative market contested by the Venetians. The fortress is the subject of Mickiewicz's penultimate poem in his 1826 cycle of Crimean Sonnets.

In 1475 the Turks conquered Cembalo and renamed it Balyk-Yuva, meaning Fish's Nest, from which the name Balaklava came. Russian troops invaded Crimea in 1771, during the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774, and Crimea was annexed by the Russian Empire thirteen years later. Afterwards the Crimean Tatar and Turkish population was forcibly replaced by Greek Orthodox settlers from the Archipelago.

The town became known for the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War and the Charge of the Light Brigade, in which a British cavalry brigade, because of a misunderstanding, was sent up a valley held on three sides by the Russians. About 250 men were killed or wounded and over 400 horses lost, reducing the mounted brigade by two thirds. Alfred, Lord Tennyson commemorated it in verse. The balaclava, a knitted garment covering the head and neck, takes its name from the place, where soldiers first wore it, and several towns in English-speaking countries were named Balaklava later in the 19th century.

In 1954 Crimea was transferred from the Russian Soviet republic to the Ukrainian Soviet republic, and in 1957 Balaklava was incorporated into Sevastopol by the Soviet government and lost its city status. An underground submarine base, built to survive a nuclear strike, was operational until 1993, when it began to be decommissioned; the last Russian submarine left in 1996. Balaklava was one of the most secret residential areas in the Soviet Union, and the base is now a naval museum complex. Monuments in the town commemorate the Crimean War, the Russian Civil War and the Great Patriotic War.
balash: Balash, in Middle Persian Wardakhsh or Walakhsh, was the brother of the Sasanian king Peroz I, who reigned from 459 to 484. In 484 Peroz was defeated and killed by a Hephthalite army near Balkh. His army was completely destroyed, his body was never found, and four of his sons and brothers also died. The eastern cities of Khorasan, Nishapur, Herat and Marw, now came under Hephthalite rule. Sukhra, a member of the Parthian House of Karen, one of the Seven Great Houses of Iran, quickly raised a new force and stopped the Hephthalites from gaining more ground. The Iranian magnates, most notably Sukhra and the Mihranid general Shapur Mihran, elected Peroz's brother Balash as shah.

Immediately after taking the throne Balash sought peace with the Hephthalites, which cost the Sasanians a heavy tribute. Little is known about him. Eastern sources see him as a mild and tolerant ruler, and his tolerance of Christianity gave him a good reputation among Christian authors, who describe him as mild and generous. He appears, however, to have been only a nominee of the powerful nobleman Sukhra, the de facto ruler.

When news of Peroz's death arrived, the Iranian nobles of Sasanian Armenia, including Shapur Mihran, wished to go to the capital Ctesiphon to elect a new sovereign, and this let the Armenians under Vahan Mamikonian proclaim independence. Given the weakness in Iran, Balash did not send an army and made peace on terms that provided: existing fire-altars in Armenia were to be destroyed and no new ones built, Christians were to have freedom of worship, conversions to Zoroastrianism were to stop and no land was to be given to converts. In 485 he appointed Vahan Mamikonian marzban of Armenia.

A few months later a son of Peroz named Zarer rebelled, and Balash, with Armenian help, put the rising down and had him killed. In 488 Balash, an unpopular figure among the nobility and clergy, was deposed after a reign of four years. Sukhra played the main part in this and made Peroz's son Kavad the new shah.
balasore: Balasore, officially Baleshwar, lies in eastern India about 215 km from the state capital Bhubaneswar and 240 km from Kolkata. It is the administrative headquarters of Balasore district. Excavations at villages near the city have shown three phases of settlement: a Chalcolithic phase (2000 to 1000 BCE), an Iron Age phase (1000 to 400 BCE) and an early historic phase (400 to 200 BCE). The area was part of the ancient kingdom of Kalinga, which later became a territory of Utkal, until the death of Mukunda Deva.

The Mughal Empire annexed the region in 1568 and held it under its suzerainty until the 1700s. The English East India Company established a factory at Balasore in 1633, and merchants of the Trieste Company set up a trading post there in 1719. Company forces bombarded the city during the Anglo-Mughal War in 1686 but were repulsed by the Mughal forces. As Calcutta grew in importance, Balasore became a centre for river pilots guiding vessels up the Hooghly River, and it gave its name to a type of cotton muslin.

The Marathas, under the Bhonsle rajas of Nagpur, later held this part of Odisha, and ceded it to the British through the Treaty of Deogaon in 1803. It belonged to the Bengal Presidency until 1912. Balasore became a separate district in October 1828, and on 7 November 1845 all of Danish India was sold to the British. Mahatma Gandhi visited in 1921, and the independence fighter Jatindranath Mukherjee, known as Bagha Jatin, was wounded and died fighting the British here. Odisha became a separate state on 1 April 1936, with Balasore as part of it. The princely state of Nilagiri merged with Odisha in January 1948 and joined the district; in 1993 Bhadrak became a district of its own.

Odia is the official and most widely spoken language, followed by Urdu, Bengali, Santali and Hindi. The census of 2011 counted 144,373 people in the municipality and its outgrowth. Chandipur is a seaside resort known for its long beach, and the Kshirachora Gopinatha Temple at Remuna was built by King Langula Narasimha Deva, who also built the temple at Konarka. Fakir Mohan University is named after the Odia novelist Fakir Mohan Senapati, who came from the town.
baldwin-i-latin-emperor: Baldwin was the son of Count Baldwin V of Hainaut and Countess Margaret I of Flanders. In 1186 he married Marie, daughter of Count Henry I of Champagne, who was a niece of Richard I of England and Philip II of France. Through her he had ties to the defenders of the Holy Land, and his uncle Count Philip I of Flanders had died on crusade at the siege of Acre in 1191. Baldwin became Count of Flanders in 1194 and Count of Hainaut in 1195.

His eight years in Flanders were taken up with recovering lands, including Artois, that had gone to the French crown as dowry. The Treaty of Péronne, signed in January 1200, made him a vassal of Philip II and returned parts of Artois to him. On 23 February 1200, at Bruges, Baldwin took the cross, and he left for the Fourth Crusade on 14 April 1202.

The crusade's leaders, short of money, were persuaded by the Venetians to divert to Constantinople, and the city fell in April 1204. The crown was first offered to Enrico Dandolo, Doge of Venice, who refused it. The choice then lay between Baldwin and Boniface of Montferrat, the nominal leader of the crusade. With Venetian support Baldwin was elected on 9 May 1204 and crowned on 16 May in the Hagia Sophia, in a ceremony that closely followed Byzantine practice.

The Latin Empire was organised on feudal lines. His own share included Constantinople and nearby regions in Europe and Asia, with the islands of Lemnos, Lesbos, Chios and Tenos. He quarrelled with Boniface, who received Thessalonica, before Dandolo and Count Louis I of Blois arranged a settlement. In February 1205 the Greeks of Thrace rose, relying on Kaloyan, tsar of Bulgaria, whose offer of alliance Baldwin had rejected.

At Adrianople on 14 April 1205 the Frankish knights were defeated, the count of Blois was killed and Baldwin was taken. His fate was uncertain for more than a year; reliable word of his death reached Constantinople only in July 1206, and his brother Henry of Flanders was crowned emperor in August. Accounts of his end differ. A tower at Veliko Tarnovo is still called Baldwin's Tower.

In 1225 a man appeared in Flanders claiming to be Baldwin and drew followers among the peasantry. He was unmasked as a Burgundian serf, Bertrand of Ray, and executed in 1226. Baldwin's daughters Joan and Margaret II both later ruled as countesses of Flanders.
baldwin-i-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born some time after 1060, the youngest son of Count Eustace II of Boulogne and Ida of Lorraine. Because he was the youngest he was intended for a church career, held prebends in cathedrals, but for unknown reasons abandoned that path and became a knight. He married a Norman noblewoman, Godehilde of Tosny. His brother Godfrey of Bouillon named him in most of his charters, which suggests that he regarded him as his heir. When the First Crusade was proclaimed in 1095, Godfrey sold or mortgaged his domains, and Baldwin received the County of Verdun in 1096. He left with Godfrey's army on 15 August 1096, taking his wife and children, which suggests that he did not plan to return.

In 1097 Baldwin and the Norman Tancred led a separate expedition into Cilicia. Their quarrel over Tarsus began an enduring conflict. Baldwin seized fortresses west of the Euphrates with the help of local Armenians. In early 1098 Thoros, the Armenian lord of Edessa, asked for his help against the Seljuks. Baldwin reached Edessa on 20 February, and after a riot against Thoros he took the town and established the first Crusader state on 10 March 1098. Having been widowed, he married the daughter of an Armenian lord to strengthen his rule. He supplied the crusader army with food during the siege of Antioch, and he held Edessa for three weeks against Kerbogha of Mosul, delaying him until the crusaders took Antioch.

When Godfrey of Bouillon died, Baldwin left Edessa on 2 October 1100 and reached Jerusalem around 9 November. The patriarch crowned him king at Bethlehem on 25 December. With Genoese and Venetian fleets he took Arsuf and Caesarea in 1101, Acre in 1104, Beirut in 1110 and Sidon in 1111, though his attempts on Ascalon and Tyre failed. After his victory at the third battle of Ramla in 1105 the Egyptians launched no further major campaigns against the kingdom. Soldiers pillaged Caesarea and massacred most of its adult population.

Baldwin was the only crowned monarch in the Latin East and claimed suzerainty over the other crusader rulers. He died on 2 April 1118 at Al-Arish, during an expedition against Egypt, and was buried beside Godfrey in the Calvary Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre. Fulcher of Chartres called him his subjects' 'shield, strength and support', and Christopher Tyerman credits him with a stable kingdom with defensible borders.
baldwin-ii-of-jerusalem: Baldwin's birth year is unknown. He was the son of Count Hugh I of Rethel and Melisende of Montlhéry, probably a younger child, and was a kinsman of the brothers Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin of Boulogne. His family spoke the Champenois dialect of Old French, and he was probably illiterate. As lord of Bourcq he joined Godfrey's army at the beginning of the First Crusade. William of Tyre describes him as very religious, with callouses on his hands and knees from frequent prayer.

Baldwin of Boulogne granted him the County of Edessa when he left for Jerusalem on 2 October 1100. Baldwin married Morphia, the daughter of the Armenian lord Gabriel of Melitene, which strengthened his position among his largely Armenian subjects. At the Battle of Harran on 7 May 1104 Sökmen and Jikirmish drew the crusaders into an ambush, and he was captured; Tancred governed Edessa as regent. Joscelin of Courtenay ransomed him in 1108, and Tancred gave back the county only after the prelates arbitrated in Baldwin's favour. He returned to Edessa on 18 September 1108.

Mawdud besieged Edessa in April 1110, and Baldwin I of Jerusalem came to relieve it. The childless Baldwin I died on 2 April 1118, and Baldwin of Bourcq was elected king by the nobles. After the army of Antioch was almost destroyed in June 1119 he became regent for Bohemond II of Antioch, and his time in the north caused discontent in Jerusalem.

Belek captured the king on 18 April 1123 while he prepared to hunt with falcons, and held him at Kharput, later at Harran and Aleppo. Jerusalem's regents captured Tyre on 7 or 8 July 1124. Baldwin was released in August 1124, but al-Bursuqi forced him to lift the siege of Aleppo in January 1125. In 1126 Bohemond II married his daughter Alice, and in 1129 his eldest daughter Melisende married Count Fulk V of Anjou. He took monastic vows and died on 21 August 1131; Melisende and Fulk were crowned on 14 September. William of Tyre called him devout and experienced in war, but others criticised his love of money.
baldwin-iii-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born in the first half of 1130, the eldest son of Queen Melisende and King Fulk. His mother was the eldest daughter and designated heir of King Baldwin II, who conferred the kingdom on the young Baldwin and his parents in 1131. Fulk had been count of Anjou before he left France to marry Melisende. Fulk died in a hunting accident on 10 November 1143, and Baldwin was crowned with Melisende on Christmas Day. Because he was only 13, his mother became his guardian and the true ruler; William of Tyre presented her rule as grounded in hereditary right, and the historian Bernard Hamilton argues she should be considered a queen regnant.

In 1144 Baldwin put down a rebellion at Wadi Musa by cutting down the inhabitants' olive trees and offering pardons, his first military success. When Zengid forces besieged Edessa that year, Melisende sent an army without involving him, and the city fell. Baldwin joined the Second Crusade's failed attempt to capture Damascus in 1148. In 1150 he arranged the sale of the last Edessan fortresses to the Byzantine Empire. His relations with his mother worsened as he sought a larger role, and in April 1152 he deposed her in a swift military action.

In January 1153 the Franks began the siege of Ascalon, which Baldwin conquered that year. After he nearly lost his life in a battle against Nur ad-Din in 1157, he allied with Emperor Manuel I Komnenos and married the emperor's niece Theodora in 1158. He spent ten days with Manuel at Antioch in 1159 and received a subsidy of 22,000 hyperpyra and 3,000 marks of silver. In 1161 he took up rule in Antioch again after Turkic forces captured Raynald of Châtillon. William of Tyre describes him as affable and quick-witted, and says he respected the rights of the Church.

In late 1162 Baldwin took pills from a Syrian physician and contracted dysentery. He was carried to Beirut and died there on 10 February 1163, aged 33. William of Tyre reports a widespread suspicion of poisoning, which the historians Peter W. Edbury and John G. Rowe dismiss. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on 18 February. William says that Nur ad-Din refused to attack while the Franks mourned. Baldwin had no children with Theodora and was succeeded by his brother Amalric. He was the longest-reigning of the 12th-century kings of Jerusalem and widened the kingdom's borders.
baldwin-iv-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born in mid-1161, probably at Ascalon, the son of Amalric, then count of Jaffa and Ascalon, and Agnes of Courtenay. His parents separated when he was two, after the High Court forced Amalric to annul the marriage on grounds of consanguinity as the price of being accepted as king in 1163. At nine he was sent to be educated by William of Tyre, who noticed early signs of leprosy, though the disease was diagnosed only after Baldwin became king.

After Amalric's death the High Court chose Baldwin unanimously, expecting that a husband would be found for his sister Sibylla to succeed him if he proved to be ill. He was crowned on 15 July 1174. Miles of Plancy and then Count Raymond III of Tripoli ruled as regent until Baldwin came of age at 15 in 1176. His planned attack on Egypt failed for lack of cooperation from his vassals.

In November 1177 Saladin invaded the kingdom while the Frankish army was in northern Syria. Baldwin and Raynald of Châtillon repelled him at Montgisard. Baldwin could not marry, and the question of succession dominated his reign. In 1180 Baldwin had Sibylla marry Guy of Lusignan, to forestall a coup by Raymond III and Bohemond III of Antioch, but Guy was opposed by much of the nobility. In 1182 Baldwin won the Battle of Le Forbelet.

From 1183 he could neither walk unsupported nor use his hands, and he went blind. He entrusted the government to Guy, but Guy's failure to lead and his insubordination led Baldwin to disinherit him, and to have Sibylla's young son crowned as Baldwin V. He was carried in a litter to lift Saladin's siege of Kerak, but failed to have Sibylla's marriage annulled.

In his last months Baldwin named Raymond regent for his nephew and died of a fever in 1185, no later than 16 May. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, near his father. Baldwin V died the next year, Sibylla made Guy king, and Saladin destroyed the kingdom at the Battle of Hattin in 1187.

Historians have traced the instability to his reign, yet the kingdom lost no territory while he ruled. His chief contribution, in the view of historians, was his refusal to abdicate before finding a suitable successor, since only he could keep the nobles united. Pope Alexander III called his leprosy a just judgement of God.
balearic-islands: The archipelago lies in the western Mediterranean off the eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula. It has two groups: the western Pityusic Islands, comprising Ibiza, Formentera and smaller islets, and the eastern Gymnesian Islands, principally Mallorca and Menorca. The Greeks called the islands Gymnesiai, and the Carthaginians and Romans used the name Baleares. Most ancient writers derived the name of the people from the Greek word for "to launch", from their skill as slingers. The earliest known habitation dates to about 2500 to 2300 BCE, by people associated with the Bell Beaker culture.

In ancient times the islanders of the Gymnesian Islands built talayots and were known for the sling. They served as mercenaries first under the Carthaginians and later under the Romans, each man carrying three slings of different lengths for stones of different sizes. Greek and Roman writers also told stories about their customs that the Romans found peculiar. The Phoenicians took possession of the islands early, and a trace survives in the town of Mago, now Mahón. Quintus Caecilius Metellus conquered the islands in 123 BCE, was given the surname Balearicus, settled 3,000 Roman and Hispanic colonists and founded Palma and Pollentia.

The Vandals under Genseric took them between 461 and 468, and Belisarius's troops restored Roman control in late 533 or early 534. In 707 the islands submitted to an Umayyad fleet, and in 903 Muslim forces captured them for the Emirate of Córdoba.

A crusade led by Pisa, with 420 ships, sacked Palma in 1115 and withdrew, and within a year the Berber Almoravids conquered the islands. King James I of Aragon captured Palma on the last day of 1229 after a three-month siege, took Menorca in 1232 and Ibiza in 1235. His will of 1276 created a Kingdom of Mallorca for his son James II, as a vassal of Aragon.

The kingdom ended when James III was killed at the Battle of Llucmajor in 1349 and the islands passed directly to the Crown of Aragon. Ottoman privateers raided them in the early 16th century, and in 1558 the corsair Turgut Reis ravaged them and 4,000 people were enslaved. Menorca was British for most of the 18th century after the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713, and returned to Spain by the Treaty of Amiens.

The islands form an autonomous community and province of Spain, with Palma as capital and largest city. They achieved self-government under a Statute of Autonomy in 1983, and Catalan and Spanish are co-official languages. They have 1,249,844 inhabitants and an area of 4,991.70 square kilometres. The four principal islands are major international tourist destinations.
balfour-declaration: Early British support for a larger Jewish presence in Palestine began in the early 1840s under Lord Palmerston and rested on geopolitical calculation, backed by evangelical sympathy for the restoration of the Jews, notably in Lord Shaftesbury. Zionism arose in the late nineteenth century in reaction to antisemitic and exclusionary nationalism in Europe. Around 1916 Jews were about 3 per cent of Palestine's population, which was mostly Muslim, with Christians second.

The British Cabinet first discussed Palestine on 9 November 1914. Within two months Herbert Samuel circulated a memorandum proposing support for Zionist ambitions to win Jewish support in the war. The first negotiations with the Zionists took place on 7 February 1917, and on 19 June Arthur Balfour asked Lord Rothschild and Chaim Weizmann to draft a public declaration. The War Cabinet decided to release it on 31 October 1917, after discussion that referred to the propaganda benefit among Jews worldwide. Palestine's Arab majority was not represented.

The text was a single sentence of 67 words, sent on 2 November 1917 from Balfour to Walter Rothschild for transmission to the Zionist Federation of Great Britain and Ireland. Two clauses promise support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, and two safeguard clauses cover the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities there and the rights and political status of Jews in other countries. The term national home had no precedent in international law and was intentionally vague about whether a Jewish state was contemplated. Lord Milner's amendment replaced the draft's reconstituted with in Palestine. The text was published in the press on 9 November.

The declaration was the first public support for Zionism by a major political power and greatly raised support for it among Jewish communities. Christians and Muslims, almost 90 per cent of Palestine's population, strongly opposed it, and in the wider Arab world it was seen as a betrayal of the McMahon-Hussein correspondence with the Sharif of Mecca. Jerusalem surrendered to the British on 9 December 1917.

The declaration became a core part of the British Mandate for Palestine. The British government acknowledged in 1939 that the wishes and interests of the local population should have been taken into account, and in 2018 that the declaration should have called for protection of the Palestinian Arabs' political rights. It is considered a principal cause of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and indirectly led to the emergence of Israel.
bali: Bali is the westernmost of the Lesser Sunda Islands, 3.2 km east of Java across the Bali Strait and about 8 degrees south of the equator. It spans roughly 153 km from east to west and 112 km from north to south. Its fauna is Asian in character, since it lies just west of the Wallace Line. The name appears in ancient inscriptions in the compound Vāli-dvīpa, "island"; one of the earliest attestations is the Belanjong pillar inscription of King Sri Kesari Warmadewa, dated about 914 CE. The meaning of Vāli is uncertain, and one proposal derives it from Sanskrit bali, "offering".

Austronesian peoples, who migrated from Taiwan through maritime Southeast Asia, inhabited Bali around 2000 BCE, and stone tools of that time have been found near Cekik in the west. Ancient Bali had nine Hindu sects, each revering a particular deity. The first known European contact came in 1512, when a Portuguese expedition led by António Abreu and Francisco Serrão sighted the northern shores. Cornelis de Houtman, a Dutch merchant-explorer, arrived in 1597.

Dutch political and economic control began in the 1840s on the north coast, where the Dutch set competing Balinese realms against each other, and was extended in the late 1890s by exploiting struggles between the kingdoms of the south. British forces took the Japanese surrender in 1945 and handed the island to the Dutch in 1946, who made it one of the 13 districts of the State of East Indonesia. Bali became part of the Republic of the United States of Indonesia when the Netherlands recognised independence on 29 December 1949, and a province in 1958.

Bali is an Indonesian province whose capital, Denpasar, is the most populous city of the Lesser Sunda Islands; the upland town of Ubud is regarded as its cultural centre. About 86 per cent of its people follow Balinese Hinduism, which combines local beliefs with Hindu ones, and Balinese and Indonesian are the most widely spoken languages. Pre-modern society had four castes. Temples and homes are oriented between the mountain Gunung Agung (kaja) and the sea (kelod). The Subak irrigation system of the rice fields was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. Gamelan orchestras and dances such as legong, barong and kecak are central to its arts, and Nyepi, the Hindu New Year, is marked by a day of silence.
balikesir: Close to modern Balıkesir stood the Roman town of Hadrianutherae, which, as its name recalls, was founded by the emperor Hadrian. He came to the region in 124 CE and, after a successful bear hunt, established a city bearing his name. In the Byzantine period the neglected small town was known as Palaiokastron, Old Castle.

When the Turkomans came from Middle Asia into Mysia, they called the place Balukiser after the castle remains. Balıkesir, formerly called Karasi, was founded by Karasi Bey in the 13th century on the remains of the small town, and 1297 is taken as the date of its establishment, one of few cities founded by Turks in Anatolia. The Ottomans annexed it in 1345. An earthquake in 1898 destroyed much of it, leaving only 51 buildings undamaged. The Greek army occupied the city on 30 June 1919 and the Turkish army retook it on 6 September 1922.

Balıkesir lies in the Marmara region and is the seat of Balıkesir Province. The urban part had a population of 314,958 in 2022. A fire on 3 August 1950 destroyed the centre of the city, burning 498 shops, and it was rebuilt; it was the second biggest disaster in the city after the 1898 earthquake. The Yildirim Mosque, built in 1388, is the oldest surviving Ottoman work in the city, and of the Zaganos Pasha Mosque, built in 1461 and named after the grand vizier of Mehmet the Conqueror, only the mosque and baths remain.
balingen: Balingen is a town in Baden-Württemberg, capital of the district of Zollernalbkreis, near the Swabian Jura. It lies about 35 kilometres south of Tübingen and 70 kilometres south-southwest of Stuttgart. After Albstadt it is the second largest town in the district, and in 1973 it became the seat of the newly formed district of Zollernalb, which continued the old tradition of an official town. It is nicknamed Waagenstadt, the city of scales, and it is the home of the scale maker Bizerba.

Balingen is first mentioned in 863, and the earliest traces of settlement in the area are Alemannic terraced graves. According to historical records the town itself was established in 1255 by Count Friedrich von Zollern, and it was fortified before 1377. In 1403 the town, its castle and the Schalksburg estate were sold to the County of Württemberg, which made it the seat of an administrative district, Amt Balingen.

Fire repeatedly devastated the town. Chroniclers say it burned in 1286 during a feud between the Zollern and Hohenberg families, and further fires followed in 1546, 1607, 1672, 1724 and 1809. The last left only 55 of 445 buildings standing, and the rebuilding gave the town its classicist character. A civic foundation established a hospital in 1489 to care for the poor and the elderly. Balingen became part of the unified Germany in 1870. From 1939 to 1945 the town was the site of a subcamp of the Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp, which after the war became a French internment camp for former Nazi war criminals.

The castle, reconstructed in 1935, stands beside the old tanners' quarter, known as Little Venice. The Protestant church, finished in 1541, escaped the fire of 1809 and has a characteristic sundial in its apse. A publicly accessible sulphur spring, whose water has the smell of rotten eggs, is said to have healing powers. Among Balingen's natives are the Carthusian monk and humanist Gregor Reisch, who produced an encyclopedia of general knowledge.
balkan-league: After the Crimean War, Russia pursued indirect expansion in the Balkans by creating friendly states under its patronage, on the basis of the Panslavic movement. It helped establish an autonomous Bulgaria after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 and expanded Serbia. After its humiliation in the Bosnian Crisis, Russia pressed the two to compromise and ally against Austria-Hungary and the Ottomans. The Italo-Turkish War, which began in September 1911, exposed Ottoman weakness, and the Albanian Uprising of 1911 raised Serbian fears of an Albanian state closing its last direction of expansion. Serbia and Bulgaria signed an alliance on 13 March 1912; a secret chapter redirected it against the Ottoman Empire, and Serbia then allied with Montenegro and Bulgaria with Greece.

Their agreement stipulated that Bulgaria would receive all of Macedonia south of the Kriva Palanka–Ohrid line, while Serbia would expand to the north of it, including Kosovo, and westward to the Adriatic coast. Bulgaria refused to agree on any division of gains with Greece, as it expected its own army to occupy most of Macedonia and Thessaloniki first. Greece, led by Eleftherios Venizelos, was nevertheless essential, since alone of the four it had a major fleet that could prevent Ottoman reinforcements from crossing from Asia by sea. Montenegro, a small country and a close ally of Serbia, was regarded as a second-class partner with limited aims around Shkodër.

The Great Powers officially agreed on the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and warned the Balkan states, but their private signals differed, and the warning had no effect. Russia was the prime mover of the League, and France refused to support Russia in any conflict with Austria-Hungary caused by it. Montenegro declared war on 8 October 1912, and the other three states did so on 17 October, after an ultimatum on 13 October. The allied armies destroyed Ottoman power in Europe in a series of victories.

The old rivalries returned after victory, above all over the partition of Macedonia.
