Two other groups live among the Moros: the Lumad, of whom the Teduray are the largest group, and settler communities, mainly Christian, including Tagalog, Ilocano and Visayan peoples. Cebuano and Tagalog serve as lingua francas.

The westernmost and west-central parts of Mindanao have been the traditional homeland of Muslim Filipinos since the 15th century, before the Spanish began to colonize most of the Philippines in 1565. Most of Mindanao was the homeland of indigenous Lumad groups who were neither Christian nor Muslim. Spanish rule did not fully conquer the archipelago because of Moro resistance, and modern Moro leaders see centuries of resistance to the Spanish, Americans and Japanese as one national liberation movement.

The American colonial government began promoting migration to Mindanao in 1903, and later presidents continued it. The share of indigenous peoples fell from a majority in 1913 to a minority by 1976, and the best lands went to settlers and corporate agriculture. The Tripoli Agreement of 23 December 1976 between the government and the MNLF promised an autonomous region, but its implementation collapsed and hostilities resumed. Salamat Hashim then led a splinter faction that became the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

The MILF rejected the validity of the earlier autonomous region and called for one with more powers. In 2014 the government and the MILF negotiated the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, and the Bangsamoro Organic Law was signed on 26 July 2018. A two-part plebiscite on 21 January and 6 February 2019 approved the new region, which replaced the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. Cotabato City voted to join, and 63 barangays of Cotabato province were added.

The organic law provides for a parliamentary system headed by a chief minister, and states that the region remains an integral part of the national territory. Kulintang gong music is central to the culture of Muslims, Lumads and Christians alike, and the region includes Lake Lanao and the Liguasan Marsh.
banjarmasin: Banjarmasin lies on a delta island near the confluence of the Barito and Martapura rivers, and the Martapura bisects it. The land is flat and low-lying, and several smaller rivers affected by the tides form its drainage. The city sits in a swampy region, generally below water level, and is prone to flooding by tidal bores. Its climate is tropical monsoon, with heavy rain from November to June.

The name is thought to be a corruption of Bandar Masih, Port Masih, after Patih Masih, who ruled the port and surrounding villages. Dayaks from the interior visited the port to trade, and some settled there.Europeans first met the Banjar through trade, mostly at Banten from 1596. Dutch traders came to the port only after Banten's rulers banned them. On 17 July 1607 the Sultan took revenge on a Dutch ship at Banjarmasin by hijacking it and massacring the crew. A trade agreement gave the Dutch East India Company a monopoly of trade in the port, but the sultan expelled the company in 1638 after waging war and burning much of its property around the port.

The Imperial Japanese Army occupied the city in the Second World War, and control then passed to the Imperial Japanese Navy, whose rule locals described as harsher. Australian forces liberated the city in September 1945. The people opposed the return of Dutch rule, which led to the four-year Kalimantan Physical Revolution between Indonesian nationalists and the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, ending with Dutch recognition of Indonesia in 1949. The city was granted city status in 1959 and became the capital of the new province of South Kalimantan.

Banjarmasin is the largest city in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, and the centre of Banjarese culture. The provincial capital was legally moved to Banjarbaru on 15 February 2022. The culture of the Banjar people is described as a river culture, influenced by Dayak, Javanese, Malay, Arab and even Persian peoples, and keeps elements of a Hindu-Buddhist past despite a Muslim majority.
banjul: Banjul stands on St Mary's Island, also called Banjul Island, in the Gambia River where it enters the Atlantic Ocean. Bridges connect the island to the mainland, and ferries cross the river. There are several explanations of the name. One tradition says that Bandjougou, son of Barafin, came to the island fleeing the attacks of Soumaoro Kante on the Manding region, and that his name became Bandjoulou. Another derives it from Bang julo, the Mandinka word for the rope fibre gathered on the island.

In 1651 the island was leased from the King of Kombo by the Duke of Courland and Semigallia, as part of the Curonian colonization. On 23 April 1816 Tumani Bojang, the King of Kombo, ceded it to Alexander Grant, the British commandant, in exchange for an annual fee of 103 iron bars. Grant's expedition of 75 men had been ordered by Charles MacCarthy to establish a military garrison. Grant founded a trading post and base to control the entrance to the Gambia estuary and suppress the slave trade.

The British renamed the island St Mary's and called the town Bathurst, after the 3rd Earl Bathurst, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies. The streets were laid out in a modified grid and named after Allied generals at the Battle of Waterloo.

Within a few years the town drew migrants: Africans of various origins, Levantines and Europeans. Most of its people were Muslim, with a significant Christian minority including the Aku. The Wolof, mainly from Gorée and Saint-Louis, were the largest African group, rising from 829 in 1881 to 10,130 in 1944. Islamic schools called dara were founded early, and the first Muslim court in 1905. Bathurst was declared capital of the Protectorate of the Gambia in 1889, and became a centre of British activity in the colony. It was an important Allied naval and air hub in the Second World War, when its population rose from 14,370 in 1931 to 21,154 in 1944. After independence the town was renamed Banjul on 24 April 1973.

Banjul is the capital of the Gambia and its economic and administrative centre, with the Central Bank of the Gambia and a port that ships groundnut products, beeswax, palm oil and hides. The city proper had 26,461 people at the 2024 census, and the Greater Banjul Area, which includes the Kanifing municipality, 405,809. Arch 22, 35 metres tall, was built as an entrance portal to commemorate the bloodless coup of 22 July 1994 and houses a textile museum. The Gambian National Museum, the Albert Market and the State House are in the city.
bank-of-england: After the Revolution of 1688 brought William III and Mary II to the throne, a national bank became possible. During the Nine Years' War the Royal Navy was defeated by the French at the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690, and the government decided to rebuild it, but low public funds and poor credit made it impossible to borrow the £1.5 million it wanted. The idea of a public bank was two decades old. John Locke was an early supporter and, once it was set up, an early investor, and in 1691 the Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a national bank to bolster public finances. It was chartered in 1694.

The Ways and Means Act of 1715 authorised the bank to take subscriptions for a government issue of 5% annuities meant to raise £910,000; this began its role in managing government stocks, which it kept until 1998. The bank has been on Threadneedle Street since 1734, and a satirical cartoon by James Gillray in 1797 gave it the nickname the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street. Its first branches opened in 1826, and by 1829 there were eleven; the last five closed in 1997.

Britain was on the gold standard until 1931, when the Great Depression forced the bank to take it off. Banknotes were issued from 1694, hand-written at first and fully printed from 1855. After the First World War the bank withdrew increasingly from private and commercial accounts to concentrate on central banking. It was privately owned by stockholders until its nationalisation in 1946 by the Attlee ministry.

The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and the model on which most modern central banks have been based. It is the world's second oldest central bank, after Sweden's of 1668. In 1998 it became an independent public body, and the Debt Management Office took over government debt. The bank is custodian of the official gold reserves of the United Kingdom and holds a monopoly on issuing banknotes in England and Wales.
banska-stiavnica: Banská Štiavnica stands in the middle of an immense caldera created by the collapse of an ancient volcano, known for its size as the Štiavnica Mountains. Its fate has been closely linked to the exploitation of abundant silver ore. Excavations show that the site was settled in the Neolithic period. The Slavic population named the settlement in the valley Štiavnica, meaning acidic stream, and the settlement on the hill above came to be called Bánya, the mine.

The first mining settlement was founded by Celts in the 3rd century BCE, probably by the Cotini tribe. The site was called terra banensium, the land of miners, as early as 1156. Skilled German settlers began arriving in the 13th century and adapted the local name to Schemnitz. Banská Štiavnica gained the status of a royal town in 1238, one of the first in the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the High and Late Middle Ages it was the main producer of silver and gold in the kingdom.

During the Ottoman Wars the town built powerful fortifications, including two castles, in the 16th century. It was also a centre of mining innovation: in 1627 gunpowder was used in a mine there, one of the first uses in the world. In the 18th century local scientists, among them Jozef Karol Hell, Maximilian Hell and Samuel Mikovíny, designed a system of reservoirs and channels called tajchy to drain flooded mines.

Samuel Mikovíny founded a Mining Academy in 1735, the first mining school in the Kingdom of Hungary. From 1763 it became the Academy of Mining with the support of Queen Maria Theresa, and in 1848 the Academy of Mining and Forestry, described as the first technical university in the world. In 1782 the town was the third biggest in the kingdom, but mining declined progressively from the second half of the 19th century.

Banská Štiavnica is a town in central Slovakia with a population of less than 10,000. The surviving urban centre was formed during the 16th century, and the town and its surroundings were proclaimed a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 11 December 1993. Sixty reservoirs were built between the 15th and 18th centuries, connected by more than 100 kilometres of channels, and they are now used mainly for recreation. The old and new castles have become museums.
banten: Banten lies at the western tip of Java. It is bordered by the Java Sea on the north, the Sunda Strait on the west and the Indian Ocean on the south, and by West Java and Jakarta on the east. The Sunda Strait carries sea lanes linking Australia and New Zealand with Southeast Asia, and Banten forms a link between Java and Sumatra. The province covers 9,355.76 square kilometres and ranges from sea level to 2,000 metres, with lowlands in the north and south and hills in the centre.

In the fourth and fifth centuries the area belonged to the kingdom of Tarumanagara. A Sanskrit inscription found in 1947 in Munjul describes life under Purnawarman. After Tarumanagara fell to an attack by Srivijaya, western Java became part of the Sunda Kingdom. Islam began to spread in the 15th century and by the late 16th century had replaced Hinduism and Buddhism as the main religion, with the establishment of the Banten Sultanate. According to the Babad Banten, Sunan Gunung Jati and Maulana Hasanuddin spread Islam widely.

The Portuguese were established in Banten before the Dutch, and the English, French and Danish also traded there. The Portuguese left in 1601 after the Dutch destroyed their fleet off the coast. The Dutch East India Company gradually weakened the sultanate, and on 22 November 1808 Governor-General Herman Willem Daendels declared it absorbed into the Dutch East Indies. Japan occupied the region from March 1942 and built the Saketi-Bayah railway to carry brown coal, using about 1,000 forced labourers, rōmusha, drawn mainly from Banten; casualties are estimated at 20,000 to 60,000, not counting mine workers. Banten became a separate province on 17 October 2000.

The capital of the province is Serang and its largest city is Tangerang. Most residents are Muslims, and the Bantenese, at 47 per cent, are the largest ethnic group. The Baduy people of Kanekes practise Sunda Wiwitan and keep their ancestral customs. The Great Mosque of Banten and Ujung Kulon National Park, a sanctuary of the Javan rhinoceros, are among its notable sites.
bantu-peoples: The Bantu peoples are a grouping of about 400 distinct Indigenous African ethnic groups who speak Bantu languages, of which there are between 440 and 680 depending on how language and dialect are defined. They are not a single ethnic group. The term Bantu is an artificial one, introduced into modern scholarship by Wilhelm Bleek in 1857 or 1858, based on a reconstructed Proto-Bantu word for people. Proto-Bantu is estimated to have been spoken 4,000 to 3,000 years ago in the area of modern Cameroon. The spread of Bantu speakers across Central, East and Southern Africa, the Bantu expansion, took roughly two millennia, during the 1st millennium BCE and the 1st millennium CE.

In the course of the expansion Bantu-speaking peoples absorbed or displaced many earlier inhabitants. Central African Pygmy groups, the Hadza of northern Tanzania and various Khoisan populations of southern Africa remained. Genetic analysis shows admixture with earlier local populations, and interaction with Cushitic, Nilotic and Central Sudanic speakers. Pioneering groups had reached parts of KwaZulu-Natal before the 3rd century CE and the Northern Cape by 500 CE.

Between the 9th and 15th centuries Bantu-speaking states began to emerge in the Great Lakes region and in the savanna south of the Central African rainforest, and from the 12th century state formation became more frequent. Examples include the Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba Empire, the Lunda Empire, Buganda, Rwanda and the Zulu Kingdom. The Monomotapa kings built the Great Zimbabwe complex, ancestral to the Shona. On the East African coast contact with Arab and Persian traders produced Swahili culture, whose language holds many Arabic loanwords.

Speakers of Bantu languages number in the hundreds of millions, roughly 350 million in the mid-2010s, about 30 per cent of Africa's population. About 90 million are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo alone.

In South Africa the term Bantu came into use in the 1920s in preference to Native. After World War II the National Party governments adopted it officially, and it became identified with apartheid, which named its eleven rural reserves Bantustans. It is now used there only in its linguistic sense.
bantustan: From 1913 successive white-minority South African governments set up reserves to segregate the black population, as the Natives Land Act of 1913 limited black people to seven percent of the land. When the National Party came to power in 1948, Hendrik Verwoerd, Minister for Native Affairs and later Prime Minister, built on this with measures such as the Group Areas Acts and the Natives Resettlement Act of 1954. The creation of homelands was central to the strategy, since the long-term goal was to make them independent, so that black people would lose their South African citizenship and voting rights and whites would remain in control.

The word, first used in the late 1940s, was coined by supporters of the policy to echo Pakistan and Hindustan, and it quickly became a pejorative; the National Party preferred homelands. Nelson Mandela wrote in 1959 that the word was a complete misnomer that helped the Nationalists perpetrate a fraud, since Africans would have no rights outside the reserves.

The Bantu Authorities Act of 1951 established homelands for the black ethnic groups, amounting to 13% of the country's land. The Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a plan called Separate Development, in four steps: a single Territorial Authority, a legislative assembly with limited powers, self-governing status, and nominal independence. Cooperative chiefs ran the homelands, and uncooperative ones were forcibly deposed. The Black Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 designated all black South Africans citizens of the homelands, even if they lived in white South Africa, and cancelled their South African citizenship.

By 1984 all ten homelands in South Africa were self-governing, and four, Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda and Ciskei, had been declared independent between 1976 and 1981. Only South Africa recognised them. An estimated 3.5 million people were forced from their homes from the 1960s to the 1980s, many resettled in the homelands, yet only about 39% of black South Africans lived in them in 1986. Following the Odendaal commission, ten homelands were also set up in South West Africa from 1968.

The homelands were generally poor, with few local jobs. Bophuthatswana, with deposits of platinum, was the wealthiest, and the casino resort of Sun City was built there, taking advantage of laws that differed from those of South Africa. Homeland leaders were widely seen as collaborators with the apartheid system, though some gained a following. All the Bantustans were dismantled and reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994, when the Interim Constitution came into force; in Ciskei South African security forces intervened in March 1994 to defuse a crisis. The term is now used more generally, in a disapproving sense, for any area where people are forced to live without full civil and political rights.
bao-dai: Bảo Đại was born Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh Thụy on 22 October 1913, the only child of Emperor Khải Định. The Nguyễn dynasty had ruled Vietnam since 1802, but after the French conquest of 1883 the country was divided into the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin and the colony of Cochinchina, and the dynasty kept only nominal rule of Annam and Tonkin. In 1922 the boy was adopted by a former French Resident-Superior of Annam and sent to France to study. He was the first Vietnamese monarch to receive a full Western education.

Khải Định died in 1925, and on 8 January 1926 Vĩnh Thụy was enthroned at the age of twelve, taking the era name Bảo Đại, meaning keeper of greatness. A regent governed for him while he returned to France to study. He came back to Vietnam in 1932 and began to reform the court, abolishing the kowtow and the rule against looking directly at the emperor.

In March 1945 the Japanese, who had occupied French Indochina since 1940, ousted the French administration and kept Bảo Đại as emperor. On 11 March he signed a declaration of independence, prepared by the Japanese, that cancelled the treaty of 1884 with France and proclaimed the Empire of Vietnam, in practice a client state of Japan. After Japan surrendered, the Viet Minh forced the imperial government to hand over power, and he abdicated, saying that he would prefer to be a citizen of an independent country than emperor of an enslaved one.

Hồ Chí Minh invited him to Hanoi as supreme adviser to the new Democratic Republic of Vietnam, a post he held for nearly a year. In 1946 he left a delegation to China and settled in Hong Kong. From 1949 to 1955 he was chief of state of the French-associated State of Vietnam. He was criticised for being too closely tied to France and for spending much of his time outside Vietnam, and in 1955 Prime Minister Ngô Đình Diệm removed him in a referendum.

Bảo Đại lived in exile in France. He died in Paris on 31 July 1997, aged 83, and was buried in the Passy Cemetery. The Communist Party of Vietnam regarded him as a traitor, and many overseas Vietnamese opposed to communism also judged him weak, though recent studies have questioned both views.
baoji: Baoji is a prefecture-level city that covers 18,159 square kilometres and had a population of 3,321,853 at the 2020 census. It is surrounded on three sides by hills and lies in a valley opening out to the east. Its location is strategic, because it controls a pass on the Qin Mountains between the Wei River valley and the Jialing River. Since the early 1990s it has been the second largest city in Shaanxi.

South of the city lies the beginning of a plank road into the Qin Mountains, and the Jialing Jiang Fountainhead has small waterfalls and forests. To the north is Bei Puo, a giant hill of loess with a view over the city and the surrounding farming villages.

The area has roots reaching back to about 2000 BCE, and a number of Longshan archaeological sites have been found north of the Wei River near the Northern Silk Road. The city thrived early in the Tang dynasty. The Northern Silk Road, the northernmost of the routes, ran for about 2,600 kilometres through Baoji. It connected the ancient capital Chang'an to the West over the Wushaoling Mountain to Wuwei and on to Kashgar, where it linked to ancient Parthia.

Mount Taibai still has traces of roadways from the Three Kingdoms period (220 to 280 CE), built as wooden plank bridges along the mountainside. They are generally unusable through decay but remain a popular attraction. Zhuge Liang's Memorial Temple stands about 20 kilometres from the city, and visitors interested in the Three Kingdoms go there.

The Baoji area was home to Yandi, traditionally regarded as a forefather of the Han Chinese. His tomb lies in the southern part of the city and his temple in the north. Famen Temple in Fufeng County holds one of the Buddha's finger bones. Railways first reached Baoji in 1937 and have been key to its modern growth.

Baoji is a large industrial centre and is regarded as the gateway between western and eastern China, since most trains from Beijing, Shanghai and Xi'an pass through it on their way to Gansu, Sichuan, Xinjiang and Tibet. The Baoji Bronze Museum holds more than 120,000 cultural relics, primarily of the Zhou dynasty. Baoji University of Arts and Sciences is based in the city.
bar-le-duc: Bar-le-Duc, formerly known as Bar, is the capital of the Meuse département in the Grand Est region of north-eastern France. The lower town, the more modern and busier part, extends along a narrow valley shut in by wooded or vine-clad hills, and the Ornain runs through it. The upper town, the Ville Haute, lies on the left bank of a small arm of the river, the Canal des Usines.

Bar-le-Duc was the seat of a county and, from 1354, of the Duchy of Bar. The town is probably of ancient origin but was unimportant until the 10th century, when Frederick I of Upper Lorraine fortified it. Bar was an independent duchy from 1354 to 1480, when the Duchy of Lorraine acquired it.

In 1916, during the Battle of Verdun, Bar-le-Duc was the assembly point for the supplies sent to the besieged city of Verdun. Thousands of trucks carrying men, equipment and food travelled north around the clock on the road linking the two towns, which the writer and politician Maurice Barres named the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, in April 1916.

The Ville Haute is crossed by a long, quiet street lined with houses of the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries, and holds 16th-century remains of the château of the dukes of Bar, dismantled in 1670. The church of Saint-Étienne contains the Cadaver Tomb of René of Châlon, who died in 1544, a carved white stone effigy of a half-decayed corpse by the 16th-century artist Ligier Richier. Among the natives of Bar-le-Duc are Mary of Guise, mother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and the mathematician Henri Poincaré. Bar-le-Duc jelly, made from currants and first mentioned in 1344, is known as Bar caviar.
bar-montenegro: Bar lies on the Adriatic shore in the coastal region of Montenegro, about 53 kilometres from Podgorica, with Lake Skadar, the largest lake in southern Europe, to the east. Its name is thought to be a shortened Slavic form of Antivari, from the Latin Antibarum or Antibari, meaning opposite Bari, for its position across the Adriatic from that Italian city. It is called Tivari in Albanian. Finds from the Neolithic show that people lived there in prehistoric times, and the name Antibarium is first quoted in the 10th century.

In the Middle Ages Bar was linked to the Slavic state of Duklja. Stefan Vojislav, ruler from 1018 to 1043, defeated the Byzantines in a battle on a hill near Bar and made it his seat. His son Mihailo I established the Archdiocese of Antivari, founded in 1089. Byzantium held the town from 1166 to 1183, until Stefan Nemanja conquered and destroyed it. The Nemanjić dynasty ruled it until 1360, then the Balšić family. The Venetians controlled Bar from 1405 to 1412, when it grew most and became a city-state, with its own Statute of Communes and coinage. They ruled again from 1443 to 1571, until the Ottomans captured Antivari and held it until 1878.

The Ottomans ceded Antivari to Montenegro at the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, and the town was made militarily neutral. In the late 1850s it had 4,000 inhabitants, 62.5 per cent of them Muslims; more than half left or were expelled after 1878. On 30 August 1904 Guglielmo Marconi made a radio link between Antivari and Bari, and in 1908 the first railway in this part of the Balkans opened there. In 1914 and 1915 Austro-Hungarian ships bombarded the port, and on 16 August 1914 a French fleet sank the cruiser SMS Zenta off the town in the Battle of Antivari. Bar joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918.

The old town of Stari Bar and the newer settlement by the sea are distinct: the district of Pristan was demolished in 1976 to enlarge the port, and its people moved mostly to Topolica. The Port of Bar and the Belgrade–Bar railway, opened in 1976, are the basis of its economy. King Nikola's castle at Topolica, built in 1885, houses the Bar Homeland Museum. Bar is the birthplace of Saint Jovan Vladimir, and has Orthodox and Catholic churches and mosques built by the Ottomans.
bar-sur-aube: The town is old. Remains of an Iron Age oppidum survive, and a coin bearing a horse and the name of Togirix, a chief of the Lingones, was found on the hill of Sainte Germaine. In Roman times it appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana as Segessera, and villas of the 1st to 4th centuries have been found in and around it. Tradition tells that the city was devastated by Attila, and Sainte Germaine is said to have been beheaded on his order in 451. After the division of the kingdom of Clovis it became part of Austrasia, and under Charles the Bald coins were struck with its name on the reverse. The name Bar comes from a Gallic word meaning summit.

Under the counts of Champagne the town was of great importance because of the Champagne fairs, where merchants from Flanders and Italy traded oriental spices and silk for the textiles and raw materials of northern Europe. The town was later joined to the crown of France. In 1318 Philip V the Tall sold it to Jacques de Croÿ; the residents then bought it themselves, so that the king could no longer sell or alienate their lands. A long plague in 1636 ended the fair.

The fortifications were demolished in 1862 and replaced by a boulevard. The French Revolution was well received there, and from 1790 to 1800 the town was the chief town of its district. On 27 February 1814, near the end of the Napoleonic era, the Battle of Bar-sur-Aube was fought in the town and its surroundings.

Bar-sur-Aube is a commune and sub-prefecture in the Aube department of the Grand Est region, about 30 kilometres west-north-west of Chaumont. It lies on the Aube among hills and Champagne vineyards. Its heritage includes the 12th-century church of Saint Maclou, the 16th-century church of Saint Peter, which holds most of the commune's more than 200 registered historical objects, and the chapel of Saint John, held in turn by the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller.
baracoa: Baracoa, whose full original name is Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de Baracoa, lies near the eastern tip of Cuba on the Bay of Honey, which is Bahía de Miel. A wide mountain range, including the Sierra del Purial, surrounds it and kept it isolated: until the 1960s the only access was by sea, when a 120-kilometre mountain road called La Farola was built from Guantánamo. The name is thought to come from a Taíno word meaning the presence of the sea. The nearby table mountain of El Yunque shelters several species of ferns and palms found nowhere else.

The original inhabitants of the island included the Guanahatabey, Ciboney and Taíno, who were almost wiped out by European diseases. Hatuey, who fled the Spanish on Hispaniola and raised an army against them in Cuba, is remembered as a local hero. According to the story, he was betrayed and sentenced to burn at the stake, and when a priest offered him salvation he asked whether the Spanish dead went to heaven, and said that he would rather go to hell.

Christopher Columbus landed in Cuba on 27 November 1492 at a place he named Porto Santo, generally taken from his description to be Baracoa, though Gibara has also been claimed. Tradition says he set up a cross, the Cruz de la Parra, on the sand. About 15 August 1511, the official foundation day, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, first governor of Cuba, built a town here, making it the island's first capital. In 1518 it received the title of city and the first Cuban bishop was appointed there. Spanish fortifications, El Castillo, Matachín and La Punta, and a cemetery remain.

In the 17th and 18th centuries its isolation made Baracoa a haven for illegal trade with French and British merchants. In 1744, during the War of Jenkins' Ear, the officer Luis de Unzaga, as chief commander, used a network of Irish merchants and French military personnel to be warned of British attacks, which kept the town at peace and let trade between Saint-Domingue and Cuba prosper. Early in the 19th century refugees from the Haitian Revolution settled and began growing coffee and cocoa. From the middle of that century, expeditions of independence fighters, among them Antonio Maceo and José Martí, landed here.

Baracoa is Cuba's main chocolate-manufacturing area, with cacao grown under royal palms by the rivers Miel, Toa and Yumuri, as well as bananas and coconuts. The Catedral Nuestra Señora de la Asunción holds the Cruz de la Parra. Carbon dating places it at about the period of Columbus, but it is made of a local wood, so part of the tradition cannot be right.
barbary-coast: The Barbary Coast, also called Barbary, Berbery or the Berber Coast, covered the coastal areas of central and western North Africa, more precisely the Maghreb and the Ottoman borderlands. It was never a single political entity. From the sixteenth century it was divided into four states, from west to east: the Alawi Sultanate of Morocco and the Regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli. Their main rulers were the sultan of Morocco, the dey of Algiers, the bey of Tunis and the pasha of Tripoli. The name comes from an exonym for the Berbers, now called Amazigh.

The slave trade was an economic lifeline of the Barbary states. Most captives came from piracy at sea and from raids on coasts around the Mediterranean, although there were also Atlantic raids as far as Iceland. In 1625 the pirate fleet of Algiers, by far the largest, numbered 100 ships carrying 8,000 to 10,000 men, and the corsair industry accounted for a quarter of the city's workforce. The corsairs were Arabs and Berbers but also Turks, Greeks, Albanians, Syrians and renegade Italians, especially Corsicans.

Spain fought back after the fall of Granada completed the Reconquista. Ferdinand II launched campaigns to curb Barbary piracy and took North African cities including Melilla. In the seventeenth century pirates, now including expelled Moriscos, adopted European naval tactics. The Moriscos of the Republic of Salé used their knowledge of Spanish shores to raid the Spanish Levante, and from 1617 raids struck Galicia, which led Spain to form a fleet around 1621, with limited success.

The United States fought the Barbary Wars from 1801 to 1805 against some of the states, leading to the Battle of Derna, the second overseas military land action of the United States. The Second Barbary War ended with an agreement that American ships had free passage without paying tribute. Slaving came to an end in the early 1830s after the French conquest of Algeria.
barbastro: Barbastro is a city in the Somontano county of the province of Huesca, at the junction of the rivers Cinca and Vero. It was known originally as Barbastra or Bergiduna. An ancient Celtiberian city called Bergidum or Bergiduna stood there; in Roman times, as Barbastro, it lay within Hispania Citerior and later Hispania Tarraconensis, and after the fall of the Western Roman Empire it belonged to the Visigoth kingdom.

Musa bin Nusair overtook Barbastro and the surrounding Barbitaniya in 717, as part of the Umayyad push into the northern territories of the Marca Hispanica, and the town was called Madyar. It was later settled by the Banu Jalaf, who made it the capital of an emirate of Barbineta and Huesca until 862, and it was known as the Emirate of Brabstra until 882.

In 1064 Sancho Ramírez, King of Aragón, and Frankish Christian forces led by William VIII of Aquitaine and a Norman commander called Le Bon Normand invaded the city, which then belonged to the emirate of Zaragoza. The attack is known as the Siege of Barbastro. Contemporary sources state that 50,000 people were killed or captured, but modern historians regard this as an exaggeration, since the whole population of the town probably did not exceed 8,000. Muslim forces reconquered the city in 1065.

A Sephardic Jewish community flourished in Barbastro in the Middle Ages and suffered little compared with others in Spain; the first written record of it dates from 1144. After the Disputation of Tortosa its members all became conversos, and the old synagogue became a centre of converso life. In June 1837, during the First Carlist War, the French Foreign Legion, attached to the liberal government's army, fought the Carlist foreign legion there, and its commander, Colonel Joseph Conrad, was killed.

In the Spanish Civil War 51 Catholic Claretians, mostly young seminarians, were executed in Barbastro by anarchist militia of the Popular Front, and the diocese suffered the highest proportion of clergy killed in the war. The city's economy flourished until the early 20th century, declined, and recovered from the 1960s with the growth of agricultural production.
barbed-wire: Fencing of flat, thin wire with bristling points was first proposed in France by Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans in 1860. In April 1865 Louis François Janin proposed a double wire with diamond-shaped metal barbs. In 1867 alone six patents were issued, only two of them for livestock, one to Lucien B. Smith of Ohio, regarded as the American inventor. After the Civil War the plains were extensively settled, and ranchers, railroads and farmers all needed to fence large open spaces where wood and stone were costly and hedges unreliable.

In 1873 Joseph Glidden, a farmer, saw at a fair in DeKalb, Illinois a display by Henry B. Rose of a wooden strip with metallic points. With the hardware dealer Isaac L. Ellwood and the lumber merchant Jacob Haish he began experimenting, twisting two wires round the barbs with a grindstone and shaping barbs with a coffee mill. Glidden applied for a patent in October 1873; Haish, who held patents of his own, accused him of interference, and approval of Glidden's wire, nicknamed The Winner, was deferred until 24 November 1874.

In 1876 John Warne Gates demonstrated the wire in Military Plaza, San Antonio, showing cattle held by it, and sales rose sharply. Between 1873 and 1899 as many as 150 companies made barbed wire, then consolidated, notably into the American Steel and Wire Company, later part of U.S. Steel. A US District Court upheld the Glidden patent in 1880 and the Supreme Court affirmed it in 1892. Wire cut the cost of enclosing land and set farmers against open-range ranchers in the range wars. Heavy penalties were set for cutting fences, and some historians date the end of the Old West to the wire's spread.

Portuguese troops used barbed wire in the Battle of Magul in 1895, and it was used extensively in the Boer War, where it held the captured Boer population in concentration camps. In the First World War all combatants placed entanglements before their trenches to halt charges or funnel soldiers into machine-gun fire. The tank defeated it, as the Allied breakthrough at Amiens on 8 August 1918 showed.

Barbed wire is still the standard fencing for enclosing cattle in most regions of the United States. Fences are built between heavy braced posts and kept under great tension, often up to half a ton. The wire is galvanized, and high-tensile wire is thinner but resists stretching better. Razor wire, which replaces the barbs with near-continuous cutting surfaces, is used where humans must be kept out.
barbuda: Barbuda lies north of Antigua and covers about 160 square kilometres. Coral limestone makes up most of the island, which has very little variety in its landscape. Hills in the Barbuda Highlands on the eastern side reach about 38 metres, while the northwest corner holds many lagoons, and Codrington Lagoon dominates the western part. Salty ponds and scrubland are spread across the interior. The climate is tropical marine. Codrington, which grew up as the main residential area by 1666, is still the only town and the main settlement.

The first settlers arrived by canoe, as hunter-gatherers, around 2,900 to 3,000 BCE. Sources disagree on whether they came from South America, the Greater Antilles or the Yucatán region. They made cutting blades, hoes and picks from the shells of conch, trumpet and whelk. They were followed by Arawak people, present on Barbuda and Antigua from at least 1,000 BCE, whose numbers on Barbuda peaked between 1,500 and 800 years ago. They probably came from present-day Venezuela and Guyana, grew sweet potatoes, corn, cotton and tobacco, and made pottery in the Saladoid style, with white-on-red designs.

English colonisation was attempted from St. Kitts under a patent of 1625 granted to the Earl of Carlisle, and the island appears there as Barbado. In 1668 about 240 Kalinago attacked the 20 English inhabitants, and eight settlers died. Strong Kalinago resistance and drought caused this attempt to fail. In 1685 the crown granted the island to the brothers John and Christopher Codrington. The colonisers intended Barbuda to be a colony for the forced reproduction of enslaved people, but this never went through. Slavery was abolished there in 1834. Because a single land grant had covered the whole island, Barbudans went on farming communal property on their own account.

Barbuda forms part of the twin-island state of Antigua and Barbuda as an autonomous entity. It gained autonomy in 1976 through the Barbuda Local Government Act, which created the Barbuda Council, and gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1981 as part of Antigua and Barbuda. The Council has eleven members and sits in Codrington. Under the Barbuda Land Acts, land is held communally. The 2011 census counted 1,634 people. Fishing, especially for lobster, supplies most exports, and tourist attractions include the Frigate Bird Sanctuary in Codrington Lagoon, a 19th-century Martello Tower and the ruins of Highland House, the Codrington family home.
barcelona: Barcelona lies on the north-east coast of the Iberian Peninsula, facing the Mediterranean Sea, on a plain about 5 km wide limited by the Collserola mountain range, the Llobregat river to the south-west and the Besòs river to the north. It lies 120 km south of the Pyrenees. The escarpment of Montjuïc overlooks the harbour and is topped by Montjuïc Castle, a fortress built in the 17th and 18th centuries to control the city.

According to tradition Barcelona was founded by Phoenician or Carthaginian settlers, and some historians credit the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca with naming it Barcino in the 3rd century BCE, though this theory has been questioned. Coins of the 3rd century BCE found at the foot of Montjuïc carry the name Barkeno in Iberian script.

In the Middle Ages Barcelona became the capital of the County of Barcelona. After the union with Aragon it remained capital of the Principality of Catalonia and the most important city of the Crown of Aragon, until Valencia overtook it shortly before 1516. Its industrial rise began in 1833, when Catalonia's textile industry began to use steam power. It became capital of autonomous Catalonia in 1931 and was taken by the fascists in 1939.

Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia and the second most populous municipality of Spain. Its old centre, the Barri Gòtic, has buildings from medieval times and some from the Roman settlement. Works of Antoni Gaudí and Lluís Domènech i Montaner are World Heritage Sites, and the city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics.
bard: The word goes back to the Proto-Celtic noun *bardos, a poet-singer, itself derived from a Proto-Indo-European compound meaning praise-maker. It is attested in Gaulish as bardus in Latin and bárdoi in Greek, and survives in Middle Welsh bardd, Middle Irish bard and Middle Breton barz. The fullest early accounts descend from the lost history of Posidonius, who travelled in southern Gaul in the early 1st century BCE, and reach us through Diodorus Siculus, Strabo and Athenaeus. Because these writers share one source they count as a single tradition. Caesar, who wrote at length about the druids, does not mention the bards at all.

The sources agree on what the bard did: praise poetry and satire, sung to a stringed instrument that Diodorus compares to a lyre. The power to raise or lower a patron's standing gave successful bards a privileged and well-paid position. Athenaeus, citing Posidonius, tells of the Arvernian Louernios, to whom a poet arrived late after a feast and sang of the king's greatness; Louernios threw him a bag of gold, and the poet answered with a second song. Appian describes a singer in the train of an embassy sent by the Arvernian king Bituitus, who praised the king, his people and the envoy. Diodorus adds that bards, together with druids, could step between two armies and halt them.

In medieval Wales the court poet held an office set out in the Laws of Hywel Dda, with the pencerdd, or chief of song, at its head. The Gogynfeirdd of the 12th and 13th centuries composed praise and elegy for the princes of independent Wales, and the order broke up in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. In Ireland the professional poet was the file, and the baird were held to rely on talent rather than formal learning. Irish bardic poetry lasted into the 17th century, and in Gaelic Scotland the MacMhuirich family kept the classical tradition into the early 18th century.

A Welsh tradition holds that Edward I had the Welsh bards put to death after the conquest of 1282, but no medieval source records it, and the historian Prys Morgan treats it as a fable. Thomas Gray's ode The Bard, published in 1757, fixed the legend in the public mind. James Macpherson's Works of Ossian, published in the 1760s as the verse of an ancient Highland bard, was read across Europe. In Wales, Edward Williams, writing as Iolo Morganwg, founded the Gorsedd Beirdd Ynys Prydein in 1792, supporting his claims with forgeries exposed only after his death. The image of an aged, visionary bard that grew from these works remains familiar in popular culture.
bardiya: The prince's name appears in several forms. In Darius the Great's Behistun inscription he is Bardiya or Bardia, called Pirtiya in the Elamite version and Barziya in the Akkadian. Herodotus calls him Smerdis, the usual Greek form, and Ctesias calls him Tanyoxarces. English histories traditionally followed Herodotus and used Smerdis, but recent ones tend to prefer Bardiya.

He was the younger son of Cyrus the Great and a full or half-brother of Cambyses II. According to Ctesias, Cyrus on his deathbed named Cambyses king and appointed Bardiya satrap of Bactria, Chorasmia, Parthia and Carmania. Darius's inscription says instead that Cambyses killed Bardiya in secret, after becoming king and before leaving for Egypt.

The sources agree that in the spring of 522 BCE a man claiming to be Bardiya was proclaimed king, but they differ on who he was. According to Darius, he was a Median magus named Gaumata. In Herodotus the usurper is a magus whose brother, the palace steward Patizeithes, had put him forward after Bardiya's secret murder; Ctesias names him Sphendadates, who was said to resemble Tanyoxarces and took his place after Cambyses had the prince killed.

In these accounts the new king was widely accepted, helped by granting tax relief for three years, and ruled for about seven months, moving the seat of government to Media. Herodotus has Cambyses die of a wound to his thigh while marching against him. In Herodotus the nobleman Otanes grew suspicious and had his daughter Phaedymia, who was in the king's harem, check whether the king had ears, since the impostor's had been cut off. Seven nobles then plotted against him.

In September 522 BCE the seven nobles, among them Darius, surprised the ruler in a castle at Nisa and killed him. Darius was proclaimed king, and Herodotus and Ctesias say he won the throne by a trick in a horse-neighing contest. Another man claiming to be Bardiya, Vahyazdāta, rose in eastern Persia the next year, had great success and was finally captured and executed. Persia is said to have marked the death of the false Bardiya each year in a feast called the killing of the magian.

Most modern historians do not find Darius's version convincing. They assume that the man who ruled was the real Bardiya and that Darius invented the impostor to justify seizing the throne, though others call this hypothetical. Contracts of his reign survive from Babylonia. Darius claimed that Bardiya had destroyed some temples and seized herds and houses. Bardiya's only daughter, Parmys, married Darius.
bareilly: Bareilly lies in the Indo-Gangetic Plains on the bank of the Ramganga River, about 252 kilometres north-west of Lucknow and 265 kilometres east of New Delhi. The plain is level and well watered, with fertile alluvial soil, although the lower plain is flood-prone. According to the Mahabharata, the region, called Panchala, was the birthplace of Draupadi, and folklore says that Gautama Buddha visited the ancient fortress city of Ahichchhatra.

The earliest settlement was founded in 1537 by the Rajput chieftain Jagat Singh Katehriya, who named it after his two sons Bansaldev and Baraldev. The town came under Mughal rule in 1569, and in 1657 the Mughal governor Mukrand Rai laid the foundation of the modern city. As Mughal power weakened, the Kingdom of Rohilkhand rose, with Bareilly as a major centre. Under Hafiz Rahmat Khan Barech, Rohilkhand blocked Maratha expansion into northern India at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

In 1774 the combined forces of Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the East India Company defeated Hafiz Rahmat Khan, who was killed in battle, ending Rohilla rule. The Nawab of Awadh surrendered Rohilkhand to the Company in a treaty of 10 November 1801. A military station was established south of the city in 1811, and a fort was built in 1816. Bareilly was freed by rebels during the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and remained independent under Khan Bahadur Khan until the British re-annexed it in 1858.

Bareilly is a city in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh and the centre of the historical region of Rohilkhand. It is the place of origin of the Barelvi movement, a Sunni Islamic movement formed by the scholar Ahmad Raza Khan to counter the growing influence of the Deobandi movement; his shrine at the Bareilly Dargah is visited by millions of followers each year. The city has been known as Nath Nagri because of its ancient Shiva temples, and is a centre of furniture manufacturing and of trade in cotton, cereal and sugar.
bari: Bari stands on the Adriatic coast of southern Italy, the largest urban area on that sea. Its old town is closely built on a peninsula between two modern harbours and holds the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, the Cathedral of San Sabino, built between 1035 and 1171, and the Norman-Swabian Castle. To the south lies the Murat quarter, laid out on a rectangular grid after Joachim Murat, King of Naples, began a new urbanisation in 1813. The port has long linked the city to Greece, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean.

In antiquity Bari was Barium, a harbour of the Iapygian Peuceti, with strong Greek influence. It became part of the Roman Republic in the 3rd century BCE and gained importance as the junction of the coast road and the Via Traiana and as a port for eastern trade. After 476 it was occupied by the Ostrogoths, taken by the Byzantines in the Gothic wars and then disputed for two centuries with the Lombards of Benevento. Through the Middle Ages it was one of the major slave depots of the Mediterranean, in particular for Slavic slaves bound for Byzantine and Muslim lands.

Its first emir, Kalfun, took Bari in 847. The Frankish emperor Louis II conquered the city and ended the emirate in 871 after a five-year campaign, helped by a Byzantine fleet. In 885 it became the residence of the Byzantine catapan. Robert Guiscard captured Bari in 1071 after a three-year siege. The former praetorium became the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, where the relics were installed in 1087 and which Pope Urban II consecrated in 1089. Peter the Hermit preached the First Crusade there in 1095.

Bona Sforza, widow of King Sigismund I of Poland, settled in Bari in 1556, fortified the castle and died in the city in 1557, after which the kings of Naples ruled it directly. On 2 December 1943 a German air raid destroyed the American ship SS John Harvey, which carried a secret cargo of mustard gas bombs, and the gas killed and injured sailors and civilians; the number of deaths is disputed.
barometer: On 27 July 1630 Giovanni Battista Baliani wrote to Galileo Galilei about a siphon led over a hill about 21 m high that failed to work: the water in the limb sank to about 10 m above the reservoir. Galileo answered that the power of a vacuum held the water up until its weight grew too great, a restatement of the old doctrine that nature abhors a vacuum. After his Discorsi reached Rome in December 1638, Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti sought a better way to produce a vacuum. W. E. Knowles Middleton places their experiment between 1639 and 1643, with Athanasius Kircher and Niccolò Zucchi present.

Torricelli, who had been Galileo's amanuensis in the last three months of his life, read the results differently. In a letter to Michelangelo Ricci in 1644 he argued that the weight of the atmosphere explained the resistance, and that it was foolish to attribute to a vacuum what followed from another evident cause.

Marin Mersenne was shown the experiment by Torricelli toward the end of 1644, and in 1646 Blaise Pascal and Pierre Petit repeated and perfected it. Pascal tested the Aristotelian claim that vapours from the liquid filled the space above it by comparing water with wine, thought more spiritous. He did so in public, inviting the Aristotelians to predict the result. They expected the wine to stand lower, and it did not.

Mercury barometers broke at sea, and in 1668 Robert Hooke's marine barometer, made by Henry Hunt, was presented to the Royal Society. The compact sympiesometer was widely used on ships in the early 19th century. Leibniz proposed an aneroid barometer around 1700, and Lucien Vidi invented a working one in 1844.

Pressure readings and the pressure tendency, the change over time, have been used in weather forecasting since the late 19th century. Combined with wind observations they allow reasonably accurate short-term forecasts, and readings from a network of stations produced maps of air pressure, the first form of the modern weather map. A rapid fall suggests an approaching low-pressure system and more chance of rain, while a rapid rise follows a cold front and goes with clearing skies. Readings are corrected for temperature, since the density of mercury changes, and reduced to sea level.
baroque: The word comes into English from French, and its roots are disputed. One line of explanation traces it to the Portuguese barroco, a flawed pearl; another to baroco, a term of medieval scholastic logic that by the 16th century had come to describe anything absurdly complex. The French philosopher Michel de Montaigne helped give it the sense of bizarre and uselessly complicated.

The style itself was shaped by the Catholic Church. The Council of Trent, meeting in 1545–1563, decided that the arts should reach a wide public and communicate religious themes with direct and emotional involvement, in response to the Protestant Reformation. The first Baroque façade in Rome was that of the Church of the Gesù in 1584, plain by later standards but a break with Renaissance façades. Lutheran Baroque art also developed, as a marker of confessional identity.

Baroque painters used intense, warm colours and strong contrasts of light and dark to direct attention to the central action. They chose moments of most intense movement and drama, and their figures show clear emotion. Allegory was essential: a picture carried a message in symbols that an educated viewer was expected to read. The dominant sculptor was Gian Lorenzo Bernini, who worked under Pope Urban VIII and made the Chair of St. Peter beneath the dome of St. Peter's Basilica.

Architecture varied by country. In Central Europe many ornate cathedrals, abbeys and pilgrimage churches were built between 1680 and 1750, and the princes of the German states chose Baroque for their palaces. French Baroque, associated with Louis XIV, is more restrained and has no broken pediments or curved façades. Louis XIV invited Bernini to design the east wing of the Louvre but chose a more classical design by Claude Perrault and Louis Le Vau. In Russia, Peter the Great's visit to western Europe in 1697–1698 preceded the Petrine Baroque of Saint Petersburg.

Beyond Europe, the style travelled with Spanish and Portuguese rule. In the Americas, European artists and missionaries were joined by Criollo and indigenous craftsmen, who gave it local features; the Cusco School of painting and the Quito School are examples. In Portuguese Goa, Baroque forms mixed with Hindu elements, and its churches and convents were declared a World Heritage Site in 1986.

By the 1730s the style had turned into the Rococo, which began in France as a reaction against the grandeur of Versailles. The Baroque itself was condemned by Johann Joachim Winckelmann, who praised classical art, and in the 19th century the British critic John Ruskin called its sculpture morally corrupt. Interest returned through Romanticism and later through Postmodernism, which promoted the inclusion of elements of historic styles in new designs.
barthelemy-boganda: Boganda was born around 1910 to a family of farmers in Bobangui, a large M'Baka village in the Lobaye basin, at the edge of the equatorial forest some 80 kilometres south-west of Bangui. His father, Swalakpé, was a village head and the wealthy owner of several palm plantations who had taken numerous wives; his mother, Siribé, was the third. French companies exploited the region through forced labour, and coercive labour practices, violence and disease had badly disrupted traditional society. After the death of his parents Boganda was adopted and educated by Roman Catholic missionaries, and in 1938 he was ordained a priest.

After the Second World War the Bishop of Bangui urged Boganda to enter politics. On 10 November 1946 he was elected deputy for Oubangui-Chari to the National Assembly of France, winning 10,846 votes, almost half of those cast, and became the first Oubanguian member. In Paris he spoke against racism and colonial abuses but found little support for his proposals. Returning to the territory, he launched a co-operative in 1948 and in 1949 founded the Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa (MESAN), which became popular among villagers and peasants. He was later laicized after marrying Michelle Jourdain, a parliamentary secretary.

He became the first Mayor of Bangui on 18 November 1956, and MESAN won every seat in the Territorial Assembly on 31 March 1957. Worried that a single small state would be weak, Boganda promoted a wider union of central African territories. On 1 December 1958 he declared the Central African Republic for Oubangui-Chari alone, and on 6 December he became president of its Council of Government. He designed its flag and wrote the words of its anthem, La Renaissance.

On 29 March 1959 Boganda boarded a Nord Noratlas plane at Berbérati for a flight to Bangui. The plane went missing and its wreckage was found the next day in the district of Boda; all nine people aboard had died. Experts found a trace of explosives in the wreckage, but a full report was never published and the possibility of an assassination remains unresolved. His funeral on 3 April was attended by thousands.
The Legislative Assembly declared him Father of the Nation in June 1959, and Boganda Day is observed each year on 29 March. His phrase zo kwe zo was placed in the state's coat of arms.
bartolome-de-las-casas: Bartolomé de las Casas was born in Seville on 11 November 1484. For centuries his birth was dated to 1474, until archival work in the 1970s uncovered records of a contemporary lawsuit showing that he was born a decade later. His father, Pedro de las Casas, was a merchant. He arrived in Hispaniola as one of the first Spanish settlers and took part in the colonial economy built on forced Indigenous labour. In 1513, as a chaplain, he joined the conquest of Cuba, where he witnessed many atrocities against the Ciboney and Guanahatabey. He later wrote that he saw cruelty on a scale no living being has ever seen.

In 1515 he gave up his Indigenous laborers and his encomienda and met King Ferdinand to argue against the encomienda system. He was given the title Protector of the Indians. In his early writings he advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labour, a position he later retracted, writing that black slavery was as unjust as Indian slavery. His attempt at peaceful settlement in Venezuela failed, and in 1522 he entered the Dominican monastery of Santa Cruz in Santo Domingo, taking vows in 1523.

He worked as a missionary among the Maya of Guatemala and lobbied for the abolition of the encomienda, winning an important victory in the New Laws of 1542. He was consecrated Bishop of Chiapas on 30 March 1544. Conflicts with the encomenderos and colonists forced him back to Spain. In 1550 he took part in the Valladolid debate, in which Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that the Indians were less than human. De Las Casas maintained that they were fully human and that forcible subjugation was unjustifiable.

De Las Casas resigned his bishopric and spent the rest of his life at the imperial court, where he had great influence on matters concerning the Indies. He died on 18 July 1566. A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written in 1542 and published at Seville in 1552, was one of the first attempts by a colonial-era Spanish writer to describe the mistreatment of Indigenous peoples. His efforts improved the legal status of Indigenous people and sharpened the ethical debate over colonialism, though he did not change Spanish policy as a whole. After his death he was widely venerated, and a cause for beatification was opened.
bartolome-esteban-murillo: Murillo was probably born in December 1617 to Gaspar Esteban, a barber surgeon, and María Pérez Murillo, and was baptised in the parish of Santa María Magdalena in Seville on 1 January 1618. After his parents died in 1627 and 1628 he became the ward of his older sister Ana and her husband Juan Agustín Lagares, and he stayed in their house until his marriage in 1645.

He studied in Seville in the workshop of Juan del Castillo, his uncle and godfather. His first works were also influenced by Francisco de Zurbarán, Jusepe de Ribera and Alonso Cano. According to the painter and art historian Antonio Palomino he travelled to Madrid in 1642, but there is little evidence for this, and Palomino denied claims by Joachim von Sandrart that he went to Italy.

In 1645 Murillo married Beatriz Cabrera y Villalobos, with whom he had ten children. The year of his marriage he received his first major commission, eleven canvases for the convent of San Francisco in Seville, on which he worked until 1648. They show a range from the tenebrism of the Ecstasy of St Francis to the softly luminous style, seen in the Death of St Clare, that became typical of his mature work. Also about 1645 he painted The Young Beggar, now in the Louvre, the first of his many paintings of children, in which the influence of Velázquez is apparent.

After a pair of pictures for Seville Cathedral he specialised in the Virgin and Child and the Immaculate Conception. He was again in Madrid from 1658 to 1660. On returning to Seville he was one of the founders of the Academia de Bellas Artes, sharing its direction in 1660 with the architect Francisco Herrera the Younger. This was his period of most activity, and the paintings for Santa María la Blanca were completed in 1665.

Murillo died in Seville on 3 April 1682, a few months after he fell from a scaffold while working on a fresco at the church of the Capuchines in Cádiz. He had many pupils and followers, and the imitation of his paintings ensured his reputation in Spain and his fame throughout Europe. Before the 19th century his work was more widely known than that of any other Spanish artist, and Gainsborough and Greuze were among those influenced by his style. His paintings of flower girls, street urchins and beggars form an extensive record of the everyday life of his times.
bartolome-mitre: Bartolomé Mitre was born on 26 June 1821 in Buenos Aires. His father was of Greek descent, and the family name was originally Mitropoulos. In 1831 the family settled in Uruguay, and in 1839 he graduated from the Military School of Montevideo as a second lieutenant of artillery. He wrote for newspapers in support of Fructuoso Rivera and joined the Colorado Party against the Blancos, which led him to side with the unitario opponents of the Rosas regime. He then went to Bolivia and Chile, where he wrote for newspapers and met fellow exiles Juan Bautista Alberdi and Domingo Faustino Sarmiento.

Mitre returned to Argentina after Juan Manuel de Rosas was defeated at the Battle of Caseros in 1852. He helped lead the revolt of Buenos Aires Province against Justo José de Urquiza's federal system on 11 September 1852. His victory at the Battle of Pavón in 1861 won concessions, notably an amendment providing for indirect elections through an electoral college. The college elected him president, with Marcos Paz as vice president, and he took office on 12 October 1862.

He later founded the newspaper La Nación, in 1870. In 1874 he ran again for president against Nicolás Avellaneda, took up arms when the electoral college awarded him only three provinces, was defeated and was spared only by Avellaneda's commutation. After the Revolution of the Park in 1890 he co-founded the Civic Union with Leandro Alem; it split in 1891, Mitre founding the National Civic Union and Alem the Radical Civic Union.

The Supreme Court began to operate on 15 January 1863, and federal courts were organised in the provinces. National colleges were founded in the provinces and railways began with British capital. In the Paraguayan War Mitre was first named head of the allied forces. His government also fought the federal rebels of La Rioja, and Mitre wrote that he wanted a police war there, declaring the montoneros thieves so that prisoners could be executed. The caudillo Chacho Peñaloza surrendered on 12 November 1863 and was murdered by Pablo Irrazábal. Mitre also wrote poetry, plays and histories and translated Dante into Spanish. He died on 19 January 1906.
bartolomeu-dias: Dias came from a family with a maritime background. One of his ancestors, Dinis Dias e Fernandes, explored the African coast in the 1440s. Tracing his own biography is complicated by the existence of several Portuguese seafarers of the same name. In 1481 he accompanied an expedition led by Diogo de Azambuja to build the fortress and trading post of São Jorge da Mina in the Gulf of Guinea, and indirect evidence suggests he may have joined Diogo Cão's first expedition to the Congo River. On 10 October 1486 King John II of Portugal granted him an annuity of 6,000 reis for services to come.

Probably in July or August 1487 Dias left Lisbon with three ships, to continue the exploration advanced by Cão and to look for Prester John, a Christian ruler believed to reign somewhere beyond Europe. He carried stone pillars, padrões, to mark landfalls, and six Africans kidnapped by Cão and taught Portuguese, whom he meant to leave along the coast. On 8 December 1487 he reached modern Walvis Bay. The ships then turned southwest, away from land; historians debate whether a storm drove them or they sought better winds. After 30 days at sea, on 4 February 1488, they reached the southern cape of Africa at what became Mossel Bay.

They continued east until 12 March 1488, when they anchored at Kwaaihoek. The crew were restless and the ships battered, and the officers unanimously urged a return, which Dias accepted. In May 1488 he first saw the Cape of Good Hope; tradition says he named it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it. He reached Lisbon in December 1488 after 16 months. Almost all maritime records were destroyed in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, and much comes from João de Barros, writing about sixty years later. His reception at court was muted.

Dias contributed to the design and construction of the São Gabriel and São Rafael used by Vasco da Gama, and accompanied da Gama's fleet to the Cape Verde Islands in 1497. In 1500 he was a captain on Pedro Álvares Cabral's expedition, which reached Brazil on 22 April 1500. He died on 29 May 1500 when four ships, his among them, were lost in a storm off the Cape of Good Hope. His grandson Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Luanda in 1576.
bartoszyce: Bartoszyce lies on the left shore of the Łyna River in a valley, about 90 kilometres east of Elbląg and 55 kilometres south of Kaliningrad, at an altitude of 3 metres. It is the capital of Bartoszyce County and has 20,767 inhabitants. The Teutonic Knights built their castle on the border between the Old Prussian regions of Natangia and Bartia, and it belonged to the district of Balga.

The Old Prussians besieged the castle for four years during an uprising that began in 1260, and it was destroyed in 1264. The Order rebuilt it, and after the uprisings ended it was rebuilt in stone in 1274–80. A settlement developed across the river, first documented in 1326 as Rosenthal; it received town privileges from the Grand Master Luther von Braunschweig in 1332 and was renamed Bartenstein. Poles settled there in sizeable numbers from the 14th to the 17th century and used the names Bartoszyce and Barsztyn. In 1440 the town joined the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation, and by the Peace of Toruń of 1466 it became part of Poland as a fief held by the State of the Teutonic Order.

The town became Protestant in 1525, when the Order's Prussian lands were secularised as the Duchy of Prussia, and in 1701 it passed to the Kingdom of Prussia. Prussia and the Russian Empire signed the Treaty of Bartenstein there on 26 April 1807. A railway reached it in 1868 and brought an iron foundry, a machine factory and a train-car factory. It became the district capital in 1902, and the district was renamed Landkreis Bartenstein in 1927. About half the town was destroyed in fighting between German and Soviet forces in 1945, and on 15 June 1945 the Soviets handed it to Polish authorities. The remaining German residents were evacuated or expelled and the town was repopulated with Poles.

Bartoszyce belongs to the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship, which it joined in 1999 after lying in Olsztyn Voivodeship from 1946. It is a member of Cittaslow. The future priest Jerzy Popiełuszko did his military service in a special unit there in 1966–1968, and a memorial to him stands in the town. A scene of Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace is set there.
baruch-spinoza: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam on 24 November 1632 to a marrano family that had fled Portugal for the more tolerant Dutch Republic. His ancestors, adherents of crypto-Judaism, had faced persecution during the Portuguese Inquisition. His father, Michael, was a prominent merchant whose business had a wide reach and who was elected an administrative officer of the congregation Talmud Torah in 1649. Spinoza attended the congregation's school, where pupils were taught in Spanish to read the prayerbook and the Torah in Hebrew. His name does not appear on the school's registry after the age of fourteen, and he was needed in his father's business after his brother died in 1649.

Between 1654 and 1657 he began studying Latin with Franciscus van den Enden, a former Jesuit and political radical, who likely introduced him to scholastic and modern philosophy, including Descartes. Many of his friends were freethinkers or belonged to dissenting Christian groups such as the Collegiants. In 1654, when his father died, Spinoza became public and defiant in a series of financial and legal clashes with the synagogue, and the community, anxious for its reputation, expelled him permanently in 1656. He then supported himself by grinding lenses.

Around 1660 to 1661 Spinoza moved to Rijnsburg, near Leiden, where he wrote a Short Treatise on God, Man, and His Well-Being, which he never published, and began his Ethics. His Descartes' Principles of Philosophy, a geometric exposition in the manner of Euclid, appeared in 1663. He published sparingly in his lifetime to avoid persecution.

The Tractatus Theologico-Politicus, published in 1670, questioned the divine origin of the Hebrew Bible and argued that ecclesiastical authority should have no role in a secular, democratic state; it caused an uproar across Europe. The Ethics, which he regarded as his chief work, is written in a mathematical form modelled on Euclid. It equates God with nature, a view that scholars interpret as pantheist, panentheist or atheist. Spinoza denied that God has personality, intelligence or will, which is why he was often called an atheist. His unfinished Tractatus Politicus treats forms of government.

Spinoza's health failed in 1676, and he died at The Hague on 21 February 1677, aged 44, of a lung ailment, probably tuberculosis, perhaps worsened by glass dust. His friends published his works after his death. In 1785 Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi condemned his pantheism after Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was thought to have confessed to being a Spinozist, which then meant much the same as atheist, and Moses Mendelssohn disagreed with him. Later he came to be seen as a cultural hero and the first secular Jew. According to his biographer Jonathan I. Israel, thinkers from Lessing and Goethe to Kant, Hegel and Nietzsche remained preoccupied with him throughout their lives.
bas-rhin: Bas-Rhin, meaning Lower Rhine, is a department of Alsace in the Grand Est region of France. The name refers to its lower altitude, since it lies downstream of Haut-Rhin. The Rhine forms its eastern border, and the area includes foothills of the Vosges Mountains. To the north lies the Palatinate Forest in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and to the east the state of Baden-Württemberg. Strasbourg is its prefecture and most populous commune. With Haut-Rhin it formed the traditional region of Alsace, which until 1871 also included the area now called the Territoire de Belfort. It is the last French department to keep the term Bas in its name.

Bas-Rhin is one of the original 83 departments, created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution. On 14 January 1790 the National Constituent Assembly decreed that Alsace be divided into two departments with Strasbourg and Colmar as their capitals. Its borders then changed many times. In 1793 it absorbed newly annexed territories such as the County of Sarrewerden and the County of Drulingen. In 1808 some territories east of the Rhine, including the city of Kehl, were annexed, and in 1814 and 1815 the treaties of Paris first gave France the lands north of the Lauter, including Landau, and then took them away. Troops from Baden and Saxony occupied the department from June 1815 to November 1818.

In 1871 the Treaty of Frankfurt annexed it to Germany, and it became the Bezirk Unterelsass in the Reichsland Elsaß-Lothringen. It became French again in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles and kept the cantons of Schirmeck and Saales that Germany had taken from the Vosges. The Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp operated there between 1941 and 1944. Kehl was attached to Bas-Rhin in 1944 and reassigned to West Germany in 1953. In 1982 the department joined the newly created Alsace region.

Strasbourg is the official seat of the European Parliament and of the Council of Europe. The department had 1,163,810 inhabitants in 2023 and is densely populated, with more than twice the French average density. The Rhine has always been of great historical and economic importance to the area. On 1 January 2021 the departmental councils of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin merged into the European Collectivity of Alsace. Its inhabitants are known as Bas-Rhinois.
basel-landschaft: Basel-Landschaft, also called Basel-Country, and informally Baselland or Baselbiet, is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation. It is composed of five districts, with Liestal as its capital, and is traditionally considered a half-canton, the other half being Basel-Stadt. It lies essentially south of the Rhine and north of the Jura Mountains, in the northwestern corner of Switzerland, and borders Basel-Stadt, Aargau, Solothurn and Jura, with international borders with France and Germany. The Ergolz and the Birs drain its lands. Its shape is very irregular, and its borders cut across several towns.

In Roman times the area was a centre of Roman activity. The remains of Augusta Raurica, in what is now Augst, show a city of about 20,000 people around 200 CE, and the site includes the best-preserved amphitheatre north of the Alps. With Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft formed the historic canton of Basel, which joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. Until the end of the 16th century most of its land belonged to the city of Basel, on which the countryside was economically dependent, and the castles and residences of Basel merchants dominated much of the landscape. After Napoleon's visit in 1798 the country achieved equality with the city.

After 1830 political quarrels and armed conflict broke out in the canton, partly over the rights of the rural population. They culminated in the uprising of 1833, including the Battle of the Hülftenschanz near Frenkendorf, and led to the separation of Basel-Landschaft from the city on 26 August 1833.

A movement for reunification gained momentum after 1900, when many parts of Basel-Landschaft became industrialised. The two half cantons agreed in principle to merge, but in 1969 the people of Basel-Landschaft voted down the proposal, perhaps because the economic gap between the two had closed. Since then they have signed agreements to co-operate, such as the canton's contribution to the University of Basel since 1976. In 1988 the canton wrote into its constitution the aim of recognition of the two Basels as full cantons. The population is predominantly German-speaking.
basel-stadt: Basel-Stadt, or Basel-City, is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation, composed of three municipalities, Basel, Riehen and Bettingen, with Basel as its capital. It is traditionally a half-canton, the other half being Basel-Landschaft. It is the smallest canton by area, just 37 square kilometres, and one of the northernmost and lowest, lying on both sides of the Rhine. Basel stands at the Rhine knee, where the river turns from a westerly to a northerly flow, marking the change from the High Rhine to the Upper Rhine. The territories of Switzerland, France and Germany meet in the middle of the Rhine, about 150 metres north of the Dreiländereck monument.

Together with Basel-Landschaft, Basel-Stadt was part of the Canton of Basel, which joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. After political quarrels and armed conflict, partly over the rights of the population of the agricultural areas, the canton was divided and Basel-Landschaft separated from the city on 26 August 1833. A movement for reunification gained momentum after 1900, when many parts of Basel-Landschaft became industrialised, but the people of Basel-Landschaft voted against reunion in 1969 and again in September 2014.

The present constitution of the canton dates from 1889. In 1966 Basel-Stadt became the first German-speaking canton to allow women to vote, five years before the right was extended to all Swiss women in 1971.

The chemical and pharmaceutical industries are the most significant industries in the canton, and Basel is the worldwide seat of the Bank for International Settlements. The port on the Rhine offers landlocked Switzerland its only direct connection to the sea, and the airport of Basel-Mulhouse lies 4 kilometres inside French territory. The Carnival of Basel, whose central tradition, the Morgestraich, begins at 4 a.m. and is followed by 72 hours of festivities, and the Autumn Fair, the biggest in Switzerland, are major events. The canton is known for two biscuits, the Basler Läckerli and the Basler Brunsli.
basf: BASF is an acronym for Badische Anilin- und Sodafabrik, the Baden Aniline and Soda Factory. It was founded by Friedrich Engelhorn on 6 April 1865 in Mannheim, in the state of Baden. Engelhorn had set up a gasworks and street lighting for the town council in 1861, and used the tar it produced as a by-product of coal to extract aniline for dyes. The plant was built across the Rhine at Ludwigshafen because the Mannheim council feared air pollution, and dye production moved there in 1866.

William Henry Perkin's discovery in 1857 that aniline could make intense colouring agents had begun the commercial production of synthetic dyes in England. BASF recruited the chemist Heinrich Caro as its first head of research. He developed a synthesis for the red dye alizarin and applied for a British patent on 25 June 1869, one day before Perkin applied for a virtually identical one; the two companies reached a commercial agreement. A synthetic indigo reached the market in 1897, and in 1901 about 80% of production was dyestuffs.

Other processes followed. In 1890 a unit using the contact process produced sulfuric acid at 98% concentration, the result of research by Rudolf Knietsch. After the Haber process, developed from 1908 to 1912, made it possible to synthesise ammonia, BASF acquired exclusive rights and in 1913 opened a plant at Oppau, adding fertilizers. In 1916 it opened a site at Leuna where explosives were made during the First World War. An explosion at Oppau on 21 September 1921 killed 565 people, the biggest industrial accident in German history.
