Napoleon retreated from the dominant Pratzen Heights near Austerlitz and gave every sign that his army was in poor state. He deliberately weakened his right flank to tempt the Allies to attack it, and hid his main force in dead ground. The Allies adopted the plan of the Austrian chief of staff Franz von Weyrother, a main drive against the French right. Napoleon began with some 72,000 men against about 85,000, since the corps of Marshal Davout was still far to the south.

The battle began about 8 am on 2 December 1805 with Allied attacks on the village of Telnitz, where Davout's first men arrived in time to hold the French right. At about 8:45 am Napoleon saw the weakness of the Allied centre, which had been stripped to extend against his right, and ordered Marshal Soult's corps to storm the Pratzen Heights, saying that one sharp blow would end the war.

The Allies lost about 36,000 men, 186 guns and 45 standards; the French lost around 9,000. France and Austria agreed an armistice at once, and the Treaty of Pressburg of 26 December took Austria out of the war. It confirmed Austria's loss of lands in Italy and Bavaria to France and in Germany to Napoleon's German allies, and imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs. The victory also allowed the creation of the Confederation of the Rhine.

The battle is often cited by military historians as one of Napoleon's tactical masterpieces, in the company of Hannibal's Cannae and Alexander the Great's Gaugamela. It did not establish a lasting peace, since neither Russia nor Britain was driven to settle. The battlefield has been protected by law as a landscape monument zone since 1992.
battle-of-bannockburn: The Wars of Scottish Independence began in 1296, and by 1304 Scotland had been conquered, but in 1306 Robert the Bruce seized the throne and reopened the war. Edward I died in 1307, and his son Edward II proved unable to give the same determined leadership.

In 1313 Bruce demanded that remaining supporters of the ousted John Balliol acknowledge him or lose their lands, and he demanded the surrender of the English garrison at Stirling Castle. His brother Edward Bruce besieged it in 1314, and the English agreed that it would surrender if not relieved by midsummer. Edward II summoned troops from England, Wales and Ireland and raised the largest army ever to invade Scotland.

The battle lasted two days. Bruce drew up his army at New Park in four divisions of schiltrons, dense squares of men with pikes. On 23 June 1314 Henry de Bohun, a nephew of the Earl of Hereford, charged Bruce, who killed him with an axe. Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, then routed a second English force. That night the Scottish knight Alexander Seton, serving in Edward's army, deserted and told Bruce that English morale was low.

On 24 June the Scots advanced from the wood and knelt briefly in prayer. The Earl of Gloucester, accused of cowardice by the king, led a charge and was surrounded and killed. The schiltrons pushed the English back against the Bannock Burn, where their cavalry could not manoeuvre, and Scottish horse under Sir Robert Keith dispersed the longbowmen. Edward fled, was refused entry to Stirling Castle and escaped by ship from Dunbar to Berwick.

Stirling Castle surrendered and Bruce razed it. The Earl of Hereford was among the nobles taken, and Edward exchanged them for Bruce's wife Elizabeth de Burgh, his sisters, his daughter Marjorie and Bishop Robert Wishart, held in England for eight years. By 1315 only Berwick remained outside Bruce's control. The defeat opened northern England to Scottish raids. The exact site is debated, and the National Trust for Scotland accepts the Carse of Balquhiderock as the most likely site of the second day.
battle-of-bir-hakeim: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.
battle-of-blenheim: By 1704 the War of the Spanish Succession was in its fourth year. Louis XIV of France sought to knock the Holy Roman Emperor, Leopold, out of the war by seizing Vienna and so gain a favourable peace. Maximilian II Emanuel and Marshal Ferdinand de Marsin threatened the city from Bavaria, a large army under the Duke of Vendôme in northern Italy posed a second danger, and Rákóczi's Hungarian revolt pressed from the east. The fall of Vienna would almost certainly have led to the collapse of the Grand Alliance.

The Duke of Marlborough resolved to relieve the danger. Leaving Bedburg on 19 May with about 21,000 men, he marched 400 km to the Danube in five weeks, concealing his destination, and by the time he arrived his army numbered 40,000.

After Marshal Tallard reached the Danube with 34,000 men and joined Maximilian and Marsin, Eugene and Marlborough combined their forces at Donauwörth by noon on 11 August. On 13 August the Allies advanced before dawn and reached Schwenningen, three kilometres from Blenheim, by about 06:00. The marshy Nebel stream fronted the French line. Marlborough would command 36,000 troops against Tallard's 33,000, while Eugene's 16,000 faced Maximilian and Marsin's 23,000.

Lieutenant-General John Cutts attacked the village of Blenheim, but repeated French volleys drove his men back, and Eugene's Prussians and Danes were repulsed at Lutzingen. In the centre Marlborough crossed the Nebel, and five English squadrons under Colonel Francis Palmes pushed back the elite Gens d'Armes. By 16:00 the Allied centre was planted among the French line, and large parts of the Franco-Bavarian army were penned in Blenheim and Oberglau. Marlborough then sent more infantry to storm Blenheim, where the fighting was hand to hand.

French losses were immense, over 27,000 killed, wounded and captured, among them Tallard, who was taken to England. Munich, Augsburg, Ingolstadt, Ulm and the rest of Bavaria soon fell to the Allies, and by the Treaty of Ilbersheim, signed on 7 November, Bavaria was placed under Austrian military rule.

Historians regard the battle as perhaps the most important of the war's early years, since it saved the Habsburg Empire and kept the Grand Alliance together, though it did not win the war. The war continued until 1714.
battle-of-bosworth-field: In 1471 the Yorkists defeated their rivals at the battles of Barnet and Tewkesbury, and the House of Lancaster was left with no direct claimants. Henry Tudor, whose mother Lady Margaret Beaufort was a great-granddaughter of John of Gaunt, had only a weak claim, and Edward IV regarded him as a nobody. The Tudors took refuge in Brittany under Duke Francis II. Richard III took the throne in 1483, after his twelve-year-old nephew Edward V was declared illegitimate. The boy and his younger brother soon disappeared, and their fate remains a mystery. Henry's first invasion in 1483 foundered in a storm.

Henry sailed from Harfleur with thirty ships and landed at Mill Bay, near Dale, on 7 August 1485, and marched inland through Wales. Richard learned of the landing on 11 August and called his lords to Leicester. The Yorkist army, estimated at 7,500 to 12,000 men, formed on a ridge in three groups under Richard, the Duke of Norfolk and the Earl of Northumberland. Henry's force, estimated at 5,000 to 8,000, was commanded by the experienced Earl of Oxford. Lord Stanley and Sir William Stanley stood nearby with 4,000 to 6,000 men, lending Henry only four knights at first.

Norfolk's vanguard attacked but struggled against Oxford's men, and some of Norfolk's troops fled. Northumberland took no action when signalled to help the king, so Richard gambled on a charge across the field to kill Henry. When the Stanleys saw the king's knights separated from his army, Sir William led his men to Henry's aid and Richard was surrounded and killed. According to Polydore Vergil, Lord Stanley found Richard's circlet, and Henry was proclaimed king on Crown Hill near Stoke Golding.

Henry seized the crown by right of conquest and married Elizabeth of York. Richard was the last English monarch to fall in battle. Henry hired chroniclers to present his reign as a modern age that began in 1485, and Tudor writers depicted Bosworth as a clash of good and evil, as Shakespeare does in his play Richard III. The battle is poorly recorded; contemporary accounts come from the Croyland Chronicle and from the foreigners Vergil, Jean Molinet and Diego de Valera. The site is disputed: surveys by the Battlefields Trust between 2003 and 2009 suggested a place about three kilometres south-west of Ambion Hill, where a silver-gilt boar badge was found among lead shot.
battle-of-britain: Germany had rapidly overwhelmed France and the Low Countries in the Battle of France, leaving Britain to face the threat of invasion by sea. The German high command recognised the difficulty of a seaborne attack while the Royal Navy controlled the English Channel, and its primary objective was to compel Britain to accept a negotiated peace. On 16 July 1940 Adolf Hitler ordered preparation of Operation Sea Lion, an amphibious and airborne assault to follow once the Luftwaffe had air superiority over the Channel. Britain officially dates the battle from 10 July to 31 October 1940.

The Luftwaffe first attacked coastal convoys and ports. On 1 August it was directed to achieve air superiority and incapacitate RAF Fighter Command, and twelve days later it shifted its attacks to airfields and infrastructure. The RAF's Hurricanes and Spitfires faced the Bf 109, and Fighter Command relied on the Chain Home radar and a system of reporting chains named for Hugh Dowding. About 20 per cent of the pilots were from outside Britain, among them 145 Poles, 127 New Zealanders and 112 Canadians.

On 7 September the Luftwaffe began the night attacks on London and other cities known as the Blitz. At a conference on 14 September Hitler acknowledged that it had not gained the air superiority that Sea Lion required. On 15 September the Luftwaffe made its largest bombing attack yet, which forced the whole of the RAF to defend London and the south-east and ended in a decisive British victory. In September RAF Bomber Command night raids also disrupted the German preparation of converted barges.

On 19 September Hitler ordered a reduction in work on Sea Lion. The Luftwaffe proved unable to sustain daylight raids, though its night bombing continued until 11 May 1941. By 2 November the RAF fielded 1,796 pilots, over 40 per cent more than in July. The battle was the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces and the first major defeat of Germany's military forces. Churchill summed it up with the words, Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few, and the pilots have been known as The Few ever since.
battle-of-cannae: Hannibal crossed the Pyrenees and the Alps in 218 BCE and beat the Romans at the Trebia and at Lake Trasimene. The Romans then appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus dictator, and he avoided pitched battles and cut Hannibal's supplies. The policy grew unpopular, and Rome feared its allies would defect. In 216 BCE the consuls Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus were given a newly raised army of unprecedented size, about 86,000 Roman and allied troops, and told to engage Hannibal.

In the spring Hannibal seized the supply depot at Cannae in Apulia, between the Romans and their supplies. The consuls found him on the left bank of the Aufidus. Roman law made them alternate command daily, and Varro commanded on the day of the battle. The sources, none contemporary, make him reckless, though some historians suggest he was made a scapegoat.

The Romans massed their infantry in a deeper formation than usual to break through Hannibal's centre. Hannibal advanced his centre, held by Hispanics and Celts, into a crescent and kept his African infantry on the flanks. As the Roman centre pressed forward, the Africans wheeled in on its flanks while Carthaginian cavalry closed behind, surrounding most of the army, which was slaughtered.

The figures are uncertain. Polybius gives 70,000 Roman and allied infantry killed and 10,000 captured; Livy gives a considerably lower count of the dead. Among the dead were the consul Paullus and 29 of 48 military tribunes. Only about 15,000 Romans survived, mostly from the camp garrisons.

Rome was gripped by panic. The authorities consulted the Sibylline Books, sent Quintus Fabius Pictor to the Delphic oracle and buried four people alive as a sacrifice. They lowered the draft age and enlisted criminals, debtors and slaves. Capua and other Italian cities went over to Carthage, but Rome refused Hannibal's offer to ransom prisoners and fought on until victory at Zama 14 years later. The defeat led Rome to adopt smaller, more flexible infantry units, and Cannae became the model of a battle of annihilation, studied by later commanders such as Alfred von Schlieffen.
battle-of-caporetto: Through spring and summer 1917 the Italians launched repeated offensives on the Isonzo front, the most successful being the 11th Battle of the Isonzo. Emperor Karl, expecting a breakthrough as both sides ran out of men, asked Kaiser Wilhelm II for German forces. In August 1917 Paul von Hindenburg and Arthur Arz von Straußenburg agreed to send troops from the Eastern Front, over Erich Ludendorff's opposition. In September experts led by the chemist Otto Hahn found a suitable site for a gas attack in the quiet Caporetto sector, where a good road ran west through a mountain valley to the Venetian Plain. A new 14th Army was formed under Otto von Below.

At 02:00 on 24 October, with no wind and the front misted over, 894 tubes dug into a reverse slope fired gas canisters into the Italian trenches near Bovec. The defenders fled, but 500 to 600 were killed. At 06:41 some 2,200 guns opened fire, and at 08:00 two large mines were exploded and the infantry attacked. Stormtrooper units led the assault with light machine guns, mortars, flamethrowers and grenades, while Alpine troops infiltrated the ridges. The attackers in the valley advanced almost unopposed, some for 25 kilometres on the first day, breaching the Italian Second Army.

Luigi Capello, the Second Army's commander, was bedridden with fever and asked to withdraw to the Tagliamento, but Luigi Cadorna refused. On 30 October Cadorna ordered most of the army to retreat across it, and by 10 November he had established a position on the Piave River and Monte Grappa. The attackers, with stretched supply lines and exhausted soldiers, could not follow up.

Italian losses were 13,000 killed, 30,000 wounded and 265,000 to 275,000 prisoners, most of whom surrendered willingly because of low morale under Cadorna's harsh discipline. The Austro-Hungarians and Germans suffered about 70,000 casualties. The army's strength fell from 1,800,000 to 1,000,000 and Paolo Boselli's government collapsed. Cadorna was forced to resign and was replaced by Armando Diaz. The last Austro-German push was repelled in the First Battle of Monte Grappa. The name Caporetto became in Italy a word for a terrible defeat, and Ernest Hemingway described its aftermath in A Farewell to Arms.
battle-of-carrhae: Marcus Licinius Crassus, Pompeius Magnus and Julius Caesar formed the First Triumvirate. After meetings at Ravenna and Luca in 56 BCE, the alliance secured for Crassus the province of Syria, with the evident intention of going to war with Parthia. Ancient writers, particularly Plutarch, put his motive down to greed, while the historian Erich S. Gruen believes he wished to enrich the public treasury. Cicero called the war one with no justification, since Parthia had a treaty with Rome. Crassus left Rome on 14 November 55 BCE despite protests and dire omens. In Parthia, meanwhile, a war of succession had followed the killing of King Phraates III by his sons Orodes II and Mithridates IV.

According to Plutarch, Crassus raised seven legions of about 28,000 to 35,000 heavy infantry, with some 4,000 light infantry and 4,000 cavalry. King Artavasdes II of Armenia twice offered him reinforcements if he marched through Armenia, but Crassus chose the direct route through Mesopotamia. Orodes took most of the Parthian army to punish the Armenians and sent the spahbod Surena with an all-cavalry force to harass the Romans. Surena's force numbered about ten thousand including slaves and vassals, supported by a baggage train of a thousand camels.

The armies met near Carrhae on 9 June 53 BCE. Crassus formed his men in a hollow square, which protected them from being outflanked but cost them mobility. Surena's horse archers surrounded the square and shot from beyond the range of the Roman javelins, while his cataphracts charged whenever the legionaries locked their shields. Crassus sent his son Publius with 1,300 Gallic cavalry, 500 archers and eight cohorts; they were drawn away and destroyed. The Romans retreated to Carrhae, leaving 4,000 wounded to be killed. At a truce meeting the next day violence broke out and Crassus was killed.

Plutarch gives Roman losses as about 20,000 killed and 10,000 captured, with minimal Parthian casualties. The Parthians took several legionary eagles. Gaius Cassius Longinus led about 10,000 survivors back to Syria and held the province against Parthian attack. Orodes II, jealous of Surena's victory, had him executed.

Some historians see the loss of Crassus as weakening the ties that held the First Triumvirate together and so as a step towards Caesar's civil war, though others note the lapse of time between the two. In the longer run the defeat did little lasting harm to Rome: the Parthian invasion of 40 BCE was repulsed by Publius Ventidius Bassus. The modern historian Gregory Hospodor argues that blaming Crassus alone oversimplifies the defeat, which also exposed the limits of the Roman military system of the late Republic.
battle-of-chaeronea-338-bce: Philip II ended the Third Sacred War in 346 BCE and concluded the Peace of Philocrates with Athens, which made Athens a reluctant ally. The peace was never popular. The orator Demosthenes led the war party, and in 340 BCE persuaded the assembly to ally with Byzantium, which Philip was besieging. Philip took this as a declaration of war.

In 339 BCE a Fourth Sacred War against Amphissa gave him a pretext to march south, and Thebes and Athens allied against him. After months of stalemate Philip marched down the main road from Phocis into Boeotia in August 338 BCE.

Diodorus Siculus gives the Macedonian army as roughly 30,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry. Philip took the right wing and placed his 18-year-old son Alexander on the left, with experienced generals. The allies, mostly Athenians and Thebans, held a line about 2.5 miles long between Mount Thurion and the Kephisos River, the Athenians on the left and the Thebans on the right. Modern opinion holds the armies about equal in size.

Diodorus says the battle was hotly contested for a long time until Alexander broke the allied line and put the right wing to flight while Philip routed the left. Polyaenus, of varying reliability, suggests Philip drew the Athenians forward by withdrawing. Plutarch says Alexander was first to break the Sacred Band of Thebes. Diodorus reports over 1,000 Athenians dead and 2,000 captured. Excavations beneath the Lion of Chaeronea found 254 bodies, generally accepted as the Sacred Band's grave.

The Athenian orator Lycurgus said that with the dead of Chaeronea the freedom of the Greeks was also buried. Philip treated Thebes severely, with a Macedonian garrison and a ransom for its prisoners, but treated Athens leniently, probably wanting its navy against Persia. In 337 BCE a congress he organised formed the League of Corinth, joined by every state except Sparta, and voted him strategos for a war on Persia. Philip was assassinated in 336 BCE, and Alexander conducted the campaigns from 334 to 323 BCE.
battle-of-chaldiran: After his struggle against his brothers for the Ottoman throne, Sultan Selim I turned to the Qizilbash, a Twelver Shi'i warrior-dervish group that had sided with other members of the dynasty against him. He feared they would incite the population against him in favour of their leader, the Safavid ruler Ismail I, whom his partisans believed to be descended from Muhammad and infallible. Selim obtained a jurist's opinion describing Ismail and the Qizilbash as unbelievers and heretics, and before the campaign he ordered the execution of some 40,000 Qizilbash in Anatolia. He also tried to block the import of Iranian silk.

When Selim marched east, the Khanate of Bukhara attacked the Safavids from the other side, and Ismail used a scorched earth policy against the Ottomans. Selim's army was discontented, because supply was hard, the terrain of the Armenian highlands was rough and the men were marching against fellow Muslims. At one point the janissaries fired their muskets at the sultan's tent. Learning that the Safavid army was forming at Chaldiran, Selim moved quickly to fight, partly to quiet this discontent.

The battle took place on 23 August 1514. The Ottomans had a larger army, of 60,000 to 100,000 men, and many heavy artillery pieces. The Safavid army numbered 40,000 to 80,000 and had no artillery. The Ottomans placed their guns and thousands of janissaries with gunpowder weapons behind a barrier of carts. The Safavid cavalry attacked the wings to avoid the guns at the centre, but the artillery was highly mobile and the Safavids suffered disastrous losses. Ismail was wounded and almost captured, and his wives were taken by Selim. Kurdish tribes fought on both sides, since the battle was fought in the Kurdish heartland.

The Ottomans entered the Safavid capital Tabriz on 7 September, pillaged it and left, though the Friday sermon that week was delivered in Selim's name. Selim could not press further because of the janissaries' discontent. The Ottomans annexed Eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia. Control of these regions changed hands several times, was settled in the Peace of Amasya of 1555 and was made firm by the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639. Ismail withdrew from government and never again took part in a military campaign.

The defeat undermined belief in the infallibility of the Qizilbash leader, and Kurdish chiefs shifted their allegiance from the Safavids to the Ottomans. The Safavids made firearms a part of their armies, and Ismail's son Tahmasp I used cannon in later battles. Selim next turned south against the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516 and 1517.
battle-of-covadonga: Texts written by Mozarabs in northern Hispania in the late ninth century say that the Visigoths elected a nobleman named Pelagius as their princeps in 718. He was the son of Favila, a dignitary at the court of King Egica, and he set up his headquarters at Cangas de Onís. Since the start of the Muslim invasion, refugees and fighters from the south had moved north, and some took refuge in the mountains of Asturias, where Pelagius recruited his band. Remnants of the Hispano-Gothic aristocracy supported him and, with the local leaders, formed a new aristocracy. The mountain population included Astures, Galicians, Cantabri and Basques.

Pelagius refused to pay the jizya to the Muslims and attacked small Umayyad garrisons, eventually expelling a provincial governor named Munuza. At first the revolt posed no threat to the new rulers of Hispania, who held power at Córdoba, and their forces were occupied with raids on Narbonne and Gaul. A Muslim defeat at the Battle of Toulouse on 9 July 721 probably set the stage for Covadonga.

In 722 the Umayyad commanders Alqama and Munuza were sent to Asturias, and according to legend Bishop Oppas of Seville went with them and tried without success to persuade his fellow Christians to surrender. Pelagius retreated deep into the mountains to a narrow valley that could not be attacked on a broad front.

Alqama came to Covadonga and sent an envoy to demand surrender, which Pelagius refused. Alqama then ordered his best troops into the valley. The Asturians shot arrows and stones from the slopes, and at the decisive moment Pelagius led some of his men out of a cave where they had been hiding. Christian accounts describe a horrific slaughter of the Muslims, while Umayyad accounts call it a mere skirmish. Alqama fell, and his soldiers withdrew.

Afterwards the people of the villages emerged with their weapons and killed hundreds of Alqama's retreating troops. Munuza gathered survivors and later met Pelagius and his enlarged force near the modern town of Proaza, where Pelagius won again and Munuza was killed. Pelagius soon founded the Kingdom of Asturias, which became a Christian stronghold against further Muslim expansion.

The battle is traditionally regarded as the foundational event of that kingdom and so as the starting point of the Christian Reconquista of Iberia after the Umayyad conquest of 711. It is commemorated at the shrine of Our Lady of Covadonga.
battle-of-crecy: English monarchs had held lands in France since the Norman Conquest of 1066, which made them vassals of the kings of France. On 24 May 1337 the Great Council of Philip VI in Paris agreed that Edward III's lands in France should be taken back into the king's hands because he had breached his obligations as a vassal, and the Hundred Years' War began. Eight years of costly and inconclusive fighting followed. In 1345 Henry, Earl of Derby, led a rapid campaign in Gascony, defeating two large French armies at Bergerac and Auberoche. Edward landed at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in Normandy on 12 July 1346, achieved complete strategic surprise and stormed Caen on 26 July, where more than 5,000 French soldiers and civilians were killed.

The English burned a path to within 2 miles (3 km) of Paris, then marched north hoping to meet an allied Flemish army. Edward chose a sloping hillside facing south-east at Crécy-en-Ponthieu, with Wadicourt anchoring the left flank and Crécy and the River Maye protecting the right. His men dug pits in front of their positions and set up several primitive gunpowder weapons. The English army, estimated by modern historians at between 7,000 and 15,000, was substantially smaller than the French, which Clifford Rogers puts at twice to three times its size.

Late on 26 August the French advanced, unfurling the oriflamme, the sacred banner that meant no prisoners would be taken. A rainstorm broke. Genoese crossbowmen engaged the longbowmen, who outranged them and shot more than three times as fast, and the crossbowmen fled. The French then charged uphill in a series of cavalry attacks, disordered by the fleeing crossbowmen, the mud and the pits, and broken up by archery that killed or wounded many of the unarmoured horses. By the time the charges reached the dismounted English men-at-arms they had lost much of their impetus. They continued late into the night, each ending in fierce fighting and a French retreat.

English losses were very low; a roll-call after the battle gave about forty dead, though some modern historians think around three hundred. The English heralds counted 1,542 bodies of French noble men-at-arms on the field, perhaps not including those killed the following day, and no count was made of lower-born foot soldiers. Edward then besieged Calais, which fell after eleven months and stayed in English hands until 1558. The battle was reported to the English parliament on 13 September as a sign of divine favour. Rogers calls it a total English victory, and Andrew Ayton says England's reputation as a military power was established in an evening's hard fighting. It confirmed the longbow as a dominant weapon of Western European warfare.
battle-of-culloden: Charles Edward Stuart landed in the Western Isles on 23 July 1745 to reclaim the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart. After a victory at Prestonpans in September the Jacobites controlled much of Scotland, and their invasion of England reached Derby before retreating. Recruitment brought their strength to more than 8,000, and on 17 January 1746 they repulsed a government force under Henry Hawley at the Battle of Falkirk Muir. When the Duke of Cumberland took over command, the Jacobites abandoned the siege of Stirling Castle and withdrew to Inverness.

A Royal Navy blockade left them short of money and food. When Cumberland resumed the campaign on 8 April, Charles and his advisers agreed their best option was a set-piece battle. On the night of 15 April Lord George Murray led a march to attack the government camp at Nairn, but it was slow and confused, and he turned back before reaching it, leaving the army tired and hungry.

On 16 April the Jacobites, about 5,400 strong, formed on Drummossie Moor with the Highland regiments in the first line and the River Nairn about a kilometre to their right. Cumberland's army marched across country and formed line within about 500 metres. The artillery of both sides opened fire at about 1:30 pm, though accounts differ on how long the Jacobites waited under bombardment.

When Charles ordered the advance, government gunners switched to canister shot, and the Highland regiments came on into heavy fire. In the centre and on the right the regiments swerved and became entangled. Many reached the government lines, where the brunt fell on Barrell's 4th Foot and Dejean's 37th Foot, but a second line counterattacked and surrounded them on three sides. The Jacobite first line collapsed, French regulars covered the retreat, and the fleeing Highlanders were pursued by dragoons. Jacobite losses were between 1,500 and 2,000 killed or wounded, many in the pursuit. Cumberland reported 50 dead and 259 wounded.

The army was ordered to disperse until Charles returned with French support, and by 18 April most of it had disbanded, though at least a third had missed the battle. Of 3,471 prisoners, only one in twenty was tried; about 1,200 were transported, 905 were released under the Indemnity Act 1747, 362 were exchanged with France, and 120 were executed. The defeat effectively ended Jacobitism as a significant element in British politics.

Commemoration was slight before the 1840s. A cairn was raised on the battlefield in 1881, and the Gaelic Society of Inverness began an annual ceremony in 1925. The site is now protected, with a visitor centre opened in December 2007 and the farmhouse of Leanach standing where a cottage probably served as a government field hospital.
battle-of-dien-bien-phu: By 1953 the First Indochina War had defeated a succession of French commanders, who had been unable to suppress the Viet Minh insurrection. In 1952 and 1953 the Viet Minh overran much of Laos. Navarre looked for a way to protect it, and Colonel Louis Berteil formulated the hedgehog concept: a fortified airhead, supplied by air, beside Viet Minh supply lines to Laos.

In June 1953 Major General René Cogny proposed Dien Bien Phu, which had an old airstrip built by the Japanese. Navarre chose it, and every major subordinate officer protested; Cogny warned of a new Nà Sản under worse conditions. Operation Castor began on 20 November 1953, when the French dropped or flew about 9,000 troops into the area in three days.

The French had assumed that the Viet Minh had no anti-aircraft capability. Under General Võ Nguyên Giáp the Viet Minh surrounded the camp and hauled heavy artillery, anti-aircraft guns among it, up the rear slopes of the mountains, where tunnels let them pull the guns out, fire and withdraw. Their attack began on 13 March 1954 against the outpost Béatrice. On 14 March the airstrip was put permanently out of commission, so supplies had to come by parachute. On 17 March most of the Tai troops defending Anne-Marie left or defected.

Fighting then centred on the strong points Eliane and Dominique, and from 5 April Giáp changed to entrenchment and sapping. By the end of April the outpost Isabelle was nearly out of water and ammunition. On 6 May the Viet Minh used Katyusha rockets for the first time and exploded a mine under Eliane 2. The garrison was overrun, and the survivors surrendered on 7 May.

Dien Bien Phu was the decisive battle of the First Indochina War, and the loss of the garrison cost roughly one-tenth of the French Union manpower in Indochina. The Viet Minh counted 11,721 prisoners on 8 May, of whom 4,436 were wounded. The able-bodied were force-marched over 600 km to prison camps, and hundreds died of disease on the way.

The Geneva Conference opened on 8 May, and its agreement in July partitioned Vietnam into a communist North and the State of Vietnam in the south, temporarily, with elections in 1956 that were never held. The last French forces left Vietnam in 1956. The defeat did not significantly alter the strategic situation, but it brought a profound psychological shock to France.
battle-of-falkirk-1298: After the Battle of Stirling Bridge, William Wallace led a Scottish army south from November 1297 until January 1298, raiding the countryside from Newcastle upon Tyne to Carlisle. Edward I made a truce with the French king Philip the Fair in October 1297 and returned to England on 14 March 1298. He moved the centre of government to York, where it stayed for six years, and declared the Scottish magnates traitors when none came to a council of war there. His army assembled at Roxburgh on 25 June and may have included about 2,000 armoured cavalry and some 12,000 paid infantry, though one estimate puts the infantry at only 8,000.

Edward was about to fall back on Edinburgh when he learned that the Scots were at Torwood, near Falkirk. On 22 July he placed his army south of the town. The Scots were chiefly spearmen drawn up in four great schiltrons, with archers between them and about 500 mounted knights at the rear. The Comyns and Robert Bruce were absent, and Andrew Moray, who had shared the victory at Stirling Bridge, had died of wounds from that battle.

The English cavalry advanced in four divisions. They routed the Scottish cavalry and overran the archers under Sir John Stewart, but the schiltrons held, and 111 English horses were killed against the spears. Edward's archers, crossbowmen and slingers then shot into the packed, poorly armoured spearmen, who could neither retreat nor attack. When the ranks were thin and disordered, the English cavalry and infantry broke the schiltrons.

Scottish leaders were not lost in great numbers, but the dead included Wallace's second-in-command Sir John de Graham, Sir John Stewart and Macduff of Fife. Wallace resigned as Guardian of Scotland shortly afterwards. Edward occupied Stirling and raided Perth, St Andrews and Ayrshire, but was back at Carlisle by 9 September, and he invaded again in the summer of 1300. The historian Stuart Reid judged that Wallace, a good partisan leader, was not suited to leading a conventional army. The exact site of the battle is uncertain, with three proposed locations. The Falkirk Roll, a list of the arms of English bannerets present, is the oldest known English occasional roll of arms.
battle-of-fort-sumter: South Carolina adopted an ordinance of secession on 20 December 1860, soon after Abraham Lincoln's victory in the presidential election, and by February 1861 six more Southern states had done the same. The seceding states seized federal property. President James Buchanan protested but took no action.

In Charleston Harbor the garrison under Major Robert Anderson held Fort Moultrie, whose defences against land attack were feeble. On 26 December 1860 Anderson secretly moved his command by small boat to Fort Sumter, a substantial fortress controlling the harbour entrance. South Carolina's governor, Francis Wilkinson Pickens, considered this a breach of faith. An attempt to resupply the fort with the unarmed ship Star of the West failed when shore batteries fired on it on 9 January 1861. Brigadier General P. G. T. Beauregard took command of Confederate forces in Charleston, and the garrison of 85 men reported only six weeks of rations left.

Lincoln, inaugurated on 4 March, faced the crisis as his first. Both he and Jefferson Davis preferred that the other side be seen as the aggressor, since each believed the side that used force first would lose support in the border states. Lincoln informed Pickens that he was sending supply ships, which brought a Confederate ultimatum for immediate evacuation, and Anderson refused.

At 4:30 am on 12 April a single mortar round fired from Fort Johnson signalled a bombardment by 43 guns and mortars around the harbour, fired in sequence under Beauregard's orders. Anderson held fire until daylight, and of his 60 guns he could safely use only the 21 on the lowest level. The fort had been designed against naval attack, and the high-arcing fire of land-based guns reached parts of it that ships' guns could not.

On 13 April the flagpole was shot down. Anderson, short of ammunition with fires burning and his men exhausted, agreed to a truce at 2 pm after enduring over 3,000 rounds, 34 hours after the first shot. No one on either side died in the fighting, although a gun explosion during the surrender ceremony on 14 April killed two US Army soldiers.

The bombardment was the first military action of the American Civil War. Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers for 90 days, and four more slave states then declared secession and joined the Confederacy; the governors of Missouri and Kentucky refused to send troops. The war lasted four years, effectively ending in April 1865 with Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House.

Charleston Harbor stayed in Confederate hands almost throughout, and the Confederates evacuated Fort Sumter and Charleston in February 1865. On 14 April 1865 Anderson returned to the ruined fort to raise the flag he had lowered.
battle-of-france: France and Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the German invasion of Poland. The French army began the limited Saar Offensive but by mid-October had withdrawn to its start line, and a period of inaction known as the Phoney War followed. In the 1930s the French had built the Maginot Line along the border with Germany, intended to divert a German invasion into Belgium, where the best French divisions would meet it. The hills and woods of the Ardennes were thought to cover the area to the north of the line.

The German plan, Fall Gelb, was reshaped on the advice of Manstein and Heinz Guderian, who proposed concentrating most of the armour at Sedan. The invasion began on 10 May 1940 with attacks on Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and the French sent their best forces north into Belgium. German armour advanced through the Ardennes, crossed the Meuse and raced down the Somme valley, cutting off the units that had gone into Belgium. British, French and Belgian forces were pushed back to the sea, and the British and French navies evacuated much of the British Expeditionary Force and the French and Belgian armies from Dunkirk in Operation Dynamo.

The Germans began Fall Rot on 5 June against the Somme and Aisne, where the French resisted strongly but were beaten by German air superiority and armoured mobility. Italy declared war on 10 June. Paris was declared an open city and occupied by German forces on 14 June. Paul Reynaud resigned as Prime Minister on 16 June and was succeeded by Philippe Pétain, who asked for an armistice.

The armistice was signed at Compiègne on 22 June 1940, the site Hitler chose because the 1918 Armistice had been signed there. France was divided into a German occupation zone in the north and west and a zone libre in the south. Pétain's Vichy government replaced the Third Republic, and De Gaulle refused to accept its legitimacy; his Appeal of 18 June was the beginning of Free France. German losses are commonly put at 27,074 killed, 111,034 wounded and 18,384 missing, little more than a third of those at Verdun in the First World War.
battle-of-gaugamela: Darius III had lost the Battle of Issus to Alexander in November 333 BCE, and his wife, mother and two daughters were captured. Alexander then took the Levant after the Siege of Tyre and Egypt, whose satrap Mazaces surrendered peacefully. Ancient historians report that Darius tried diplomacy three times, finally offering land west of the Euphrates, joint rule, a daughter in marriage and 30,000 talents of silver. The accounts differ in detail. Diodorus Siculus has Parmenion say he would accept, and Alexander reply that so would he, if he were Parmenion. Alexander refused, insisting there could be only one king of Asia.

In the summer of 331 BCE Alexander crossed the Euphrates and followed a northern route, easier for foraging and cooler. He crossed the Tigris with great difficulty, and captured scouts told him that Darius waited at Gaugamela, where the ground was being levelled. Calculations put the battle on 1 October 331 BCE.

Modern scholars reject the very high ancient figures for Darius's army and accept Arrian's for Alexander's: 7,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry. Darius cleared the ground for scythed chariots and placed himself at the centre with his best infantry, with Bessus commanding the left flank and Mazaeus the right. Alexander took the right wing himself with the Companion cavalry and left Parmenion to hold the left.

Alexander led the Companions toward the right, drawing the Persian cavalry to the flanks and forcing Darius to attack. A long cavalry battle followed, in which the outnumbered Macedonians held on by careful use of reserves. The scythed chariots were intercepted by javelin-throwers, and those that got through were let pass between gaps in the ranks. Alexander then formed a wedge and struck the weakened centre, and Arrian says Darius was the first to turn and flee.

Alexander went first to help Parmenion, whose wing was encircled, and the fiercest fighting of the day followed against the Persian right. Babylon was surrendered by Bagophanes, and 4,000 talents and the war elephants were captured. Darius escaped east with a small force, but Bessus murdered him. Alexander gave him a full burial at Persepolis and executed Bessus the next year. The Achaemenid Empire is traditionally considered to have ended with Darius's death. The site of the battlefield is uncertain, and the most commonly accepted location is Karamlesh in the Nineveh Plains.
battle-of-gettysburg: After the Confederate victory at the Battle of Chancellorsville, General Robert E. Lee decided on a second invasion of the North. It would upset the Union's plans for the summer, might reduce the pressure on the besieged Confederate garrison at Vicksburg, and would let his army live off Northern farms while Virginia rested. His army of about 72,000 men could also threaten Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington and might strengthen the growing peace movement in the North. Lee began to move north from Fredericksburg on 3 June, and on 28 June President Abraham Lincoln replaced Major General Joseph Hooker with Major General George Meade as commander of the Army of the Potomac.

On 1 July the armies met northwest of Gettysburg. Brigadier General John Buford's Union cavalry delayed the Confederates until infantry arrived, but two large Confederate corps broke the hastily formed Union lines, which fell back to the hills south of the town. On 2 July the Union line stood in a fishhook shape. Lee attacked the Union left, with fierce fighting at Little Round Top, the Wheatfield, Devil's Den and the Peach Orchard, and assaulted Culp's Hill and Cemetery Hill on the right, but the Union held its lines.

On 3 July around 1 p.m. 150 to 170 Confederate guns opened what was probably the largest bombardment of the war, which did little to the Union position. About 3 p.m. between 10,500 and 12,500 Confederate soldiers advanced three-quarters of a mile towards Cemetery Ridge in the assault known as Pickett's Charge. Union artillery and rifle fire devastated them, and the few who briefly reached the ridge were driven back. On 4 July Lee began his retreat.

Union casualties were 23,055, of whom 3,155 were killed, and the Confederates lost 23,231 by one recent count, though many authors give as many as 28,000. Nearly a third of Lee's general officers were killed, wounded or captured. On 4 July the Vicksburg garrison surrendered to Major General Ulysses S. Grant, and news of Gettysburg ended lingering hopes of European recognition of the Confederacy.

Historians often call Gettysburg the turning point of the war, usually together with Vicksburg, since Lee conducted no more strategic offensives afterwards, though it was not seen as decisive at the time and the war went on for almost two years. On 19 November 1863 Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, now Gettysburg National Cemetery, in his Gettysburg Address of 271 words.
battle-of-grunwald: In 1230 the Teutonic Order, a crusading military order, moved to Chełmno Land and launched the Prussian Crusade, conquering and converting the pagan Prussians by the 1280s. It then turned on the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania and for about 100 years raided its lands, particularly Samogitia, which separated the order's lands in Prussia from its branch in Livonia, but gained very little territory. In May 1409 an uprising began in Teutonic-held Samogitia, which Lithuania and Poland supported. Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen declared war on both on 6 August 1409.

The Polish and Lithuanian troops gathered at Czerwińsk and crossed the Vistula over a pontoon bridge between 24 and 30 June 1410. They then marched towards Marienburg (Malbork), the capital of Prussia, and crossed the Prussian border on 9 July. No contemporary source gives reliable troop counts; the highest estimates, 39,000 Polish–Lithuanian and 27,000 Teutonic men, are often cited as commonly accepted. The Teutonic army was outnumbered but had advantages in discipline, training and equipment.

On 15 July the armies met between the villages of Grünfelde, Tannenberg and Ludwigsdorf. Vytautas attacked the Teutonic left flank, and after more than an hour the Lithuanian light cavalry retreated. Heavy fighting between Poles and Teutons followed, and Jungingen led 16 banners to the Polish right flank. The Lithuanians returned and struck from the rear, Jungingen was killed, and the leaderless Teutonic forces retreated to their camp, where the defence was broken. The battle lasted about ten hours.

The victors delayed three days on the battlefield and reached Marienburg only on 26 July, which gave Heinrich von Plauen time to organise its defence. Many Teutonic fortresses surrendered, but the siege of Marienburg failed, and the Peace of Thorn of 1411 cost the order minimal territory. The order never recovered its former power, and the burden of war reparations caused internal conflicts and an economic downturn in its lands.

The battle shifted the balance of power in Central and Eastern Europe towards the Polish–Lithuanian union. It is regarded as one of the most important victories in the history of Poland and Lithuania and is also commemorated in Ukraine and Belarus. In 1914 Germany named a victory over Russia the Battle of Tannenberg and framed it as revenge for 1410.
battle-of-hastings: King Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066, leaving several claimants to the throne. Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, was elected king by the Witenagemot and crowned by Ealdred, the Archbishop of York. Duke William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to agree, and the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also made a claim.

Hardrada and Harold's exiled brother Tostig Godwinson defeated an English army at the Battle of Fulford on 20 September 1066, and Harold defeated them at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Three days later William landed at Pevensey. Harold marched about 200 miles south in roughly a week and camped on Caldbec Hill on the night of 13 October.

The armies met on Saturday 14 October 1066 about 7 miles north of Hastings, near the present town of Battle. The fighting began at 9 am and lasted until dusk. The numbers are unknown; most modern historians argue for 7,000 to 8,000 English troops. The English were almost entirely infantry, in a shield wall at the top of a steep slope, with few archers. About half of William's army was infantry, and the rest was split between cavalry and archers.

Norman arrows shot uphill had little effect, and attacks by infantry and then cavalry failed to break the shield wall. A retreat began on William's left, and a rumour spread that he was dead; he rode through his men showing his face and led a counter-attack. The Normans then used the tactic of feigned flight. Accounts of Harold's death conflict, and the traditional arrow in the eye is first mentioned in the 1080s. He appears to have died late in the battle, and most of his army then retreated.

Some historians estimate that 2,000 invaders died, along with about twice that number of Englishmen. Harold's body was identified the day after the battle. William was crowned king on Christmas Day 1066. Rebellions and resistance continued, but Hastings effectively marked the culmination of his conquest of England. William founded a monastery on the site, with the high altar of the abbey church said to mark the spot where Harold died.
battle-of-hattin: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was divided. Guy of Lusignan became king in 1186 in right of his wife Sibylla, and his court faction, which included Raynald of Châtillon, Gerard of Ridefort and the Knights Templar, was opposed by a nobles' faction led by Raymond III of Tripoli. Saladin, who had become vizier of Egypt in 1169, had taken Damascus in 1174 and Aleppo in 1183 and controlled the southern and eastern flanks of the crusader states. In 1187 Raynald raided a Muslim pilgrim caravan while a truce was in force. Saladin's son al-Afdal and the emir Gökböri then raided around Acre, and in May 1187 they heavily defeated the Templars at the Battle of Cresson.

Saladin assembled about 40,000 men and crossed the Jordan on 30 June. On 2 July he stormed Tiberias, where Raymond's wife Eschiva of Bures held out in the citadel, hoping to draw the Crusader army away from its well-watered camp at La Saphorie. Raymond advised against marching, but Gerard and Raynald accused him of cowardice, and Guy resolved to advance.

On 3 July the Crusaders marched under constant attack by mounted archers and found the springs inadequate. They were forced to camp on a dry plateau near Meskenah, surrounded overnight, while Muslim troops set fire to dry grass. On 4 July, blinded by smoke and tormented by thirst, they were blocked from the water. Raymond broke through to the lake with two charges and escaped to Tyre. Most of the infantry fled onto the Horns of Hattin. The knights made three charges on Saladin's position and were broken when Guy's tent fell.

Guy, Raynald and other barons were captured. Saladin had Raynald killed for breaking the truce, assuring Guy that kings do not kill kings. About 200 captive Templar and Hospitaller Knights were beheaded, except the Grand Master of the Temple, and the captured turcopoles were executed. Other prisoners were sold into slavery, while the high-ranking barons were treated well; Guy was released in 1188.

Having sent most of their men to the field, the Crusaders had little left to defend their castles. Fifty-two towns and fortifications fell, among them Acre, Nablus, Jaffa and Beirut, and Queen Sibylla, Patriarch Heraclius and Balian negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem on 2 October. Tyre held, saved by Conrad of Montferrat. The defeat led Pope Gregory VIII to call a new crusade, and the Third Crusade began in 1189. Crusader military power in Outremer finally collapsed at La Forbie in 1244.
battle-of-issus: Alexander the Great crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and defeated the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the Battle of the Granicus. He then occupied most of Asia Minor and took the coastal settlements, in order to negate the power of the superior Persian fleet. While he was at Tarsus he heard that Darius III was massing a great army at Babylon. Alexander sent Parmenion ahead to occupy the coast around Issus. Darius took a northern route and captured Issus without opposition, cutting off the hands of the sick and wounded Alexander had left there. In doing so he put his army behind Alexander's and cut his supply lines.

The two armies met on either side of a small river, the Pinarus, on a coastal plain only 2.6 kilometres wide between the sea and the mountains, where Darius could not use his superior numbers. Ancient writers gave Persian totals from 250,000 to 600,000, but most modern historians estimate no more than 100,000. Alexander's army may not have exceeded 40,000. The fighting is dated to 5 November 333 BCE.

The Persian cavalry charged first against Parmenion. In the centre the Macedonian phalanx suffered severely crossing the river against the Greek mercenaries. Then Alexander's hypaspists broke through the Persian line, and Alexander led the Companions in a direct assault on Darius and his bodyguard, who fled. Alexander then turned on the rear of the Greek mercenaries, who also gave way. The Persians, seeing their king gone, fled in rout, and the cavalry pursued them while the light lasted.

The battle was a decisive victory for Alexander and marked the beginning of the end of Persian power. It was the first time the Persian army had been defeated with the king present. The Macedonians captured Darius's wife, his daughters and his mother, who had accompanied the campaign. Alexander, who later married the younger daughter Stateira, treated the women with great respect. The Spartan king Agis III later recruited 8,000 of the Greek mercenary survivors, and in 331 BCE he defeated a Macedonian general but was finally beaten at the Battle of Megalopolis.
battle-of-iwo-jima: After the American capture of the Marshall Islands in early 1944, Japanese commanders expected a drive toward the Marianas and set up an inner line of defences running north to Japan through the Volcano Islands. The American invasion, called Operation Detachment, aimed to capture Iwo Jima and its two airfields. In June 1944 Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi took command of the defence. He knew his garrison could not win, but hoped to inflict such casualties that the Americans would reconsider invading Japan.

The Japanese positions were heavily fortified, with bunkers, hidden artillery and 18 kilometres of tunnels. Major General Harry Schmidt, commanding the Marine landing force, asked for a ten-day bombardment, but Rear Admiral William H. P. Blandy insisted on three days, a decision the Marines resented.

The landings began on 19 February 1945. After about an hour, once men and equipment crowded the beach, the Japanese opened fire with machine guns, mortars and heavy artillery. Loose volcanic ash stopped the amphibious tractors, and the Marines had to go forward on foot. The 28th Marines crossed the island at its narrowest, about 800 metres, and isolated Mount Suribachi. Kuribayashi had forbidden banzai charges as a waste of resources, and the Japanese fought from their fortifications.

On 23 February six Marines raised a flag on Suribachi, in the second flag-raising there that day, and Joe Rosenthal's photograph of it won a Pulitzer Prize. The north was harder: rocky terrain favoured the defenders, and the Motoyama Plateau became what the Marines called the meatgrinder. Flamethrowers were used to clear pillboxes and caves.

Of some 21,000 Japanese on the island, only 216 were taken prisoner, and 3,000 or more kept fighting in the caves until they were hunted down. The 36-day assault cost more than 26,000 American casualties, including 6,800 dead. It was the only Marine battle in which American casualties exceeded Japanese. Two Japanese soldiers held out until January 1949. The value of the island remains disputed: William V. Pratt, a retired Chief of Naval Operations, called it useless to the Army and the Navy, though its airfield served escort fighters and emergency landings of B-29s. Lessons from it guided the Battle of Okinawa.
battle-of-jena-auerstedt: Napoleon began his campaign against the Fourth Coalition by thrusting a force of 180,000 through the Franconian Forest. The Prussian army awaited him with about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons. Its command was bloated and inefficient: the post of chief of staff was held by three officers, there was no courier system, and five competing plans of battle were debated until the initiative passed to the French. Prussian doctrine had barely changed in over fifty years, and the Prussian musket of 1806, the 1754 model, was called the worst in Europe by one authority. The French army, by contrast, had been reorganised into the corps system.

At Jena on 14 October 1806 Napoleon's troops met the force of Prince Hohenlohe, who remained disoriented about the enemy's strength throughout. Marshal Michel Ney attacked without orders and was nearly cut off, but Napoleon held the centre with the Imperial Guard until he was relieved. Around 1 p.m. Napoleon ordered his flanks forward and broke the Prussian line. The Prussians lost 10,000 killed or wounded, 15,000 prisoners and 150 guns.

Further north, at Auerstedt, Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout's III Corps ran into the Prussian main force of 64,000, which included King Frederick William III and the Duke of Brunswick. Outnumbered more than two to one, Davout held Hassenhausen, and the Duke of Brunswick was carried from the field mortally wounded shortly before 10 a.m. Davout counter-attacked at 11 a.m., and by noon the Prussian centre was broken and the King ordered a withdrawal. Davout lost 7,052 men killed or wounded, against 13,000 Prussian casualties. Marshal Bernadotte, within earshot, took no part, because he kept to the last orders he had received.

Napoleon at first doubted that one corps had beaten the Prussian main body, and he made Davout Duke of Auerstedt. Murat's cavalry pursued the beaten army, and the Capitulation of Erfurt on 16 October gave up a large body of troops with hardly a shot fired. Davout entered Berlin on 25 October, and Blücher surrendered at Lübeck on 7 November after the city was stormed.

The defeat showed the need for reform in a Prussian state and army that was still largely feudal. Gerhard von Scharnhorst, August Neidhardt von Gneisenau and Carl von Clausewitz, all of whom served in the battle, were among the later reformers. Their work, with civil reforms in the following years, began Prussia's transformation into a modern state, and the memory of Prussia as a French vassal became a part of German nationalism. Napoleon named a bridge in Paris after the battle, and a Metro station there bears the same name.
battle-of-jutland: The German High Seas Fleet had 16 dreadnought-type battleships against the Royal Navy's 28 and stood little chance of a head-on clash, so the Germans planned to lure out and destroy parts of the British fleet. In January 1916 Vice-Admiral Reinhard Scheer took command. His plan was to use Vice-Admiral Franz Hipper's five battlecruisers to draw Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty's battlecruisers into the path of the main fleet, with submarines across the likely British routes. The British, however, held a copy of the German codebook, taken in 1914 from the cruiser SMS Magdeburg, and usually knew of German activities. Admiral Sir John Jellicoe sailed with the Grand Fleet on 30 May 1916 to meet Beatty.

On the afternoon of 31 May Beatty met Hipper earlier than the Germans expected, and in the exchange he lost two battlecruisers. When at 16:40 he sighted the German battleships, he turned back north, drawing the Germans towards Jellicoe. At 18:30 the main fleets engaged for the first time, with Jellicoe crossing the T of Scheer's line. Scheer, taken by surprise and hampered by poor visibility, ordered a turn away at 18:33. Jellicoe crossed his line again at 19:15, and the leading German battleships were badly damaged.

At 21:00 Jellicoe, aware of the fleet's weakness in night fighting, chose to avoid a major engagement until dawn and moved south to block Scheer's escape. Scheer instead crossed Jellicoe's wake and escaped by Horns Reef, and most of the British light forces failed to report their night encounters with the Germans. Fourteen British and eleven German ships were sunk.

Both sides claimed victory, and historians have not agreed on who won, or whether anyone did. The British lost more ships and far more sailors, but the German fleet had not broken the blockade. By the end of 1916 the German navy accepted that its surface ships had been contained and turned to unrestricted submarine warfare, which together with the Zimmermann Telegram led to the United States declaring war in April 1917.

Jellicoe was criticised for caution in letting Scheer escape, became First Sea Lord, and was replaced as commander of the Grand Fleet by Beatty. His supporters blamed Beatty for the failure to achieve a complete victory. The Admiralty's own review found that British armour-piercing shells often exploded outside German armour instead of penetrating it.
battle-of-kadesh: After expelling the Hyksos around 1550 BCE, the rulers of the Egyptian New Kingdom reclaimed their borders and fought as far north as the Orontes, but Egyptian influence in Syria declined in the late Eighteenth Dynasty, as the Amarna letters show. In the Nineteenth Dynasty Seti I set out to restore the empire. He reoccupied abandoned posts, made an informal peace with the Hittites and captured Kadesh and Amurru, with his son Ramesses II campaigning beside him. In his fourth year Ramesses marched into Syria, and in the spring of his fifth year, in May 1274 BCE, he set out from his capital Pi-Ramesses. The Hittite king Muwatalli II gave the recovery of Amurru as his reason for marching south.

Ramesses led four divisions, named Amun, Re, Set and Ptah, together with Sherden troops and a contingent called the Ne'arin. Muwatalli had gathered allies, and Ramesses recorded nineteen of them. Two captured nomads, who were Hittite spies, told Ramesses that the Hittite army was far off at Aleppo, and he hurried towards Kadesh with the Amun division while the others were strung out behind him. Hittite chariots then crossed the river and struck the Re division in the open, scattering it, and went on to attack the Egyptian camp.

Ramesses, by his own account abandoned and surrounded, rallied his bodyguard and the survivors and led several charges. The Hittites stopped to plunder the camp and were driven back towards the Orontes. Muwatalli sent another thousand chariots, but the Ne'arin arrived suddenly and the Ptah division threatened the Hittite rear. After six unsuccessful charges the Hittites were pinned against the river, and many drowned trying to swim it. They kept Kadesh itself.

Unable to besiege the walled city, Ramesses went south and then back to Egypt, proclaiming victory. Hittite records tell a different story, and modern historians regard the battle as a draw. Muwatalli went on to capture the Egyptian province of Upi. Ramesses took Dapur and Tunip in his eighth and ninth years, but they returned to Hittite control within a year. A peace treaty with Hattusili III was signed in the twenty-first year of Ramesses's reign, about 1258 BCE. It was inscribed on a silver tablet; a clay copy was found at Hattusa and an Egyptian version survives on papyrus.

More texts and wall reliefs record this battle than any other in the Ancient Near East, almost all from the Egyptian side. The main sources are the Poem and the Bulletin, repeated in temples at Abydos, Luxor, Karnak, Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, and the bombastic nature of Ramesses's version is recognised.
battle-of-karbala: After the assassination of the third caliph Uthman ibn Affan in 656, Ali ibn Abi Talib was proclaimed caliph, but Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, denounced his legitimacy. After Ali was assassinated in 661, his son Hasan handed power to Mu'awiya by treaty, on condition that Mu'awiya rule justly and let his successor be chosen by consultation. After Hasan's death in 670 his brother Husayn became head of the Banu Hashim clan. Before his death in 680, Mu'awiya named his son Yazid successor, making the caliphate hereditary.

Husayn declined to pledge allegiance to Yazid and went to Mecca. There the people of Kufa sent him many letters inviting him to overthrow Umayyad rule, and his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil reported favourably on their support. Husayn set out for the city on 9 September 680 with about fifty men and his family.

On the way Husayn learned that Muslim ibn Aqil had been executed in Kufa, and told his followers they could leave. Most who had joined him on the road did, and his companions from Mecca stayed. A force of 1,000 sent by the caliph intercepted his caravan, and he camped at Karbala on 2 October, where a further 4,000 Umayyad troops arrived. The governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad refused safe passage unless Husayn submitted to his authority, which Husayn rejected.

On 10 October 680 Husayn addressed his opponents, reminding them that he was Muhammad's grandson. Al-Hurr ibn Yazid al-Tamimi went over to his side. Husayn was struck by an arrow and then surrounded and killed. Seventy or seventy-two died on his side, and the surviving women and children were taken to Kufa and then Damascus.

Kufan supporters felt guilty at having abandoned Husayn and formed the Tawwabin movement, with the slogan Revenge for Husayn, which was crushed in January 685. Mukhtar al-Thaqafi then ruled much of Iraq for eighteen months, killing several of those responsible for Husayn's death. Heinz Halm writes that there was no religious aspect to Shi'ism before 680 and that the deaths at Karbala created it. Shia commemorate Husayn's martyrdom in the ten days of Muharram, ending on Ashura, and the Imam Husayn Shrine at Karbala is a holy site of Shia Islam, the destination of the Arba'in pilgrimage.
battle-of-koniggratz: At the start of the war in June the Prussian armies stood along the Prussian border: the Army of the Elbe under Karl Herwarth von Bittenfeld, the First Army under Prince Friedrich Karl, and the Second Army under Crown Prince Frederick William in Silesia. Benedek's Austrian army was gathered at Olmütz and left it reluctantly on 18 June. Moltke ordered the two armies under his command to Jitschin, a daring move meant to keep the war short.

Benedek was indecisive and did not use his larger numbers to beat the Prussian armies one by one. On 29 June Prince Friedrich Karl won at Jitschin over General Clam-Gallas. Benedek asked Emperor Franz Josef to make peace and, when this was refused, drew up his army against the Elbe between Sadová and Königgrätz.

The Prussians sighted the Austrians on the eve of 2 July. The telegraph to the Second Army was down, so two mounted officers rode 32 kilometres through the night and reached it at 4 am. The battle began at dawn on 3 July in rain and mist. The Prussian 7th Division under Fransecky advanced into the Swiepwald and held there while the Austrian artillery pinned the Prussian right. Benedek refused to order a cavalry charge that later writers argue might have won the day.

The Prussian needle gun fired much faster than the Austrian muzzle-loaders and could be used lying down. At 2:30 pm the Crown Prince arrived with nearly 100,000 men and struck the Austrian right flank, and the Army of the Elbe broke the left. The 1st Guard Division took Chlum behind the centre. Benedek ordered a general retreat at 3 pm, covered by cavalry charges that cost 2,000 men and almost as many horses, and crossed the Elbe near 6 pm.

The Prussians lost nearly 9,000 men killed, wounded or missing. The Austrians and their allies lost roughly 31,000, among them 9,291 prisoners, with 187 cannon and 51 colours. Austrian medical staff withdrew with the army, because Austria had refused to sign the First Geneva Convention, leaving the wounded on the field; the Saxon nurse Marie Simon tended them for 17 weeks and went on with Carola of Vasa to found the Albert Association, a precursor of the German Red Cross.

The last skirmish was fought at Blumenau on 22 July, as the Peace of Prague was being signed. The victory cleared the way to the Little German solution and the North German Confederation. The French public demanded revenge for Sadová, which formed part of the background to the Franco-Prussian War of 1870.
battle-of-koppam: From his accession Rajadhiraja Chola I sought to subdue the Chalukyas, who ruled parts of northern Karnataka and the south of present-day Maharashtra, and to add their lands to the Chola Empire. His first invasion, in 1047–48, had failed. On the second expedition he led a large army north and plundered the province of Rattamandalam, with his brother and heir-apparent Rajendra Chola II following in the rear.

According to the Chola sources and the Thiruvalandur copper plate, Rajadhiraja had personally led the attack on Kalyanapura, also called Kalyani, the modern Basavakalyan. Someshvara I fled when the city was attacked, returned with an army and was beaten again, and the Chola king then withdrew towards Kollapura. The copper plate says that Someshvara gathered a huge army and called out for battle as the Chola withdrew, and that the Chola turned to meet him at the place called Koppam.

The copper plate describes columns of foot soldiers, horses and elephants engaging their counterparts, with Rajadhiraja fighting from his elephant until a downpour of Chalukya arrows killed him. The Chola troops, who had been holding the upper hand, panicked and began to retreat. Rajendra II, commanding the reserve, took over the army, rallied it and inflicted heavy losses, forcing Someshvara to flee. Chola sources record that the elephants, horses and camels of the Chalukyas, a large booty and the queens of Someshvara fell into Chola hands. Rajendra is reported to have set up a victory pillar at Kolhapur before returning to his country.

The battle is known chiefly from the Chola side: an inscription dated to 1054 and Rajendra Chola II's Manimangalam record of 1055. The latter gives the victory to Rajendra and says that Ahavamalla, as it calls the Chalukya king, became afraid, incurred disgrace and ran away. The year is given as 1054, or as 1052 by the historian Sen. The site is also uncertain. The Manimangalam inscription places Koppam on the bank of the great river; the scholar Fleet identified it with Khidrapur, 30 miles south-east of Kolhapur, taking the river to be the Krishna, while other historians have put it near Maski.
battle-of-kosovo: After the death of Stefan Uroš V in December 1371 and the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa earlier that year, the Serbian Empire had broken into virtually independent principalities. Prince Lazar, ruler of Moravian Serbia, the northern part of the former empire, prepared for a campaign against the Ottomans. After Ottoman defeats at Pločnik in 1386 and Bileća in 1388, Sultan Murad I moved his troops through Kratovo and Kumanovo to Pristina, where he arrived on 14 June 1389. Lazar gathered troops near Niš and moved to Kosovo, a crossroads that let him control the routes Murad could take. Lazar's army included his own troops, a contingent under his son-in-law Vuk Branković and Bosnian forces under Vlatko Vuković sent by King Tvrtko I.

Reliable accounts are scarce, and no first-hand account from a participant exists. The army sizes are disputed; the leading estimate accepted by Western scholars is 15,000 to 20,000 for Lazar and 27,000 to 30,000 for Murad. Murad's son Bayezid commanded the right wing and his son Yakub the left. It is believed that the battle began with Ottoman archers shooting at the Serbian cavalry, which broke through the Ottoman left wing, but light Ottoman cavalry and infantry then counterattacked and the Serbian heavy armour became a disadvantage. Bayezid led a counterattack and the Ottomans routed the Serbian infantry.

Lazar was captured and Murad was killed. Murad's death is attributed to a Serbian knight named Miloš Obilić, and accounts of how he did it differ. In popular tradition Vuk Branković betrayed Lazar by fleeing, a theory first presented by Mavro Orbini in 1601 that is largely seen as unfounded. Both armies were largely destroyed, and the battle is the only time an Ottoman sultan was killed in battle.

Bayezid killed his brother Yakub on hearing of their father's death and became sole heir. The Serbs had too few men left to field large armies, while the Ottomans could draw on reserves from the east. Hungary tried to expand in northern Serbia, and the Ottomans renewed their campaign in the south in 1390 to 1391. Some Serbian principalities that were not already vassals became so in the following years, and Lazar's daughter married Bayezid. Serbia became an Ottoman province, and the capture of Smederevo on 20 June 1459 marks the end of medieval Serbian statehood.

The battle was mythologised soon afterwards, and the Kosovo Myth became central to Serbian folklore. In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić collected the epic poems of the Kosovo cycle. The battle is seen in Serbian public discourse as important to Serbian history, tradition and national identity, and Vidovdan commemorates it.
battle-of-kulikovo: After the Mongol invasion of Rus' in the 13th century the Russian principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde. Moscow grew in power and often challenged its neighbours, and in 1300 it seized Kolomna from Ryazan. After the killing of Khan Berdi Beg in 1359 the Golden Horde fell into what were called the Great Troubles, and the commander Mamai, Berdi Beg's son-in-law, took power in its western part and enthroned khans of his own. He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, so his hold on power was tenuous, and he had to fight both for supremacy and against separatism while Lithuania, Moscow and Ryazan rose as new powers.

In August 1380 Dmitry of Moscow learned that Mamai's army was approaching. Mamai's envoys demanded a tribute raised to the level of the time of Khan Jani Beg, and Dmitry agreed only to the amount of his earlier agreement. He gathered an army at Kolomna and marched south, reaching the Don on 6 September. Jogaila of Lithuania was marching to join Mamai. On the morning of 8 September, in thick fog, the Russian army crossed the Don.

The early sources give few details of the fighting. The fullest account, The Tale of the Rout of Mamai, dates from the 16th century, and it is unknown whether it rests on an earlier source. It describes six regiments, with an ambush regiment hidden in an oak grove and Dmitry exchanging his coat and helmet with a boyar so as to fight unrecognised. The main forces clashed at about 10.35 in the morning, and Russian sources agree that a long and cruel melee followed in which many died on both sides. A third of the commanders of the banners were killed. Dmitry survived, wounded and exhausted, and was found among the corpses.

Jogaila turned back on hearing of Mamai's defeat. Dmitry made Prince Oleg of Ryazan accept him as his older brother. Mamai escaped to the Genoese stronghold of Caffa in Crimea and raised a new army, but without a legitimate khan his nobles went over to his rival Tokhtamysh, who gained full power and ended the twenty-year split of the Golden Horde. Mamai fled to Caffa again and was killed.

The victory did not end Mongol domination, but it is traditionally regarded as the turning point at which Mongol influence began to fade and Moscow's power to rise. Only five primary sources survive, none from the Tatar side, yet the battle produced a larger body of medieval Rus' literature than any other event, the Kulikovo cycle, which includes the epic Zadonshchina.
battle-of-kursk: After Stalingrad the Red Army moved to a general offensive in the south, and by February 1943 the southern sector of the German front was in strategic crisis. Kursk was retaken by the Soviets on 8 February. Short of infantry and artillery, the Germans would have to rely chiefly on their panzer divisions for any offensive in 1943. On 10 March Manstein presented a plan to pinch off the Kursk salient. Hitler believed that a victory would reassert German strength and improve his prestige with allies he thought were considering withdrawing from the war.

The Soviets had foreknowledge of the German plans through the Lucy spy ring in Switzerland and the spy John Cairncross at Bletchley Park. Georgiy Zhukov and other officers recommended a strategic defensive before going on the offensive. The Germans delayed the attack to build up their forces, which gave the Red Army time to construct a series of deep defensive belts and a large reserve.

Operation Citadel began on 5 July 1943, with attacks from north and south on the base of the salient. In the north, Model's 9th Army attacked the Central Front, and the fighting around Ponyri and Olkhovatka became a battle of attrition that troops called a mini-Stalingrad. In the south, Hoth's 4th Panzer Army advanced against the Voronezh Front, and the Soviets committed their strategic reserves, including the 5th Guards Tank Army, which advanced to Prokhorovka, where a large armoured clash took place from 12 July.

The Western Allies invaded Sicily on 10 July, and on 12 July Hitler decided to stop the offensive and move forces to Italy, though Manstein objected that his forces were on the verge of breaking through.
