The same day the Soviets launched Operation Kutuzov against the Orel salient, and on 3 August they began Operation Polkovodets Rumyantsev, liberating Belgorod by 5 August.

For the first time a major German offensive was stopped before it broke through; the Germans advanced at most 8 to 12 kilometres in the north and 35 kilometres in the south. The Soviet victory was costly, but the Soviet Union's industry and manpower allowed it to replace its losses. The battle was the last strategic offensive the Germans were able to launch on the Eastern Front, and the Red Army held the strategic initiative for the rest of the war. It is the single largest battle in the history of warfare and the single deadliest armoured battle.
battle-of-lake-trasimene: Carthage and Rome had fought the First Punic War from 264 to 241 BCE. Afterwards the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca expanded Carthaginian Iberia into an autonomous territory ruled by the Barcid family, which gave Carthage silver mines, manpower and shipyards. Hannibal succeeded to its rule in 221 BCE. In 219 BCE his army besieged and sacked Saguntum, which had a treaty with Rome, and Rome declared war.

Hannibal marched from New Carthage through Gaul in May 218 BCE and crossed the Alps in October with 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and elephants. He beat the consul Publius Scipio at the Battle of Ticinus and then destroyed most of a Roman army at the Battle of the Trebia. In Rome the consuls Gnaeus Geminus and Gaius Flaminius were elected, and the Romans fielded twenty-two legions in 217 BCE, ten more than the year before.

In spring 217 BCE the Carthaginians crossed the Apennines by a difficult but unguarded route and moved into Etruria, plundering, razing villages and killing every adult man they met. Flaminius, commanding the Roman army at Arretium, set off in pursuit. The historian Adrian Goldsworthy notes that his troops, marching through devastated land, would have felt humiliated and provoked. The Romans thought the Carthaginians were fleeing and pursued so fast that they could not scout properly. On 20 June the Carthaginians marched along the north shore of Lake Trasimene, and Hannibal decided to turn and fight there.

On 21 June 217 BCE, probably in poor visibility, the Romans were attacked from the flank and rear and had no chance to form even a rudimentary line. After three hours of hard fighting some 15,000 were killed. About 6,000 at the front of the column escaped the trap but were surrounded later that day and surrendered. Nearly all of Flaminius's army of about 25,000 was killed or captured. The destruction of a whole army by an ambush is widely considered unique. Several days later the Carthaginians wiped out the cavalry of the second Roman army, which did not yet know of the disaster.

News of the defeat caused panic in Rome, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus was elected dictator. The Carthaginians marched towards southern Italy, hoping to win over Greek and Italic city-states. Impatient with the Fabian strategy of avoiding major battles, the Romans elected Lucius Paullus and Gaius Varro as consuls the next year. They fought Hannibal at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE, a third and worse disaster, and thirteen more years of war followed.
battle-of-las-navas-de-tolosa: In 1195 the Almohads defeated Alfonso VIII of Castile at the Battle of Alarcos. León and Navarre then allied with the Almohad ruler Yaqub al-Mansur and attacked Castile in 1196 to 1197, and Yaqub signed a ten-year truce with Alfonso in 1197. When it expired Alfonso resumed raiding the frontier. In 1211 Yaqub's successor, Muhammad al-Nasir, brought a large army from Morocco and captured Salvatierra Castle, stronghold of the knights of the Order of Calatrava.

Pope Innocent III called Christian knights to a crusade. Alfonso was joined in person by Peter II of Aragon and Sancho VII of Navarre, by the religious orders and by volunteers from across Europe. Alfonso IX of León stood aloof, and Afonso II of Portugal, busy with civil war, sent a contingent of town militiamen and Templars.

The army gathered at Toledo in May 1212. French and other European knights disliked Alfonso's merciful treatment of defeated Jews and Muslims at Malagón and Calatrava la Vieja, having already assaulted and murdered people in Toledo's Jewish quarter. The Christians went south in mid-June, taking castles including Calatrava and Alarcos. Led by a local shepherd, Martín Alhaja, they crossed the mountains through the Despeñaperros Pass and, on 16 July 1212, took the Almohad camp by surprise. Alhaja received the hereditary title Cabeza de Vaca.

The fight was at close quarters, with no room for archers, and the Christian knights proved superior. Knights of the Order of Santiago broke the Almohad line, and Sancho VII led his Navarrese knights through the gaps to the caliph's tent, defended by a densely packed bodyguard of black warriors. A story that they were chained together is thought to come from a mistranslation. The caliph escaped but his army was routed. His tent and standard were sent to Pope Innocent III. Christian losses were about 2,000, among them the Portuguese Templar master Gomes Ramires.

Muhammad al-Nasir withdrew to Marrakesh, shut himself in his palace and died a year later. Soon after the battle the Castilians took Baeza and Úbeda. Alfonso VIII's letter to the pope claims 60,000 Muslims killed at Úbeda, with many enslaved, and the Latin Chronicle of the Kings of Castile gives almost 100,000 captured. The defeat hastened the Almohad decline in Iberia and the Maghreb and gave new impetus to the Christian conquest. Alfonso's grandson Ferdinand III took Córdoba in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and Seville in 1248, while James I of Aragon took Valencia in 1238. By 1252 the Almohad empire was almost finished. The Emirate of Granada, under the Nasrid dynasty, survived as a vassal of Castile until 1492.
battle-of-lechfeld: In 953 a rebellion in Francia under Otto I's son Liudolf, Duke of Swabia, and his son-in-law Conrad, Duke of Lorraine, led them in 954 to call in the Hungarians, who then plundered the Rhineland. The year 955 began badly for Otto, with the archbishop of Salzburg joining the enemy and Bavarian counts taking up arms. Otto defeated the rebellion at Mühldorf and besieged Regensburg, but raiders from the Polabian principalities still troubled Saxony. In early July he received Hungarian envoys, whom the Germans suspected of assessing the outcome of the rebellion.

Soon afterwards couriers from his brother Henry I, Duke of Bavaria, told him of a Hungarian invasion. The Hungarians, said to number 8,000 to 10,000 horse archers, ravaged the land between the Lech and the Iller and besieged Augsburg, which Bishop Ulrich defended. The Magyars preferred to fight at a distance with light armour, while Otto's army, perhaps 7,000 to 9,000 strong, was divided into eight legions, among them Bavarians, Swabians, Frankish troops under Conrad, a Bohemian legion and Otto's own royal legion.

After failed assaults on the city, the Hungarians learned on 9 August that Otto's army was near. As it approached Augsburg on 10 August, a Hungarian force crossed the river and attacked the Bohemian legion on the flank, routing it and damaging the two Swabian legions. The Hungarians stopped to plunder the baggage train, and Conrad led a counterattack that shattered them, preventing the army from being encircled.

Otto then led his army against the main Hungarian force, which was defeated in close combat, though it retreated in good order. The sources are brief about how the fighting went. Otto did not pursue far, since three legions in the rear had been decimated and the heat weighed on his armoured men. He ordered the river crossings held, and on 11 and 12 August heavy rain and flooding slowed the retreating Hungarians, who were hunted down by troops operating from nearby fortifications. Conrad died in the battle, struck in the throat by an arrow.

The Hungarian leaders Bulcsú, Lél and Súr were captured and hanged, and captives were executed or sent back to their prince Taksony without ears and noses. Otto's army proclaimed him father of the fatherland and emperor, and he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962. Many came to regard him as a new Charlemagne.

The Magyars ceased their campaigns westwards after 955. The Hungarian historian Gyula Kristó calls the result a catastrophic defeat, and Paul K. Davis writes that it convinced survivors to settle down, creating the basis for the state of Hungary. The battle has also been viewed as a symbolic victory of knightly cavalry over the nomadic light cavalry of the early Middle Ages.
battle-of-legnica: The Mongols considered the Cumans their subjects, but the Cumans fled west into the Kingdom of Hungary. After Béla IV of Hungary rejected Batu Khan's ultimatum to surrender them, Subutai planned the invasion of Europe. Batu and Subutai were to attack Hungary, while a third army under Baidar, Orda Khan and Kadan struck Poland as a diversion. Baidar and Kadan sacked Sandomierz, defeated Polish armies at Tursko and Chmielnik, and burned Kraków on 24 March. They failed to take Wrocław, and when they heard that Wenceslaus I of Bohemia was two days away with an army more than twice the size of Henry's, they turned to intercept Henry before the two could unite.

Henry II the Pious of Silesia commanded Poles and Moravians, with Bavarian miners from Goldberg, conscripts from Greater Poland, an army from Opole under Mieszko II the Fat and a small contingent of Templars. Estimates of his army range from 2,000 to as many as 25,000 men, and the Mongol force was at most 25,000 horsemen, perhaps far fewer. The Mongols used feigned retreats to draw the Polish cavalry away from its infantry and then attacked from the flanks, with a smokescreen to hide their movements.

Henry's army was almost destroyed, and Henry was killed while trying to flee. The Mongols paraded his head on a spear before the town of Legnica. Estimates of European casualties range from 2,000 to 40,000. Mongol losses are unknown.

Wenceslaus I fell back to gather reinforcements on hearing of the defeat. His much larger force routed the Mongol vanguard that overtook it at Kłodzko, but since Baidar and Kadan had orders only to divert, they avoided a clash with the Bohemian army and sacked small towns. They then headed south to join Batu and Subutai, who had defeated the Hungarians at the Battle of Mohi. Later raids reached Poland in 1259–1260 and 1287, the second unsuccessfully. The battle is commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw with the inscription LEGNICA 9 IV 1241.
battle-of-leipzig: Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in disaster, and in June 1813 the Duke of Wellington routed the French at Vitoria in Spain. The allies regrouped as the Sixth Coalition, which included Prussia, Russia, Sweden, the United Kingdom and smaller German states whose rulers no longer felt loyal to the French emperor. Napoleon raised another large army, but it consisted largely of teenagers and inexperienced conscripts, and his cavalry was weak. The Coalition followed the Trachenberg Plan, defeating his marshals with weaker forces while wearing out his own corps in chases across Germany.

Two attempts to take Berlin failed, at Großbeeren and Dennewitz. Napoleon withdrew westward and gathered his army around Leipzig to protect his supply lines, while the Coalition armies converged on the city. He was outnumbered but held Leipzig and its bridges, which let him shift troops between sectors faster than the Allies could.

The fighting lasted from 16 to 19 October 1813. On the first day the French won small victories at Lindenau and Wachau and had a reverse at Möckern, and the day ended in a draw. Reinforcements then favoured the Allies: 145,000 arrived by 17 October, against 14,000 for the French. On 18 October Napoleon offered to surrender his fortresses on the Oder and Vistula in return for an armistice and a withdrawal behind the Saale. Alexander I, Francis I and Frederick William III declined.

On 19 October the Allies attacked the retreating French, while Marshal Oudinot's rearguard of 30,000 fought street by street in Leipzig. A corporal blew up the only bridge over the Elster while it was crowded with retreating troops, and the rout cost thousands of French lives and 30,000 prisoners. Prince Józef Poniatowski drowned.

Leipzig was the bloodiest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, with estimates of 80,000 to 110,000 killed, wounded or missing. It ended French power east of the Rhine and brought Baden, Saxony and Württemberg over to the Coalition. Napoleon told the Senate that a year before all Europe had marched with him and now all Europe marched against him. The Coalition invaded France in 1814, and Napoleon abdicated in May and was exiled to Elba. A 91-metre Monument to the Battle of the Nations was completed in Leipzig in 1913.
battle-of-lepanto: Pope Pius V promoted the Christian coalition to rescue the Venetian colony of Famagusta on Cyprus, which the Turks were besieging in early 1571. On 1 August the Venetians surrendered after being promised they could leave freely, but the Ottoman commander Lala Kara Mustafa Pasha broke his word, imprisoned them and had Marco Antonio Bragadin flayed alive. The Holy League included Venice, the Spanish Empire, the Papal States, Genoa and other states. Its banner reached Naples on 14 August 1571, where it was consigned to John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II of Spain, the overall commander.

The Holy League fleet had 206 galleys and six galleasses, large Venetian galleys with heavy artillery. The Ottoman admiral Ali Pasha commanded 211 war galleys and 63 galliots; the oarsmen were virtually all slaves, many of them captured Christians. The Christians had an estimated 1,815 guns against 750 Ottoman guns with insufficient ammunition, and their arquebusiers faced Ottoman composite bowmen.

On the morning of 7 October 1571 the Christian fleet formed up in four divisions on a north–south line, with the Venetian Agostino Barbarigo on the left, John of Austria in the centre and the Genoese Gianandrea Doria on the right, and met the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. John of Austria had the galley slaves freed from their chains. The battle was in essence an infantry battle on floating platforms, and the Ottoman fleet was almost completely destroyed.

It was the largest naval battle in Western history since classical antiquity, with more than 450 warships, and the last major engagement fought almost entirely between rowing vessels. The Ottomans, who had not lost a major naval battle since the fifteenth century, rebuilt quickly, with about 250 ships built within six months. The League failed to capitalise, since friction among the Christian leaders ended further operations and it regained none of the territories lost earlier. The loss of qualified crews led to a sharp decrease in Ottoman naval initiative after 1580.

The victory confirmed the de facto division of the Mediterranean between an Ottoman east and a west under the Spanish Crown and its Italian allies. The League credited the victory to the Virgin Mary, and Pius V instituted the feast of Our Lady of Victory, now kept as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary.
battle-of-leuctra: The King's Peace of 386 BCE, which ended the Corinthian War, guaranteed the autonomy of Greek cities not under Persian control. Sparta used that clause to force the Boeotian League, dominated by Thebes, to disband, and in 382 BCE the Spartan general Phoebidas seized the Theban acropolis, the Cadmea. In late 379 BCE an anti-Spartan faction of Theban exiles overthrew the pro-Spartan oligarchs, and the Boeotian War began in 378 BCE.

In 371 BCE both Sparta and Athens were ready for peace. The Theban ambassadors wished to sign for the whole Boeotian League, but the Spartans demanded that each Boeotian city sign separately, and the Thebans refused. With Thebes isolated, Sparta sent King Cleombrotus I into Boeotia, where his army met a hastily repositioned Boeotian force at Leuctra, a village in the territory of Thespiae.

Ancient sources disagree on the numbers. The modern consensus is that Cleombrotus led about 10,000 Peloponnesian infantry, including 700 Spartiates, and 1,000 cavalry, against 7,000 Boeotian infantry and 700 cavalry under Epaminondas, with Pelopidas commanding the 300-strong Sacred Band. Greek phalanxes were usually about eight ranks deep with the best troops on the right. Cleombrotus's was at most twelve deep with the Spartans on the right. Epaminondas, breaking with tradition, massed the Thebans at least fifty shields deep on the left, opposite the Spartans, and held back the other Boeotians in a shallower line.

The ancient accounts differ in detail, and Xenophon, the only contemporary, gives reasons for the Spartan defeat more than a narrative. He reports that the Spartan cavalry was beaten and fled through their own infantry just as the Thebans charged. Plutarch instead has the Spartans opening out their right wing to envelop the Thebans, and the Sacred Band charging before the line was closed. The massed Theban column drove back the Spartan right, Cleombrotus was mortally wounded, and the Spartan left gave way when it saw the right pushed back. Xenophon records almost 1,000 Lacedaemonian dead, about 400 of them Spartiates.

A truce let both armies collect their dead, and the Thebans set up a victory trophy. More than a quarter of Sparta's full citizens had been lost, and Aristotle called the battle the single blow that ended Spartan dominance. Democratic factions revived in the Peloponnese, and in the winter of 370/69 BCE a Theban-led army invaded Laconia and Messenia, freeing the helots of Messenia. Within a decade Sparta had lost the Peloponnesian League and half its territory.

The years 371 to 362 BCE are known as the Theban hegemony, which ended at the Second Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE, where Epaminondas died. Epaminondas's tactics are commonly thought to have influenced Philip II of Macedon, who lived in Thebes as a hostage between 368 and 365 BCE.
battle-of-manzikert: Byzantine strength in the east weakened under Constantine IX Monomachos, who about 1053 disbanded the Iberian Army of 50,000 men, a step that contemporaries judged catastrophic for the eastern defences. A truce with the Seljuks lasted until 1064, when Alp Arslan took Ani. Romanos IV Diogenes came to power in 1068 and campaigned against the Seljuks, retaking Hierapolis but winning no decisive victory in 1069.

While Alp Arslan besieged Aleppo, Romanos led a large army into Armenia to recover lost fortresses. It numbered around 40,000, with professional troops from the western and eastern provinces, Frankish and Norman mercenaries under Roussel de Bailleul, Turkic and Bulgarian mercenaries, Georgian and Armenian troops and part of the Varangian Guard. Andronikos Doukas, son of his rival John Doukas, commanded the rear guard. Romanos took Manzikert on 23 August 1071 but had detached part of his army to Khliat, halving his force.

Alp Arslan was nearby with a large cavalry force, and his scouts knew exactly where Romanos was. Seljuk horse archers harassed the Byzantines, some Turkic mercenaries deserted, and Romanos rejected a Seljuk peace emissary. On 26 August the Byzantines advanced against a Seljuk crescent whose wings moved to surround them. They captured Alp Arslan's camp, but the Seljuk cavalry avoided a pitched battle.

At nightfall Romanos ordered a withdrawal. The right wing misunderstood, and Doukas ignored the order to cover the retreat and marched back to camp. The Seljuks attacked the confused army, the right wing and then the left broke, and the emperor and the Varangian Guard were surrounded. Romanos was wounded and taken prisoner.

Alp Arslan treated Romanos with considerable kindness and, after about a week, agreed terms. Back in the empire Romanos was defeated three times by the Doukas family, deposed, blinded and exiled, and died of an infection from the blinding. Modern scholars think Byzantine losses in the battle were relatively low, and that the civil war that followed did more harm. By 1080 the Seljuks had gained 78,000 square kilometres of Anatolia. Byzantine writers such as Anna Komnene saw the battle as a disaster, and historians date the loss of Anatolia from it.
battle-of-marathon: Athens and Eretria had each sent a force to support the Ionian cities in their revolt against Persian rule, and the Athenians and Eretrians captured and burned Sardis before retreating with heavy losses. Darius I swore to burn down the two cities. After the Persian victory at the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE crushed the revolt, he began planning to subjugate Greece. In 490 BCE he sent a naval force under Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean, which captured Eretria and then landed at the bay of Marathon, about 27 kilometres north-east of Athens.

Under Miltiades, the Athenian general with most experience of fighting the Persians, the Athenian army marched to block the two exits from the plain. The Spartans, in the middle of a religious festival, said they could not march until the full moon, but 1,000 hoplites from Plataea joined the Athenians.

Ancient sources give the Athenians and Plataeans as about 10,000 men, a figure modern historians generally accept. Modern estimates for the Persian infantry run from 20,000 to 100,000, with a consensus of perhaps 25,000. The Athenians, probably outnumbered at least two to one, had no need to seek battle, since each day brought the Spartans closer, and the marshes and mountains kept the Persian cavalry from joining the infantry.

Miltiades ordered a general attack. The Greeks thinned their centre, perhaps so that their line was as long as the Persian line, and ran for the last stretch under the Persian arrows. The Persian centre prevailed against the thin Greek centre, but on both wings the Athenians and Plataeans routed the Persian levies and turned inwards to surround the Persian centre. The Persians broke in panic towards their ships, and some ran into the swamps, where an unknown number drowned. The Athenians captured seven ships.

Herodotus records 6,400 Persian bodies counted on the battlefield and 192 Athenian dead, among them the war archon Callimachus. The Persian fleet then sailed towards Athens, but the Athenian army marched back quickly and arrived in time to prevent a landing, and the Persians returned to Asia. The Spartan army reached Marathon the next day and agreed that the Athenians had won a great victory. Darius's son Xerxes I began the second invasion in 480 BCE.

The defeat barely touched the resources of the Persian Empire, yet it was the first Greek victory over the Persians and showed that resistance was possible. It also showed that Greeks could win without the Spartans, and it raised Greek esteem for Athens.
battle-of-marengo: Bonaparte led his Army of the Reserve over the Alps in mid-May 1800, almost before the passes were open, and took Milan on 2 June. He cut the main Austrian supply route along the south bank of the Po. He hoped the siege of Genoa, held by General André Masséna, would keep Michael von Melas occupied, but Genoa surrendered on 4 June. On 9 June Jean Lannes beat Peter Karl Ott von Bátorkéz at Montebello. Melas gathered his army at Alessandria and planned to fight his way east. Through a double agent, usually known as François Toli, he tried to make Bonaparte believe the Austrians would march north, and Bonaparte sent large forces north and south.

On 14 June about 30,000 Austrians with 100 guns faced 22,000 French with 15 guns. The Austrians had to file through a narrow bridgehead over the Bormida, and their first two assaults across the Fontanone stream near Marengo village were repelled. At 11:00 Bonaparte realised the true situation and recalled the detachment of Louis Desaix. Melas renewed the assault and broke the French centre, and by 2:30 pm the French were withdrawing.

Desaix arrived at around 5:30 pm with 6,000 men. Tradition holds that he told Bonaparte the battle was lost but there was time to win another. A surprise charge by François Étienne de Kellermann's cavalry, hidden by musketry and artillery fire, threw the pursuing Austrians back into Alessandria in disorder, with about 14,000 killed, wounded or captured. French casualties were considerably fewer but included Desaix.

Within 24 hours Melas began negotiations, the Convention of Alessandria, by which the Austrians evacuated north-western Italy west of the Ticino. The victory strengthened Bonaparte as First Consul after his coup of the previous November. Marengo was mythologised in an army bulletin and three increasingly glamorous official reports; Napoleon's bulletin set a charge by Jean-Baptiste Bessières against Kellermann's, although Melas and Murat both credited Kellermann. A department of 1802 and several French ships were named Marengo, as was Napoleon's horse, and chicken Marengo is said to have been devised by his army's chef Dunan on the evening of the battle.
battle-of-midway: Japan had quickly won its first goals in the Pacific, taking Hong Kong, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies. After the Doolittle air raid on Tokyo in April 1942, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned Operation MI, an attack on Midway Atoll meant to draw out and destroy the American Pacific Fleet, above all its carriers. The plan was complex, scattered its forces over hundreds of miles of sea, and assumed that only two American carriers were available.

The United States had an advantage in intelligence. Cryptanalysts under Commander Joseph Rochefort had partly broken the Japanese naval code JN-25b and learned of an operation against a target called AF. To confirm that AF was Midway, the base broadcast an uncoded message that its water supply had failed, and a Japanese message soon reported AF short of water. Admiral Chester Nimitz sent forces under Frank Jack Fletcher and Raymond Spruance, and the carrier Yorktown, damaged at the Coral Sea, was made battle-ready in 72 hours.

On 4 June 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Midway. Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, who had kept half his aircraft in reserve, ordered them rearmed with bombs for land targets, and then received a report of an American fleet. American carrier aircraft reached his force while his carriers were rearming and refuelling. Akagi was set ablaze by a single hit that exploded among armed and fuelled aircraft, and Kaga and Sōryū were also sunk.

The last carrier, Hiryū, counterattacked and hit Yorktown with three bombs, but that afternoon American dive bombers left her unable to operate aircraft. All four Japanese fleet carriers were sunk, as was the heavy cruiser Mikuma. Japan lost 3,057 men, including many pilots hard to replace. The United States lost Yorktown and the destroyer Hammann.

American forces withdrew once pursuit became too hazardous, and returned to Pearl Harbor after 10 June. Three American airmen captured during the battle were killed by their captors. After Midway and the Solomon Islands campaign, Japan could not replace its losses in ships and trained men, while American industrial and training capacity grew. The depth of the sea made the wrecks hard to find: Robert Ballard located Yorktown in 1998, and in 1999 an expedition found wreckage of Kaga. In 2000 the atoll was designated the Battle of Midway National Memorial.
battle-of-mohacs: After the death of King Matthias Corvinus in 1490, the Hungarian magnates secured the accession of the weak-willed Vladislaus II, who gave away most royal estates and revenues. The nobility cut its own taxes by 70 to 80 per cent, the Black Army of Matthias was dissolved and border garrisons went unpaid. A peasant rebellion under György Dózsa in 1514 was crushed by the nobles under John Zápolya, leaving the country divided. In 1521 the Ottomans took Nándorfehérvár, present-day Belgrade, the strongest Hungarian fortress on the Danube.

King Louis II married Mary of Habsburg in 1522, and the Ottomans saw the alliance as a threat. After Suleiman I came to power in 1520 they offered peace at least once, and Louis refused for reasons that are unclear. Help from Europe was scarce, since the western powers were absorbed in the Italian wars. Francis I of France, defeated at Pavia in 1525, asked Suleiman to make war on the Habsburgs, and the road lay across Hungary. An Ottoman army left Constantinople on 16 April 1526.

The Hungarian nobles were slow to answer their king's call. The army that took the field numbered around 25,000 to 30,000 men, with 85 cannons against about 300 for the Ottomans. The battle was fought on the afternoon of 29 August 1526 on a waterlogged plain near Mohács. Pressed by nobles who wanted immediate battle, the Hungarians relied on heavy cavalry to break the Ottoman line.

Archbishop Pál Tomori led a charge that at first drove back the Ottoman front line. The grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha drew his centre back into a crescent, exposing the flanks of the cavalry, and Ottoman cavalry and light infantry attacked from both wings while Janissaries and artillery fired from prepared positions. The Hungarian army was encircled, and its lines collapsed within two hours. King Louis and much of the aristocracy were killed.

Suleiman did not at first grasp the scale of his victory. During four more days on the field about 2,000 captured nobles were executed. Queen Mary fled Buda, and the Ottomans pillaged the abandoned castle and left. The nobility elected two kings, John Zápolya and the Habsburg Archduke Ferdinand, and the Ottomans occupied Buda in 1541, dividing Hungary into Habsburg, Ottoman and Transylvanian parts. Many Hungarians regard Mohács as the turning point of their history, and the saying More was lost at Mohács is still used for any great loss.
battle-of-mohi: The Mongols attacked central Europe with three armies. Two crossed Poland and defeated Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia at Legnica, a southern army attacked Transylvania, and the main army under Batu Khan and Subutai entered Hungary through the Verecke Pass. On 12 March 1241 it annihilated the army of the count palatine, Denis Tomaj. Hungary was weakened by its own politics. Kings had forbidden nobles to build private stone castles, so few stood along the Mongol routes.

Béla IV had taken back the lands his father Andrew II had given away and expelled his advisers, which angered the nobles. He also sheltered some 40,000 Cuman refugees, but the Cuman khan was murdered in a riot at Pest, and the Cumans, believing themselves betrayed, left the country, pillaging as they went.

The Mongol vanguard reached Pest on 15 March. After a week of forced marches the Hungarians reached the flooded Sajó and built a camp of wagons. A Ruthenian slave of the Mongols warned them of a night attack on the bridge, and the king's brother Coloman and Archbishop Ugrin Csák, with the Templar master, beat the Mongol vanguard there, returning to camp at about 2 am. At dawn Batu attacked the bridge with seven stone throwers, Shiban crossed at a ford to the north, and Subutai built a makeshift bridge to the south and attacked the Hungarian rear.

Confined in the camp, the Hungarians were bombarded by stones and flaming arrows. The Mongols left a gap open, and those who fled through it were almost all slaughtered. Ugrin was killed with another archbishop and three bishops, and Béla escaped, though Coloman died soon afterwards of his wounds.

A near-contemporary source reports 10,000 Hungarians killed, almost the entire army. The Mongols burnt Pest, killed most of Esztergom's population and occupied the Great Hungarian Plain, Transylvania and the northern Carpathian slopes. Nearly half of the inhabited places were destroyed, and 15 to 25 per cent of the population was lost. Béla fled to Austria, where Duke Frederick arrested the royal family and extorted a ransom and three western counties, and then to the Adriatic coast at Trogir, where he stayed until the Mongols withdrew. Among the Mongols, Batu blamed Subutai for the heavy losses, while Güyük and Büri accused Batu of incompetence, and he sent them back to Karakorum.
battle-of-mycale: After the Greek naval victory at Salamis, Xerxes I retreated to Asia with a minor portion of his army and left his general Mardonius to finish the campaign the following year. The Persian fleet was stationed at Samos to defend Ionia and prevent an Ionian revolt. Its morale was breaking, and its commanders waited anxiously for news of Mardonius's land army.

Herodotus gives 300 ships and 60,000 soldiers for the Persians, but Charles Hignett and others think both figures far too high, and estimates of the Persian army range from about 4,000 to 10,000 men. The Greek fleet is usually put at about 110 ships, with perhaps 3,300 marines.

When the Persians learned that the Greek fleet was approaching, they sailed from Samos to Mycale on the mainland, possibly because they judged a sea battle hopeless. They beached their ships behind rocks, built a palisaded camp of cut wood with stakes on the ramparts, and expected a siege.

The Greek commander Leotychides decided to attack anyway and landed the fleet's marines. The Athenians and Corinthians formed the left wing along the shore, while the Spartans and others were still crossing the hills on the right. The Persians came out and set up a shield wall. The Greek left engaged first, and the right wing broke the wall by shoving. Tigranes and Mardontes were killed. The Persians fled to their camp, the Ionian contingents defected, and the ethnic Persian troops who held out were attacked in the rear when the Greek left outflanked the camp.

With Plataea and Mycale the second Persian invasion of Greece was over. The Greek fleet sailed to the Hellespont to break down the pontoon bridges, found them already destroyed, and the Peloponnesians went home. The Athenians stayed and besieged the Persians at Sestos, which fell after a long siege and began a new phase of the war, the Greek counterattack. Chios, Lesbos and Samos joined the Hellenic alliance, and Thrace and Macedonia broke away from the Persians.

Some historians treat the fighting itself as minor. George Cawkwell called it a very minor affair whose results were major because it led to an Ionian revolt. The ancient accounts also differ on the ships: Herodotus has them burned, and Iain McDougall argues that the burned vessels were mostly Ionian and too damaged to salvage. Spoils from the campaign were displayed at Delphi and, according to Vitruvius, Persian masts and spars were used in the roof of the Odeon of Pericles at Athens.
battle-of-narva-1700: Peter the Great of Russia wanted an adequate opening to the Baltic and so sought the Swedish Baltic provinces that Russia had lost during the Time of Troubles. Sweden, by contrast, had a professional army, one of the largest and most disciplined in northern Europe. Russia, Denmark-Norway and Augustus the Strong of Poland-Lithuania allied against Sweden, but Charles XII landed at Humlebæk north of Copenhagen and forced Denmark-Norway out of the alliance in August 1700. He then took part of his army across the Baltic to Estonia.

The Russian army was poorly drilled. In spring 1700 Peter retired or reassigned most of his officers, leaving up to 70 percent of company posts vacant, and filled them with young Moscow noblemen with no command experience. In November Russian troops besieged Narva. Peter left the camp the day before the battle, and the new commander, Charles Eugène de Croÿ, had never commanded a Russian unit.

Charles XII approached Narva on 29 November 1700 and the next morning positioned his army before the Russian siege lines. The Russians, stretched over four miles between two ramparts, outnumbered the relief force three or four to one. The Swedes moved forward at 2 pm, just as a snowstorm blew into the Russian faces. Charles ignored officers who wished to wait, and the Swedes attacked in two dense columns and, within 15 minutes, had filled the ditches with fascines and broken in.

The Swedes rolled up the Russian line to north and south, shattering inexperienced regiments one by one. Panic followed, and de Croÿ hurried to surrender. The Kamperholm Bridge, the only one across the Narva River, collapsed under retreating troops. Only the Preobrazhensky and Semyonovsky regiments held, in a square behind improvised barricades of wagons.

The Russian high command lost its morale and capitulated. The Swedes captured ten generals and ten colonels, 4,050 muskets and 173 artillery pieces. Regimental rolls of January 1701 show a loss of about 25 percent of personnel. Charles kept the senior Russian commanders as prisoners, explaining that he had not received the army's treasury.

The battle was not followed by a Swedish advance into Russia, and Charles turned south against Augustus the Strong in Livonia and Poland-Lithuania. Peter took Narva in a second battle in 1704. A Russian memorial to the fallen was begun in 1900, and a Swedish one reading Svecia memor was inaugurated in 2000.
battle-of-navarino: The Greeks rose against Ottoman rule in 1821, and by 1825 neither side could win. The sultan then persuaded Muhammad Ali Pasha, the wali of Egypt, to send his Western-trained army and navy, promising the Peloponnese as a hereditary fief to Ali's eldest son Ibrahim. Ibrahim landed with 16,000 men in February 1825 and overran the western Peloponnese. By 1827 the Greek government was almost bankrupt and its forces far weaker than those of its enemies. Tsar Nicholas I, who succeeded Alexander in December 1825, was more willing to act, and Britain, France and Russia signed the Treaty of London on 6 July 1827. It called for an armistice and Greek autonomy within the Ottoman Empire, and they sent squadrons to enforce it.

The British admiral Edward Codrington was to impose the armistice and cut the flow of supplies to Greece, using force only as a last resort. The Ottomans rejected the treaty on 29 August, and the Greek government accepted the armistice on 2 September. The Ottoman and Egyptian fleet lay at anchor in Navarino Bay in a horseshoe of three lines, so that small vessels could fire through gaps in the front line. On 20 October 1827 the Allied ships entered the bay in two lines, with Codrington's flagship HMS Asia in the lead. He had a band play on deck to show peaceful intent, and the captains were to fire only if attacked. Fighting broke out, and Codrington claimed the Ottomans started it.
It was the last major naval battle fought entirely with sailing ships, though most vessels fought at anchor. The Allies won through superior firepower and gunnery and destroyed the Ottoman armada.

The sultan still had some 40,000 troops in central and southern Greece, so independence was not yet secure. Russia declared war in April 1828, and a French expeditionary force landed in the Peloponnese at the end of August. The Egyptians left in October 1828, a year after the battle. In Britain, Codrington was a hero to the public, but ministers thought he had exceeded his instructions, and King George IV called the battle an untoward event. He was relieved of his command in June 1828. Pylos holds Three Admirals' Square with a monument to Codrington, Van Heiden and Rigny, and the battle is commemorated there each year on 20 October.
battle-of-nicopolis: After the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 the Ottomans had conquered most of the Balkans and reduced the Byzantine Empire to the area around Constantinople, which they blockaded from 1394. In 1393 the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Shishman lost his temporary capital Nicopolis, and his brother Ivan Stratsimir held Vidin only as an Ottoman vassal. Hungary now formed the frontier between the two religions in Eastern Europe. In 1394 Pope Boniface IX proclaimed a new crusade, although the Western Schism had split the papacy.

Philip, Duke of Burgundy, withdrew from the planned leadership and named his 24-year-old son John, Count of Nevers, to nominal command, with the experienced Enguerrand VII, Lord of Coucy, as chief counsellor. The crusade left Dijon on 30 April 1396 and joined King Sigismund of Hungary at Buda, where the French rejected his advice to let the Ottomans make the long march to them.

The crusaders besieged Nicopolis, whose governor Doğan Bey was prepared for a long siege. They had brought no siege machines, and the steep slope and strong fortifications made an assault impossible. On the morning of 25 September 1396 Sigismund asked Nevers to postpone the advance for two hours while scouts reported on the Turkish forces. Coucy and Jean de Vienne agreed, but the Constable of France, D'Eu, declared that Sigismund wished to keep the honour for himself, and the argument ended when D'Eu decided to advance. The army was routed. Estimates of the numbers are heavily contested.

Sigismund later told the Master of the Hospitallers: "We lost the day by the pride and vanity of these French." On 26 September Bayezid had the prisoners assembled. Nevers, Coucy, D'Eu and a few other nobles were spared for ransom, those under 20 were taken as slaves, and the rest, thought to number several thousand, were killed in front of the sultan. Accounts of the number killed that day range from 300 to 3,000.

Western Europe made no further move to halt the Turkish advance in the Balkans until the 1440s. In 1402 Bayezid was defeated and captured by Timur. Nicopolis is widely regarded as the end of the Second Bulgarian Empire, and Ivan Stratsimir was captured and killed in Bursa. The Turks tightened their control of the Balkans and became a greater threat to Central Europe.
battle-of-okinawa: The battle, codenamed Operation Iceberg, followed a long campaign of island hopping. The Allies planned to use Kadena Air Base on Okinawa as a staging point for Operation Downfall, the invasion of the Japanese home islands 550 kilometres away. The United States formed the Tenth Army, combining Army and Marine divisions, with its own tactical air force. Against it stood Lieutenant General Mitsuru Ushijima's Thirty-Second Army, a mixed force of regular troops, naval infantry and conscripted local Okinawans, about 100,000 Japanese troops in all at the start.

The 77th Infantry Division captured the Kerama Islands from 26 March 1945. On 28 March, 394 civilians on Tokashiki island were forced by Japanese soldiers to kill themselves after American troops landed. The main landing took place on 1 April on the Hagushi beaches on the west coast, and the Tenth Army quickly took the Kadena and Yomitan airbases. The 6th Marine Division cleared the north, while two Army divisions turned south and met fierce resistance at fortified outposts guarding the Shuri Line. The Japanese fought from prepared cave positions, and the advance cost many lives on both sides. The land battle lasted about 81 days.

At sea, Japanese attacks came in waves. Between 1 April and 25 May seven major kamikaze attacks involved more than 1,500 planes. In April the battleship Yamato and nine other warships sailed from Japan on a suicide sortie, Operation Ten-Go; American carrier aircraft sank Yamato and five other warships before they reached Okinawa.

The Americans suffered some 48,000 casualties, more than 12,000 of them killed or missing. Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr., the commander of the Tenth Army, was killed by artillery fire four days before the campaign ended, the highest-ranking American officer killed by enemy fire in the war. Okinawa had a large civilian population, and about 40,000 of the Okinawans killed had been drafted or impressed by the Japanese army. The Cornerstone of Peace at Mabuni, erected in 1995, lists the names of all the known dead, civilian and military, Japanese and foreign.

Japan surrendered soon after, so the planned invasion of the home islands never took place. Some military historians hold that the cost of Okinawa led American planners to seek an alternative in the atomic bombings, while others point to the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and Japan's depleted resources.
battle-of-passchendaele: The Third Battle of Ypres was fought from July to November 1917 for control of the ridges south and east of Ypres in West Flanders, as part of a strategy decided by the Entente in November 1916 and May 1917. Passchendaele lies on the last ridge east of Ypres, 8 kilometres from Roulers, whose station was on the main supply route of the German 4th Army. The campaign was controversial from the start. David Lloyd George and Ferdinand Foch opposed it, and Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig did not receive the War Cabinet's approval until 25 July. The first stage was the Battle of Messines in June, after mines filled with nearly 454 tonnes of explosives were fired under the ridge.

The first Allied attack was the Battle of Pilckem Ridge on 31 July. General Hubert Gough's offensive was not planned as a breakthrough. The Germans held the Gheluvelt Plateau in August, though their casualties worsened a manpower shortage. On 25 August Haig shifted the main effort to the Second Army, whose commander Plumer planned to take the plateau in four limited steps at six-day intervals. Unusually wet weather in August and the autumn rains in October turned the ground to mud. The campaign ended in November when the Canadian Corps captured Passchendaele, and a British night attack towards Westroosebeke on 1 and 2 December failed.

Casualty figures have been published with acrimony. James Edmonds put British casualties at 244,897 and estimated German losses at 400,000, while A. J. P. Taylor, who rejected Edmonds's calculations, gave 300,000 British and 200,000 German. The British claim of 24,065 prisoners is undisputed. Lloyd George later called Passchendaele one of the worst disasters of the war, while a German General Staff publication wrote that Germany had been brought near to certain destruction by the Flanders battle. Jack Sheldon argued that it pinned the German army to Flanders and caused unsustainable casualties. The German submarine bases on the coast had not been captured. The Menin Gate Memorial commemorates Commonwealth dead of the Ypres Salient who have no known grave.
battle-of-pavia: The French had held Lombardy at the start of the Italian War of 1521 to 1526 but lost it after the Battle of Bicocca in 1522. A French invasion in late 1523 under Guillaume Gouffier, Seigneur de Bonnivet, was defeated at the Battle of the Sesia. An imperial invasion of Provence then stalled at the Siege of Marseille and withdrew when Francis I arrived at Avignon with the main French army. In mid-October 1524 Francis crossed the Alps, entered Milan and advanced on Pavia, where Antonio de Leyva held out with about 9,000 men, paying them by melting the church plate.

The French besieged the city from late October. An assault on 21 November was beaten back, and Francis decided to starve the garrison. He then divided his forces, sending the Duke of Albany south to aid Pope Clement VII, while about 5,000 Grisons Swiss left for home. In January 1525 Georg Frundsberg arrived with 15,000 fresh landsknechts, and Charles de Lannoy renewed the offensive. Short of supplies, the imperial commanders decided on 21 February to attack, Pescara arguing that battle was their only way.

On the night of 23 February the imperial engineers breached the wall of the Visconti Park at the Porta Pescarina. By 5:00 am some 3,000 arquebusiers under Alfonso d'Avalos, Marquis of Vasto, were inside and advancing on Mirabello Castle. A full infantry battle developed by 7:00 am, when Frundsberg's landsknechts met Swiss pikemen. Around 7:40 am Francis led his gendarmes in a charge that scattered Lannoy's cavalry, but it carried him away from his infantry and masked the fire of his own artillery.

By 8:00 am imperial pikemen and arquebusiers had surrounded the French cavalry in the wooded ground and killed them systematically. The Black Band of landsknechts was exterminated, and Richard de la Pole and François de Lorraine were killed. Francis's horse was killed under him and he was taken prisoner. By 9:00 am the battle was over.

Many leading French nobles died, among them Bonnivet, La Trémoille and La Palice, and Anne de Montmorency was captured. Who took Francis is uncertain: candidates include Lannoy, three Spanish soldiers, the Count of Salm and the condottiero Cesare Hercolani, and Charles V in his autobiography credited his principal captains. Francis was held at Pizzighettone and taken to Spain, and under the Treaty of Madrid he gave up his claims in Milan and Burgundy. The peace was broken in the same year, and a new war lasted from 1526 to 1529.
battle-of-pharsalus: After the war began, Caesar captured Rome, forced Pompey and his allies out of Italy and defeated Pompey's legates in Spain. In 48 BCE he crossed the Adriatic and besieged Dyrrachium but was defeated there. He then withdrew east into Thessaly, partly to relieve a legate threatened by Metellus Scipio's forces arriving from Syria, and besieged Gomphi after it resisted him. Pompey pursued, seeking to end the war on Greek soil and spare Italy invasion. His overconfident allies pressed him, accusing him of prolonging the war to extend his command.

Caesar's army, by his own account, had 22,000 legionaries in eight understrength legions, most of them veterans of the Gallic Wars, with 1,000 Gallic and Germanic cavalry. Pompey had about 45,000 Roman infantry according to Caesar, Appian and Plutarch, and between 5,000 and 7,000 cavalry, besides thousands of archers, slingers and light infantry from the east. Both armies formed in three lines, with Pompey's right and Caesar's left resting on the river Enipeus. Pompey massed his cavalry on his left under Labienus, intending it to sweep round Caesar's flank and rear. Caesar, thinning his ranks to six men deep, secretly formed a fourth line on his right.

Pompey ordered his men to wait rather than charge. Caesar's infantry advanced under Mark Antony and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus. Labienus's cavalry pushed back Caesar's, but Caesar's hidden fourth line, ordered to thrust with their pila rather than throw them, surprised the horsemen, who panicked and fled to the hills. Caesar's third line then broke Pompey's exposed left wing. Seeing his cavalry and legions give way, Pompey retreated to his camp and then fled, and the camp fell after brave resistance by seven cohorts of auxiliaries.

Caesar claimed to have lost about 200 soldiers and 30 centurions and put Pompeian losses at 60,000; Appian gives 1,200 and 6,000, and the larger figures seem exaggerated. Caesar captured Pompey's camp, burned his correspondence and announced that he would forgive all who asked for mercy. Marcus Junius Brutus sought his pardon, and Cato regrouped with supporters and went to Libya. Pompey fled to Mytilene and Cilicia, then to Egypt, where he was assassinated on arrival on the order of Ptolemy XIII; Caesar reached Alexandria on 2 October 48 BCE. The battle did not end the civil war, but it gave Caesar legitimacy, and former allies of Pompey began to align themselves with him.
battle-of-philippi: After the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BCE, Brutus and Cassius, known as the Liberators, left Italy and took control of the eastern provinces from Greece to Syria and the allied eastern kingdoms. In Rome the three main Caesarian leaders, Antony, Octavian and Lepidus, established the Second Triumvirate and crushed the Senate's opposition. They declared a civil war ostensibly to avenge Caesar, though the underlying cause was a long conflict between the Optimates and the Populares.

Lepidus stayed in Italy while Antony and Octavian moved to northern Greece with 28 legions, sending an advance force of eight legions along the Via Egnatia. The Liberators, with the Republican admiral Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus commanding 130 ships, wished to avoid a decisive battle and to use their naval superiority to cut the triumvirs' supplies from Italy. They took a fortified position about 3.5 kilometres west of Philippi, Brutus to the north of the Via Egnatia and Cassius to the south.

Each side probably had only 40,000 to 50,000 legionaries. After Antony cut a causeway through the southern marshes, Cassius built a transverse wall against him, and a general battle began on 3 October 42 BCE. Brutus's troops attacked without waiting for orders, routed Octavian's army and captured its camp, though Octavian himself was not found in his tent. To the south Antony stormed Cassius's fortifications. Unable to see what had happened on Brutus's wing, and believing the day lost, Cassius ordered his freedman Pindarus to kill him. Brutus called him the last of the Romans.

On the same day the Republican fleet destroyed a convoy of reinforcements led by Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus. Over the next three weeks Antony advanced south, forcing Brutus to extend his line. Brutus attacked on the afternoon of 23 October. After close combat his thinned centre gave way, the triumvirs turned on his flank and rear, and his army could not re-form. Brutus retreated into the hills with the equivalent of four legions and took his own life.

Antony covered Brutus's body with a purple garment, according to Plutarch. Many young aristocrats died in the battle or by suicide, among them Marcus Porcius Cato, the son of Cato the Younger, and the father of Livia. About 14,000 survivors were enrolled in the triumvirs' army, and some veterans settled at Philippi, which became the Roman colony Colonia Victrix Philippensium. Antony stayed in the East and Octavian returned to Italy to find land for the veterans. Sextus Pompey still held Sicily, but Republican resistance had been crushed.
battle-of-plassey: Siraj-ud-Daulah, who succeeded his maternal grandfather Alivardi Khan as Nawab of Bengal in 1756, ordered the British to stop extending their fortifications. He attacked British-controlled Calcutta, an episode that included the Black Hole massacre. The British sent reinforcements from Madras under Colonel Robert Clive and Admiral Charles Watson, recaptured Calcutta, and then seized the French fort at Chandannagar. The conflict took place during the Seven Years' War, and a small French contingent fought against the British. The Nawab also feared attack from the Afghans under Ahmad Shah Durrani in the north and from the Marathas in the west, so he could not commit his whole army against the British.

The British formed a conspiracy with Siraj-ud-Daulah's demoted commander-in-chief Mir Jafar, with Yar Lutuf Khan, Rai Durlabh and others. Clive promised to make Mir Jafar Nawab. He marched on Murshidabad with about 3,000 men, and the Nawab's army, about 50,000 strong with 40 cannons and 10 war elephants, took position at Plassey by 21 June 1757.

On 23 June the Nawab's artillery opened fire at 8:00, and Clive withdrew into a grove sheltered by an embankment. After a heavy rainstorm, in which the British covered their ammunition and the Nawab's army did not, Mir Madan Khan led a cavalry charge that was driven back with grapeshot. Siraj, disturbed, appealed to Mir Jafar, who sent word of it to Clive, and on the advice of Rai Durlabh the Nawab withdrew and left for Murshidabad. Clive's troops took the French position at 15:00. Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh and Yar Lutuf Khan had made no move to join the battle, which lasted about eleven hours.

On 24 June Clive greeted Mir Jafar as Nawab of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, and on 29 June he placed him on the throne at Murshidabad. The French were no longer a significant force in Bengal. By 1759 Mir Jafar resented his subordination to the British and encouraged the Dutch to send ships from Java; Clive defeated them at the Battle of Chinsura on 25 November 1759, and the British then deposed Mir Jafar and installed Mir Qasim. The British used the revenue and concessions they gained to increase their military strength, and historians judge Plassey one of the pivotal battles in the colonial control of the subcontinent.
battle-of-plataea: Xerxes I began preparing an invasion of Greece soon after his accession in 486 BCE, and a congress of city states, probably at Corinth, formed an alliance known as the Allies in 481 BCE. In August 480 BCE a small Allied army under the Spartan king Leonidas I held the pass of Thermopylae for three days before being outflanked. The Persians then occupied the evacuated city of Athens. The Allied navy won a decisive victory at Salamis, and Xerxes retreated to Sardis with a small part of his army, leaving his general Mardonius to finish the conquest the following year.

Mardonius retreated into Boeotia, hoping to draw the Greeks onto ground suited to his cavalry, and built a fortified camp on the north bank of the Asopos river. The Greek army, commanded by Pausanias, the regent of Sparta, crossed Mount Cithaeron and took positions on high ground opposite. According to Herodotus the Spartans sent 45,000 men, among them 5,000 full citizens and 35,000 helots. Estimates of the Persian army, drawn from the size of its camp, range from about 70,000 to 120,000, though modern historians differ widely.

The Greeks refused to descend to the plain, and a stalemate lasted eleven days. Persian cavalry then cut the Greek supply lines. On the thirteenth day the Greeks tried to withdraw, and their line broke up. Mardonius took this for a full retreat and ordered a pursuit. The Spartans, Tegeans and Athenians turned and fought, routed the lightly armed Persian infantry and killed Mardonius. Much of the Persian army was trapped in its camp and killed.

According to Herodotus the Battle of Mycale was fought on the same day, destroying what remained of the Persian fleet. After the two victories the second Persian invasion was over, and the Persian desire to conquer Greece gradually diminished. The sale of the loot paid for buildings such as the Athenian Treasury at Delphi.

A bronze column of intertwined snakes, the Serpent Column, was made from melted Persian armour and set up at Delphi, listing the 31 city-states that fought; most of it now stands in the Hippodrome of Constantinople. The poet Simonides of Ceos wrote an elegy and an encomium on the battle, and in Spartan tradition the victory avenged Thermopylae.
battle-of-poitiers-1356: English kings had held lands in France as vassals of the French crown since 1066, and by the early 14th century only Gascony remained. On 24 May 1337 Philip VI's Great Council agreed to take back Edward III's lands in France, which began the Hundred Years' War. In 1356 Edward III's son, the Black Prince, left Bergerac on 4 August with about 6,000 Anglo-Gascon fighters and devastated the countryside in three divisions. His aim was to force the French to attack him on ground of his choosing. King John II pursued with a large and unusually mobile army, and on 18 September the Anglo-Gascons took a strong position on a wooded hill 5 miles south of Poitiers, where they dug pits and trenches.

On 19 September about 14,000 to 16,000 French faced 6,000 Anglo-Gascons, who fought on foot as nearly all the French did. The first French attack, begun when a movement in the English lines was taken for a withdrawal, was driven back, and a second attack under the Dauphin Charles was also repulsed. Philip, Duke of Orléans, then led about half the third division off the field with three of John's four sons. John led the fourth division forward and had the Oriflamme unfurled, the signal that no prisoners were to be taken. A mounted force of 160 Anglo-Gascons appeared behind the French, and believing themselves surrounded the French collapsed. John II and his 14-year-old son Philip were captured, and about 2,500 French men-at-arms died.

France fell into near anarchy, and the peasant revolt known as the Jacquerie broke out in 1358. Two treaties of London were rejected in France. After a campaign in 1359 the Treaty of Brétigny was agreed in 1360, ceding large areas of France to England, and John was ransomed for three million gold écus. The French resumed hostilities in 1369 and recaptured most of the lost territory, and the war ended in a French victory in 1453.
battle-of-poltava: King Charles XII of Sweden had defeated most of the anti-Swedish coalition, and Tsar Peter I was the only enemy still fighting. Peter offered to return the Baltic provinces Russia had occupied since 1703, except Ingria, where he had begun to build St. Petersburg, but Charles refused. In the autumn of 1707 Charles marched towards Moscow with almost 44,000 men. Russian scorched-earth tactics and harsh weather forced him south into Ukraine, where he hoped for help from Ivan Mazepa, the Cossack hetman who had decided to rebel against Peter. The winter of 1708 to 1709 was the coldest in Europe in over 500 years.

By spring 1709 Charles had about 20,000 soldiers and 34 cannons. He besieged the fortress of Poltava on the Vorskla on 2 May, and Peter marched to relieve it with about 80,000 men and built a fortified camp north of the town. On 20 June Charles was shot in the foot, so Field Marshal Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld took operational command. Peter had built ten redoubts across the corridor between two woods.

The Swedish attack began before dawn, but the cavalry arrived late and the Russians sounded the alarm. The Swedes overran the first two redoubts, but a column under General Carl Gustaf Roos became isolated at the third and surrendered at 9:30 a.m. At 9:45 the Swedes advanced on Peter's 42 battalions and nearly broke the first line, but their cavalry could not reform in time and the infantry on the left flank fled. The Russians filled the gap, and Aleksandr Menshikov's cavalry outflanked the Swedes.

Charles retreated south that evening. Lewenhaupt led the survivors towards the Dnieper but, pursued by Russian cavalry and Kalmyk auxiliaries, was forced to surrender at Perevolochna on 11 July. Peter sent many Swedish prisoners to Siberia. Charles and Mazepa escaped with about 1,500 men to Bendery in Moldavia, then controlled by the Ottoman Empire, where Charles stayed five years.

The battle revived the anti-Swedish coalition, which attacked the weakened Swedish Empire on several fronts. It was the largest battle of the Great Northern War, and Sweden lost its dominant position in the Baltic, which the Russian Empire took over.
battle-of-sagrajas: After a civil war, the Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus broke up into small independent states, the taifas, of which Seville under the Banu Abbad was the strongest. Alfonso VI of Castile, with Sancho of Aragon and Navarre and Count Berengar Raymond of Barcelona, pressed them hard after the fall of Toledo, took Coria, raided as far as Tarifa and besieged Zaragoza. The taifa kings paid tribute, and Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad of Seville wrote for help in 1082 to Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the leader of the Almoravids, a Sunni Maliki reform movement of Sanhaja tribes, who had founded Marrakesh and united the western Maghreb. Yusuf promised to come once he had taken Ceuta.
Alfonso sent mocking letters to Ibn Abbad while besieging him. Ibn Abbad wrote to Yusuf again, and agreed to give him the Green Island and Algeciras as a base for his troops.

The armies camped facing each other across the Wadi Bira near Badajoz, the Andalusians in one camp and the Almoravids in another. Yusuf offered Alfonso the usual three choices of Islam, tribute or war, and Alfonso refused. The two sides agreed on a Monday for the battle, but the Muslims suspected an attack on Friday, their holy day, and set scouts to watch. Alfonso is said to have attacked first, with a force under Count García and Count Zodric sent against Ibn Abbad's camp.

On 23 October 1086 this force met the Almoravid knights under Dawud ibn Aisha, whose archers helped repel the first assault. The turning point came when Yusuf ordered 4,000 cavalry from Takrur, with large shields and javelins, to charge, destroying the Christian cavalry. One of them is said to have wounded Alfonso severely in the thigh, leaving him with a limp. Towards sunset Alfonso retreated to a hill with a small company and escaped in the dark to Coria.

Alfonso, who had reportedly come with an army of 60,000, left with only about 300 knights. The battle preserved al-Andalus from Alfonso's conquests and lifted the sieges of major cities, though he kept up his offensives. Yusuf stayed near Seville for three days and returned to Morocco on the death of his son Abu Bakr. The taifa rulers soon returned to their quarrels, and the Castilians resumed raids and took the fortress of Aledo.
battle-of-salamis: Athens and Eretria had supported the Ionian Revolt against the Persian king Darius I, and a Persian force destroyed Eretria in 490 BCE but was defeated by the Athenians at Marathon. In 480 BCE Xerxes I invaded Greece with a vast force. A small Greek force held Thermopylae, where the Spartan rearguard was annihilated, while the allied fleet fought at Artemisium and retreated with heavy losses. The Persians took Phocis, Boeotia, Attica and Euboea. The allies prepared to defend the Isthmus of Corinth, and the fleet withdrew to Salamis.

The Persians needed to finish the conquest in one campaigning season, since so large a force could not be supplied for long. To outflank the Isthmus they needed their navy, so destroying the allied fleet offered Xerxes the best hope. Herodotus has Queen Artemisia of Caria warn him that fighting at sea was an unnecessary risk.

The Athenian general Themistocles persuaded the allies to fight at sea again. By a ruse, a message telling Xerxes that much of the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, he drew the Persian navy into the straits to block both entrances. Herodotus gives the Greek fleet as 378 triremes, while Aeschylus, who fought there, says 310. Herodotus puts the Persian fleet at 1,207 ships at the outset, but most modern historians favour 600 to 800 at Salamis.

Ancient sources describe the fighting poorly. In the cramped waters Persian numbers became a hindrance, as ships struggled to manoeuvre and fouled their own lines. The Persian admiral Ariabignes, a brother of Xerxes, was killed early, and the Phoenician squadrons were pushed against the coast, many running aground. In the centre a wedge of Greek ships split the Persian fleet in two.

Xerxes tried to build a causeway across the straits, but the Greek fleet now patrolled them. He retreated to Asia with much of his army and left Mardonius to complete the conquest. The next year the Persians lost at Plataea and Mycale and made no further attempt on the Greek mainland, and over thirty years Thrace, the Aegean islands and Ionia were removed from their control. Many historians count Salamis among the most significant battles in history. In 2017 archaeologists announced the discovery of the anchorage used by the Greek warships before the battle.
battle-of-sedan-1870: After the costly Battle of Gravelotte on 18 August, Marshal François Achille Bazaine's Army of the Rhine retreated to Metz, where Prussian forces besieged it from 19 August. Napoleon III and Marshal Patrice de MacMahon formed the Army of Châlons to relieve him and marched north-east towards the Belgian border. The march depleted the French and left both flanks exposed, and Helmuth von Moltke took the Prussian Third and Fourth Armies north to catch them. At the Battle of Beaumont on 30 August MacMahon lost 7,500 men and 40 cannons and fell back on the obsolete fortress of Sedan to rest and resupply. He refused General Félix Douay's request to dig trenches, saying the army would not stay long.

Moltke divided his forces into three groups, one to hold the French where they were, one to catch them if they retreated and a smallest to hold the river bank. By 09:00 on 1 September the Prussian V and XI Corps had completed the encirclement to the north-west. The fighting opened at Bazeilles, where French marines held stone houses before Bavarian artillery shelled the village into rubble.

MacMahon was wounded early. General Auguste-Alexandre Ducrot, who took command, ordered a retreat, but General Emmanuel Félix de Wimpffen overruled him and attacked at La Moncelle, which gave the French a brief rally. By 11:00 German artillery had taken a heavy toll. A cavalry attack led by General Jean Auguste Margueritte, who was mortally wounded, was beaten back by infantry fire. French troops were driven into the Bois de la Garenne, which the Prussian Guards took at 14:30, and the troops inside it surrendered. Napoleon III then raised a white flag over the fortress, although Wimpffen launched one more failed attack.

Wimpffen signed the surrender of the army and the fortress at 11:30 on 2 September. Moltke had refused him an honourable capitulation, pointing to the French lack of ammunition and food. The Germans counted 9,860 casualties, while the French lost 3,220 killed, 14,811 wounded and 104,000 captured, with 558 guns. Napoleon III left for captivity at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel on 3 September.

On 4 September protesters stormed the imperial palace and the Second French Empire collapsed in a bloodless revolution. A Government of National Defense, which later became the French Third Republic, carried on the war for five more months. The German armies besieged Paris from 19 September. Because of the battle's part in German unification, many Germans marked 2 September as Sedantag, the Day of Sedan, until 1919, though the Kaiser did not make it an official holiday.
battle-of-sekigahara: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's heir, Toyotomi Hideyori, was only five years old when Hideyoshi died, which left a power vacuum. After the Imjin War, factional disputes arose between Ishida Mitsunari and seven former Toyotomi generals including Katō Kiyomasa. Tokugawa Ieyasu won over Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori to challenge Mitsunari, who claimed to fight for the Toyotomi clan. Mitsunari met Ōtani Yoshitsugu, Mashita Nagamori and Ankokuji Ekei to raise an anti-Tokugawa army, with Mōri Terumoto as overall commander. This became the Western Army. Terumoto captured Osaka Castle while the main Tokugawa army was on its way to suppress Uesugi Kagekatsu. Mitsunari had hoped to hold Gifu Castle and Ōgaki Castle, but the Eastern Army, the Tokugawa-led coalition, captured Gifu Castle first.

On 21 October 1600, in what is now Gifu Prefecture, the Tokugawa advance guard stumbled into Ishida's army in dense fog. Ii Naomasa, commanding his 3,600 crimson-clad troops, attacked the Western Army's centre, and Fukushima Masanori engaged Ukita Hideie's troops. The fighting then reached a deadlock, which the chronicler Ōta Gyūichi describes as friends and foes pushing each other.

Several Western commanders defected. The most notable was Kobayakawa Hideaki, Hideyoshi's nephew. The conventional account says he hesitated until around noon, when Ieyasu supposedly ordered arquebuses fired at his position. Modern historians such as Jun Shiramine and Stephen Turnbull doubt this and think he had already agreed to defect. Ukita's ranks broke, and Ōtani Yoshitsugu, outnumbered, killed himself. Mitsunari began to retreat as Shima Sakon fell, and Shimazu Yoshihiro's men escaped encirclement with only 200 soldiers. Large forces on both sides never reached the field, among them Tokugawa Hidetada's 38,000 held up at the Siege of Ueda.

Authority to assign ranks and redistribute land passed from the Toyotomi to Ieyasu, who immediately redistributed domains worth 6.8 million koku, mostly to the allies who had made his victory. Katō Kiyomasa's domain rose from 195,000 to 515,000 koku. The battle is generally regarded as the beginning of the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan until 1868. Jakob Meckel, a Prussian general advising Meiji Japan, judged from a map that the Western Army's greater numbers and higher ground should have won. Japanese historians point instead to resentment of Mitsunari among powerful daimyo, particularly veterans of the invasions of Korea.
battle-of-siffin: After the third caliph Uthman was killed in 656 CE by Egyptian rebels, the Basrans, Kufans and most of the Ansar supported Ali for the caliphate. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the Umayyad governor of Syria, refused to pledge allegiance and sent Ali a formal declaration of war, charging him with Uthman's murder and demanding that the killers be surrendered. Ali answered that he was innocent and that Mu'awiya should first pledge allegiance and then bring his case to Ali's court.

Modern authors often regard Mu'awiya's call for revenge as a pretext to keep his rule over Syria or to seize the caliphate. Mu'awiya won the support of Amr ibn al-As, who was promised the governorship of Egypt for life.

Siffin lay on the right bank of the Euphrates, near Raqqa in present-day Syria. Ali's army, which drew on Kufa, reached it early in the summer of 657, and found Mu'awiya's forces already there and holding the watering place. The size of the armies is uncertain, with reports ranging from 100,000 to 150,000 on each side.

The main battle seems to have begun on Wednesday, 26 July 657 and continued to Friday or Saturday morning. Ali probably did not initiate the fighting. Mu'awiya fared better on the first day, but by the second the Iraqis began to gain the upper hand. Before noon some Syrians raised pages of the Quran on their lances, calling for the Book of God to judge between them, and the fighting stopped. Ali is said to have urged his men to continue, calling it a deception, but the majority of his army wanted a truce, and he agreed under pressure. By this point Ali may have lost 25,000 men and Mu'awiya 45,000.

A minority in Ali's camp opposed the arbitration, and about 12,000 are said to have seceded outside Kufa. Some later left for al-Nahrawan and became the Kharijites, who fought Ali at the Battle of Nahrawan in 658. The arbitration itself was inconclusive, and the accounts of it are highly tendentious. The arbitrators could not agree on the next caliph.

The Syrians recognised Mu'awiya as caliph at Jerusalem, and in July 658 Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt from Ali's governor. Ali was assassinated by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam in January 661. That summer Mu'awiya invaded Iraq and compelled Ali's son Hasan to give up the caliphate, and his rule was acknowledged throughout the caliphate. The battle is regarded as a major step towards the Umayyad Caliphate.
battle-of-sluys: The war began after disagreements between Philip VI of France and Edward III of England. By 1337 English monarchs held only Gascony and Ponthieu in France, and on 24 May 1337 Philip's Great Council agreed that the Duchy of Aquitaine should be taken back into Philip's hands because Edward had breached his obligations as a vassal. At sea the French began with the advantage. Their galleys, partly hired from Genoa and Monaco, raided the English coast and razed Portsmouth in 1338, while Edward owned only three warships and relied on merchant cogs fitted with wooden castles at bow and stern.

The balance shifted in 1340. Genoese crews had mutinied in 1339, and in January 1340 an English raid on Boulogne destroyed 18 galleys and 24 other ships. Philip then assembled a Great Army of the Sea of about 200 ships, most of them requisitioned merchantmen, under Hugues Quiéret and Nicolas Béhuchet. It reached Sluys on 8 June 1340 and cut English communications with Edward's allies in Flanders.

Merchants had been reluctant to supply ships, but after an angry council Edward assembled between 120 and 150 ships at the River Orwell, carrying 1,300 men-at-arms and 1,000 longbowmen. He sailed on 22 June. The French chained their ships in three lines across the estuary of the Zwin. Pietro Barbavera, who commanded the galleys, advised putting to sea, but Béhuchet insisted on blocking the inlet.

On 24 June Edward entered at high tide with the wind and tide in his favour. The French ships had drifted eastward and become entangled. The English attacked in groups of three, two ships of archers flanking one of men-at-arms, and the longbowmen outshot the crossbowmen, according to the historians Jonathan Sumption and Robert Hardy. At night the rear line tried to break out, and apart from the galleys only 17 ships escaped. The English captured 166 merchant ships and sank or burned 24. French losses are put at 16,000 to 20,000 dead.

The victory let Edward land his army, which went on to besiege Tournai without success. It gave the English naval supremacy in the Channel, but Philip's greater resources allowed him to rebuild his navy quickly, and French raids continued, including attacks on the Isle of Wight, Plymouth and the Channel Islands later in 1340. In 1341 French, Castilian and Portuguese squadrons cut English communications with Gascony. Edward later issued a gold noble showing himself seated in a ship, inscribed with a line from the Gospel of Luke used as a protection in battle.
battle-of-solferino: The early weeks of the Second Italian War of Independence went well for the Piedmontese and French, who largely pushed Austria out of northern Italy, took Milan and marched east to finish Austria off before Prussia could become involved. On 22 June the allied army, 96,000 French and 37,000 Piedmontese, advanced from the Chiese to the Mincio. The Austrian Emperor Franz Joseph moved his 1st Army of 57,000 men and 2nd Army of 45,500 across the Mincio, and both sides converged on Medole, Solferino and San Martino.

It was the last major battle in which all the armies were under the personal command of their monarchs, and the largest since Leipzig in 1813. Napoleon III led the French and Victor Emmanuel II the Sardinians, while the Austrian high command was hindered by rivalry between its chief of staff, Heinrich von Heß, and the emperor's adjutant general, Karl Ludwig von Grünne.

With no fixed plan, the fighting was uncoordinated and fell into three engagements, at Medole in the south, Solferino in the centre and San Martino in the north. At Medole, from around 4 am, General Niel's 4th Corps held a thin line and kept three Austrian corps from helping the 2nd Army at Solferino. At Solferino the Austrians held their positions all day against repeated French attacks, until Napoleon III fed in the Imperial Guard.

Near 3 pm the French reserves attacked Cavriana, occupying it at 6 pm and breaking the Austrian centre, which forced both Austrian armies to retreat. In the north the Sardinians fought Benedek's VIII Corps from 7 am, and San Martino changed hands three times before a fourth assault took it at 8 pm.

The battle lasted over nine hours. Austrian losses were 2,386 killed, 10,634 wounded and 9,290 missing, and the Allies lost 2,313 killed, 12,102 wounded and 2,776 captured or missing. The Austrians retreated to the fortresses of the Quadrilateral.

Napoleon III, moved by the losses, ended the war with the Armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859. The Piedmontese won Lombardy but not Venetia, and Cavour resigned. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861. Henry Dunant, who toured the field afterwards, was horrified by the suffering of the wounded and began the campaign that led to the Geneva Conventions and the International Red Cross, which he described in A Memory of Solferino. Memorials, ossuaries and museums mark the field, among them the 70-metre Tower of San Martino della Battaglia, built in 1893.
battle-of-stalingrad: By the spring of 1942 the Wehrmacht held Ukraine, Belarus and the Baltic republics, and Adolf Hitler chose the south of the Soviet Union as the target of the summer campaign. Germany's fuel supplies had dwindled, and the plan, code-named Fall Blau, aimed to seize the Soviet oil fields in the Caucasus.
