Stalingrad was one of the largest industrial centres of the Soviet Union and a transport hub on the Volga River, and controlling it would block Soviet shipments along the river. The city also carried the name of the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. Hitler split the army group, sending one part south to the Caucasus and the other, including Paulus's 6th Army, east towards the Volga.

German forces first met the Red Army's Stalingrad Front on 17 July 1942. On 23 August the 6th Army and part of the 4th Panzer Army began their offensive, supported by Luftwaffe bombing that reduced much of the city to rubble. The fighting became house-to-house. The Soviet commander Chuikov kept his front line as close to the Germans as possible, so that German artillery and aircraft could not strike without risking their own men, and used small units moving through the city's sewers. After 27 September the struggle moved to the factory district, and by November the Germans held 90 per cent of the ruined city, with the Soviet defenders confined to two narrow pockets on the Volga's west bank.

On 19 November the Red Army launched Operation Uranus against the Romanian armies guarding the German flanks. The flanks were overrun and about 330,000 Axis troops were trapped. Hitler forbade a breakout; attempts to supply the army by air failed, and Manstein's relief attempt, Operation Winter Storm, did not reach it. On 7 January 1943 Soviet envoys offered terms of surrender, which Hitler refused to let Paulus accept. On 2 February 1943 the 6th Army, out of ammunition and food, capitulated, the first of Hitler's field armies to do so.

The Axis suffered between 800,000 and 1,500,000 casualties, killed, wounded or captured, among the German armed forces and their allies. Of the troops trapped in the pocket, 105,000 eventually surrendered and 60,000 died. The German public was told of the disaster only at the end of January 1943; on 31 January state radio broadcast the Adagio of Anton Bruckner's Seventh Symphony before announcing the defeat. On 18 February Joseph Goebbels gave his Sportpalast speech calling for total war.

The defeat ended Germany's 1942 summer offensive and passed the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front to the Soviet Union. It is generally regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe. Stalingrad was named a Hero City in 1945, and the monument The Motherland Calls was erected on Mamayev Kurgan in 1967.
battle-of-stamford-bridge: The death of the childless King Edward the Confessor in January 1066 set off a struggle for the English throne among contenders from across north-western Europe, among them Harald Hardrada of Norway. The Norwegian army, with reinforcements from Orkney, most likely numbered between 7,000 and 9,000 men. Hardrada was joined by forces Tostig Godwinson had recruited in Flanders and Scotland. Tostig, exiled in 1065 after being ousted as Earl of Northumbria, was at odds with his brother Harold, who had been elected king. On 20 September the invaders defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar at the Battle of Fulford and received the surrender of York.

Harold was in southern England awaiting an invasion by William, Duke of Normandy. On hearing of the Norwegians he marched north with his housecarls and as many thegns as he could gather, covering about 185 miles from London to Yorkshire in four days. On 25 September he took the Norwegians completely by surprise at Stamford Bridge, where they had gone to collect hostages and supplies. According to Snorri Sturluson's saga, Harold himself rode up beforehand and offered Tostig his earldom.

A Norwegian with an axe was said by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Henry of Huntingdon to have blocked the narrow bridge alone and cut down more than 40 Englishmen. The delay allowed the Norse to form a shield wall, but they had left their armour behind. The battle raged for hours and went far beyond the bridge. When the shield wall broke, Hardrada was killed by an arrow in the throat and Tostig was slain. Eystein Orre's men ran 16 miles from the ships at Riccall and briefly checked the English, but were overwhelmed.

Harold granted a truce to the survivors, among them Hardrada's son Olaf and Paul Thorfinnsson, Earl of Orkney, who pledged not to attack England again. Only 24 ships of a fleet of over 300 were needed to carry them home. Three days later, on 28 September, William landed at Pevensey, and Harold marched south and was defeated and killed at Hastings on 14 October. The battle has traditionally marked the end of the Viking Age, although major Scandinavian campaigns in Britain followed, such as Sweyn Estrithson's in 1069–1070 and Magnus Barefoot's in 1098.
battle-of-stirling-bridge: In 1296 John de Warenne, 6th Earl of Surrey, defeated the Scots at the Battle of Dunbar, King John Balliol surrendered to Edward I on 10 July, and the Scottish landholders were made to acknowledge Edward's overlordship. In 1297 Andrew Moray began a revolt in northern Scotland and by late summer controlled Urquhart, Inverness, Elgin, Banff and Aberdeen. William Wallace joined him in September near Dundee, and they marched to Stirling, traditionally regarded as the key to Scotland. Surrey and Edward's treasurer in Scotland, Hugh de Cressingham, had both reached Stirling by 9 September, by which time the Scots held Abbey Craig.

The Forth was crossed near Stirling Castle by a long causeway and a narrow wooden bridge wide enough for only two horsemen abreast. Surrey saw the risk and delayed for several days to negotiate. Walter of Guisborough reports that Wallace answered the envoys that the Scots were there not to make peace but to fight and free their kingdom. A Scots knight, Sir Richard Lundie, offered to cross at a ford two miles upstream, but Cressingham persuaded Surrey to order a direct attack over the bridge.

Wallace and Moray waited until, by one estimate, about 2,000 English troops had crossed. Their spearmen then came down from the high ground, held off the heavy cavalry and cut off the bridge. Most of those trapped in the loop of the river were probably killed. Marmaduke Thweng fought his way back across. Surrey ordered the bridge destroyed and retreated towards Berwick, leaving Stirling Castle isolated.

Walter of Guisborough recorded English losses as 100 cavalry and 5,000 infantry. Scottish losses are unrecorded except for Moray, who was mortally wounded and was dead by November. The Lanercost Chronicle says Wallace had a strip of Cressingham's skin made into a sword belt. The Scots raided as far south as Durham, and Wallace was appointed Guardian of Scotland. Edward was already planning another invasion, which led to the Battle of Falkirk. Wallace's later fame rests largely on the poet Blind Harry, writing about 1470, whose account of the battle is a blend of fact and fiction and is highly improbable in its details.
battle-of-talas: Tang China and the Arab caliphates had met in Central Asia since the early eighth century. In 715 a Tang force defeated a Tibetan-Arab army at the Battle of Namangan and restored the king of Fergana, and in 717 Tang troops and Karluks defeated the Umayyads and Tibetans at the Battle of Aksu. In 747 the Tang general Gao Xianzhi established control over the Gilgit region, and in 750 the Abbasids took power after the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate.

The immediate cause was a quarrel over Shash, the region of modern Tashkent. Gao Xianzhi led Tang and Karluk soldiers against its king, who surrendered and was taken to the Tang capital Chang'an and executed. His son then appealed to the Abbasids, and the Abbasid commander Ziyad ibn Salih received reinforcements from Abu Muslim in May 751.

In July 751 the armies met on the Talas River, near the present border of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, though the exact site is unconfirmed. According to the Chinese account, the two sides fought to a stalemate for five days, with crossbowmen and archers behind a shield wall of infantry. On the fifth day the Karluk mercenaries, who made up two thirds of the Tang army, attacked it from the rear while the Abbasids attacked from the front.

Gao Xianzhi escaped with some of his regulars, helped by his officer Li Siye, but most of his troops were captured. Numbers are uncertain. Chinese sources put the Tang dead at 20,000 to 30,000, and Arabic sources at 45,000 to 50,000 with 20,000 to 25,000 captured. Sources also differ on whether the Karluks changed sides during the battle or were Abbasid allies from the start.

Historians judge the battle differently. One view holds that it ended Tang influence in Transoxiana and secured Abbasid control of the region and the spread of Islam among the Turkic peoples. Another holds that it was little more than a border clash: borders barely moved, Arab envoys visited the Tang court four times in 752 and 753, and the Tang kept considerable influence in eastern Central Asia until the An Lushan rebellion of 755 forced them to withdraw troops from the Protectorate General to Pacify the West.

Chinese prisoners taken at Talas are said to have introduced papermaking to West Asia, but several findings dispute this. The Arabic historian al-Maqdisi reports that Abu Muslim took 5,000 Chinese prisoners. The battle is recorded in both Chinese and Arabic sources, which differ in their accounts of it.
battle-of-the-atlantic: At its core was the Allied naval blockade of Germany, announced the day after the declaration of war, and Germany's counterblockade. The United Kingdom was an island highly dependent on imports and needed more than a million tons of imported material a week to survive and fight, so the battle became a tonnage war. The Germans targeted merchant shipping, and from 1942 the Axis also sought to stop the build-up of Allied supplies in Britain for an invasion of occupied Europe. The name came into use in 1941, when the First Lord of the Admiralty, A. V. Alexander, asked Parliament on 5 March for more ships and men to fight the Battle of the Atlantic.

The Kriegsmarine lacked the strength in 1939 to challenge the British and French navies directly, and relied on commerce raiding. The German occupation of Norway and France in 1940 gave U-boats bases on the Atlantic coast, and from June to October 1940 over 270 Allied ships were sunk, a period U-boat crews called the Happy Time. The British answered with permanent escort groups, and the Royal Canadian Navy grew from a handful of destroyers into a large escort force. United States ships and aircraft began to aid convoys on 13 September 1941.

In February 1942 the U-boats changed to a new four-rotor Enigma key that the Allied codebreakers could not read for ten months, and the Germans read about 80 per cent of the Admiralty messages sent in Naval Cipher 3 from March 1942 to June 1943. Against this the Allies developed shipborne direction-finding radio, the Leigh Light for night attacks by aircraft and long-range B-24 Liberator aircraft that closed the mid-Atlantic gap. In March 1943, 120 ships were sunk and 12 U-boats destroyed; by mid-1943 the U-boats had been defeated, although losses continued until the end of the war.

The German tonnage war failed, and the supplies and troops needed for the D-Day landings were built up in Britain. Between 1939 and 1945, 72,200 Allied naval and merchant seamen died. The Germans lost about 30,000 U-boat sailors, three quarters of a force of 40,000. United States yards built 2,710 Liberty ships of 38.5 million tons, far more than the 14 million tons the U-boats sank in the whole war.

Historians disagree about which measures mattered most. Max Hastings holds that in 1941 alone Ultra saved between 1.5 and two million tons of shipping, while a former U-boat commander writing for the Admiralty after the war attributed the defeat first to Allied radar developments.
battle-of-the-boyne: The battle was part of James II's attempt to regain the thrones of England and Scotland after the Glorious Revolution, and it had wider European roots in the League of Augsburg and the Grand Alliance against the ambitions of Louis XIV of France. In Ireland the war was also a sectarian and ethnic conflict. Catholic landowners had lost almost all their lands after Cromwell's conquest, and under Richard Talbot, Earl of Tyrconnel, they raised an army for James and by 1690 controlled all of Ireland except Derry and Enniskillen. Protestants feared for their lives and property under a Catholic king.

William, a seasoned commander who had yet to win a major battle, saw Ireland as one front in the war against France, while James could count on Louis XIV, who sent 6,000 French troops. The Duke of Schomberg, aged 74, had been sent to Ireland in 1689 with 20,000 men, but fever and Jacobite blocking forces left the campaign static. William landed at Carrickfergus on 14 June 1690 and marched south.

The Williamite army numbered about 36,000, of whom only about half were British; its best infantry were 7,000 Danish infantry and 6,000 Dutch with flintlock muskets, plus 3,000 French Huguenots. James had 23,500 men, mostly Irish Catholics with some French regiments. His Irish cavalry were good troops, but many of the infantry were pressed peasants, some armed only with scythes, and those with firearms had obsolete matchlocks.

On 1 July 1690 William sent about a quarter of his men west to cross at Roughgrange as a diversion, led by Schomberg's son Meinhardt. James sent much of his army, including his best French troops, to meet it, but a swampy ravine kept the two forces apart. At the main ford near Oldbridge the Dutch Blue Guards crossed and held off Jacobite cavalry under the Duke of Berwick with platoon fire. The Jacobites retired in good order, and about 2,000 of some 50,000 participants died, three quarters of them Jacobites.

William's forces entered Dublin two days later. James fled to France and never returned, and his Irish supporters nicknamed him Séamus a' chaca. The war ended only after Aughrim in 1691 and the Treaty of Limerick. On the continent the battle was treated as the first real victory of the League of Augsburg. The Twelfth of July was first a commemoration of Aughrim, and the two battles were combined in the late eighteenth century after the founding of the Orange Order in 1795.
battle-of-the-bulge: After the breakout from Normandy at the end of July 1944, the Allies advanced toward Germany faster than expected, leaving troops tired and supply lines stretched thin. They captured Antwerp intact in September, but it was not operational until 28 November. Adolf Hitler believed that a blow in the west could split the Allies and force the Americans and British to a separate peace, giving Germany time to produce new weapons and concentrate in the east. After the war this was generally judged unrealistic given Allied air superiority.

The offensive aimed to stop Allied use of Antwerp and to split their lines. The Germans called it Unternehmen Wacht am Rhein, a name implying a defensive posture. The name Battle of the Bulge came from the press, from the way the Allied line bulged inward on wartime news maps.

At 5:30 on 16 December 1944 the Germans opened with a 90-minute barrage along a front of 130 kilometres. They achieved total surprise, through Allied overconfidence, poor air reconnaissance in bad weather and faulty intelligence. The region was a rest area held thinly by tired troops and inexperienced replacements. In the north the 2nd and 99th Infantry Divisions held Elsenborn Ridge and forced the German spearhead onto less favourable routes. Waffen-SS troops under Joachim Peiper shot American prisoners near Malmedy.

In the centre the Germans encircled two regiments of the 106th Division at the Schnee Eifel, the most serious American reverse of the campaign. Bastogne was surrounded, and the farthest German advance, to Foy-Notre-Dame, was stopped by the 2nd Armored Division on 24 December. The weather improved from 23 December, letting Allied aircraft strike, and on 26 December the lead element of George S. Patton's Third Army reached Bastogne from the south.

The offensive was effectively broken by 27 December, but fighting went on for another month as Patton attacked north and Bernard Montgomery south to reduce the bulge. On 1 January 1945 the Luftwaffe attacked Allied airfields in Operation Bodenplatte, destroying about 465 aircraft but losing 277, and was left ineffective for the rest of the war. It was the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in the war. German casualties are put at 81,000 to 103,900 by Allied estimates. The battle destroyed much of Germany's armoured strength and set back the Allied advance into Germany by several weeks.
battle-of-the-camel: Many senior companions of Muhammad, Ali among them, criticised the third caliph Uthman for nepotism and for deviating from the Quran and the Sunna. Discontented groups from the provinces came to Medina, and Ali mediated between them and Uthman. Uthman was assassinated by Egyptian rebels in June 656, and Ali had played no part in the attack. The Ansar and the Basrans and Kufans favoured Ali as the next caliph, and he accepted at last, though he preferred to be a minister. Talha and Zubayr pledged to him but then left for Mecca on the pretext of performing the lesser pilgrimage. Aisha, who had opposed Uthman, also blamed Ali for the assassination.

The opposition demanded that Ali punish Uthman's killers, and also called for his removal and a Qurayshite council to choose a successor. In October 656 some six to nine hundred rebels led by Aisha, Talha and Zubayr marched on Basra, where they killed many people and took control of the city and its treasury. Ali gathered an army at Kufa and marched to Basra, and negotiations in a tent between the armies failed after three days. Ali ordered that the wounded and captives were not to be killed and that fugitives were not to be pursued.

The fighting took place on a December day in 656, from noon to sunset, and was mostly hand-to-hand combat. Aisha rode a red camel in an armoured palanquin, and the fiercest fighting was around it. Talha was killed, reportedly by Marwan ibn al-Hakam. Zubayr left the field and was later killed near Basra. Ali's troops killed Aisha's camel and captured her. The lowest estimate of the dead is 2,500 on Aisha's side and 400 to 500 on Ali's.

Aisha was treated with respect, reprimanded for causing loss of life, and sent back to Mecca or Medina with her half-brother Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. Her defeat ended her political ambitions. Ali announced a general pardon, freed prisoners, forbade the enslavement of women and children, and returned seized property. Some of his soldiers objected, and the orders later became a rallying cry for the Kharijites. He then moved to Kufa, which became his main base, and the Medinan elite permanently lost authority over the community. Kufa remained the main centre of Shia Islam until Baghdad was founded in the mid-eighth century.
battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains: By 450 the Romans had restored their authority in much of Gaul, though control of the provinces beyond Italy was diminishing. Germanic peoples occupying Roman territory were bound by treaty as foederati under their own leaders: the Visigoths on the Garonne were restive, the Burgundians awaited an opening for revolt, and the Alans on the Loire were more loyal. When Attila invaded, the general Flavius Aetius moved his army rapidly from Italy to Gaul and tried to persuade the Visigothic king Theodoric I to join him. Theodoric hesitated, and Aetius turned to the former Praetorian Prefect of Gaul, Avitus, who according to tradition persuaded the Visigoths and other wavering peoples.

The coalition assembled at Arles and Toulouse and marched to Orléans, reaching it on 14 June. Jordanes lists among Aetius's allies Franks, Burgundians, Alans and other Celtic or German tribes; Peter Heather suggests the Visigoths may have fielded about 25,000 men.

Attila was leaving Gaul with most of his objectives achieved when Aetius and his allies pursued him from Orléans. The armies met on the Catalaunian Plains on or about 20 June. The exact site is uncertain; scholars place it near Châlons-en-Champagne or Troyes, and the ridge at Montgueux, west of Troyes, is the most thoroughly researched proposal.

The account of Jordanes, who wrote long afterwards and is described as notoriously unreliable on Gothic history, tells of a struggle for the ridge, with the Alans in the centre. Theodoric was killed on the right, and his son Thorismund attacked the Hunnic centre and nearly killed Attila. Darkness fell in confusion, and neither side knew the outcome until morning. Hydatius says almost 300,000 men are said to have fallen. Attila withdrew.

From Cassiodorus in the early sixth century the battle was increasingly seen as a Roman allied victory. Edward Gibbon called it the last victory achieved in the name of the Western Roman Empire, and Edward Shepherd Creasy called it a triumph of Christian Europe. Most modern authors have moved away from this view. J. B. Bury held that its significance had been enormously exaggerated, since the decisive moment was the defence of Orléans and the battle was fought as Attila retreated, though it damaged his prestige and weakened his forces.

In 452 Attila invaded Italy and razed Aquileia after a three-month siege; Pope Leo I took part in an embassy that brought a treaty, and Attila retreated, most likely because of famine and disease in his army. Attila died in 453, and after the Battle of Nedao in 454 the coalition of the Huns and their Germanic vassals gradually disintegrated.
battle-of-the-golden-spurs: The battle belongs to the Franco-Flemish War of 1297–1305. King Philip IV of France hoped to reassert control over the County of Flanders, a semi-independent polity notionally part of his kingdom, and perhaps to annex it. The French invaded in 1297 and again in 1300, and by May 1300 they controlled the county; Guy of Dampierre was imprisoned.

After Philip left, unrest returned in Bruges against the new governor, Jacques de Châtillon. On 18 May 1302 rebels who had fled the city came back and killed every Frenchman they could find, an act known as the Bruges Matins. Most towns joined the rising, though Ghent did not, and most of the Flemish nobility took the French side.

Philip sent a force under Count Robert II of Artois, built around a core of 2,500 noble cavalry. The Flemish army, led in the field by William of Jülich, was mostly town militia organised by guild, between 8,000 and 10,000 infantry. They carried pikes, crossbows and the goedendag, a thick wooden shaft topped with a steel spike. The Flemish besieged the castle of Courtrai from 26 June and fought the French on 11 July beside the Groeninge stream.

The ground was crossed by ditches and streams that the Flemish had dug and in places hidden, which robbed the French charge of momentum. Artois sent his heavy cavalry across the brooks. The Flemish pikemen did not flinch, and many knights were knocked from their horses and killed with the goedendag. Artois ordered his rearguard forward, but it turned back to protect the baggage. The count was cut down, and the surviving knights were driven into the marshes and slaughtered. The Flemish took few prisoners for ransom.

Courtrai castle surrendered on 13 July. The patrician regimes in Ghent and Ypres were overthrown and the guilds were officially recognised. The Annals of Ghent put French losses at more than 1,000 men, including 75 important nobles. The 500 pairs of spurs taken from the dead were given to the Church of Our Lady. The French soon reversed the result, winning at Mons-en-Pévèle in 1304, and the Peace of Athis-sur-Orge in 1305 made the Flemish pay substantial tribute.

Later writers saw the battle as an early sign of an infantry revolution, copied or adapted at Bannockburn, Crécy and Agincourt. In the 19th and 20th centuries it became the centre of a cult in Flanders: Hendrik Conscience's 1838 novel The Lion of Flanders made it known, and in 1973 its date was made the official holiday of the Flemish Community.
battle-of-the-granicus: After winning the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip II of Macedon forced most Greek states into the Hellenic League, whose aim was war on the Achaemenid Empire to avenge the Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. The Persian empire had been in crisis since the murder of Artaxerxes III in 338 BCE, and in spring 336 BCE Philip sent an expeditionary corps to the western coast of Asia Minor.

In early spring 334 BCE Alexander marched to the Hellespont with around 32,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry. Darius left the defence of Asia Minor to his satraps, perhaps because Alexander had not yet proved himself abroad. The satraps, led most probably by Arsites, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, and including Spithridates and Memnon of Rhodes, were camped near Zeleia when Alexander crossed.

The battle was fought in May 334 BCE at the crossing of the Granicus, now called the Biga River, on the road from Abydus to Dascylium. Arrian's account, the longest, describes Alexander's army as 18,100 men, and gives the Persians almost 20,000 Greek mercenary infantry and 20,000 cavalry. Diodorus and Justin give far higher figures, which modern historians regard as exaggerated.

In Arrian's account Alexander first sent Amyntas against the Persian left, but the Persians held the higher bank and threw back the attack with javelins. Alexander then charged with the Companion cavalry and fought personally against Persian nobles, among them Rhosaces and Spithridates. The Persian cavalry broke, the Foot Companions crossed the river and the Persian infantry routed, except the Greek mercenaries, who withdrew to higher ground and fought hard.

Arrian gives 115 Macedonian dead. Arsites escaped to Phrygia but later killed himself after being blamed for the defeat. Arrian says 1,000 cavalry were killed and 2,000 Greek mercenaries taken prisoner, and Alexander sent the prisoners to Macedon to work the land as slaves, because they had fought for Persia against fellow Greeks.

Alexander sent 300 suits of Persian armour to Athens as an offering to Athena, with an inscription that left out the Spartans. He also set up at Dion a bronze group by Lysippus of twenty-five of his companions who had died in the first cavalry charge; it was later taken to Rome by Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus in 146 BCE. The Persians were forced onto the defensive in the cities they still held. Sardis surrendered to Alexander, and Miletus, which resisted, was besieged.
battle-of-the-hydaspes: After Alexander the Great defeated the last Achaemenid forces under Bessus and Spitamenes in 328 BCE, he began a campaign towards India in 327 BCE. He entered India through the Khyber Pass, and a smaller force under his own command took the fortress of Aornos. In the early spring of the next year he allied with Taxiles, king of Taxila, against his neighbour Porus, who had refused to surrender and was preparing for war.

Alexander had to subdue Porus to keep marching east, since leaving a strong opponent on his flank would have been dangerous, and he could not show weakness to the Indian princes already subdued. Porus chose the ground well.

Alexander camped on the north bank of the Hydaspes, now the Jhelum, and in the spring of 326 BCE Porus drew up on the south bank. The river was too deep and fast for a direct crossing, so Alexander moved his cavalry up and down the bank each night with Porus shadowing him. He found a crossing about 27 km upstream, where a wooded island divided the river, and left Craterus in camp with most of the army to make feints. According to Arrian he took 6,000 foot and 5,000 horse. A storm that night drowned the noise of the crossing. Porus's son, sent to meet them, was routed and died.

Porus came with the best of his army, with cavalry on the flanks, chariots in front and elephants before the infantry. Alexander attacked the flanks with cavalry first, and the Indian horsemen were routed. The elephants then advanced against the Macedonian phalanx and caused heavy losses, but were driven back and trampled their own side. The phalanx advanced while the cavalry charged from the rear, and Craterus, who had crossed, pursued the fleeing army.

Porus, who had fought on, finally dismounted and was taken to Alexander. Asked how he wished to be treated, he is said to have replied, treat me as a king would treat another king. Alexander let him keep his lands and made him a satrap. He founded two cities, Nikaia at the site of the battle and Boukephala across the river in honour of his horse Bucephalus, which died during or after the battle.

Alexander then marched east to the Hyphasis, now the Beas, where his troops, who had campaigned nearly eight years, refused to go on. He turned south along the Indus. The battle exposed the Indian subcontinent to Greek political and cultural influence.
battle-of-the-kalka-river: After Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarezmian Empire in 1219, the generals Jebe and Subutai pursued the Khwarezmian sultan and then asked leave to continue their conquests for a year or two, returning to Mongolia by way of the Caucasus. With an army of 20,000, each general commanding a tumen, they sacked Rey, Zanjan and Qazvin and raided the Kingdom of Georgia. Crossing the Caucasus at heavy cost, they met a league of Lezgians, Alans and Cherkesses joined by the Cumans. The Mongols persuaded the Cumans to leave the alliance by appealing to Turkic-Mongol friendship and promising booty, then routed the others and turned on the Cumans themselves.

The Cuman Khan Koten fled to his son-in-law Mstislav Mstislavich of Galicia, known as Mstislav the Bold. He warned him that the Mongols had taken the Cuman land that day and would take his the next. Mstislav gathered the Rus' princes, among them Mstislav III of Kiev, but no commander-in-chief was appointed, so each prince could act as he pleased. The Mongols sent envoys saying they had no quarrel with the Rus', but Mstislav of Kiev had them executed.

The Mongols drew the Rus' forces eastward in a feigned retreat for nine days, then turned to face them on the Kalka River, whose exact location is unknown. Mstislav the Bold crossed and attacked with his Cuman allies without waiting for the rest. According to the chronicles the Cumans broke and ran through the Rus' ranks, causing confusion and a rout that began very quickly. Mstislav the Bold cut his way out with part of his army, while Mstislav of Kiev withdrew with some 10,000 men to a stockaded camp on a hill by the Dnieper.

After three days Mstislav of Kiev surrendered on a promise of safe conduct. The Mongols then killed his men and executed him and the Kievan nobles by burying and suffocating them under a victory platform, in the traditional Mongol manner of killing royalty without shedding blood. The number present is disputed, since no primary source gives it: estimates of the Rus' army range from 8,000 to 80,000. The Novgorod First Chronicle, the most reliable, gives no figures but says that only one soldier in ten returned home.

The Mongols did not stay. They plundered a few towns in the south and marched east, were defeated by the Volga Bulgars at Samara Bend, and rejoined Genghis Khan east of the Syr Darya. Their raid is described as history's longest cavalry raid, with 5,500 miles (8,900 km) ridden in three years. In 1237 Subutai and Batu returned and conquered the Kievan Rus'.
battle-of-the-little-bighorn: The battle belonged to the Great Sioux War of 1876 and was fought on land the Lakota had taken from other tribes since 1851, without the consent of the Crow, who had a treaty claim there. The Lakota had been displaced by the United States around Fort Laramie and reacted to white encroachment into the Black Hills, which they consider sacred. Around 5 June 1876, during a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek, Sitting Bull, the spiritual leader of the Hunkpapa Lakota, reportedly had a vision of soldiers falling into his camp like grasshoppers from the sky.

The army sent three columns to force the Lakota and Cheyenne back to their reservations, one of them under Alfred Terry, which included the 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer. Plans rested on the Indian agents' figure of no more than 800 hostiles, which was correct until several weeks before the battle, when thousands of reservation Indians joined Sitting Bull for the summer buffalo hunt.

On 25 June, after Custer's Crow scouts reported that the village was being alerted, Major Marcus Reno's detachment of three troops was ordered to charge. His force crossed the Little Bighorn around 3:10 p.m. and found the Lakota and Northern Cheyenne present in force. The details of Custer's own fight are largely conjectural, because none of the men who went forward with his five companies survived. Lakota accounts say far more of their casualties occurred in the attack on Last Stand Hill than anywhere else, and that the command structure broke down rapidly, though smaller last stands were made by several groups.
The Lakota and Northern Cheyenne then turned on Reno and Benteen, and the fight continued until dark and for much of the next day. On 27 June Terry's column approached and the warriors drew off.

The 7th Cavalry had 16 officers and 242 troopers killed or dead of wounds, and Custer's two brothers, nephew and brother-in-law died with him. Estimates of Native casualties range from 36 to 300. Six women and four children are known to have been killed at the start of the battle, among them two wives and three children of Gall.

Congress authorised an increase in the size of the army, and the Indian Appropriations Act of 1876 cut off rations for the Sioux until they ended hostilities and ceded the Black Hills; the Agreement of 1877 took their land. Custer's widow Libbie Custer worked to burnish his memory, and his heroic image began to tarnish after her death in 1933. An army court of inquiry in 1879 found Reno's conduct without fault. The battlefield was renamed the Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument in 1991.
battle-of-the-nile: After Napoleon Bonaparte's victories in northern Italy, Britain remained the only major European power still at war with the French Republic. The French Directory considered invading Britain or Ireland but found British control of northern waters an obstacle, and the French navy was dominant only in the Mediterranean. Bonaparte proposed an invasion of Egypt as a first step in a campaign against British India.

His fleet sailed from Toulon on 19 May 1798, took Malta from the Knights of St. John of Jerusalem in June, and reached Alexandria. The Royal Navy sent a squadron under Rear-Admiral Sir Horatio Nelson to find out the purpose of the expedition and defeat it. He pursued the French for more than two months and several times missed them by hours.

Vice-Admiral François-Paul Brueys d'Aigalliers anchored his line in Aboukir Bay, a shallow anchorage about 32 km north-east of Alexandria, and believed his position was strong. His crews were needed ashore to find provisions, so he had no scouts out. Nelson's fleet was sighted on 1 August and attacked at once. His ships split into two divisions, one passing between the French line and the shore and the other engaging its seaward side, so the leading French ships were caught in a crossfire.

The French vanguard surrendered during the evening. At 21:00 fire was seen on the lower decks of the flagship Orient, and at 22:00 it reached the magazines and the ship exploded. Brueys had been killed. Fighting resumed at dawn on 2 August, and the surviving French ships of the line gradually pulled away to the east. Only two ships of the line and two frigates escaped.

British losses were recorded as 218 killed and about 677 wounded. French losses are harder to calculate; estimates range from 2,000 to 5,000, with a suggested median of 3,500, and about half the dead died on Orient. Nelson was wounded in the battle.

The victory reversed the strategic position in the Mediterranean and left Napoleon's army trapped in Egypt. British naval dominance off the Syrian coast contributed to the French defeat at the siege of Acre in 1799, before Napoleon left Egypt. The result also encouraged other European states to turn against France and was a factor in the outbreak of the War of the Second Coalition. Nelson was made Baron Nelson of the Nile and Burnham Thorpe, though he was privately dissatisfied with the reward.
battle-of-the-pyramids: After landing in Ottoman Egypt and capturing Alexandria on 2 July 1798, General Napoleon Bonaparte marched his army across the desert towards Cairo. His aim was to break the power of the Mamluk beys who dominated Egypt and to secure the capital before Ottoman reinforcements could arrive. Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey, two Georgian Mamluks who commanded the country's military forces, prepared to resist, with elite heavily armoured cavalry supported by fellahin militia as infantry. On 13 July French scouts found Murad's camp near Shubra Khit. French artillery destroyed the Mamluk flagship on the Nile and forced a retreat, an early demonstration of how concentrated firepower could stop cavalry.

On 21 July, after marching all night, the French reached the village of Embabeh. Napoleon formed each of his five divisions into a hollow rectangle with cavalry and baggage in the centre and cannon at the corners. He told his troops that forty centuries looked down on them from the pyramids, from which he named the battle. The divisions of Louis Desaix, Jean-Louis-Ébénézer Reynier, Charles-François-Joseph Dugua, Honoré Vial and Louis André Bon advanced in echelon, with the Nile on their left.

Murad anchored his right on the Nile at Embabeh, which was fortified with infantry and artillery, and his left on Biktil, planning to hold the flanks and strike the French centre with cavalry. Across the river Ibrahim Bey's army watched but could not cross. At about 15:30 Murad ordered his defterdar, Ayyub Bey, to lead a mass assault. The squares of Desaix, Reynier and Dugua repelled the horsemen with musketry and artillery. Meanwhile Bon's division formed attack columns and stormed Embabeh. The garrison broke, and many fled into the Nile, where hundreds drowned. The chronicler ʻAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jabartī wrote that the fighting lasted about three-quarters of an hour.

French reports listed 29 killed and 260 wounded. Murad's losses were far heavier, with thousands killed or wounded, including Ayyub Bey and perhaps 3,000 of the elite cavalry. Wounded in the cheek, Murad escaped to Upper Egypt, where he fought a guerrilla campaign until Desaix defeated him in late 1799. Napoleon entered Cairo on 24 July and set up a French administration, putting down later rebellions by force. The battle marked the beginning of the end of seven centuries of Mamluk dominance in Egypt. Its strategic effect was brief, because ten days later Admiral Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile, cutting Napoleon's army off from France.
battle-of-the-somme: The Chantilly Conference of December 1915 agreed on simultaneous offensives in 1916 by the Russian, Italian, British and French armies. The Somme offensive was the Franco-British share, with the French army to take the main part, supported on the northern flank by the British Fourth Army. When the Germans began the Battle of Verdun on 21 February 1916, French commanders diverted many of the divisions intended for the Somme, and the British attack became the principal effort. The British force was a mixture of wartime volunteers from the Territorial Force and Kitchener's Army with the remains of the pre-war army.

A five-day artillery bombardment preceded the attack, which began on 1 July 1916. The French Sixth Army and the right wing of the British Fourth Army inflicted a considerable defeat on the German Second Army, but from the Albert–Bapaume road north to Gommecourt, where the Germans had made their main defensive effort, the British attack was a disaster. British casualties on the first day were 57,470, including 19,240 killed, the worst in the history of the British Army.

Douglas Haig abandoned the attack north of the road to reinforce the success in the south, and the offensive became the capture of fortified villages and woods that offered observation for artillery. The Battle of Flers–Courcelette on 15 to 22 September saw the first use of tanks on the Somme and the debut of the Canadian Corps and the New Zealand Division. The battle is dated to 18 November.

More than three million men fought in the battle, and more than one million were wounded or killed. The Anglo-French operational objectives were not achieved, since they failed to capture Péronne and Bapaume. In March 1917 the Germans made a strategic retreat of about 25 miles to the Hindenburg Line in Operation Alberich.

In the United Kingdom and Newfoundland the Somme became the central memory of the First World War, commemorated on 1 July each year at the Thiepval Memorial to the Missing of the Somme. Some historians see it as the beginning of modern all-arms warfare, in which Kitchener's Army learned to fight a mass-industrial war. Debate continues over the necessity, significance and effect of the battle.
battle-of-the-teutoburg-forest: Julius Caesar conquered most of western Europe in the Gallic Wars and twice crossed the Rhine, but his engagements with Germanic tribes were inconclusive. Rome then neglected the continent for two decades, and the Gauls rebelled when troops left in 31 BCE. Publius Quinctilius Varus, appointed by Augustus to command in Germania in 7 CE, had been consul and governor of Africa and Syria. The historian Michael McNally judges that he was sent for his political skill in handling the Germanic factions rather than for military ability.

Arminius of the Cherusci had been taken to Rome as a hostage as a boy, received an aristocratic education, joined the Roman cavalry and commanded auxiliaries. He then returned home, still nominally loyal to Rome. His Roman training let him anticipate Roman tactics and deceive Varus.

Varus planned a simple campaign for 9 CE: the army would cross the Rhine and set up a summer camp in nominally pacified Cherusci territory. Sources say he took little military action that summer and held court instead, though the only contemporary account comes from Velleius Paterculus, who had reason to dislike him. In late summer Arminius invented reports of a local rebellion. Others advised Varus that there was too little time to suppress it, but Arminius proposed a shorter route through the territory of the Angrivarii, and Varus took it.

The army set out on 8 September, strung out for 15 to 20 kilometres on forest tracks, and Arminius meant to lead it toward Kalkriese, where the Angrivarii lay in ambush. In the late morning his Bructerii allies attacked along the line in a brief skirmish aimed at tiring the Romans. A torrential downpour began, and Varus ordered a camp. The fighting went on between 8 and 11 September.

Suetonius records that Augustus struck his head against the palace walls, shouting for Varus to give him back his legions. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used for Roman legions again. Tiberius took effective control, and Germanicus raided Germania in 14 CE. Arminius was poisoned by fellow Germans in 21 CE. Since the 15th century the battle has been seen as the event that ended Roman expansion at the Rhine, and in the 19th century it became part of German nationalist mythology. Recent scholars point to other reasons for the frontier, such as supply from the Mediterranean by river and the greater wealth of the Rhine lands.
battle-of-the-trebia: The Second Punic War followed the First Punic War of 264 to 241 BCE, in which Carthage was defeated by Rome. Hamilcar Barca then expanded Carthaginian Iberia into a quasi-monarchical territory ruled by his family, the Barcids, which gave Carthage silver mines, manpower and the means to resist Roman demands. In 218 BCE Hannibal led an army from Iberia through Gaul and across the Alps, reaching northern Italy in October with 38,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry.

The Gallic tribes of Cisalpine Gaul had risen against the Romans after colonists were settled at Placentia and Cremona. At the Battle of Ticinus, Publius Scipio led the Roman cavalry and light infantry against the Carthaginian cavalry, was beaten and wounded, and the Romans withdrew to a fortified camp near Placentia. The Senate ordered the second consul, Sempronius Longus, whose army in Sicily had been meant for an invasion of Africa, to march north. Because Scipio was partly incapacitated, Sempronius took overall command.

After a day of heavy skirmishing in which the Romans gained the upper hand, Sempronius was eager for battle. Hannibal had his brother Mago take 1,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry in the night to hide in an old brush-filled watercourse beside the flood plain where he meant to fight. His Numidian cavalry then lured the Romans out of their camp onto ground of his choosing. The armies were each about 40,000 strong, the Carthaginians stronger in cavalry and the Romans in infantry.

Fresh Carthaginian cavalry routed the outnumbered Roman cavalry, and light infantry outflanked the Roman infantry. Hannibal had also placed his elephants on either side of the infantry to discourage the Romans from approaching the flanks, and he thinned his line, especially the Gauls in the centre, to match the Roman length. The hidden force then struck the Roman infantry in the rear. Most Roman units collapsed, but about 10,000 under Sempronius kept formation and fought their way out to Placentia.

Historians disagree about Roman losses. Paul Erdkamp puts them at 20,000 killed, half the force, not counting prisoners. Carthaginian losses were several thousand, mostly Gallic infantry in the centre, and several elephants. News of the defeat caused panic in Rome at first, but this calmed when Sempronius arrived to preside over the consular elections. Gnaeus Servilius Geminus and Gaius Flaminius were chosen, and the new consuls raised fresh legions and built a fleet of 60 quinqueremes.

Gallic recruits flocked to Hannibal, whose army grew to 60,000. In spring 217 BCE he crossed the Apennine Mountains and won the Battle of Lake Trasimene, and in 216 BCE the Battle of Cannae, the last of what modern historians call the three great military calamities of the Romans in the first three years of the war.
battle-of-the-yarmuk: Emperor Heraclius had defeated the Sasanian Empire in 627 and restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in 629. The Muslims had seized Emesa, a march from Aleppo and from Antioch, where Heraclius resided. Alarmed, he prepared a counteroffensive, and in 635 Yazdegerd III of Persia sought an alliance, planning a simultaneous attack in Iraq. When Heraclius launched his offensive in May 636, Yazdegerd could not coordinate with it. The Muslims learned of the preparations from Byzantine prisoners, and on Khalid ibn al-Walid's advice Abu Ubayda pulled the army back from Palestine and Syria and concentrated it on the plain near Jabiyah and the Yarmuk River.

Estimates of the armies are uncertain. Early accounts give the Muslims 36,000 to 40,000 men and the Byzantines 60,000 to 70,000, while some modern estimates put the Byzantine army at 40,000 at most or even 15,000 to 20,000, and Warren Treadgold suggests 80,000 to 100,000 or more. The only early Byzantine source is Theophanes, who wrote a century later. Heraclius had told his commander Vahan to avoid battle until diplomacy was exhausted, and negotiations delayed the fighting for a month.

The battle began on 15 August 636 and lasted six days. On the first days the Byzantines tried limited attacks and then thrusts against the Muslim right wing and centre, which fell back, but Khalid used his mobile guard of cavalry to counterattack and the Byzantines made no breakthrough. On 20 August, with some 8,000 cavalry massed, Khalid rode round the Byzantine left wing and drove the Byzantine cavalry from the field. The infantry was left exposed and was forced towards the ravine to the west.

Khalid pursued the survivors towards Damascus. Vahan, who had escaped the fighting, was probably killed there, and Khalid entered Damascus, where he was welcomed. When news reached Heraclius at Antioch, he accepted that the defeat was God's decision and a result of the sins of the people, himself included. Lacking men and money to defend Syria, he sailed for Constantinople by night and, according to tradition, bade farewell to Syria.

The battle effectively ended Byzantine rule in Syria and is regarded as one of the most decisive in military history. It marked the culmination of the first great wave of early Muslim conquests after the death of Muhammad, which saw the Rashidun Caliphate advance into both the Sasanian and the Byzantine empires. It was also the most important victory of Khalid ibn al-Walid.
battle-of-thermopylae: Athens and Eretria had aided the Ionian Revolt against Darius I in 499–494 BCE, and Darius vowed to punish them. His first invasion of Greece ended in 490 BCE with the Greek victory at the Battle of Marathon. A decade later his son Xerxes had assembled a very large land and naval force to conquer Greece. The Athenian general Themistocles proposed that the allied Greeks block the Persian army at the pass of Thermopylae while the fleet held the Straits of Artemisium. The Spartans sent an advance force under King Leonidas I, with the 300 men of the royal bodyguard, to block the pass.

The Greek force numbered approximately 7,000. Ancient authors gave the Persian army in the millions; modern scholars estimate between 120,000 and 300,000. Xerxes attacked on the fifth day after the Persians reached the pass, first with 5,000 archers, whose arrows the Greeks' shields and bronze helmets deflected, then with waves of about 10,000 men. The Greeks fought at the narrowest part of the pass in a phalanx of overlapping shields, and the Persians could make no headway on the first day or the second.

On the second day Ephialtes, a local man motivated by the desire for a reward, told Xerxes of a mountain path around the pass. His name came to mean nightmare in Greek and to stand for the archetypal traitor. On the third day a Persian column bypassed the Phocians guarding the path. Leonidas, aware that he was being outflanked, dismissed most of the Greek army and stayed to guard the retreat with 300 Spartans and 700 Thespians; up to 900 helots and 400 Thebans are also reported to have remained. Most of the Thebans reportedly surrendered, and the others fought to the death.

The Persians now held the pass, and the Greek fleet at Artemisium withdrew to Salamis. The Persians overran Boeotia and captured the evacuated city of Athens, but the Greek fleet defeated them at the Battle of Salamis in late 480 BCE. Xerxes withdrew to Asia with much of his army, leaving Mardonius, who was decisively defeated at the Battle of Plataea the following year. Writers ancient and modern have used Thermopylae as an example of an army defending its native soil.
battle-of-tours: The Umayyad troops under Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani, governor-general of al-Andalus, overran Septimania by 719 and made Narbonne their capital from 720. Duke Odo the Great broke the siege of Toulouse, taking them by surprise, and Al-Samh ibn Malik was mortally wounded, but the Umayyads raided into Burgundy in 725. When Odo was later defeated, he appealed to the Franks for help, which Charles Martel granted only after Odo agreed to submit to Frankish authority.

In 732 the Umayyad advance force under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was heading north towards the Loire, having outpaced its supply wagons and part of its army. It was caught off guard to find a large Frankish force sitting directly in its path to Tours. Charles chose not to attack but to take up a defensive formation, and according to Arab sources the Franks drew up in a large square with hills and trees in front of them to break up cavalry charges. For a week the armies skirmished.

The battle was fought on 10 October 732 at a site between Poitiers and Tours that the sources do not fix exactly. Abd al-Rahman trusted in his cavalry and had it charge repeatedly through the day. According to Arab sources the cavalry broke into the Frankish square several times, but the Franks did not break. Al-Ghafiqi was killed in combat, and the Umayyad army withdrew.

The Umayyad army retreated south over the Pyrenees, and Charles continued to expand southwards. The Umayyads remained in control of parts of Septimania for another 27 years; Charles failed to take Narbonne in 737, and his son Pepin the Short forced its surrender in 759. Ninth-century chroniclers gave Charles the nickname Martel, the hammer.

Historians disagree about the battle's importance. Edward Gibbon and others held that it halted the spread of Islam in Western Europe. Alessandro Barbero writes that historians now tend to play down its significance, since the Muslim force aimed to pillage the monastery of St-Martin of Tours rather than conquer the Frankish kingdom. Arab historians who mention it at all present it as a minor skirmish. Most historians agree the battle helped lay the foundations of the Carolingian Empire.
battle-of-trafalgar: In 1805 Napoleon Bonaparte's First French Empire dominated the European continent by land, while the Royal Navy held the seas through blockades. Napoleon renewed his determination to invade Britain, and to bring his invasion flotilla across the English Channel he needed to wrest control of it from the Royal Navy. Vice-Admiral Villeneuve's fleet evaded Horatio Nelson's blockade of Toulon, joined the Spanish fleet at Cádiz and sailed for the Caribbean. Nelson pursued it across the Atlantic and missed it by a few days. Villeneuve returned to Europe and ended at Cádiz, where Napoleon ordered him in September to sail to Naples.

Villeneuve changed his mind several times, and on 18 October he ordered the combined fleet to sail, though the winds were very light. On 21 October, off Cape Trafalgar, it met Nelson's fleet of 27 ships of the line, against Villeneuve's 33. Nelson sailed at the flank of the Franco-Spanish line in two columns, hoping to break it up and force a melee in which his well-trained crews could fight ship to ship, instead of the usual parallel lines of battle.

At 11:45 Nelson signalled to the fleet, England expects that every man will do his duty. The light winds meant the leading British ships were under heavy fire for almost an hour before their own guns could bear. Nelson's flagship HMS Victory led one column and was almost knocked out of action; Nelson was shot by a French marksman and died shortly before the battle ended. The columns split the Franco-Spanish fleet into three groups and isolated the rear, which was overwhelmed. The British lost no ships, and Villeneuve was captured.

A storm followed the battle and wrecked or sank several of the captured ships. On 4 November 1805 a British squadron under Sir Richard Strachan captured four French ships that had escaped the battle. The victory confirmed Britain's naval supremacy and ended any real effort by Napoleon to invade Britain; Britain's command of the sea was not tested for over a century. Nelson's death in victory secured his place as a British national hero.
battle-of-tsushima: The Russo-Japanese War began on 8 February 1904, when Japanese destroyers made a surprise attack on the Russian Far East Fleet at Port Arthur. Japan needed to neutralise Russian naval power in order to secure its supply lines to the mainland and fight a ground war in Manchuria. After the Russian First Pacific Squadron fell inactive and Port Arthur came under siege, the Tsar agreed to form a Second Pacific Squadron from the Baltic Fleet, including 11 of its 13 battleships. The voyage lasted over seven months and covered 18,000 nautical miles. In the Dogger Bank incident the squadron mistook British fishing trawlers for Japanese torpedo boats, killing several fishermen.

Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky revealed his choice of the Tsushima Strait, the shortest route, only on 25 May 1905. The fleet approached in radio silence, but a Japanese ship located it early on 27 May and reported by wireless, and Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō sailed with the Combined Fleet. In the afternoon Tōgō turned his line in sequence across the Russian course. The Russian gunnery proved surprisingly good, but Rozhestvensky was wounded and knocked unconscious, and four Russian battleships were sunk by sunset.

At night 21 destroyers and 45 torpedo boats attacked for three hours without a break, and the Russians dispersed into small groups. On the morning of 28 May the Japanese surrounded the squadron of Admiral Nebogatov, who ordered the four remaining battleships to surrender. Tōgō's greater battle experience, extensive Japanese gunnery practice, high-explosive shells, wireless telegraphy and British help with guns, ships and intelligence are all credited with the result.

All 11 Russian battleships were lost, seven sunk and four captured. Only a cruiser and two destroyers reached Vladivostok. Russian losses were 216 officers and 4,614 men killed, with about 6,000 taken prisoner. Japan lost three torpedo boats and 117 men killed, and none of its heavy ships.

The loss forced Russia to seek peace, and the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed in September 1905. In Japan Tōgō was revered as a national hero, and his flagship Mikasa is preserved as a museum ship at Yokosuka. It was the only decisive engagement ever fought between modern steel battleship fleets and the first in which wireless telegraphy played a critical role. It showed that faster battleships with long-range big guns were superior to mixed batteries, which led to the dreadnought arms race. Russia's prestige was badly damaged and the defeat was a blow to the Romanov dynasty.
battle-of-uhud: After the Muslims migrated to Medina, hostilities with the Quraysh of Mecca grew, largely because of Muslim raids on Meccan caravans. In 624 the Muslims defeated a more numerous Meccan force at Badr, where several Quraysh leaders were killed, including Amr ibn Hisham. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, chosen as their leader, vowed revenge, and wealthy Meccans who had lost relatives gave money for another expedition. He mobilised more than 3,000 men against Medina.

Muhammad had meant to stay in Medina and use its fortifications, but many Muslims who had missed Badr wanted open battle, and he gave way. Shortly before the battle Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, chief of the Khazraj, withdrew with 300 men. The Muslim force of around 700 took position on the slopes of Mount Uhud, which protected its rear. Muhammad posted 50 archers on a nearby hill to guard the flank against the Meccan cavalry and ordered them not to leave their places.

The battle took place on 23 March 625. It opened with duels in which the Meccan standard-bearer Talha ibn Abi Talha was killed by Ali ibn Abi Talib, and others of his family who took up the banner fell one after another. In the general engagement the Muslims swept through the Meccan ranks. Believing the battle won, most of the archers left the hill to collect spoils. Khalid ibn al-Walid, commanding the Meccan cavalry, attacked the few who stayed and then struck the Muslim flank and rear.

Many Muslims were killed, among them Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's uncle. Rumour spread that Muhammad had died, but he had been wounded in the face. Umar ibn al-Khattab rallied the troops, and a counter-charge drove Khalid's men from the slopes. The Meccan cavalry could not climb the slope, and Abu Sufyan returned to Mecca without attacking the wounded Muslims again.

Scholars differ on the result. Chase F. Robinson writes that a disheartening Muslim defeat is clear enough, while William Montgomery Watt notes that the Meccans failed to destroy Muhammad and his followers. The Qur'an, in a verse revealed soon after, attributes the setback to disobedience and desire for loot and treats it as a test. Abu Sufyan then sought alliances with nomadic tribes, and the Quraysh returned in 627 with a larger confederate force at the Battle of the Trench. Khalid ibn al-Walid's leadership at Uhud was an early sign of the career that made him one of the best-known Arab generals of the later conquests.
battle-of-valmy: The battle came early in the War of the First Coalition, when the monarchies of Europe sought to stop the French Revolution or contain it to France. King Frederick William II of Prussia, supported by Great Britain and Austria, sent the Duke of Brunswick towards Paris with a large army. Longwy fell on 23 August and Verdun on 2 September 1792. About 54,000 French troops in the Army of the North under Charles Dumouriez and the Army of the Centre under François Kellermann faced Brunswick's coalition army of about 84,000, which included Hessians and French royalist émigrés. Just over half of the French infantry were regulars of the old Royal Army, as were nearly all the cavalry.

Dumouriez abandoned his plan to attack the Austrian Netherlands and approached the invaders from the rear. Kellermann joined him at Sainte-Menehould on 19 September, which put the French east of the Prussians and behind their lines. Brunswick, troubled by bad weather and sickness, turned back to fight. On 20 September Kellermann took position on slopes near Valmy, around an old windmill that he had razed, and his artillery opened what is called the Cannonade of Valmy.

Kellermann had about 36,000 men and 40 cannon, Brunswick about 34,000 and 54 cannon. The French batteries proved superior, and the Prussian infantry made a cautious, fruitless advance under fire. Kellermann is said to have raised his hat and cried Vive la Nation, and the troops sang La Marseillaise and Ça Ira. To general surprise Brunswick broke off the action. Casualties were no more than three hundred French and two hundred Prussians. Brunswick withdrew towards Germany on 30 September without being attacked.

Historians have never settled why the Prussians withdrew. Most point to the strong French position, growing reinforcements and the unexpected spirit of the volunteers, together with Prussian worries about the Russian invasion of Poland. Stories of a secret plea by Louis XVI or of bribery are doubted; Munro Price finds no convincing proof of bribery.

Beset by food shortages and dysentery, the Prussians retreated beyond the Rhine, and French troops took Mainz in October. On the day of the battle the Legislative Assembly had transferred its power to the National Convention, which then abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the French Republic. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who was with the Prussian army, later wrote that a new epoch in the history of the world had begun. Kellermann was ennobled by Napoleon in 1808 and became Duke of Valmy.
battle-of-varna: The Hungarian kingdom fell into crisis after the death of King Sigismund in 1437, and his successor Albert died in 1439. Hungarian nobles then called the young Władysław III of Poland to the throne, expecting help against the Ottomans, and he ruled beside the nobleman John Hunyadi. The sultan Murad II signed a ten-year truce with Hungary and in 1444 resigned the throne to his twelve-year-old son Mehmed II.

Cardinal Julian Cesarini insisted that Władysław should break the truce, arguing that it was invalid because it had been made with infidels. Hungary worked with Venice and Pope Eugene IV to raise a new crusader army under Hunyadi and Władysław. Çandarlı Halil Pasha recalled Murad II, who commanded the Ottoman army. The crusaders numbered some 20,000, mainly Hungarian, Polish, Bohemian and 4,000 Wallachian troops.

An Ottoman army of around 40,000 or 60,000 approached Varna on 9 November. Cesarini first urged withdrawal, then a defence behind the Hussite Wagenburg until the fleet arrived. The young Władysław and Hunyadi rejected defensive tactics, and Hunyadi declared: "To escape is impossible, to surrender is unthinkable."

On 10 November Hunyadi drew up the army in an arc 3.5 kilometres long between Lake Varna and the Franga plateau. Ottoman light cavalry assaulted the Croats, and when the Christians pursued them in disorder, the Anatolian cavalry ambushed them. The right wing fled into the marshland, where Cesarini met his end. Against Hunyadi's advice, Władysław led 500 Polish knights at the Ottoman centre and almost reached Murad, but in front of his tent the king's horse fell or was stabbed.

Hunyadi organised the retreat of the remains of the army, which had suffered thousands of casualties. The king's head and body were never found. Turkish chroniclers say a mercenary beheaded him, but Murad II's own memorandum says he survived the battle and was executed later in captivity. Hunyadi became Governor of Hungary on 5 June 1446.

Hungary passed to the four-year-old Ladislaus the Posthumous, while Poland had a three-year interregnum before Casimir IV Jagiellon. The Ottoman victories at Varna and at the Second Battle of Kosovo in 1448 deterred European states from sending help to the Byzantines in 1453. The fallen king was given the name Ladislaus of Varna (Władysław III Warneńczyk), and the battle is commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw.
battle-of-verdun: By late 1914 the war of movement on the Western Front had ended, and offensives gained little ground at heavy cost. According to his memoirs, the German Chief of the General Staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed that the French army could still be defeated if it suffered enough casualties. He offered five corps for an offensive at Verdun, but only on the east bank of the Meuse. Verdun, a town that had played an important part in the defence of France for centuries, was ringed by a double line of 28 forts, but in 1915 guns and ammunition had been removed from many of them.

Bad weather delayed the German attack from 12 to 21 February 1916. It began with a ten-hour bombardment by 808 guns, which fired about 1,000,000 shells, and German stormtroopers followed with flamethrowers and grenades. The Germans captured Fort Douaumont four days later. Philippe Pétain ordered that there be no retreat and that German attacks be counter-attacked. The Germans extended the offensive to the west bank of the Meuse to eliminate the French artillery there, but the attacks failed to reach their objectives.

The Germans captured Fort Vaux in June and came within 4 kilometres of the Verdun citadel, but the Brusilov Offensive and the opening of the Battle of the Somme on 1 July forced them to transfer artillery from Verdun. In September and December French counter-offensives recaptured much ground on the east bank, including Fort Douaumont and Fort Vaux. The battle lasted 302 days, the longest of the First World War.

In 2000 Hannes Heer and Klaus Naumann calculated that the French suffered 377,231 casualties and the Germans 337,000, a total of 714,231. Rain and constant bombardment turned the clay soil into mud full of debris and human remains, and forests were obliterated. Accounts of men breaking down with insanity and shell shock were common.

In France, Verdun came to symbolise the determination of the French Army and the destructiveness of the war, and it has become for the French the representative memory of the First World War, as the Somme is for the British. In 1920 a ceremony was held in the citadel of Verdun to choose the body for the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Arc de Triomphe.
battle-of-vienna-1683: Capturing Vienna had long been an Ottoman aim, because the city controlled the Danube and the trade routes to Germany. Suleiman's advance had been stopped at Szigetvár in 1566, and Vienna was not threatened again until 1683. Under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha the Ottomans made extensive preparations. In Habsburg Hungary, unrest against Leopold I's Counter-Reformation had grown into rebellion, and in 1681 the Ottomans reinforced the forces of Imre Thököly. A peace had held between the two empires for twenty years.

The Ottomans laid siege to Vienna on 14 July 1683. Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg, commanding the garrison, refused to surrender, having heard of the massacre at Perchtoldsdorf, where townspeople who had surrendered were killed. The Viennese demolished houses near the walls, and the Ottomans dug trenches and mines towards the city.

Delays in the siege gave a relief force time to arrive. Poles and Imperial troops assembled in only six days under King John III Sobieski, with money from bankers, noblemen and the Pope. Kara Mustafa left his rear to the Khan of Crimea, who refused to attack the relief force as it crossed the Danube. The Wallachian prince Șerban Cantacuzino, sympathetic to the Christian side, also proved unreliable.

On 12 September the Ottomans attacked at 4:00 in the morning to disturb the deployment. Charles of Lorraine's Imperial troops counterattacked and took the villages of Nussdorf and Heiligenstadt, and ten Ottoman mines under the walls were found and disarmed. In the afternoon Polish infantry advanced on the Ottoman right and took Gersthof, and as the Imperial troops closed in, the Polish cavalry charged, in what is noted as the largest cavalry charge in history.

Ottoman losses in the battle itself are put at 8,000 to 15,000 dead, and the relief force lost about 3,500 killed and wounded. The Ottoman raiding of 1683 in the Austrian and Hungarian border zone took 57,220 people as slaves. Kara Mustafa was executed in Belgrade on 25 December. The war continued until 1699, when the Treaty of Karlowitz ceded most of Ottoman Hungary to the Habsburgs. Historians see the battle as the end of Ottoman expansion into Europe, and Pope Innocent XI extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church in commemoration.
battle-of-vouille: The battle was fought at Vouillé, near Poitiers, around the spring of 507 in the Franco-Gothic War, between the Franks under Clovis and the Visigoths under Alaric II. Clovis had already defeated the Alemanni east of the Rhine and the Burgundians in the Rhone Valley, and the growing power of the Franks threatened Alaric's territory in Aquitaine and Hispania. Theodoric the Great tried to broker peace between the two kings, but Clovis began a campaign to seize Aquitaine and Alaric's centre of power at Toulouse. Alaric marched north with his army and an Auvergnat militia commanded by Apollinaris of Clermont.

Clovis's army was slowed by the rain-swollen Vienne River, but it still engaged the Visigoths south of Vouillé. He kept his missile troops at the rear and sent the rest of the army forward to fight hand to hand. Although Alaric's army was larger and better equipped, his soldiers wavered after all the Auvergnat commanders except Apollinaris were killed. In the melee Clovis allegedly killed Alaric himself, whereupon the Visigothic army broke and fled. Clovis's army then went south and plundered Alaric's treasure at Toulouse.

The Franks conquered Gallia Aquitania, and the Visigoths withdrew to Septimania, which they continued to hold. The Byzantine emperor Anastasius made Clovis an honorary consul and patrician. Alaric's illegitimate son Gesalec tried to organise a counterstroke at Narbonne but was deposed and eventually killed when Narbonne was taken by the Burgundian allies of the Franks. Clovis later drove the Goths out of Angoulême, and his son Theuderic I defeated them in Hispania.
battle-of-wagram: In 1809 Napoleon had moved a number of soldiers from the Confederation of the Rhine to the Peninsular War. The Austrian Empire saw its chance to recover some of its former sphere of influence and invaded the Kingdom of Bavaria, a French ally. Napoleon beat the Austrian forces and occupied Vienna at the beginning of May 1809, but Archduke Charles of Austria-Teschen salvaged an army and retreated north of the Danube, so the war went on.

Towards the end of May, Napoleon suffered a surprise defeat at the Battle of Aspern-Essling, which cost some 53,000 casualties, almost equally divided between the two armies. It took him six weeks to prepare his next offensive, for which he gathered a French, German and Italian army of over 150,000 men near Vienna.

The battle began after Napoleon crossed the Danube with the bulk of his forces during the night of 4 July and attacked the Austrian army, which had over 130,000 men. On the first day he tried for an early breakthrough with a series of evening attacks. The Austrians were thinly spread in a wide semicircle but held a naturally strong position, and the attacks failed. Napoleon knew by that night that he had sustained high losses.

At dawn on 6 July Archduke Charles launched attacks along the whole line, hoping to take the French in a double envelopment. The offensive failed against the French right but nearly broke Napoleon's left. He redeployed IV Corps under Masséna to steady that wing and set up a grand battery, while Marshal Davout attacked the Austrian left. With his flank collapsing and no reserves left, Charles ordered an orderly retreat.

Napoleon was the uncontested winner but did not secure an overwhelming victory. With more than 300,000 combatants, it was the largest battle in European history up to that time, and with at least 72,000 casualties it was the bloodiest engagement of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars thus far. The cause was an unprecedented concentration of artillery on a flat battlefield; each army fired at least 90,000 roundshot. French casualties numbered 34,000, including over thirty generals.

On 7 July Napoleon made General MacDonald a Marshal of the Empire on the field, the only man so raised, and later gave Louis-Alexandre Berthier the title of 1st Prince of Wagram. The Treaty of Schönbrunn meant the loss of one sixth of the Austrian Empire's subjects.
battle-of-warsaw-1920: Poland fought after the First World War to keep its newly regained independence and to fix its eastern borders. In April 1920 Józef Piłsudski allied with the Ukrainian leader Symon Petlyura, and their forces entered Kiev on 7 May. A Soviet counter-offensive then forced the Poles back, and the Red Army's 1st Cavalry Army under Semyon Budyonny broke through in early June. On 4 July Mikhail Tukhachevsky's Western Front began an assault from the Berezina River, and by the end of July it had reached Białystok.

Vladimir Lenin viewed Poland as a bridge to Central and Western Europe, and Bolshevik speeches held that the shortest route to Berlin and Paris lay through Warsaw. Foreign observers expected Poland to collapse.

On the night of 5-6 August Piłsudski conceived a plan in which Polish armies would hold Warsaw while a strike group of about 20,000 men, under his own command, attacked northward from the Wieprz River into the weak point between the Soviet fronts. Many officers called it amateurish, and Piłsudski himself called it a gamble. Tukhachevsky meanwhile planned to cross the Vistula north-west of Warsaw and encircle the city.

The Soviet assault on Warsaw began on 12 August, and Radzymin, east of the city, fell on 14 August. Polish forces retook it on 15 August. Budyonny's army, influenced by command quarrels, marched on Lwów rather than Warsaw. On 16 August Piłsudski's group advanced 45 kilometres against almost no opposition and cut the communications of the Soviet 16th Army. Polish radio units also broke Soviet ciphers. On 18 August Tukhachevsky ordered a retreat, but by 21 August organised resistance had ceased.

Three Soviet armies and a cavalry corps largely disintegrated, and between 25,000 and 30,000 Soviet troops crossed into East Prussia, where they were briefly interned. Polish victories followed at the Battle of Komarów on 31 August and at the Niemen River in September. A ceasefire was signed on 12 October under pressure from France and Britain, and the Treaty of Riga was signed on 18 March 1921.

The name Miracle on the Vistula was coined by the deputy Stanisław Stroński, who disapproved of Piłsudski's Ukrainian campaign. Prime Minister Wincenty Witos replied that this was the miracle of 1920. Many participants credited the Virgin Mary, since 15 August is the feast of the Assumption. The Soviet defeat ended plans for revolutions in Germany and elsewhere, and cancelled a planned Soviet move against Lithuania.
battle-of-waterloo: When Napoleon I returned to power in March 1815, at the start of the Hundred Days, the powers at the Congress of Vienna declared him an outlaw, and the United Kingdom, Russia, Austria and Prussia mobilised armies as the Seventh Coalition. Critically outnumbered, Napoleon judged that his only chance was to attack before the coalition was ready. Wellington's and Blücher's armies were cantoned close to the north-eastern border of France, and he planned to strike them separately. On 16 June he defeated the bulk of the Prussian army at the Battle of Ligny, while a smaller French force fought the Battle of Quatre Bras. The Prussians withdrew in good order, and Wellington fell back in parallel to the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean near Waterloo.

On Sunday 18 June the French army of around 74,500 men and 254 guns faced a multinational army under Wellington. Napoleon had sent a third of his forces after the Prussians, and they were held at the Battle of Wavre. The French attacked the farm of Hougoumont in the morning, then bombarded the centre with the 80 guns of the grande batterie and sent infantry columns forward. British heavy cavalry charged in support of the hard-pressed infantry. Around 16:00 Marshal Ney, mistaking the movement of wounded to the rear for a retreat, led massed cavalry, about 9,000 horsemen, against Wellington's centre, but they could not break the infantry squares. The French later captured the farm of La Haye Sainte.

At about 13:15 Napoleon had seen Prussian columns approaching his right flank, and from about 16:30 Prussian corps under Bülow, Zieten and Pirch arrived in strength and fought through Plancenoit. At about 19:30 Napoleon committed his last reserve, the Imperial Guard. Wellington's line repulsed it, the Prussians broke through on the French right, and the French army was routed.

Wellington lost around 17,000 killed or wounded and Blücher some 7,000. Napoleon lost between 24,000 and 26,000 killed or wounded, including 6,000 to 7,000 captured, and about 15,000 more deserted in the following days. Wellington called the battle the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life. Napoleon abdicated four days later, and coalition forces entered Paris on 7 July. The defeat ended the Hundred Days and the First French Empire.

Later generations in Europe saw Waterloo as the turning point that ended the wars convulsing Europe since the French Revolution and ushered in the Concert of Europe, a period of relative peace often called the Pax Britannica. The battlefield lies about 15 kilometres south of Brussels. In 1820 King William I of the Netherlands ordered a monument there, and the Lion's Mound, a hill built from 300,000 cubic metres of earth taken from the ridge, now dominates the site.
battle-of-white-mountain: Most Bohemian estates, though under the Holy Roman Empire, had large Protestant populations and rights granting them religious and political freedom. In 1617 Ferdinand, a devout Catholic and supporter of the Counter-Reformation, was named successor to Emperor Matthias as emperor and King of Bohemia. Protestants feared for their property and their semi-autonomy, under which the king was elected, and Rudolf II's 1609 Letter of Majesty seemed violated.
