Germanic tribes settled from about 500 BCE, the Burgundians followed the Semnones after about 200 CE, and in the 7th century Slavic tribes, later known as the Hevelli and Sprevane, reached the region.

Berlin was first documented in the 13th century, at the crossing of two important trade routes. It was capital of the Margraviate of Brandenburg from 1417, the Kingdom of Prussia from 1701 and the German Empire from 1871. In 1685 the Edict of Potsdam granted religious freedom and tax-free status to French Huguenot refugees.

The Greater Berlin Act of 1920 raised the population from 1.9 million to 4 million, and in the 1920s Berlin was the third-largest city in the world. It was capital of the Weimar Republic and of Nazi Germany until 1945. After the Second World War it was split into West Berlin and East Berlin, divided by the Berlin Wall, and Bonn became the West German capital. Berlin again became the capital of all Germany after reunification on 3 October 1990.

Berlin covers 891 km2 and is the most populous city proper in the European Union. Since 1990 it has been one of three city-states among the 16 states of Germany, governed by the Senate and the 141-seat Abgeordnetenhaus. The bombing of the Second World War devastated the city, and many surviving buildings were later demolished; after reunification many heritage structures were reconstructed.

Museum Island, designated a district dedicated to art and antiquities by royal decree in 1841, is one of three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Charité hospital traces its origins to 1710, and Robert Koch and Rudolf Virchow worked in Berlin. The city hosted the 1936 Summer Olympics.
berlin-conference: Until the later 19th century European power in Africa was largely confined to the coast, where traders held posts protected by gunboats. In 1876 King Leopold II of Belgium founded the International African Association and invited Henry Morton Stanley to join him; from 1878 to 1885 Stanley returned to the Congo as Leopold's agent.

France answered in 1881 by sending the naval officer Pierre de Brazza, who raised the French flag over Brazzaville, and Portugal made a treaty with Great Britain on 26 February 1884 to block the Congo Society's access to the Atlantic. Germany began expeditions of its own, which alarmed British and French statesmen. With British support and on Portugal's initiative, Otto von Bismarck called representatives of thirteen European nations and the United States to Berlin.

The conference met on 15 November 1884 and closed on 26 February 1885 with the signing of the General Act of Berlin. Fourteen countries sent plenipotentiaries, each with a single vote; the United States reserved the right to accept or decline its conclusions. No African state took part.

Sultan Barghash bin Seyyid of Zanzibar asked to send a representative, but British pressure from the Anti-Slavery Society, which objected to Zanzibar's part in the slave trade, led to refusal. Six of the fourteen countries, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden-Norway and the United States, came home without any zone of interest in Africa.

The General Act confirmed the holdings of Leopold's International Congo Society, and on 1 August 1885 the territory was named the Congo Free State, a name absent from the Act. It decreed free trade among the signatories throughout the Congo Basin and made the Niger and Congo rivers free for shipping. Article 6 called on the powers to strive for the suppression of slavery.

Under the principle of effective occupation a power could acquire rights only if it had treaties with local leaders, flew its flag and set up an administration, and it had to notify the other signatories of any possession or protectorate it took in Africa. The Act concerned lands on the coast, and allowed a state to claim the hinterland after occupying the coast.

The conference is usually seen as formalising the Scramble for Africa, and by 1914 about 90 per cent of the continent was under European control. Some historians, among them Sybil Crowe, Matthew Craven and Simon Katzenellenbogen, caution against overstating its role, pointing to the many bilateral agreements before and after it. The only borders set at the conference were those of the Congo region, and these were later revised.
berlin-wall: After the Second World War, Germany west of the Oder-Neisse line was divided into four occupation zones, and Berlin, the seat of the Allied Control Council, into four sectors, although it lay wholly within the Soviet zone. The inner German border was closed officially in 1952, but the border in Berlin, administered by all four powers, stayed far more open, and Berlin became the main route by which East Germans left for the West. Before the Wall, 3.5 million East Germans, 20% of the population, had left the GDR.

Emigrants tended to be young and well-educated, which fed official fears of a brain drain. On 15 June 1961 Walter Ulbricht told a press conference that no one had the intention of erecting a wall. A transcript of a telephone call of 1 August suggests the initiative came from Nikita Khrushchev, though other sources say he was wary of Western reaction and that Ulbricht had pushed for a closure.

Construction began on 13 August 1961. The Wall was more than 140 kilometres long, with guard towers and concrete walls, an outer wall and an inner wall, and between them a wide area later known as the death strip. This held anti-vehicle trenches, a strip of raked sand that showed footprints, beds of nails and clear fields of fire. It went through four versions, from a wire fence and concrete block wall in 1961 to the Grenzmauer 75 of 1975 to 1989.

Eastern Bloc propaganda presented it as the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart, while West Berlin's mayor, Willy Brandt, called it the Wall of Shame. There were nine official crossings, the best known being Checkpoint Charlie, restricted to Allied personnel and foreigners.

More than 100,000 people attempted to escape, and about 5,000 succeeded. A research group in Potsdam confirmed at least 140 deaths, while others estimate well above 200. In 1989 revolutions in Poland and Hungary and the Pan-European Picnic set off a peaceful development in which the Iron Curtain largely broke. On 9 November 1989 the East German government announced that all GDR citizens could visit West Germany and West Berlin. Crowds crossed and climbed onto the Wall, and souvenir hunters chipped away pieces of it. Full demolition began on 13 June 1990 and ended in 1994, and German reunification took place on 3 October 1990.
bermuda: Bermuda is an archipelago of 181 islands, though the most significant are connected by bridges and appear to form one landmass. Its land area is 54 square kilometres. The nearest land is the coast of North Carolina, about 1,035 kilometres to the west-northwest. The islands lie in the west of the Sargasso Sea and have a tropical climate; a coral reef gives them some protection from tropical cyclones. When discovered, they had no human population and were dominated by forests of Bermuda cedar.

Bermuda was discovered in the early 1500s by the Spanish explorer Juan de Bermúdez and appears on Spanish charts of 1511. Spanish and Portuguese ships used it to take on fresh meat and water. Legends of spirits and devils, now thought to stem from the calls of birds and the noises of introduced wild hogs, together with storms and dangerous reefs, gave it the name Isle of Devils, and neither Spain nor Portugal tried to settle it.

In 1609 a flotilla bound for the Jamestown colony was broken up by a storm, and its flagship, the Sea Venture, was driven onto Bermuda's reef to prevent her sinking, so that all aboard survived. Having heard the true conditions in Jamestown, the settlers were unwilling to move on and made several attempts to rebel and stay. The new settlement became a prison labour camp and built two ships, the Deliverance and the Patience. The Somers Isles Company suppressed shipbuilding, wanting the colonists to farm, but the islanders turned to maritime trades, and in 1684 the company's charter was revoked. The House of Assembly dates from 1620.

After the American Revolution the Royal Navy began improving the harbours, and in 1811 work began on the Royal Naval Dockyard on Ireland Island, guarding the western Atlantic shipping lanes. In the War of 1812 the British attacks on Washington, D.C., and the Chesapeake were planned and launched from Bermuda. In the early 20th century it became a popular destination for tourists, and the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 ended its agricultural export trade to America and encouraged tourism.

Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory and a self-governing parliamentary democracy, with a bicameral parliament in the capital Hamilton; the United Kingdom is responsible for foreign affairs and defence. It is divided into nine parishes. An independence referendum in 1995 produced a large majority against independence. The historic Town of St. George's is a World Heritage Site.
bernal-diaz-del-castillo: Bernal Díaz was born around 1492 in Medina del Campo, a prosperous commercial city in Castile. His father, Francisco Díaz del Castillo, was a regidor, or city councillor, which gave the family some prominence. He later showed a knack for languages, learning Taíno in Cuba, Nahuatl in Mexico and Cakchiquel in Guatemala.

In 1514, aged about eighteen, he left home as a common foot soldier in the expedition of Pedrarias Dávila, the largest fleet yet sent to mainland America, with 19 vessels and 1,500 people. At Darien, in present-day Colombia, famine and an epidemic killed more than half of the settlers. In 1517 he joined Francisco Hernández de Córdoba's expedition to Yucatán, and in 1518 he returned to the Yucatán coast under Juan de Grijalva.

Back in Cuba, Díaz enlisted in the expedition of Hernán Cortés and took part in the campaigns against the Mexica, or Aztec Empire. He later described many of the 119 battles in which he fought, ending with the defeat of the Aztecs in 1521. Cortés awarded him an encomienda in 1522, confirmed and added to in 1527 and 1528. He settled in Guatemala in 1541 and in 1551, during a trip to Spain, was appointed regidor of Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala, now Antigua Guatemala.

Like many conquistadors, he was discontent that he had not won the wealth he hoped for and felt that the Spanish government had failed to acknowledge his efforts. He died in Guatemala at the age of 92, in early January 1584.

His Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, finished in 1568, was begun almost thirty years after the events and expanded after he read the biography of Cortés by Francisco López de Gómara. The title answers Cortés's own letters to the king and the claims of Gómara, Bartolomé de las Casas and others who were not on the campaign. Díaz held that Cortés took most of the credit and minimised the sacrifices of the other Spaniards and of Indigenous allies such as the Tlaxcaltecs, and he thought Bernardino de Sahagún too sympathetic to the Aztecs.

The book describes the peoples of New Spain, the Aztec palaces, marketplaces and gardens, and the human sacrifice and cannibalism he says he witnessed. Of the ruined Tenochtitlan he wrote that nothing remained of the wonders he had seen. It was published in 1632. Written decades afterwards and containing inaccuracies and biases, it is one of only two first-hand accounts of the Spanish overthrow of the Aztecs.
bernard-of-clairvaux: Bernard's parents, Tescelin de Fontaine, lord of Fontaine-lès-Dijon, and Alèthe de Montbard, belonged to the highest nobility of Burgundy. He was the third of seven children, six of them sons. At nine he was sent to a school at Châtillon-sur-Seine run by the secular canons of Saint-Vorles, where he was drawn to literature and rhetoric. After his mother died he decided to go to Cîteaux, the abbey founded near Dijon in 1098 by a group led by Robert of Molesme to live by a literal reading of the Rule of St Benedict.

Three years after entering Cîteaux, Bernard was sent with twelve monks to found a new house at the Vallée d'Absinthe in the diocese of Langres, which he named Clairvaux on 25 June 1115. Its beginnings were austere, but candidates flocked to it, and more than sixty abbeys followed in his lifetime. He defended the Cistercians against criticism from the Benedictines of Cluny in his Apology, and Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, answered with admiration and friendship.

At the Council of Troyes in 1128 he traced the outlines of the Rule of the Knights Templar. When Honorius II died in 1130 and the election of Innocent II and the Antipope Anacletus II split the Church, Bernard was chosen at the council of Étampes to judge between them and decided for Innocent, then spent years winning over rulers and cities; the schism ended with Anacletus's death in 1138. In 1141 he secured the condemnation of Peter Abelard at a council at Sens.

In 1146 Pope Eugene III commissioned him to preach the Second Crusade, and on 31 March, with King Louis VII present, he preached to an enormous crowd at Vézelay. He also opposed attacks on Jews in the Rhineland and silenced the monk Radulf, who was inspiring them.

The failure of the Second Crusade saddened his last years and put the whole responsibility on him; he wrote that the sins of the crusaders had caused it. He died on 20 August 1153, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Clairvaux. After his remains were destroyed in 1792 by the French Revolutionary government, they were transferred to Troyes Cathedral.

He was canonized 21 years after his death and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830. Against the rational approach of the scholastics he preached poetically and stressed personal friendship with Christ, and he helped spread devotion to Mary. His sermons on the Song of Songs are his best known. Bernard appears as Dante's last guide in the Divine Comedy.
bernardino-rivadavia: Bernardino Rivadavia was born in Buenos Aires on 20 May 1780, the fourth son of Benito Bernardino González de Rivadavia, a wealthy Spanish lawyer, and María Josefa de Jesús Rodríguez de Rivadeneyra. He was educated at the Royal College of San Carlos but left without finishing. During the British invasions he served as a lieutenant of the Galicia Volunteers, and on 22 May 1810 he took part in the open Cabildo that voted to depose the viceroy. In 1811 he became the dominant member of the governing triumvirate, whose government aimed at a strong central authority and an organised army until its fall in October 1812.

In 1814 Rivadavia and Manuel Belgrano were sent to Europe to seek support from Spain and Britain for the United Provinces. The mission failed, but in Britain he saw the Industrial Revolution and tried to promote similar development in Buenos Aires. In June 1821 Governor Martín Rodríguez named him minister of government of Buenos Aires province. Over five years he built avenues and schools, paved and lit streets, and founded the University of Buenos Aires, academies of theatre, geology and medicine, and the continent's first museum of natural science.

He also persuaded the legislature to authorise a loan of one million pounds, sold in London through the Baring Brothers; the government received only £552,700, and the debt was transferred to the nation in 1825. Liberal historians praise his work for education, culture and the separation of church and state, while revisionist authors condemn his free-trade policy and the Baring loan.

Rivadavia was named the first President of the United Provinces on 8 February 1826, as war with Brazil over territory in modern Uruguay required a national government. He made Buenos Aires the capital, and the constitution enacted on 24 December 1826 adopted a representative, republican and unitary government. Most provinces rejected it, and Facundo Quiroga defeated Rivadavia's ally Lamadrid at Rincón de Valladares on 6 July 1827.

In May 1827 his envoy Manuel José García signed a preliminary peace with Brazil that contradicted his instructions; the government rejected it. Rivadavia resigned on 27 June 1827. He left for Spain, was refused a landing in 1834 on trying to return, lived in Uruguay and died in Cádiz on 2 September 1845. His remains were repatriated in 1857 and now lie in a mausoleum in the Plaza Miserere.
bernardo-houssay: Bernardo Alberto Houssay was born on 10 April 1887 in Buenos Aires, the son of Albert and Clara Houssay, immigrants from France. A precocious youngster, he was admitted to the Pharmacy School of the University of Buenos Aires at 14 and to its Faculty of Medicine at 17, studying there from 1904 to 1910. While a third-year medical student he took a post as research and teaching assistant in the Chair of Physiology.

After graduating he presented a doctoral thesis on the physiological activities of pituitary extracts, published in 1911, a theme he pursued for the rest of his scientific career. He became Professor of Physiology in the university's School of Veterinary Medicine, worked as an assistant physician at the municipal hospital of Buenos Aires, and in 1913 became Chief Physician at the Alvear Hospital. In 1915 he became Chief of the Section of Experimental Pathology at the National Public Health Laboratories. In 1919 he was appointed to the chair of physiology at the university's medical school and held it until 1943, turning the department into a research centre of international standing.

In 1943 the military government deprived him of his university posts because of his liberal political ideas, and he re-established his research and staff at a privately funded Instituto de Biología y Medicina Experimental. The Peronist government dismissed him a second time in 1945. When Perón was ousted in 1955 he was reinstated at the University of Buenos Aires, where he stayed until his death. From 1957 he also directed the National Scientific and Technical Research Council.

Houssay worked in many fields of physiology, but his main contribution was experimental research on the part played by the anterior pituitary gland in the metabolism of carbohydrates, particularly in diabetes mellitus. In the 1930s he demonstrated the diabetogenic effect of anterior pituitary extracts and the lessening of diabetes after removal of the gland. These findings stimulated the study of hormonal feedback control, central to modern endocrinology. The work won him the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, shared with Carl Ferdinand Cori and Gerty Cori.

He published more than 600 scientific papers and several specialised books. With his disciples Eduardo Braun-Menéndez and Miguel Rolando Covian he wrote a textbook of human physiology, published since 1950 in Spanish and Portuguese and used in almost all medical schools of Latin America. Covian became the father of Brazilian neurophysiology at the University of São Paulo's medical faculty in Ribeirão Preto. Houssay was elected to the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1940 and became a Foreign Member of the Royal Society in 1943. He died on 21 September 1971.
bernardo-ohiggins: Bernardo O'Higgins was born on 20 August 1778 in Chillán, the illegitimate son of Ambrosio O'Higgins, a Spanish officer born in County Sligo who became governor of Chile and later viceroy of Peru, and of Isabel Riquelme. His father never acknowledged him, and the two never met in person, though Ambrosio supported him financially. At seventeen he was sent to London, where he met the Venezuelan Francisco de Miranda and joined the Lautaro Lodge, a society dedicated to the independence of Latin America. After his father's death in 1801 he inherited a large estate and returned to Chile in 1802 as a gentleman farmer.

On 18 September 1810 O'Higgins joined the revolt that created the Government Junta of Chile, a date now Chile's Independence Day. The patriots were split between the Carrera family and the circle of O'Higgins in Concepción. In October 1814 O'Higgins garrisoned the main square of Rancagua rather than the gorge he and José Miguel Carrera had agreed on; Carrera did not arrive with reinforcements, and the royalists won. O'Higgins broke out with a few men and spent three years in Argentina, where he met José de San Martín, assembled the Army of the Andes and returned to Chile in 1817 to win at Chacabuco.

He was granted dictatorial powers as Supreme Director on 16 February 1817 after San Martín declined the post, and Chile proclaimed itself independent on 12 February 1818. He founded the Chilean Military Academy and, with Lord Cochrane, the modern Chilean Navy, and sent an expedition to liberate Peru. His proposals to establish democracy and abolish titles of nobility met resistance from landowners, and he offended the Church and then the business community. The government went bankrupt, and Carrera's execution in 1821 damaged his name. A conservative coup deposed him on 28 January 1823.

O'Higgins left Valparaíso in July 1823 and never saw Chile again. Simón Bolívar's government granted him two haciendas in Peru but gave him no command. In 1842 the National Congress of Chile voted to allow his return, but he fell ill with heart trouble at Callao and died in Lima on 24 October 1842. His remains were brought to Chile in 1869 and now lie in the Crypt of the Liberator. A region of Chile, a national park and the main avenue of Santiago bear his name.
bernburg: The town centre lies in the fertile Magdeburg Börde lowland on the Saale river, about 40 km downstream from Halle and 45 km upstream from Magdeburg. It is dominated by the huge Bernburg Castle, which holds a museum and a bear pit in its moat. Bernburg is the capital of the Salzlandkreis district and a stop on the Romanesque Road. Near the town, in Lower Triassic deposits, the type fossil of the amphibian Trematosaurus brauni was found.

Archaeological sites in the area belong to the Walternienburg-Bernburg Culture, a mid-Neolithic funnel-beaker culture of about 3200 to 2800 BCE. Around 150 CE a settlement named Luppia appears in Ptolemy's Geography. In the early Middle Ages the Saale marked the border between the German stem duchies in the west and the lands of the Polabian Slavs in the east. Bernburg itself is first mentioned as civitas Brandanburg in a deed of King Otto I of 961. Enemies set fire to the castle, then held by the Ascanian prince Albert the Bear, in 1138, and in 1252 the rebuilt castle became the residence of his great-grandson Prince Bernhard I of Anhalt-Bernburg.

During the Nazi dictatorship a wing of the town's mental hospital was used for the mass murder of an estimated 15,000 people in Action T4 and Action 14f13. The victims included Jews, people with physical and mental illnesses and concentration camp inmates. The site now holds a memorial to them.
bernkastel-kues: Bernkastel-Kues lies on the Middle Moselle in the Bernkastel-Wittlich district, roughly 50 km from Trier. It consists of four quarters: Bernkastel and Andel on the right bank of the river, Kues and Wehlen on the left. The Eifel shields the town from west winds, putting it in a rain shadow. Historically the most important economic sector has been winegrowing, mostly on steep slopes, and Riesling is the customary grape.

The earliest evidence of human habitation, from about 3000 BCE, was found at Kues. About 370 CE the Roman poet Ausonius wrote his poem Mosella. Bernkastel is first documented in the first half of the 11th century, when Adalbero von Luxemburg, provost of the monastery of St. Paulin at Trier, became its lord. On 29 May 1291 King Rudolph I granted Berrincastel town rights, which Emperor Louis the Bavarian confirmed in 1332. The castle, built then under the archbishops of Trier, took the name Landshut in the 16th century and burned in 1692, after which it remained a ruin.

Nikolaus von Kues, known as Cusanus, was born in 1401 in the house of the Moselle shipowner Henne Cryfftz, and in 1451 the St.-Nikolaus-Hospital for the poor was built. By the Golden Bull of 1356 Bohemond II became Elector, and legend says he was restored to health from serious illness by a glass of wine, which gave rise to the story of the Bernkasteler Doctor vineyard. From 1794 to 1814 the town was under French rule and in 1815 it passed to Prussia. The town in its present form was created on 1 April 1905 by merging Bernkastel with the winemaking village of Kues. In 1938 the synagogue was destroyed on Kristallnacht.

The medieval marketplace has gabled timber-frame houses of the 17th century, among them the narrow Spitzhäuschen of 1416, a fountain of 1606 and a Renaissance town hall of 1608. The Graach Gate is the only town gate still standing, and the ruins of Landshut castle, once a summer residence of the archbishops of Trier, are now a lookout over the Moselle valley. At Kues the late Gothic St. Nikolaus-Hospital, founded by Cusanus, holds his library, and its chapel holds his heart. About 7,794 people live in the four quarters. The town hosts a wine festival of the Middle Moselle each September.
bertolt-brecht: Eugen Berthold Friedrich Brecht was born on 10 February 1898 in Augsburg. His mother was a devout Protestant and his father a Roman Catholic who had been persuaded to have a Protestant wedding; his Pietist grandmother influenced him in childhood, and the Bible shaped his writing for life. At school he met Caspar Neher, who designed many of the sets for his dramas. Brecht had his first successes as a playwright in Munich and moved to Berlin in 1924, where he worked as a dramaturg. His collection of poems Devotions for the Home was completed with the help of the assistant Elisabeth Hauptmann and published in January 1927.

He fled Germany in February 1933, just after Hitler took power. After brief spells in Prague, Zurich and Paris, he and Helene Weigel accepted an invitation from the writer Karin Michaëlis to Denmark, and lived for six years in Svendborg on Funen, where guests included Walter Benjamin and Hanns Eisler.

In April 1939 he moved to Stockholm and then to Helsinki, where he co-wrote Mr Puntila and His Man Matti with Hella Wuolijoki. During the war he settled in Southern California as a screenwriter, under FBI surveillance. In September 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee subpoenaed him; he testified and returned to Europe the next day, eventually settling in East Berlin, where he co-founded the Berliner Ensemble with Weigel.

Brecht developed his epic theatre by synthesising and extending the experiments of Erwin Piscator and Vsevolod Meyerhold, treating the theatre as a forum for political ideas. An epic play should not make the spectator identify emotionally with the characters; it should provoke rational self-reflection and a critical view of the action. Brecht thought that a climactic catharsis left an audience complacent, and he wanted audiences to recognise social injustice and to act on it outside the theatre.

He used techniques that remind the spectator the play is a representation and not reality, in the hope of showing that the audience's own reality is equally constructed and so changeable. He later preferred to call it dialectical theatre. He also wrote hundreds of poems, the last new collection published in his lifetime being the Svendborger Gedichte of 1939, and worked in collaboration with composers, designers and actors.

Brecht died of a heart attack on 14 August 1956, aged 58, and is buried in the Dorotheenstadt Cemetery in Berlin. According to Stephen Parker, he had had rheumatic fever as a child, which left him with chronic heart failure. Helene Weigel managed the Berliner Ensemble, which was devoted mainly to his plays, until her death in 1971. His aesthetic theories strongly influenced radical cinema of the 1960s and 1970s, in the work of Jean-Luc Godard, Rainer Werner Fassbinder and Nagisa Ōshima among others.
bertrand-russell: Russell was born on 18 May 1872 at Ravenscroft, a country house in Trellech, Monmouthshire, to John Russell, Viscount Amberley, and Katharine, Viscountess Amberley, both early advocates of birth control. His mother died of diphtheria in June 1874, followed shortly by his sister Rachel, and his father died in January 1876. He was raised by his paternal grandparents at Pembroke Lodge in Richmond Park, chiefly by his grandmother, the Countess Russell, whose progressive views on social justice and standing up for principle remained with him all his life.

He began at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1890 on a scholarship to read for the Mathematical Tripos, graduating seventh Wrangler in 1893 and becoming a Fellow in philosophy in 1895. His first major publication was An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry (1897).

Russell started in British idealism, the dominant philosophy of the time, but his friendship with G. E. Moore led him to analytic philosophy, and the two led a revolt against idealism. With Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica, published in 1910–1913. His article On Denoting has been considered a paradigm of philosophy. In 1916 he was convicted under the Defence of the Realm Act 1914 for his pacifist activity in the First World War and dismissed from Trinity. After a campaign by the Fellows, he was offered reinstatement and accepted it in 1920, but he resigned in 1921.

In August 1920 he visited Soviet Russia as part of a delegation and met Vladimir Lenin, whom he found disappointing. The visit ended his tentative support for the revolution, and he wrote The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism. He opposed rearmament against Nazi Germany, but changed his view in 1940 and in 1943 adopted a position he called relative political pacifism, that war may in extreme circumstances be the lesser of two evils. His History of Western Philosophy (1945) was a best-seller.

Russell is credited as one of the founders of analytic philosophy, and Willard Van Orman Quine named his work as a chief influence on his own. He made language a central part of philosophy and influenced Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilbert Ryle, J. L. Austin and P. F. Strawson. In lectures of 1918 he set out logical atomism, the view that knowledge can be reduced to atomic propositions and their truth-functional compounds.

He argued that religion is largely harmful and was a member of the advisory council of the British Humanist Association. He became the 3rd Earl Russell in 1931 and held the title until his death on 2 February 1970.
berwick-upon-tweed: Berwick-upon-Tweed lies at the mouth of the River Tweed on the east coast, 4 km south of the Anglo-Scottish border, 90 km south-east of Edinburgh and 105 km north of Newcastle upon Tyne. Its name has the same origin as the word berewick, a portion of farmland detached from a manor for the lord's own use, from the Old English berewíc, meaning corn farm. The earliest recorded spelling, Berewich, dates from 1167, and the medieval town seal showed a bear and a wych tree as a pun on the name.

The town was founded as an Anglo-Saxon settlement in the Kingdom of Northumbria. It remained part of the Earldom of Northumbria until control passed to the Scots after the Battle of Carham of 1018. David I of Scotland, who reigned from 1124 to 1153, made it a royal burgh and county town of Berwickshire, and a mint was present by 1153. In 1174, after the defeat of William I of Scotland, the Treaty of Falaise ceded Berwick to Henry II of England, until the treaty was annulled in 1189 when William paid Richard I 10,000 marks.

By the middle of the 13th century Berwick was prosperous. William Edington, a bishop and chancellor of England, wrote that it was so populous and of such commercial importance that it might be called another Alexandria, whose riches were the sea and the water its walls. Its position on the border led to centuries of raids, sieges and changes of ownership. The last came when Richard, Duke of Gloucester, later Richard III, retook it for England in 1482.

The Treaty of Norham of 1551, ending the Rough Wooing, left Berwick in English hands and declared it a free town independent of either kingdom, although in practice England controlled it. Under Elizabeth I large sums, one source giving £128,648, were spent on fortifications in the Italian style, to which Sir Richard Lee and the engineer Giovanni Portinari contributed. After the Act of Union of 1707 Berwick stayed within the legal system of England and Wales.

Berwick is a market town in Northumberland and the northernmost town in England, with 12,043 inhabitants at the census of 2011. Its medieval walls, the Elizabethan ramparts, the Georgian Town Hall and the barracks built by Nicholas Hawksmoor in 1717 to 1721 survive, as do the ruins of the 13th-century castle and the Old Bridge of 1610 to 1624. Berwick Rangers Football Club and Berwick Rugby Football Club play in Scottish leagues.
bes: Bes, also written Bisu, was an ancient Egyptian deity, paired with a female counterpart, Beset, and probably of Nubian or C-Group origin. People in Upper Egypt venerated him long before those in Lower Egypt, which points to a southern origin. In Nubian the word bes means cat, and the god is regularly shown with feline features. The feathered crown he wears was also common dress in ancient Kush. Donald Mackenzie suggested in 1907 that Bes was a Middle Kingdom import from Nubia, whose cult spread widely only at the beginning of the New Kingdom, but figurines resembling Bes, thirteen of them at Tell el-Farkha, have since been found in deposits of the pre-dynastic Naqada period.

Bes is first mentioned in the Pyramid Texts but seems to have been best known and most widely worshipped in the Middle Kingdom. Evidence of his worship continues into Coptic Egypt, the latest being a jug showing Bes from Tell Edfu, dated to the 10th century CE.

Bes protected households and, in particular, mothers, children and childbirth. His tasks included killing snakes, driving off evil spirits and watching over children, and he was present with Taweret at births. Where Egyptian gods were normally shown in profile, Bes appeared in a full-face portrait, ithyphallic and sometimes in a soldier's tunic, ready to attack any approaching evil. Because he drove off evil, he also came to symbolise the good things in life, music, dance and sexual pleasure. Some modern scholars, among them James Romano, hold that in its earliest form Bes represented a lion rearing on its hind legs.

Images of Bes were kept in homes. From the Middle Kingdom he appears on masks, amulets, infant feeding bottles, magic knives, furniture, toiletries and game pieces, and many jugs and storage jars bear his image. In the New Kingdom dancers, musicians and servant girls wore tattoos of him on the thigh, as a wall painting of the 19th Dynasty from Deir el-Medina shows. In the Ptolemaic period chambers at Saqqara were painted with Bes and Beset, which Egyptologists think were used for curing fertility problems or for healing rituals.

His worship spread abroad. Beset was more popular in Minoan Crete, while Bes found favour with the Phoenicians and the ancient Cypriots. From the end of the 6th century BCE his image spread across the Achaemenid Empire, to which Egypt then belonged, and has been found at Susa and as far off as central Asia. Over time he came to be shown in Persian clothes and headdress. His cult reached Syria and the Balearic Islands as well.
besalu: Besalú is a town in the comarca of Garrotxa, in the province of Girona in Catalonia. Its name derives from the Latin Bisuldunum, meaning a fort on a mountain between two rivers. It was designated a historical national property, a conjunt historicoartístic, in 1966, and its urban layout is almost identical to the original one.

The town was most important in the early Middle Ages, as capital of the county of Besalú. The county had roughly the territory of the present Garrotxa, but sometimes extended as far as Corbières in the Aude, in France. In 894 Besalú became a county with its own dynasty. Wilfred the Hairy, credited with the unification of Catalonia, was Count of Besalú, and the troubadour Raimon Vidal was born in the town.
In 1111 Besalú lost its independence to the county of Barcelona. Centuries later the town entered a period of decline, made worse by wars with the French and the Carlist wars.

The emblem of Besalú is its 12th-century Romanesque bridge over the Fluvià, which has seven uneven arches and two towers, with a gateway at its midpoint. Parts of the old walls survive. The narrow streets nearest the bridge belong to the former Jewish quarter, where a mikveh, a ritual bath dating from the 11th or 12th century, is the only Romanesque one remaining in Spain, and the remains of a medieval synagogue lie near the river.

The church of Sant Pere was consecrated in 1003, and of the Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere only a three-nave church and one apse remain. Other monuments include the Royal Curia, the apse of Santa Maria and a tower of the old counts' castle, and the parish church of Sant Vicenç. Industry and tourism are now the main sources of income.
besame-mucho: The song was written in 1932 by the Mexican songwriter Consuelo Velázquez, and its title means "Kiss Me A Lot". She took her inspiration from a piano piece, "Quejas, o la Maja y el Ruiseñor", from the 1911 suite Goyescas by the Spanish composer Enrique Granados. Granados later included the same music as the "Aria of the Nightingale" in his 1916 opera of the same name. English lyrics for the bolero were written by Sunny Skylar, and Velázquez herself recorded it as a piano instrumental on her album Piano Interpretations in 1955.

The song reached a wide audience in 1944. It was heard in two films that May: Follow the Boys, released on 5 May 1944, in which it was played by Charlie Spivak and his Orchestra, and Cowboy and the Senorita, released on 13 May 1944, with a vocal by Dale Evans. The version by Bob Eberly and Kitty Kallen with Jimmy Dorsey and His Orchestra reached number one in the United States that year, and Andy Russell's recording reached number eight. As the song crossed the Atlantic in 1944, it became one of the most recognisable melodies of the decade.

Later recordings include those of Pedro Vargas, who was inducted into the Latin Grammy Hall of Fame in 2001, and Ray Conniff and His Orchestra and Chorus, who recorded it on 25 March 1960 for the album Say It with Music (A Touch of Latin). The Beatles played it at their Decca audition on 1 January 1962 and again at their first session at Abbey Road Studios on 6 June 1962. Dalida reached number five in France with it in 1976, João Gilberto recorded it for the bossa nova album Amoroso in 1977, and Luis Miguel included it on Romances in 1997. In 1999 it was recognised as the most recorded and covered Spanish-language song of all time.

In 1990 the song played a part in a Brazilian political scandal. A clandestine affair between two government ministers, Bernardo Cabral, the Minister of Justice, and Zélia Cardoso de Mello, the Minister for Economy, Finance and Planning, became public when the couple danced cheek to cheek to "Bésame Mucho" at a birthday party held for her. Cabral, a married father of three, was forced to resign. A few days later the regimental band of the presidential guard, Os Dragões da Independência, struck up the song as Cardoso de Mello received the Order of Military Merit, and its musical director was given three days' detention for insubordination.
besancon: Besançon lies in the north-east of France on the river Doubs, at the edge of the Jura Mountains, about 325 kilometres east of Paris. The old city developed in a natural meander of the Doubs, almost 1,000 metres across, known as la Boucle, closed on the south by a hill, Mont Saint-Étienne, which rises to 371 metres. Because the Alps rise abruptly to its south, the town had military importance from the 1st century BCE onward.

Tribes of Gauls settled the oxbow of the Doubs around 1500 BCE. The city is first recorded in 58 BCE as Vesontio in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and it became an important city of Roman Gaul. It acquired a bishop's see in the 3rd century. The name became Besançon in 1243. The Treaty of Verdun in 843 made it part of Lotharingia.

In the 15th century Besançon came under the dukes of Burgundy, and after the marriage of Mary of Burgundy to Maximilian I it was in effect a Habsburg fief. In 1519 Charles V became its master as Holy Roman Emperor, and in 1526 the city won the right to mint coins, which it kept until 1673, all bearing the name of Charles V. French conquest followed in 1674. The Austrians bombarded the city in 1814, and the Germans occupied the citadel in the Second World War, executing some one hundred resistance fighters there.

Besançon is the capital of the department of Doubs and has about 120,000 inhabitants. Its university was founded in 1423, and it is the historical capital of watchmaking in France. Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban designed most of its fortifications, including the citadel across the neck of la Boucle, which are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with eleven other sites as the Fortifications of Vauban. The Palais Granvelle, a Renaissance palace built for Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, chancellor of Charles V, now houses the Museum of Time.
bessarabia: Bessarabia is bounded by the Dniester to the north and east, the Prut to the west, and the lower Danube and the Black Sea to the south, and has an area of 45,630 square kilometres. It is mostly hilly plains and flat steppe, very fertile. About two thirds of it lies in modern Moldova, with the Budjak in the south and a small part of the Chernivtsi Oblast in the north in Ukraine. According to the traditional explanation the name derives from the Wallachian Basarab dynasty, who allegedly ruled the south in the 14th century; some scholars argue that it began as an exonym used by Western cartographers and was first used in local sources only in the late 17th century.

In antiquity the region was inhabited by Thracians and, for shorter periods, by Cimmerians, Scythians, Sarmatians and Celts. Greek settlers founded the colony of Tyras in the 6th century BCE, and the Roman Empire defeated the Dacian kingdom in 106 CE. From the 3rd to the 11th century it was invaded in turn by Goths, Huns, Avars, Bulgars, Magyars, Pechenegs, Cumans and Mongols. After the 1360s it was gradually included in the Principality of Moldavia, which by 1392 controlled Akkerman and Chilia. Stephen the Great ruled from 1457 to 1504 and built churches and monasteries near his battlefields, many along the Dniester. In 1484 the Ottomans captured Chilia and Akkerman, and in 1538 more land in the south.

By the Treaty of Bucharest of 28 May 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the land between the Prut and the Dniester to Russia, and the whole of it was then called Bessarabia. German settlers arrived from 1814, and Bulgarians and Gagauz settled in the south. The south returned to Moldavia in 1856, and Russian rule over the whole region was restored in 1878, when Romania exchanged it for the Dobruja. On 9 April 1918 its assembly, the Sfatul Țării, voted for union with Romania; the Soviet Union never recognised this. In 1940, under an ultimatum, Romania withdrew; it retook the region in 1941 and lost it in 1944, and the Treaty of Paris of 1947 recognised the border along the Prut.

When the Soviet Union dissolved, the Moldavian and Ukrainian republics declared independence in 1991 and kept the existing division of Bessarabia, so that most of it forms the core of Moldova and its northern and southern fringes lie in Ukraine. Chișinău, the former capital of the Russian Bessarabia Governorate, is the capital of Moldova.
bessarion: Bessarion was born in Trebizond, the Black Sea port in north-eastern Anatolia that was the heart of Pontic Greek culture. His baptismal name was Basil, and he took the name Bessarion on entering a monastery. He was educated in Constantinople and in 1423 went to Mystras in the Peloponnese to study Neoplatonism under Gemistus Pletho, with an emphasis on mathematics, astronomy and geography. His Neoplatonism stayed with him throughout his life, even as a cardinal, and he wrote to Pletho's two sons, Demitrios and Andronikos, on the death of his still-beloved teacher in 1452.

In 1436 Bessarion became abbot of a monastery in Constantinople, and in 1437 Emperor John VIII Palaiologos made him metropolitan of Nicaea and took him to Italy to seek a reunion of the Orthodox and Catholic churches. The emperor hoped to win help from Western Europe against the Ottoman Empire. Although Bessarion had first belonged to the anti-unionist party, he became the most eminent unionist in the Byzantine delegation to the Council of Ferrara-Florence, and on 6 July 1439 he read the Greek declaration of union in Florence cathedral. Some historians doubt his sincerity, but one has defended it from his own Oratio Dogmatica.

On his return East he was bitterly resented. Pope Eugene IV made him a cardinal on 18 December 1439, and from then on he lived in Italy. He was legate at Bologna from 1450 to 1455, was an early candidate at the conclave of 1455, and in 1463 received the ceremonial title of Latin Patriarch of Constantinople. He died at Ravenna on 18 November 1472 and was buried in the basilica of the Santi Apostoli in Rome.

His palazzo in Rome was a virtual academy of humanist learning and a centre for learned Greeks and Greek refugees, for whom he commissioned transcripts of Greek manuscripts and Latin translations. He is known as the original patron of Greek exiles such as Theodore Gaza, John Argyropoulos and Janus Lascaris. He translated Aristotle's Metaphysics and wrote a treatise against George of Trebizond, a vehement Aristotelian, entitled In Calumniatorem Platonis. Though a Platonist, he sought to reconcile the two philosophies. In 1468 he presented his library of 482 Greek and 264 Latin manuscripts to the Senate of Venice, where it became the core of the Biblioteca Marciana.
bessemer-process: Henry Bessemer later wrote that the idea came from a conversation with Napoleon III in 1854 about the steel needed for better artillery, during the Crimean War. At that time steel was used only for small items such as cutlery and tools and was too expensive for cannon. He began work in January 1855, filed his first related patent in October of that year and patented the method in 1856. The American inventor William Kelly had experimented with a similar method in the early to mid-1850s and was awarded a priority patent in 1857; whether both invented the same process remains controversial, and Kelly's version is thought to have been less developed.

Bessemer licensed the process to four ironmasters for £27,000, but they could not make steel of the promised quality, and he bought the licences back for £32,500. The fault lay in impurities in the iron. The English metallurgist Robert Forester Mushet found the remedy: burn off nearly all impurities and carbon, then add carbon and manganese in the form of spiegeleisen. Bessemer acquired Mushet's patent after it lapsed. Commercial production began in Sheffield in 1858, using imported Swedish charcoal pig iron.

Air is blown through molten pig iron in a converter, which oxidises silicon, manganese and carbon. The oxides escape as gas or form slag, and the heat of oxidation keeps the iron molten. The blow lasted about 20 minutes, and its progress was judged by the flame at the mouth of the converter. Carbon was then added back. A converter treated a batch of 5 to 30 tons, and converters usually worked in pairs. Bessemer himself used a ganister sandstone lining, the acid process. In 1878 Sidney Gilchrist Thomas, with his cousin Percy Gilchrist, patented a dolomite or limestone lining that removed phosphorus, giving the basic Bessemer process.

In the United States Alexander Lyman Holley secured a licence in 1863 for John F. Winslow and John Augustus Griswold, and a mill opened at Troy, New York. Andrew Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Steel Works opened in 1875, and most American Bessemer steel went into railroad rails.

Steel rails lasted ten times longer than iron rails and carried heavier locomotives. Quality problems, including brittleness caused by nitrogen in the air blast, kept Bessemer steel out of many structural uses, for which open-hearth steel was suitable. By 1895 observers in the UK judged the process to be in decline. The basic process lasted longer, especially in continental Europe, where ores were rich in phosphorus. Commercial Bessemer production in the United States stopped in 1968, and basic oxygen steelmaking, in essence an improved Bessemer process, replaced it.
bessus: Nothing is known about the background of Bessus except that he belonged to the ruling Achaemenid dynasty. Under Darius III he became satrap of Bactria, a prosperous and populous province in the east that had been under Achaemenid rule since 545 to 540 BCE. From there he ruled Sogdia to the north and the regions bordering India, and he kept the loyalty of the Iranian nomadic groups of Central Asia: the Saka, the Dahae and the Massagetae. The Iranologist Richard Foltz describes the eastern satrapies as practically his personal domain.

After the defeat at Issus in 333 BCE Darius III summoned Bessus to his aid. At Gaugamela in 331 BCE Bessus supplied Bactrians, Sogdians, Indians and Saka and led the cavalry on the Persian left wing. After the defeat he followed Darius to Ecbatana, where he conspired with the chiliarch Nabarzanes and Barsaentes, satrap of Arachosia and Drangiana. They arrested Darius in mid-330 BCE and chose Bessus to lead the forces, probably because of his descent. To gain time they killed Darius near Hecatompylus in July 330 BCE, and Alexander had the body buried at Persepolis.

In the autumn of 330 BCE, at Bactra, Bessus declared himself King of Kings under the name Artaxerxes V. His realm soon fell apart: Nabarzanes surrendered and was pardoned, and Satibarzanes was killed in 329 BCE. According to Diodorus Siculus, Bessus raised 8,000 Bactrians, but many dispersed when Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush, and he fled across the Oxus into Sogdia. At Nautaca his Sogdian officers, among them Spitamenes and Dataphernes, arrested him and handed him to the general Ptolemy. Bessus was flogged, and his ears and nose were cut off, a traditional Persian punishment. He was executed at Ecbatana under the supervision of Oxyathres, the brother of Darius. The Shahnameh tells of him as Janusipar.
bethel: Most scholars identify Bethel with the modern village of Beitin, in the West Bank, 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) northeast of Ramallah. Edward Robinson, in his Biblical Researches in Palestine, was among the first to propose this, on the strength of the location described in ancient texts and the similarity of the names. A minority view equates Bethel with al-Bireh, but those who worked on the excavations have hardly taken it seriously. In the 4th century Eusebius and Jerome described it as a small village 12 Roman miles north of Jerusalem.

The Hebrew Bible first mentions Bethel as lying near the place where Abram pitched his tent, close to Ai. In Genesis 28 Jacob, fleeing his brother Esau, sleeps on a stone and dreams of a ladder between heaven and earth; on waking he anoints the stone and names the place Bethel. Both accounts say its original name was Luz, a Canaanite name, and Genesis 35 makes it the site where Jacob's name was changed to Israel.

Later books show Bethel as a religious centre. In Judges the descendants of Joseph capture it, and the Israelites go there to seek counsel before attacking the tribe of Benjamin. The prophet Samuel is said to have made a yearly circuit of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah. After the kingdom divided on the death of Solomon, about 931 BCE, Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan. The prophet Amos, about 750 BCE, spoke against the shrine, and its priest Amaziah expelled him.

Excavations by William F. Albright and James L. Kelso at Beitin, begun in 1934, found settlement from the Chalcolithic period. About 1750 BCE the site became a fortified Canaanite town, believed to be biblical Luz, with two city gates and a temple destroyed by an earthquake. The Late Bronze Age city was destroyed in the late 13th or early 12th century BCE. Bacchides the Syrian fortified the place in the time of the Maccabees, and Vespasian captured it in the summer of 69 CE.

Bethel appears on the 6th-century Madaba Map as Louza. A church there fell into ruin after the Rashidun conquest and was rebuilt by the Crusaders in the 12th century, when Baldwin V of Jerusalem gave the village as a fief to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. After Saladin's Ayyubid forces defeated the Crusaders in 1187 the church was destroyed and the village abandoned. The site stayed uninhabited for centuries, until the modern village of Beitin was established in the mid-19th century.
bethlehem: Bethlehem stands in the Judean Mountains at about 775 metres above sea level, some 30 metres higher than Jerusalem, which lies about ten kilometres to the north. The Arabic name Bēt laḥm means house of meat, while the Hebrew Bet Leḥem means house of bread or house of food. Beit Jala and Beit Sahour form an urban cluster with the city, and the refugee camps of Aida and Azza lie within its limits.

A possible earliest reference is in the Amarna correspondence of ancient Egypt, where Abdi-Heba, the Egyptian-appointed governor of Jerusalem, appeals for help in retaking a town near Jerusalem called Bit-Lahmi after attacks by Apiru mercenaries. The reading is uncertain and has met with objections. The Hebrew Bible names Bethlehem as the birthplace of David. In 2012 excavators in the City of David found a clay seal impression reading From the town of Bethlehem to the King, which they date to the 8th or 7th century BCE and take to have sealed a tax shipment.

The Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke place the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, though scholars regard the two accounts as contradictory and are divided on his actual birthplace. Under the Roman Empire Hadrian destroyed the city, and Constantine the Great later commissioned the Church of the Nativity in 327 CE. It was heavily damaged in 529 by Samaritans in revolt and rebuilt by Justinian I. In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered it demolished, but local Muslims, who were permitted to worship in its southern transept, spared it.

Crusaders took Bethlehem in 1099 and replaced the Greek Orthodox clergy with Catholic ones. The Mamluk Sultanate demolished its walls in the mid-13th century, and the Ottoman Empire rebuilt them in the 16th. From 1517 the Catholic and Greek Orthodox churches bitterly disputed custody of the basilica. Bethlehem was part of Mandatory Palestine from 1920 to 1948, was held by Jordan after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War and was captured by Israel in 1967. Refugees from the 1947–48 war settled near the city and helped turn its Christian majority into a Muslim one.

Bethlehem is the capital of the Bethlehem Governorate and had 28,591 inhabitants in 2017. Its economy is closely tied to tourism and to pilgrimage to the Church of the Nativity at Christmas, and it is known for olive wood and mother-of-pearl carving, a craft said to have been introduced by Franciscan friars from Italy in the 15th century. Bethlehem University, founded in 1973, was the first university established in the West Bank.
bettino-ricasoli: Bettino Ricasoli, 1st Count of Brolio and 2nd Baron Ricasoli, was born in Florence on 9 March 1809. Left an orphan at eighteen with an estate heavily in debt, he was declared of age by special decree of the grand duke of Tuscany and entrusted with the guardianship of his younger brothers. He withdrew from his studies to Brolio and by careful management cleared the family possessions of debt.

In 1847 he founded the journal La Patria and addressed to the grand duke a memorial suggesting remedies for the difficulties of the state. Elected Gonfaloniere of Florence in 1848, he resigned because of the grand duke's anti-Liberal tendencies. He led the Moderate Party.

As Tuscan minister of the interior in 1859 he promoted the union of Tuscany with Piedmont, which took place on 12 March 1860. Elected an Italian deputy in 1861, he succeeded Cavour as premier. He admitted Garibaldian volunteers to the regular army, revoked the decree of exile against Mazzini and attempted a reconciliation with the Vatican, which the pope's non possumus made ineffectual. Disdainful of the intrigues of his rival Rattazzi, he resigned in 1862.

He returned to power in 1866 and refused Napoleon III's offer to cede Venetia to Italy on condition that Italy abandon the Prussian alliance. After French troops left Rome at the end of 1866 he proposed a convention under which Italy would restore to the Church the property of the suppressed religious orders in return for gradual payment of 24,000,000, and he conceded the exequatur to forty-five bishops. The Vatican accepted, but the Italian Chamber proved refractory and returned more hostile after he dissolved it. He resigned without waiting for a vote and thereafter practically disappeared from political life.

Ricasoli died at his Castello di Brolio on 23 October 1880. His private life and public career were marked by integrity and a rigid austerity that earned him the name of the Iron Baron. He is also credited with creating the modern recipe of Chianti wine; a formula of specific grape percentages is often wrongly attributed to him, but his switch of focus to Sangiovese as the lead grape had lasting implications for Tuscan and Italian wine. The firm Ricasoli 1141 still produces wine at Brolio.
betty-friedan: Betty Friedan was born on 4 February 1921 to Harry and Miriam Goldstein, whose secular Jewish families came from Russia and Hungary. Her father owned a jewelry store in Peoria, and her mother wrote for a newspaper's society page when he fell ill, a life outside the home that seemed much more gratifying. As a girl she was active in both Marxist and Jewish circles, and later wrote that her passion against injustice originated in the injustice of anti-Semitism. At Peoria High School, after her application to write a column was turned down, she and six friends launched a literary magazine, Tide.

After leaving Berkeley she became a journalist for leftist and labour union publications. She wrote for Federated Press from 1943 to 1946 and for the United Electrical Workers' UE News from 1946 to 1952, where she reported on the House Un-American Activities Committee. She married Carl Friedan in 1947, and was dismissed from UE News in 1952 because she was pregnant with her second child. She then wrote freelance for magazines including Cosmopolitan. Her biographer Daniel Horowitz argues that her feminism began in the 1940s, though she disputed this.

NOW grew from the failure of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. At a conference of state commissions on the status of women, delegates were not allowed to pass a resolution urging it to act, and they met in Friedan's hotel room, where she wrote the acronym NOW on a paper napkin. With Pauli Murray she wrote its statement of purpose. In 1970 she helped defeat the Supreme Court nomination of G. Harrold Carswell, and she supported the Equal Rights Amendment, which passed the House by 354 to 24 and the Senate by 84 to 8.

Friedan pushed the movement to concentrate on economic issues, such as equality in employment and business and provision for child care, and wished to lessen its emphasis on abortion and on rape and pornography. She opposed equating feminism with lesbianism and coined the term lavender menace at a NOW meeting in 1969. Her later books included It Changed My Life, The Second Stage, The Fountain of Age and Beyond Gender, and her autobiography, Life So Far, appeared in 2000. She died of congestive heart failure at her home in Washington, D.C., on 4 February 2006, her 85th birthday.
bevagna: Bevagna lies in the flood plain of the Topino river, in the western part of the Umbrian valley and about 225 metres above sea level. It is 25 km south-east of Perugia, 8 km west of Foligno and 16 km south of Assisi. The Clitunno runs close to its ancient walls, and the Timia waters a fertile, well-cultivated plain. In antiquity Classical authors, among them Columella, Silius Italicus and Lucan, refer to the fertility of this valley.

As Mevania the town was an important Umbrian city on the Via Flaminia, between Carsulae and Fulginium. It was already a significant centre before the Roman conquest, and Umbrian forces were stationed there in 308 BCE when the consul Fabius advanced against them. Strabo lists it among the strongest Umbrian cities, and Pliny records that it was enclosed by brick walls and that its territory produced a prized wine called Irtia. Inscriptions show that it belonged to the tribus Aemilia and had quattuorviri among its magistrates.

The city suffered serious damage in barbarian incursions in the 6th century. After the 11th century it became a free municipality governed by consuls, and in 1249 Pope Innocent IV granted it the right to choose its chief magistrate. In November of that year the imperial vicar Thomas I of Aquino besieged and badly damaged it, in the context of Frederick II's claim to the Duchy of Spoleto.

It was under the Trinci family of Foligno from 1371 to 1439, when Cardinal Giovanni Vitelleschi returned it to the direct rule of the Holy See. From 1562 to 1566 its governor was Cardinal Charles Borromeo.

Under the Roman Republic of 1798 Bevagna was assigned to the Canton of Spello. The papal government was restored on 14 May 1814, Pope Leo XII granted the town the title of city in 1825, and in 1860 it joined the Kingdom of Italy.

Roman remains include a temple of the 2nd century, converted into the church of the Madonna della Neve, and the arcaded substructures of a theatre of the 2nd century, which shaped the later streets. A bath building preserves a floor mosaic in black and white of the same century, showing tritons, hippocamps, octopuses, dolphins and lobsters.

The medieval square holds the church of San Michele Arcangelo, with a façade of the early 13th century, the Romanesque church of San Silvestro, built by the architect Binello, whose plaque is dated 1195, and the Palazzo dei Consoli of the later 13th century, which has housed the Teatro Torti since 1886. Medieval festivals are held each year, including the Mercato delle Gaite in June, in which four quarters of the town compete.
beylerbey: Beylerbey, from the Turkic for 'bey of beys', also rendered 'commander of commanders' or governor-general, was a high rank in the western Islamic world in the late Middle Ages and early modern period. It began with the Seljuks, who used it in the Sultanate of Rum for the army's commander-in-chief, and it was also used by the Ilkhanids, the Golden Horde, possibly the Mamluks, and later the Safavids of Iran. Its Arabic equivalent was amir al-umara and its Persian equivalent mir-i miran.

In the early Ottoman state the beylerbey was a commander-in-chief held by princes of the dynasty: Orhan under Osman I, then Alaeddin Pasha and Süleyman Pasha. The change towards a governorship began when Murad I gave the title to Lala Shahin Pasha for capturing Adrianople, with military authority over the Ottoman lands in Europe (Rumelia). In 1393 Bayezid I named Kara Timurtash beylerbey in Anatolia, and the beylerbeyliks of Rumelia and Anatolia, soon joined by Rûm, were the first and most important.

A beylerbey ran a province, termed a beylerbeylik or vilayet, and after 1591 an eyalet. Provinces were divided into sanjaks under sanjakbeys. As the empire grew in the 15th and 16th centuries the number of beylerbeys rose to a peak of 44 by the end of the 16th century; a list of 1609 names 32 eyalets. Their size varied from two sanjaks to twenty. The beylerbey of Rumelia ranked first and, after 1536, held a seat in the Imperial Council.

Within his province the beylerbey acted as a virtual viceroy, with authority over war, justice and administration. It was limited by officials appointed from the centre, chiefly the fiscal secretaries and the kadı, and the Janissary contingents stood outside his command. He kept his own court and divan and could grant timars and ziamets, though after 1530 only the smaller timars. His chief duty was to maintain the sipahi cavalry and lead it on campaign.

From Mehmed II onwards beylerbey was also an honorary court rank, below the viziers; both were pashas, the viziers with three horse-tails and the beylerbeys with two. In the 18th century the Arabic title wali increasingly replaced beylerbey for governors-general, except in Rumelia and Anatolia, and the old titles became honorifics. The vilayet reform of 1864 made wali the only official title, and beylerbey survived only as the honorary rank Rumeli beylerbeysi.
beziers: Béziers stands on a small bluff above the River Orb, about ten kilometres from the Mediterranean coast and 75 kilometres south-west of Montpellier. It is a subprefecture of the Hérault department. The Canal du Midi crosses the Orb here by the Pont-canal de l'Orb, an aqueduct claimed to be the first of its kind. Its inhabitants are called Biterrois, after Baeterrae, the Roman name of the town.

Béziers is one of the oldest cities in France. Research published in March 2013 dates its ancient Greek colony to 575 BCE. The Romans refounded it as a colony for veterans in 36–35 BCE, as Colonia Julia Baeterrae Septimanorum, and it exported wine to Rome. It was conquered by Muslims and remained part of Islamic Iberia between 720 and 752. From the 10th to the 12th centuries it was the centre of a viscounty, whose rulers controlled the coastal plain and the main east–west route through Languedoc. The Trencavels ruled for 142 years, until the Albigensian Crusade.

Béziers was a stronghold of Catharism, which the Catholic Church condemned as heretical. The crusaders arrived on 21 July 1209 and offered the Catholics of the town the choice of handing over the heretics or leaving; many refused. The town was sacked the next day, and no one was spared, not even priests or those sheltering in the churches. The papal legate Arnaud-Amaury reported to Pope Innocent III that almost 20,000 people were put to the sword. The Cathedral of Saint Nazaire burned and collapsed on those inside. Other accounts give a handful of survivors.

The city was repopulated, and repairs to the cathedral began in 1215. Béziers joined the royal domain in 1247. In 1632 the Edict of Béziers abolished the privileges of Languedoc, restored in 1649. In the 18th century it prospered through vine growing. On 12 May 1907, 150,000 people gathered in Béziers to defend southern winegrowing, and in June soldiers of the 17th regiment, sent to Agde, mutinied and returned to the town.

The Gothic Cathedral of Saint-Nazaire, rebuilt in the 14th century, rises above the town; its nave is 32 metres high. The park of the Plateau des Poètes dates from 1867, and the allées Paul Riquet carry a statue of the creator of the Canal du Midi. Every August the town holds the Feria de Béziers, centred on bullfighting.
bhagalpur: Bhagalpur, historically known as Champa Nagari, stands on the southern bank of the Ganges in Bihar, at the convergence of Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal. It is the headquarters of Bhagalpur district and division. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary lies near the town, and the Kosi and Chanan rivers also cross the district.

The city is historically the capital of Anga, an ancient region. Jain tradition holds that all five auspicious events in the life of Vasupujya, the twelfth Teerthankar, took place at Champapur, and that Mahavira spent three rainy-season retreats there. Its main Jain temple is said to be about 2,500 years old. Champa is also the setting of the story of Behula and Lakhinder, told in medieval Bengali works such as the Mansamangal, many of which were produced between the thirteenth and the eighteenth centuries.

At Antichak village lie the excavated ruins of the Vikramshila Mahavihara. Emperor Dharmapala of the Pala Empire established it as an international centre of learning, with Tantric studies among its fields, and it was considered on a par with Nalanda. Bhaktiyar Khilji destroyed it. The Khanqah-e-Shahbazia, founded in 1577, holds the grave of the saint Maulana Shahbaz Muhammad, and its library includes a Qur'an copied by Murshid Quli Khan, the Nawab of Murshidabad.

Bhagalpur is known as the Silk City, after the silk trade of ancient Champanagari. The 2011 census gave its urban agglomeration 410,210 people, making it the third largest city of Bihar. Hinduism is the majority religion, followed by Islam, and Angika is the main language of the district, with Hindi, Bengali, Urdu and Santhali also spoken. Its festivals include a Kali Puja procession so long that one phase of immersing the images takes 36 hours, and the Manasa or Bishari Puja.
bhagat-singh: Bhagat Singh was born into a Punjabi Jat Sikh family in the village of Banga, in the Lyallpur district of the Punjab, then in British India and now in Pakistan. He was the second of seven children of Vidyavati and Kishan Singh Sandhu. His father and his uncle Ajit Singh took part in progressive politics, including the agitation of 1907 around the Canal Colonisation Bill and later the Ghadar Movement. After the village school he attended the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic School in Lahore, and in 1923 he joined the National College there, which Lala Lajpat Rai had founded two years earlier in response to Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement.

When the Simon Commission visited Lahore on 30 October 1928, Lajpat Rai led a march against it. The superintendent of police, James A. Scott, ordered a lathi charge and personally assaulted Rai, who died of a heart attack on 17 November. Singh, a prominent member of the Hindustan Republican Association, probably did much to change its name to the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. On 17 December 1928 he and Shivaram Rajguru shot John P. Saunders, who had left the District Police Headquarters; the postmortem found eight bullet wounds. Chandra Shekhar Azad shot dead Head Constable Channan Singh, who had given chase. Bhagat Singh escaped by train, with his hair cut and wearing Western dress, passing as a married couple with Durgawati Devi.

In 1929 he proposed a dramatic act to gain publicity: a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly, nominally against the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Dispute Act. After it was thrown on 8 April, he and Batukeshwar Dutt dropped leaflets and were arrested. In the jail he joined Jatin Das in a hunger strike for better conditions, and Das died of starvation in September 1929.

Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were sentenced to death in the Lahore conspiracy case and hanged in the Lahore jail on 23 March 1931, 11 hours ahead of the schedule of 24 March. Their bodies were cremated in secret near Ganda Singh Wala village and the ashes thrown into the Sutlej. He had written that he held human life sacred, but that force used for a legitimate cause was morally justified, and he declined to sign a draft letter for clemency.

An atheist, he read Bakunin, Marx, Lenin and Trotsky, and in his last testament named a Marxist basis for social reconstruction. Jawaharlal Nehru wrote that he became popular because he seemed to vindicate the honour of Lajpat Rai, and that the act was forgotten while the symbol remained. A bronze statue of him was installed in the Parliament of India on 15 August 2008. Communists, Hindu nationalists and others have each claimed his memory.
bhagavad-gita: The Sanskrit title means 'God's song'. Indian tradition attributes the Gita, like the Mahabharata of which it is a part, to the sage Vyasa, and a Hindu legend says that Ganesha wrote it down using one of his broken tusks. Modern scholarship regards it as a composite work by several authors that draws on the Upanishads and the Samkhya school. It is generally dated to the second or first century BCE, though estimates run from 400 to 500 BCE to the first century CE. It stands in the Bhishma Parva, the sixth book of the Mahabharata, and is often studied on its own in eighteen chapters.

The text is a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, just before the Kurukshetra War. Seeing relatives, friends and teachers in the opposing army, Arjuna drops his bow and doubts whether he should fight. Krishna's answers form the rest of the work. He argues that one should follow one's dharma without regarding oneself as the agent of the action, and that action and renunciation are inseparable. The poem offers three disciplines, jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion) and karma (action), and does not exclude any of them. In the eleventh chapter Krishna shows Arjuna his universal form.

The 700 verses are mostly in the anushtubh metre, with eight syllables to each quarter-verse, and the tristubh metre appears at dramatic moments. Its manuscripts exist in many Indic scripts and vary little compared with those of the rest of the Mahabharata.

The Gita is part of the Prasthanatrayi, with the Upanishads and the Brahma Sutras, the foundational texts of Vedanta. The oldest surviving commentary is that of Adi Shankara, about 800 CE, who read it as a text of non-dualism. Ramanuja, in the eleventh and early twelfth centuries, read it as qualified monism, and Madhvacharya, about 1250, as a doctrine of the fundamental difference between the soul, Vishnu and the world. Modern commentators include Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Mahatma Gandhi and Sri Aurobindo.

Persian translations were made under the Mughal Empire in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Charles Wilkins published the first English translation in 1785, and French, German and Russian versions followed. The text has also been debated: B. R. Ambedkar criticised its defence of varna duty and of the warrior's duty to fight, while others read the battlefield as an allegory of the struggle within.
bhagavata-purana: Bhagavata means follower or worshipper of Vishnu, and Purana means ancient or old traditional history. The text calls Krishna Bhagavan, the Blessed One. Many Indologists give no precise date for the Puranas, because their material was passed on orally, and a date applies only to the text as it now stands. Sheridan, in a study of 1986, dated its composition between 500 and 1000 CE and argued that a version must have existed by 1030, when al-Biruni mentions it. Many scholars, Hardy among them, date its final redaction to the 9th or early 10th century. The oldest surviving manuscript dates to c. 1124-25 and is held in Varanasi.

The twelve books consist of interwoven dialogues. The main reciter is Suka, who speaks to King Pariksit and quotes an earlier speaker, Narada, addressing King Yudhisthira; the text says that the first speaker was its composer, Vyasa, whose son Suka is. The first book opens at the onset of the Kali Yuga with sages performing a thousand-year sacrifice in the forest of Naimisaranya. Later books cover creation, genealogies, avatars of Vishnu such as Rama and Parashurama, and the destruction of the Yadu dynasty. The tenth book, of 90 chapters, tells of Krishna's life.

Its theology uses Vedanta and Samkhya in the service of bhakti. Traditions of Vedanta, among them the Advaita of Adi Shankara, the qualified monism of Rāmānujachārya, the dualism of Madhavacharya and the Bhedābheda of Vallabha and Caitanya, have each read its verses through their own commentaries.

The Bhagavata Purana is widely recognised as the best known and most influential of the Puranas and is called the Fifth Veda. It is among the most commented texts in Indian literature: over eighty medieval commentaries in Sanskrit alone are known, and a version exists in almost every Indian language. Its legends are retold in festivals such as Holi and Diwali, it inspired Ras Leela, dramatic enactments of Krishna's pastimes, and it played a significant part in the Krishna-bhakti movement of Chaitanya in Bengal.

A French translation of a Tamil version appeared in 1788, and the Bhagavata was the first Purana translated into a European language. In the 20th century it spread beyond India and was translated into over twenty languages.
bhaktapur: Bhaktapur lies in the eastern corner of the Kathmandu Valley and is a major Newar settlement. Locally it is called Khwopa, and it was historically known as Bhadgaon. The name Bhaktapur, first attested in an inscription of 928, is widely held to be a Sanskrit rendering of the older Newar name Khōpring, from words meaning cooked rice and village, which appears in a Licchavi inscription of 594. Folklore says the valley was once a lake, drained when the Bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gorge with his sword; the Swiss geologist Toni Hagen showed that it was indeed a lake, which began to drain about thirty thousand years ago.

The 14th-century Gopal Raj Vamshavali credits Ananda Deva, who ruled from 1146 to 1167, with founding the city, probably by joining earlier settlements, and with making it the capital with a royal court, Tripura Rājkula. Shrines of eight Matrikas around the city and that of Tripura Sundari at the centre make the whole town a sacred mandala. As seat of government Bhaktapur attracted invasions, because divisions in the royal family brought in Tirhut and the Khasa Kingdom. Rudra Malla married his sister to the king of Tirhut in the 1310s to end its attacks.

After Nepal Mandala divided into three kingdoms, Bhaktapur stayed a wealthy and powerful Newar kingdom, helped by its place on the India-Tibet trade route. Queen Ganga Devi, the only queen regnant, ruled jointly with her two sons, and under her it reached its territorial zenith. In 1769 the Gorkha Kingdom annexed Bhaktapur, which lost importance to Kathmandu and Lalitpur and stayed isolated. After 1846 Dhir Shumsher Rana, as mayor, had many old palaces demolished and replaced with buildings in British style.

Bhaktapur is predominantly Hindu, and about 90 per cent of its people are Newar. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The Nyatapola, a five-roofed pagoda completed in 1702 and commissioned by King Bhupatindra Malla, stands in Taumadhi Square, and Durbar Square holds the palace complex and the stone temples of Vatsala Devi and Siddhi Lakshmi. The city has about 104 hitis, carved water spouts, and 50 artificial ponds, the two oldest built in 1118 and 1168.
bharatiya-janata-party: The party's origins lie in the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, founded in 1951 by Shyama Prasad Mukherjee in collaboration with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and widely regarded as its political arm. Its aims included protecting India's Hindu cultural identity and countering what it saw as the appeasement of Muslims and of Pakistan by the Congress party under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. The RSS lent it several full-time workers, among them Deendayal Upadhyaya, who became General Secretary. The Jana Sangh won three Lok Sabha seats in 1952 and kept a minor presence in parliament until 1967.

After Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of emergency in 1975, thousands of Jana Sangh members were imprisoned in the protests. In 1977 the party merged with the Socialist Party, the Congress (O) and the Bharatiya Lok Dal to form the Janata Party, which won a majority and formed a government under Morarji Desai. The former Jana Sangh supplied 93 of its seats, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee became Minister of External Affairs.
