The mid-10th-century chronicle De Administrando Imperio first mentions it, as Biogradon, among the populated towns of christened Croatia, and it was then the centre of the county of Sidraga.

A three-naved basilica was built there in the 9th century under Duke Branimir, on the base of an older 6th-century church, and it later became the cathedral of the bishop of Biograd. The Venetians held the town briefly around the year 1000. By the 1050s it was the seat of the Diocese of Alba Maritima, and King Peter Krešimir IV founded the monasteries of St John the Evangelist and St Thomas in 1059 and 1066. It was a major port in the later 11th century, and the Norman princess Felicia of Sicily landed there in 1096 to marry King Coloman of Hungary. Coloman was crowned there in 1102 by Bishop Bono, as the crown of Croatia passed to the Hungarians.

Rule alternated between Venice and the Árpád family, and the town is called a royal city in surviving documents from this time. Venice destroyed it in 1125, when, according to the Historia Ducum Veneticorum, its citizens alone dared resist the doge. The bishopric was abolished and the population moved to Skradin. In 1202, citizens of Zadar sheltered there during the Fourth Crusade. Venice acquired the town in 1409 and held it until 1797, and it was destroyed and burned in 1521 and 1646 in the Venetian-Turkish wars.

Biograd na Moru is part of Zadar County and has 5,601 inhabitants according to the 2021 census, most of them Croats. It is regarded as another capital of the medieval Kingdom of Croatia, and its rulers included Stephen Držislav and Peter Krešimir IV.
bioko: Bioko lies in the Bight of Biafra on the Gulf of Guinea, 32 km south of the coast of Cameroon and about 160 km northwest of the mainland part of Equatorial Guinea. It covers 2,017 km2 and is about 70 km long. The island is volcanic and mountainous, mostly basalt, and its highest peak, Pico Basilé, rises to about 3,012 m. Only 60 metres of water over the continental shelf separate it from the mainland, to which it was joined until about 10,000 years ago. Rainfall is very heavy in the south, and tropical rainforest covers most of the island.

Bioko had an indigenous population when Europeans arrived: Bantu-speaking ancestors of the Bubi probably settled there before the 7th century BCE. The Portuguese navigator Fernão do Pó sighted the island in 1472, and in 1494 it was renamed Fernando Pó in his honour. The Portuguese planted sugarcane, and in 1642 the Dutch East India Company used the island to centralise its slave trade in the Gulf of Guinea. Bubi clans withdrew from the coast to the safer interior and began to build a new kingdom under chiefs such as Molambo. Under the Treaty of El Pardo of 1778, Portugal ceded Fernando Po to Spain.

After the British abolished their Atlantic slave trade, they leased bases at Port Clarence, now Malabo, and San Carlos from 1827 to 1843 for the Preventive Squadron. Under William Fitzwilliam Owen their forces detained 20 ships and freed 2,500 enslaved people. Spain raised its flag at Port Clarence in March 1843 and revoked the British lease in 1855. Late in the 19th century Krio planters turned from palm oil to cocoa; dependent on migrant labour, they failed to pay contracts, producing de facto slavery. A League of Nations investigation between 1923 and 1930 into the shipment of contract labour from Liberia found that the abuses arose from conditions on the island.

Bioko is part of Equatorial Guinea, and Malabo, on its north coast, is its largest city. The 2015 census counted 335,048 inhabitants. The Bubi, the historic indigenous people, make up 58 per cent. Spanish, official since 1844, is the language of education and administration; Bube is spoken by about 50,000 people, and the creole Pichi also developed on the island. Two protected areas, Pico Basilé National Park and the Luba Crater Scientific Reserve, cover about 40 per cent of Bioko.
birendra-of-nepal: Birendra was born on 29 December 1945 at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace in Kathmandu, the son of Crown Prince Mahendra and Crown Princess Indra. An earlier son of Mahendra, Rabindra Shah, was born to an unmarried Gurung woman and counted as illegitimate, so Birendra became heir apparent. He studied at St Joseph's School, a Jesuit school in Darjeeling, then at Eton College from 1959 to 1964, and later at the University of Tokyo and Harvard University. On 27 February 1970 he married Aishwarya Rajya Lakshmi Devi, his second cousin.

Birendra came to the throne on 31 January 1972 after Mahendra's death, and was crowned on 24 February 1975 after a mourning year and a year astrologers judged inauspicious. He inherited a country where political parties were banned and rule ran through panchayat councils, so that he was effectively an absolute monarch. Growing pro-democracy demands led him to call a referendum between a party-less and a multi-party system in May 1980. The party-less system won by 55 per cent to 45, a result that democracy campaigners later claimed was rigged.

In 1990 strikes and pro-democracy riots led him to lift the ban on parties and agree to become a constitutional monarch. He promulgated a new constitution on 9 November 1990, making Nepal a constitutional monarchy with multiparty democracy. A civil war between Maoist rebels and government forces began in 1996 and lasted until 2006. His government set up national parks, among them Chitwan and Sagarmatha, and he promoted Nepal as a zone of peace at the United Nations, a proposal 116 countries supported.

On 1 June 2001 Birendra and his immediate family were shot dead at dinner at the Narayanhiti Palace by his son, Crown Prince Dipendra. Dipendra shot himself and, in a coma, was proclaimed king, but died a few days later. Birendra's younger brother Gyanendra then became king. Monuments named for Birendra were renamed after the political changes of 2006 and the end of the monarchy in 2008.
birgu: Birgu, also called Vittoriosa or Città Vittoriosa, "Victorious City", is an old fortified city on the south side of the Grand Harbour in the Port Region of Malta. It occupies a promontory with Fort Saint Angelo at its head and the city of Cospicua at its base. It is ideally situated for safe anchorage and has a long history of maritime, mercantile and military activity. Before Valletta was founded, any military power that wanted to rule the Maltese islands had to take Birgu in order to control the Grand Harbour.

Birgu was settled in medieval times, and Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Normans, the Aragonese and the Order of Saint John all contributed to its development. After the Order of Saint John was driven out of Rhodes by the Ottoman Empire, it received Malta. In 1526 a commission of eight knights described Birgu as a small defenceless town with old houses in poor condition. When the Order arrived in 1530 it made Birgu the capital, since Mdina lay inland and did not suit its naval needs.

The city was fortified in the 1530s and strengthened in the 1550s, and the Castle of St Angelo was built, joined to the city by a drawbridge. In the Great Siege of 1565 the Knights defended it for four months, and in August the Ottoman army almost captured it, but the Knights under Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette recaptured it. Reinforcements from Sicily arrived a month later and the Ottomans abandoned the siege. A new capital, Valletta, was then built on Mount Sceberras, and in 1571 the Knights moved their convent and seat there. Birgu lost some importance but was given the title Città Vittoriosa.

After Napoleon took Malta in 1798, French forces were garrisoned in Birgu, and the Maltese rebelled soon after. The French capitulated in September 1800 and Malta became a British protectorate. The Royal Navy's Mediterranean Fleet had its base in Birgu, and British forces remained until 1979, an event commemorated by the Freedom Monument. In 1806 the gunpowder magazine exploded, killing over 200 people, and in the Second World War heavy bombing destroyed historic buildings.

Birgu has five Auberges of the Knights, and the Malta Maritime Museum stands on the waterfront. St Lawrence's Church was once the conventual church of the Order, and Fort St Angelo still stands at the centre of the Grand Harbour.
birka: Birka stood on the island of Björkö in Lake Mälaren, 30 kilometres west of present-day Stockholm. It was founded around 750 by a king or by merchants seeking to control trade, and is one of the earliest urban settlements in Scandinavia. It was the Baltic link in the Dnieper trade route through Ladoga and Novgorod to the Byzantine Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate. It most likely offered furs, iron goods and craft products for materials from Europe and Western Asia. Furs came from the Sami, the Finns and north-western Russia, and combs of reindeer antler were important. The population has been estimated at 500 to 1,000.

Rimbert's Life of Ansgar says Ansgar travelled to Birka in 829 on a mission from Emperor Louis the Pious and founded the first known Christian congregation in Sweden in 831. Its attempt to convert people from the Norse religion was unsuccessful. Adam of Bremen says Archbishop Unni died at Birka in 936. Birka was abandoned in the latter half of the 10th century, around the time Sigtuna was founded and became the main trading centre of the Mälaren area. The reasons are disputed: Gotland was better placed for Rus' and Byzantine trade, and Neil Kent has speculated that an enemy assault may have destroyed it.

No texts survive from Birka itself, and no Norse source names it. The settlement's location was lost for centuries, and the Chronicle of Sweden first claimed in 1450 that Björkö was Birka. Johan Hadorph attempted excavations in the late 17th century. Hjalmar Stolpe came in the late 19th century to study insects in amber, found so much that he suspected a trading post, and excavated between 1871 and 1895.

The remains cover about 7 hectares and include a hill fort called Borgen and more than 3,000 graves, both cremations and burials in coffins or chamber graves. Goods in the graves include glass, Rhineland pottery, Chinese silk and Byzantine embroidery with fine gold thread. Most coins found are silver dirhams from the Middle East. Ten small silver crosses and 27 pendants of Thor's hammer show that both Christianity and traditional beliefs were present. Birka and Hovgården on the neighbouring island of Adelsö have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.
birkenfeld: Birkenfeld lies in the Nahe area, north of the Nahe river, on the edge of the Saar-Hunsrück nature park, about 13 kilometres south-west of Idar-Oberstein. The name comes from Old Frankish and means something like "at the field with the birches". Finds show heavy settlement in the Iron Age, as early as the 8th century BCE, and Roman legions overran the area in the 1st century BCE. The town stands on a Roman road that linked two military roads, one from Metz to Mainz and the other from Trier through Bingen to Mainz.

The name is first recorded as Bikenuelt, about 700, and a document of Archbishop Egbert of Trier of 981 shows that Saint Leudwinus, archbishop from 695 to 713, had given the churches at Birkenfeld and Brombach to St. Paulinus' Abbey in Trier. In the 13th century the Counts of Sponheim held it. When their county was divided in 1223, Birkenfeld passed to the Rear County. The castle is first mentioned in 1293, and Emperor Louis the Bavarian granted town rights in 1332. During the Thirty Years' War the town became a theatre of war in 1635, and the plague that year killed 416 people.

In 1776 Birkenfeld became the seat of the Baden Oberamt, and an economic and cultural upswing followed, with the first higher school founded in 1779. In 1798 the left bank of the Rhine was ceded to France, and Birkenfeld belonged to the Department of Sarre. After the Congress of Vienna the Principality of Birkenfeld was awarded to the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg as an exclave, for the part played by Peter I, regent of Oldenburg, against Napoleon.

A new palace, now the district administration's seat, was built in 1821 under Oldenburg, with other Classicist buildings that still mark the town. On 1 April 1937 the region was transferred to the Prussian Rhine Province, and after the Second World War it lay in the French Occupation Zone. Since 1946 it has been a district seat in Rhineland-Palatinate.

Birkenfeld is the seat of the Birkenfeld district and of the Verbandsgemeinde of Birkenfeld, a collective municipality of 31 municipalities. The town itself has about 7,000 inhabitants. The district, of which it has been the seat since 1946, lies in the south-west of the state, and about half of its inhabitants were Evangelical and 31 per cent Catholic in 2008.
birnin-kebbi: Birnin Kebbi stands on the Sokoto River in north-western Nigeria and is connected by road to Argungu, about 45 kilometres to the northeast, Jega, about 35 kilometres to the southeast, and Bunza, about 45 kilometres to the southwest. Its people are mostly Hausa and Fulani, and Islam is the main religion. The town is also the seat of a local government area.

Birnin Kebbi was formerly the capital of the Kebbi Emirate. It remained the capital until 1805, when it was burned in the Fulani jihad. After it was incorporated into the Fulani Emirate of Gwandu, it was eclipsed in political importance by the town of Gwandu, 48 kilometres to the east, and as a caravan and riverside market by Jega, 32 kilometres to the southeast, which lay at the head of navigation on the Zamfara River, a tributary of the Sokoto. Argungu became the traditional seat of the king of Kebbi, and the Kebbi emirate moved there.
Birnin Kebbi nevertheless served as the headquarters of the Gwandu emirate after Emir Haliru was inaugurated there in 1906. In 1991 it became the capital of the newly created Nigerian state of Kebbi.

The town has declined as a river port because of silting and political conditions. It serves as a collecting point for peanuts and rice and as a local market for millet, sorghum, rice, fish, goats and cattle. It has a state polytechnic college and a government rice-research station, and is served by Sir Ahmadu Bello International Airport. Its oldest hospital is the Sir Yahaya Memorial Hospital. An estimate of 2007 gave the city a population of 125,594.
biscay: Biscay lies on the south shore of the Bay of Biscay and is bordered by Cantabria and the province of Burgos to the west, Gipuzkoa to the east and Álava to the south. The southern ranges of the Basque Mountains form a continuous barrier, with passes no lower than 600 metres, and the water divide between the Atlantic and Mediterranean basins. The middle section is occupied by the valleys of the Nervión, the Ibaizabal and the Kadagua. The coast is usually high, with cliffs and small inlets, and its main features are the estuary of Bilbao and the estuary of Gernika. The climate is oceanic, with high precipitation all year.

Biscay has been inhabited since the Middle Paleolithic, and its caves hold cave paintings, those of Santimamiñe showing bison, horses, goats and deer. Roman geographers placed two tribes there, the Caristii and the Autrigones, who are thought to have spoken Basque. The Roman presence had little impact, and the Basque language and traditions survived. The name Biscay first appears in the Chronicle of Alfonso III in the late 9th century, and the territory was then controlled by the Kingdom of Navarre.

The house of Haro, leaders of the pro-Castilian lords, was granted the rule of the newly created Biscay, and tradition names Iñigo López as its first Lord in 1043. The lordship later passed by inheritance to John I of Castile and became one of the titles of the king of Castile. Each lord had to swear to defend the fuero, the Biscayan laws derived from Navarrese and Basque customary rights, which held that sovereignty lay with the Biscayans. Lords and later kings swore the statutes to the oak of Gernika, where the assembly of the lordship sits.

In 1511 the kings granted the port of Bilbao privileges for trade with the ports of the Spanish Empire, and it was already the main Castilian harbour, shipping wool to Flanders. The Carlist Wars of the 19th century grew in part from the desire to keep foral rights, and the victory of the anti-Carlists brought successive cuts to Biscay's autonomy. Iron ore discovered in the 1850s brought foreign investment and rapid industrialization. In 1937 German aircraft under Franco's control destroyed the town of Gernika, and Bilbao fell some months later. The 1979 Statute of Guernica created the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country.

Biscay is a province of the Basque Autonomous Community with its capital and largest city at Bilbao. Its name is Bizkaia in Basque and Vizcaya in Spanish, and its institutions are the Juntas Generales and the Foral Diputation. Its population is 1,167,233.
bishkek: Bishkek stands at an altitude of about 800 metres, just off the northern fringe of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too Range, an extension of the Tian Shan whose peaks rise to 4,895 metres. North of the city a fertile, gently undulating steppe stretches far into Kazakhstan, and the river Chüy drains most of the area. The central city is laid out on a rectangular grid, with wide boulevards, marble-faced public buildings and many Soviet-style apartment blocks, and narrow irrigation channels line most streets to water the shade trees.

The site began as a caravan rest stop on a branch of the Silk Road through the Tian Shan, possibly founded by the Sogdians. In 1825 the khan of Kokand fortified it with a mud fort, Pishpek, to control the caravan routes and collect tribute from the Kyrgyz. Russian forces under Colonel Apollon Zimmermann later took and razed the fort, and a Russian settlement with the original name Pishpek was established on the site in 1868, within the General Governorship of Russian Turkestan.

In 1925 the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast was created and Pishpek became its capital. In 1926 the city was renamed Frunze after Mikhail Frunze, a Bolshevik military leader and associate of Lenin who was born there. It became capital of the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic in 1936. Until the mid-1990s Russians and other people of European descent were the majority of the population; in the 1970 census the Kyrgyz were only 12.3 per cent. The city was renamed Bishkek on 5 February 1991, and Kyrgyzstan became independent later that year. One tradition derives the name Bishkek from the paddle used to churn fermenting milk.

Bishkek is the capital and largest city of Kyrgyzstan and of the Chüy Region, with about 1.2 million people, near the border with Kazakhstan. It is the country's financial centre and its most important cultural city, with the National Library, the Kyrgyz State Historical Museum on Ala-Too Square and the Frunze House Museum. Most residents are ethnic Kyrgyz, with a sizeable Russian minority. The Dordoy Bazaar on the north-eastern edge is a major wholesale and retail market.
bishop: The English word bishop comes through Latin episcopus and Old English biscop from the Greek epískopos, meaning overseer or supervisor. The term did not originate in Christianity: it had been used in Greek for several centuries before. According to most scholars, the earliest organisation of the church in Jerusalem resembled that of Jewish synagogues, with a council of ordained presbyters, or elders, chaired, in the account of Acts, by James the Just, according to tradition the first bishop of the city. In the New Testament the word presbyter was not yet distinguished from overseer.

Around the end of the 1st century the church's organisation became clearer. In the works of the Apostolic Fathers, Ignatius of Antioch in particular, the role of the episkopos grew more important or more clearly defined, though other writers still equated bishops with presbyters. By the second century bishops were defined as the only clergy entrusted with ordaining priests and deacons. The First Council of Nicaea in the fourth century decreed that a bishop should be ordained by at least three others.

The organisation of the Roman Empire became the template for that of the church in the fourth century, particularly after Constantine's Edict of Milan. Bishops also held political office: after the 9th century they were archchancellors of the Holy Roman Empire and generally served as chancellors to medieval monarchs, and the Lord Chancellor of England was almost always a bishop until the dismissal of Cardinal Thomas Wolsey by Henry VIII. During the English Civil War the bishops' political power became a matter of heated controversy.

Traditionally a bishop is the pastor of a diocese, also called a see, bishopric or eparchy, and is understood to possess the full priesthood, so that he may ordain other clergy, including bishops. Bishops claim apostolic succession, a direct lineage back to the Twelve Apostles. They lead the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, the Anglican Communion and some Lutheran churches, while other denominations have given up the office, seeing it as a symbol of power. A bishop's usual insignia are the mitre and the crosier, and in many cathedrals a special chair, the cathedra, is set aside for his sole use.
biskra: Biskra is the main city of the Ziban region and the capital of Biskra Province in north-eastern Algeria, about 399 km from Algiers. It stands at the start of the Sahara, at an altitude of 87 metres, and is nicknamed the Queen of the Zibans and the Door of the Desert. Because of its position and its farming, especially its date oases, it has always been a crossroads between the cities of the north and the south.

In Roman times the city was known as Vescera. The Arab commander Uqba ibn Nafi al-Fihri was killed on his return from Morocco in an ambush by the Berber prince Koceila at Tahouda, a small village about 5 km from the oasis now called Sidi Okba, and was buried in the mosque of the town that bears his name. In the early 10th century Biskra and the Ziban area were conquered by the Beni Hammad. A book of the late 12th century describes a large city surrounded by fortresses and thriving villages, with a vast forest of palms and olives, and a centre of jurisprudence and learning.

In the 14th century Biskra became an important hub for the Hafsids of Tunisia, and in 1541 the Ottoman Turks began to conquer it. The French conquered it in 1844 and fortified it as a garrison, and it saw fighting during rebellions in 1849 and 1871. The local chief Bou Zian rallied people against the palm tax and seized the fortification of Zaatcha, 20 km away; a French force of 7,000 took it after fifty-three days of attack, and Bou Zian was killed.

Biskra had a recorded population of 307,987 in 2007. In the late 19th century it became a popular winter resort and gateway to the Sahara and a centre for artists and photographers. André Gide set key sections of The Immoralist there, Henri Matisse painted Blue Nude (Souvenir de Biskra) in 1907, and Béla Bartók collected traditional music in the town in 1913.
bismarck-archipelago: The Bismarck Archipelago lies just off the north-eastern coast of New Guinea in the western Pacific and is part of the Islands Region of Papua New Guinea. Its islands are mostly volcanic and have a total land area of about 49,700 square kilometres, around the Bismarck Sea.

They are grouped by province: Manus Province has the Admiralty Islands, a group of 18 islands including Manus, Los Negros and Lou, and the Western Islands; New Ireland Province has New Ireland, New Hanover, the St Matthias Islands and the Tabar, Lihir, Tanga and Feni groups; East and West New Britain provinces share New Britain and the Duke of York Islands; and others lie off Morobe, Madang and East Sepik provinces, among them Umboi, Ritter, Karkar and the Schouten Islands. The passage between New Britain and New Ireland is St George's Channel.

The first inhabitants arrived around 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. They may have come from New Guinea by boat across the Bismarck Sea or over a temporary land bridge created by an uplift of the crust. Later arrivals included the Lapita people, the direct ancestors of the Austronesian peoples of Polynesia, eastern Micronesia and Island Melanesia.

The first European to visit was the Dutch explorer Jacob le Maire in 1616, and the islands remained unsettled by western Europeans until they were annexed in 1884 as part of the German protectorate of German New Guinea. They were named in honour of Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

On 13 March 1888 a volcano on Ritter Island erupted and caused a megatsunami; almost the whole volcano fell into the sea, leaving a small rim on the east side of the original island. After the outbreak of the First World War the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force seized the islands in 1914, and Australia later received a League of Nations mandate for them. They stayed under Australian administration, interrupted only by Japanese occupation in World War II, until Papua New Guinea became independent in September 1975.
bismarck-battleship: Bismarck was the first of two Bismarck-class battleships built for the German Kriegsmarine, the second being Tirpitz. They were designed in the mid-1930s as a counter to the two Richelieu-class battleships that France began in 1935. Ordered as Ersatz Hannover, she was laid down at the Blohm & Voss yard in Hamburg on 1 July 1936, launched on 14 February 1939 with Adolf Hitler making the christening speech, and commissioned on 24 August 1940. She was nominally within the 35,000-ton limit of the Washington Naval Treaty but secretly exceeded it by a wide margin. Her main battery was eight 38 cm guns, and she reached just over 30 knots on trials.

Her only offensive operation, Rheinübung, lasted eight days in May 1941. Bismarck and the heavy cruiser Prinz Eugen were to break into the Atlantic and raid Allied shipping. In the Battle of the Denmark Strait the battlecruiser HMS Hood was destroyed by their combined fire, and HMS Prince of Wales was damaged and forced to retire; three hits from Prince of Wales damaged Bismarck enough to end the raid.

The loss of Hood set off a pursuit by dozens of Royal Navy ships. Heading for occupied France for repairs, Bismarck was attacked by fifteen Fairey Swordfish torpedo bombers from the carrier HMS Ark Royal, and one hit left her steering gear inoperable. In the final battle two British battleships and two heavy cruisers crippled her with heavy loss of life. She was scuttled to prevent boarding, although most experts agree that her damage would have sunk her in the end.

Robert Ballard, who had found the wreck of the Titanic, located Bismarck on 8 June 1989, upright on her keel at about 4,791 metres, some 650 km west of Brest. She had slid down the side of an extinct underwater volcano. Ballard's survey found no penetration of the armoured citadel. The 2002 expedition filmed by James Cameron concluded that the most extensive damage, including long gashes in the hull, came from her impact with the seabed.
bissau: Bissau lies on the estuary of the Geba River, off the Atlantic Ocean. The land around the city is extremely low-lying, and the river is accessible to ocean-going vessels for about 80 kilometres beyond it despite its modest discharge. The climate is tropical savanna, with almost no rain from November to May. The name may come from the name of a clan, N'nssassun, in its plural form Bôssassun.

From well before the arrival of Europeans until the early 20th century the island of Bissau was a kingdom of the Papel people. By oral tradition Mecau, a son of the king of Quinara, founded it and moved to the area with his pregnant sister, six wives and subjects of his father's kingdom. The kingdom had seven clans and was highly stratified, and the throne passed to the Bossassun clan, descended from the sister. When the Portuguese began to trade there in the 16th century the king of Bissau was among the most supportive monarchs of the region.

The city was founded in 1687 as a Portuguese trading post. The French were also active, and although King Bacompolco refused them leave to build a fort he granted them a trading factory, from which they shipped thousands of slaves. By 1696 the town had a fort, a church and a hospital. When the Portuguese tried to enforce a monopoly against the Papel policy of free trade, King Incinhate surrounded the unfinished fort, and they soon abandoned it. The Grão Pará and Maranhão Company rebuilt it in 1775 to store more slaves for shipment to Brazil, though real control stayed with the Papel kings.

Around the turn of the 20th century the Papels fiercely resisted Portuguese pacification campaigns. In 1915, after 30 years of war, the Portuguese under Teixeira Pinto and the warlord Abdul Injai defeated the Kingdom of Bissau and incorporated it into Portuguese Guinea. In 1941 the capital was moved from Bolama to Bissau. A dockworkers' strike was bloodily repressed in 1959 and pushed the nationalists towards armed resistance. After the military coup in Lisbon on 25 April, Bissau became the capital of the newly independent state.

Bissau is the capital and largest city of Guinea-Bissau, its main port and its administrative and military centre. Its attractions include the Fortaleza de São José da Amura, built by the Portuguese in the 18th century and containing the mausoleum of Amílcar Cabral, and the Pidjiguiti Memorial to the dockers killed in the strike of 3 August 1959.
bithynia: Bithynia occupied northwestern Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey, adjoining the Sea of Marmara, the Bosporus and the Black Sea. It bordered Mysia to the southwest, Paphlagonia to the northeast and Phrygia to the southeast. Ancient writers placed its eastern limit differently: Strabo at the river Sangarius, others at the Billaeus. Mountains and forests filled much of the land, above all the Bithynian Olympus, about 2,400 m high, above Prusa (modern Bursa), but the valleys and coasts were very fertile. Major cities stood on the shores of the Sea of Marmara: Nicomedia, Chalcedon, Cius and Apamea. Nicaea, the birthplace of the Nicene Creed, also lay in Bithynia.

The region is named for the Thracian tribe of the Bithyni, mentioned by Herodotus beside the Thyni. They probably migrated from the Balkans after the Bronze Age collapse or in the early Iron Age. King Croesus brought the Bithynians into the Lydian monarchy, which Persia conquered in 546 BCE. The Bithynians then asserted their independence under native princes, and Zipoites took the title of king in 297 BCE. His son Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia, which soon grew prosperous. The last king, Nicomedes IV, could not hold his throne against Mithridates VI of Pontus, and after the Roman Senate restored him he bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman Republic in 74 BCE.

As a Roman province Bithynia was usually joined with Pontus; Pliny the Younger governed the two together under Emperor Trajan, and his letters give historians valuable information on provincial administration. Under the Byzantine Empire the region was again divided at the Sangarius, and only the western part kept the name. Nicomedia and Nicaea long rivalled each other for the rank of capital. The Ottoman Turks conquered it between 1325 and 1333.
bitlis: Bitlis stands at an elevation of 1,545 metres in the steep-sided valley of the Bitlis River, a tributary of the Tigris, 15 kilometres from Lake Van. The origin of its name is not known. To Armenians it was Baghesh, one of the most important cities of the province of Aghdznik' in the Kingdom of Armenia, and the main fortress of the canton of Salnodzor. The fortress guarded the Baghesh Pass, which linked the southern edge of the Armenian plateau with northern Mesopotamia.

Under the Byzantine Empire the town was Balaleison. The Arabs conquered it at the end of the seventh century, and it became capital of the Zurārid emirs of Arzan, prospering on an important trade route. Later it passed to the Shaybanid and Kaysite emirs, and the Byzantine general John Curcuas captured it in the tenth century. Many Kurds settled there, and the Marwanid dynasty took the city. After Manzikert it came under Togan Arslan of Akhlat, after brief Dilmachoglu rule, and then Ayyubid rule, the Sultanate of Rûm and the Ilkhanate.

Bitlis was a Kurdish emirate, often subordinate to larger powers but keeping a measure of independence. In the 14th century its emirs, the Rusaki family, were vassals of the Karakoyunlu, and the emir submitted to Timur in 1394. In the 15th century the town flourished as a centre of Armenian manuscript production, the Kurdish emirs permitting monasteries to be built. An Ottoman army besieged it for three months and withdrew; the emir Sheref was killed in 1533 and his son submitted to the Ottoman Empire. The Ruzakid dynasty lasted until 1849, when an Ottoman governor evicted the last emir. Persian was the language of administration and scholarship, in the works of Idris-i Bidlisi and Sharaf Khan among others.

In 1915, during the Armenian genocide, Turks and Kurds led by Jevdet Bey massacred some 15,000 Armenians in Bitlis and its surroundings. Russian forces took the town in March 1916 and abandoned it in August.

Bitlis keeps more medieval and traditional architecture than any other town in eastern Turkey, much of it in the light-brown local stone called Ahlat stone. It has the 12th-century Ulu Mosque with a 15th-century minaret and large stone houses. Only one 19th-century Armenian church survives of the five monasteries and several churches that stood until 1915. Its population was 53,023 in 2021.
bitola: Bitola lies in the southwestern part of North Macedonia, in the southern part of the Pelagonia valley, surrounded by the Baba, Nidže and Kajmakčalan mountain ranges and 14 kilometres north of the Medžitlija-Níki border crossing with Greece. The Dragor River flows through the city, which stands at 615 metres above sea level at the foot of Baba Mountain. It stands at an important junction connecting the south of the Adriatic region with the Aegean Sea and Central Europe.

The earliest organised settlements nearby are early Neolithic tells near the village of Porodin, first inhabited around 6000 BCE. In antiquity the region was Lynkestis, part of Upper Macedonia, and Heraclea Lyncestis was founded by Philip II of Macedon by the middle of the 4th century BCE. Slavic tribes settled the area in the 6th and 7th centuries and built a fortress around their settlement. Bitola was part of the First Bulgarian Empire from the middle of the 8th to the early 11th centuries and was its last capital, in 1015 to 1018; the Bitola inscription is related to the fortress built in 1015. It then returned to the Byzantine Empire and was briefly part of the Serbian Empire in the 14th century.

The Ottomans conquered the city in the mid-1380s, and it was part of the Ottoman Empire as Monastir until 1912. It was the last capital of Ottoman Rumelia, from 1836 to 1867, and the many European consulates earned it the name City of Consuls. The region was a stronghold of the Ilinden Uprising of 1903, planned in Smilevo in May. In the First Balkan War the Battle of Monastir, from 16 to 19 November 1912, led to Serbian occupation, and the Treaty of Bucharest in 1913 ceded Monastir to Serbia, when its official name became Bitola.
In World War II the Germans took control on 9 April 1941, and on 11 March 1943 Bulgarian forces deported the vast majority of its Jewish community, 3,276 people, to Treblinka extermination camp.

Bitola is an administrative, cultural, industrial, commercial and educational centre of southwestern North Macedonia. Its population was historically diverse: about 37,500 at the end of the 19th century, including Aromanians, a Muslim population, a Jewish community of Sephardic origin and Slavic speakers divided between the Bulgarian Exarchate and the Greek Patriarchate.

The ruins of Heraclea Lyncestis lie 2 kilometres from the centre. Ottoman monuments include the covered bazaar, the Gazi Hajdar Kadi Mosque of the early 1560s, ascribed to the architect Mimar Sinan, and the Deboj Bath. The Church of Saint Demetrius was built in 1830 with contributions from local merchants and craftsmen. The St. Clement of Ohrid University of Bitola was founded in 1979.
black-death: The Black Death was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is primarily spread by flea bites, though it may also spread through contact with infected tissues or fluids and, in pneumonic cases, through respiratory droplets. Its origin is disputed, with some evidence pointing towards China, Central Asia, West Asia and Europe. Genetic work published in 2010 and 2011 on skeletons from mass graves, including the East Smithfield burial site in England, confirmed Y. pestis as the cause. European writers of the time called the disease pestilentia or mortalitas, and the name Black Death was not used in English for this pandemic until the 1750s.

The pandemic was reportedly first introduced to Europe during the siege of the Genoese trading port of Caffa in Crimea by the Golden Horde army of Jani Beg in 1347. From Crimea it was most likely carried by fleas on black rats travelling on Genoese ships. It spread through the Mediterranean and reached North Africa, West Asia and the rest of Europe via Constantinople, Sicily and the Italian Peninsula. Evidence suggests that once ashore it mainly spread from person to person as pneumonic plague, which explains its fast inland spread.

By autumn 1347 plague had reached Alexandria in Egypt, carried by sea from Constantinople by a single merchant ship carrying slaves. By late summer 1348 it reached Cairo, capital of the Mamluk Sultanate and the largest city of the Mediterranean Basin. The child sultan an-Nasir Hasan fled, and more than a third of the 600,000 residents died. Plague recurred in Cairo more than fifty times over the next one and a half centuries. Contemporary accounts noted above all buboes in the groin, neck and armpits, which oozed pus and bled when opened.

There are no exact figures for the death toll, and the rate varied widely by locality. A 2022 study of pollen samples across Europe found high mortality in areas of Scandinavia, France, western Germany, Greece and central Italy, but uninterrupted agricultural growth in central and eastern Europe, Iberia and Ireland. The population of Europe did not regain its 14th-century level until the 16th century. The labour shortage raised wages, and in some places rents collapsed, though many labourers lost real income to inflation.

Many Europeans blamed Jews, friars, foreigners, beggars, pilgrims, lepers and Romani for the crisis. About 2,000 Jews were murdered in the Strasbourg massacre of February 1349, and the Jewish communities of Mainz and Cologne were annihilated in August 1349. By 1351 sixty major and 150 smaller Jewish communities had been destroyed. Plague returned repeatedly to Europe through the 14th to 17th centuries, and some scholars have suggested that Italy's experience of the epidemic shaped the thought of the Renaissance.
black-forest: The Black Forest is a large forested mountain range in Baden-Württemberg, bounded by the Rhine Valley to the west and south and close to the borders with France and Switzerland. It is the source of the Danube and the Neckar. It is about 160 kilometres long and up to 50 kilometres wide, with an area of about 6,009 square kilometres, and its highest peak is the Feldberg at 1,493 metres. The gentle eastern slopes contrast with the steeply falling terrain in the west that drops into the Upper Rhine Graben. It consists of a cover of sandstone on a core of gneiss and granite, and it was covered by glaciers in the last glacial period, which left tarns such as the Mummelsee.

In ancient times the range was known as Abnoba mons, after the Celtic deity Abnoba, and in Roman times as Silva Marciana, from the Germanic marka, border; it probably marked the border area of the Marcomanni, a part of the Suebi. Apart from Roman settlements on the perimeter, such as the baths at Badenweiler, mines near Badenweiler and Sulzburg and the Roman road of the Kinzig valley, the colonization was carried out not by the Romans but by the Alemanni. They settled the valleys first and then increasingly higher areas, so that by the end of the 10th century the first settlements stood in the red sandstone region. Rötenbach, for example, was first mentioned in 819.

The ore deposits supported mining, and for several centuries logs were rafted down the Enz, Kinzig, Murg, Nagold and Rhine. This trade boomed in the 18th century and led to large-scale clearances. Most of the long, straight pine logs went to the Netherlands for shipbuilding and were called Dutchmen; used there as piles for houses, they support many historic buildings in Amsterdam. Rafting largely ended in the late 19th century with the railways and roads.

Charcoal burners, potash boilers and glassmakers also lived from the timber. Because the valleys were relatively inaccessible, industrialization arrived late. In winter many farmers made wooden cuckoo clocks, which developed in the 19th century into a precision engineering and watch industry, and the Baden state government founded a clockmaking school at Furtwangen in 1850.

The Black Forest is mainly rural, with many scattered villages and a few large towns, and the main dialect is Alemannic. It is known for its farmhouses with sweeping half-hipped roofs, the Bollenhut headdress worn in villages of the Kinzig valley, wood carving, the cuckoo clock, Black Forest ham and the Black Forest gâteau. In the 19th and early 20th centuries its rural beauty attracted artists such as Hans Thoma. Tourism is now the primary industry, and several ruined military fortifications date back to the 17th century.
black-hills: The Black Hills are an outlying subrange of the Rocky Mountain system, rising from the Great Plains in western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming. The highest summit, Black Elk Peak, rises to 2,207 metres. The range takes its name from its dark appearance from a distance, since it is covered in evergreen trees, and the Lakota call it Pahá Sápa. Its core is granite dated to 1.8 billion years, ringed by metamorphic and sedimentary rocks, and its limestone holds more than 200 caves, among them Jewel Cave and Wind Cave. Most of the hills are covered by ponderosa pine forest.

Tools show a human presence going back as far as 11,500 BCE, with the Clovis culture. The Ponca, Arikara and Mandan were among the earliest recorded inhabitants, later displaced by the Kiowa, Plains Apache and Shoshone, and then by the Cheyenne and Arapaho. After the Lakota conquered the Cheyenne in 1776 the hills became central to Lakota culture. By 1850 the Lakota were the majority, and they call the hills wamakaognaka e'cante, the heart of everything that is. The Cheyenne, Arapaho and other peoples also hold particular sites there to be sacred.

The First Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1851 recognised the Black Hills as exclusive Lakota territory. The Second Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1868 created the Great Sioux Reservation west of the Missouri and protected the hills from settlers forever. In 1874 an expedition under George Armstrong Custer found gold in French Creek, and the reporters with it announced the discovery. Thousands of miners came during the gold rush of 1875 to 1878, and the towns of Deadwood, Central City and Lead grew up in the Northern Hills.

The conflict led to the Great Sioux War of 1876. After the defeat of the Lakota and their Cheyenne and Arapaho allies, the United States occupied the hills in disregard of past treaties, relocated the Lakota to five smaller reservations and sold off 9 million acres. On 23 July 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, the Supreme Court ruled that the hills had been illegally seized and ordered payment of the original offering price plus interest. The Lakota refused the money because acceptance would end their demand for the return of the land.

The region holds Mount Rushmore National Memorial, Wind Cave National Park, Jewel Cave National Monument, Custer State Park, the Crazy Horse Memorial and, in Wyoming, Devils Tower National Monument, the first national monument of the United States. The economy has moved from mining and timber towards tourism. Rapid City is the largest city, and the former mining town of Deadwood is preserved as a historic place.
black-sea-fleet: Peter the Great tried to expand Russia to the Black Sea and set up a naval base on the Sea of Azov during the Russo-Turkish War of 1695–96, but he had to surrender those gains after the war of 1710 to 1713. Russia's position in the south advanced slowly after the war of 1735 to 1739 and then much faster under Catherine the Great, whose Greek Project envisaged partitioning the Ottoman Empire between Russia and the Habsburg Empire. Beginning with the war of 1768–1774, Russia and the Ottoman Empire fought seven more wars up to the First World War over which would dominate the Black Sea region. Prince Potemkin founded the fleet on 13 May 1783 as part of the Imperial Russian Navy.

The Russian SFSR inherited the fleet in 1918, and with the founding of the Soviet Union in 1922 it became part of the Soviet Navy. After the defeat of the anti-Bolshevik Armed Forces of South Russia the Soviet government took control of all naval elements. The few remaining ships were scrapped in the 1920s, and a large construction programme began in the 1930s, at first defensive and based on small submarines, then from about 1935 with cruisers and destroyers. Under the Montreaux Convention of 1936 the Soviet Union secured the peacetime right for its Black Sea ships to pass the Turkish Straits.

With the fall of the Soviet Union the fleet lost its major missions and much of its funding. In the early 1990s it had 645 ships and 72,000 personnel. In 1992 the greater part of its personnel, weapons and coastal facilities came under the jurisdiction of newly independent Ukraine, which ordered its own navy to be formed from it, and several ships declared themselves Ukrainian. This led to conflicts with the many officers loyal to Russia. In 1997 the fleet was partitioned between Russia and Ukraine, and Russia received title to 82 per cent of the vessels.

The fleet has its main headquarters and facilities at the Sevastopol Naval Base in Crimea. Its use of leased bases there was sometimes controversial in the years after 1991, for example over the refusal to let Ukrainians inspect aircraft cargo and the occupation of the Sarych lighthouse from 2005.
black-september: After the Six-Day War of 1967 Palestinian fedayeen guerrillas relocated to Jordan and stepped up attacks on Israel and the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They were headquartered at the border town of Karameh, which Israel targeted in the Battle of Karameh in 1968, bringing a surge of Arab support. The strength of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), led by Yasser Arafat, grew, and by early 1970 leftist groups within it were calling for the overthrow of Jordan's Hashemite monarchy, leading to violent clashes in June 1970.

King Hussein feared that an independent West Bank under PLO administration would threaten his kingdom, and he hesitated to expel the fighters. The Dawson's Field hijackings of 6 September 1970 ended his patience. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine seized three airliners; two jets landed at Azraq, and a third plane was brought to Zarqa on 9 September. The planes were blown up before the international press on 12 September.

The main fighting ran from 16 to 27 September 1970. On 17 September the Jordanian Army surrounded cities with a strong PLO presence, including Amman and Irbid, and attacked fedayeen posts in the refugee camps. The next day 10,000 Syrian troops bearing Palestine Liberation Army markings advanced towards Irbid, which the fedayeen had declared a liberated city. On 22 September the Syrians withdrew after heavy losses to a coordinated Jordanian air and ground offensive.

Pressure from Arab states such as Iraq led Hussein to halt his offensive, and on 13 October he signed an agreement with Arafat to regulate the fedayeen's presence. The army attacked again in January 1971 and drove the fighters from the cities. On 23 July 1971 some 2,000 surrendered after being encircled in the Ajlun offensive, which formally ended the conflict. The fedayeen were allowed to relocate to Lebanon through Syria.

Wasfi Tal's civilian government purged the bureaucracy and military of supporters of the guerrillas, and closed many newspapers. Palestinians and Jordanians fought on both sides in 1970, so the conflict did not reflect a Jordanian-Palestinian divide, but it paved the way for one. Hussein's resilience impressed the West and Israel, and Nixon ordered $10 million in aid to be delivered to Jordan.

Fatah members founded the Black September Organization in 1971. Its members assassinated Tal in Cairo on 28 November 1971, and in 1972 it carried out the Munich massacre of Israeli athletes. In Lebanon the enlarged PLO presence stirred internal unrest and helped to precipitate the Lebanese Civil War.
black-stone: The Black Stone was venerated at the Kaaba long before Islam, and aniconic stones called baetyls were known across the eastern Mediterranean. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad set it in the Kaaba's wall in 605, five years before his first revelation. In the account of ibn Ishaq, the clans of Mecca could not agree which should replace the stone after the Kaaba was rebuilt, so Muhammad laid it on a cloth and had each clan leader hold a corner as they carried it to the spot.

Muslim tradition gives it a longer past. One account holds that Adam placed it in the first Kaaba, and that the angel Gabriel showed Abraham where it lay so that his son Ishmael could build it into a new temple. Another holds that it was once an angel set to guard Adam.

The stone is set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba in a silver frame fastened with silver nails. It was once a single rock but now consists of several pieces cemented together, and its exposed face measures about 20 by 16 centimetres. It has never been analysed with modern techniques. It has been called basalt, natural glass or a stony meteorite, but geologists regard the meteoritic idea as doubtful.

Pilgrims circling the Kaaba seven times in the tawaf try to kiss the stone, touch it, or raise their hands towards it, following what tradition records of Muhammad. Because of the crowds, it is now acceptable to point towards it. Theologians stress that it has no divine significance; the caliph Umar is reported to have said that it could neither harm nor benefit anyone and that he kissed it only because he had seen Muhammad do so.

It is said to have been smashed by a catapult stone during the Umayyad siege of Mecca in 683, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr rejoined the pieces with a silver band. In January 930 the Qarmatians stole it and took it to Hajar in eastern Arabia, and held it for more than two decades before returning it. The custodians then had a silver frame made, and it has been enclosed in such a frame since.
blackbeard: Little is known of his early life. It is commonly believed that he was between 35 and 40 when he died, and so born around 1680. Contemporary records give his name most often as Blackbeard, Edward Thatch or Edward Teach. People who actually met him wrote Thatch or variants of it, but Teach is the form most often used, because it appears in The Boston News-Letter, North America's only newspaper at the time. He was most likely raised in Bristol, then the second-largest city in England, and could almost certainly read and write. Charles Johnson, an 18th-century author, claimed that he sailed on privateers from Jamaica in the War of the Spanish Succession.

Probably after the Treaty of Utrecht, Teach moved from Jamaica to the island of New Providence, whose harbour too shallow for the Royal Navy's larger vessels. Possibly about 1716 he joined the crew of Captain Benjamin Hornigold, who gave him command of a captured sloop. On 28 November 1717 his ships took the French slave ship La Concorde off Saint Vincent. He renamed her Queen Anne's Revenge and equipped her with 40 guns. His nickname came from his thick black beard and menacing appearance, and he was reported to tie lit slow matches under his hat to frighten his enemies.

By May 1718 he had styled himself Commodore, and his flotilla blockaded the port of Charles Town, South Carolina. About nine vessels were stopped and ransacked. Prominent citizens aboard the Crowley were held, and he demanded medical supplies from the colonial government, threatening to kill the prisoners if none came. On 10 June 1718 Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground on a sandbar at Beaufort Inlet. Teach learned of a royal pardon open to pirates who surrendered by 5 September 1718 and accepted it from Governor Charles Eden at Bath, North Carolina, but he soon returned to the sea.

Alexander Spotswood, the governor of Virginia, feared that Teach and his men would disrupt Virginian commerce and arranged for soldiers and sailors to capture him. On 22 November 1718 (3 December in the modern calendar), after a battle at Ocracoke Inlet, Teach and several of his crew were killed by a small force of sailors led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard. His loot was sold at auction for 2,238 pounds, and Spotswood used part of it to pay for the operation.

A shrewd leader, he relied on his fearsome image more than on violence. He was romanticised after his death and became the model of the archetypal pirate in fiction. Divers found the wreck of Queen Anne's Revenge in Beaufort Inlet in November 1996.
blaj: Blaj is a city in Alba County in Transylvania, lying at the confluence of the Târnava Mare and Târnava Mică rivers, where they form the Târnava River. It is 39 kilometres northeast of the county seat, Alba Iulia, in a wine-growing region. It is also known by its Hungarian name Balázsfalva and its German name Blasendorf, and the city administers eight villages. Its population was 17,816 at the 2021 census, and most inhabitants are Romanians, with Hungarian and Romani minorities.

Blaj is first mentioned in 1271 as Villa Herbordi, after the deed of a Count Herbod. In 1313 the domain passed to Herbod's son Blasius Cserei and the town was mentioned as Blasii. It began as a hamlet for the twenty families of servants at the noble's court and was awarded town status on 19 May 1737. Mănărade, one of its villages, belonged in the Middle Ages to the Cistercian Igriș Abbey, and in 1910 nearly 60 per cent of its villagers were Transylvanian Saxons.

The first public school in Romanian was established in Blaj in 1754, and Blaj was the first place to have Romanian written in the Latin alphabet instead of the traditional Cyrillic. It was also a centre of the Romanian Age of Enlightenment and the founding site of the Transylvanian School, which promoted the Roman cultural heritage of the Romanians. For this reason Romania's national poet Mihai Eminescu called it the Little Rome. In 1848 more than 40,000 Romanians met on the Câmpia Libertății, the Field of Liberty, to protest against Transylvania becoming part of Hungary, holding that their lands would be stolen from them.

Blaj was the principal religious and cultural centre of the Romanian Greek-Catholic Church in Transylvania. Its sights include the Metropolitan Palace, the Holy Trinity Cathedral, the Buna Vestire Monastery, the Greeks' Church, the Liberty Field and Avram Iancu's oak. The castle of the Bethlen dynasty is a popular site near the city.

Its schools include the Inochentie Micu Clain National College and the Sfântul Vasile cel Mare Greek-Catholic Theological High School. The Greek-Catholic bishops Samuil Vulcan and Ioan Suciu were born there, as was the priest and politician Ioan Simu.
blanche-i-of-navarre: Blanche was born on 6 July 1387, the second eldest daughter of King Charles III of Navarre and the infanta Eleanor of Castile. She became heiress to the throne of Navarre in 1413, when her elder sister Joan died. Before that she had married Martin the Younger, King of Sicily and Prince of Aragon, by proxy on 21 May 1402 in Catania, and in person on 26 December 1402. The bride was about 15 years old and the groom 28.

Martin needed legitimate heirs, having survived his previous wife, Queen Maria of Sicily, and their only son. Blanche and Martin had one child, Infante Martin of Aragon and Sicily, who lived from 1406 to 1407.

Blanche served as regent of Sicily from October 1404 to August 1405, while her husband was in Aragon, and again from August 1408 to July 1409, while he was in Sardinia. Martin died on 25 July 1409 and was succeeded by his father, Martin I of Aragon, who let her continue as regent, as she did after his death during the succession struggle in Aragon. She was a popular regent, seen as a symbol of Sicilian independence against Aragon, and there were plans to marry her to Nicolás Peralta, a descendant of the Sicilian royal house.

After Ferdinand I won in Aragon, Blanche lost her power, Sicily was annexed to Aragon in November 1415, and she went to Navarre. There she was sworn in as heir at Olite on 28 October 1415. In 1419 she married John, duke of Peñafiel, second son of Ferdinand I of Aragon, by proxy, and they married in person at Pamplona on 10 July 1420.

Charles III died on 8 September 1425 and Blanche succeeded him as queen regnant of Navarre, with John becoming king in her right as John II. They were crowned together at Pamplona on 15 May 1429. In 1433 she made a pilgrimage to Santa María del Pilar, where she founded a brotherhood inspired by chivalric traditions, whose members wore blue sashes with a gold pillar and the motto A ti me arrimo, and pledged regular fasting, prayer and almsgiving.

Blanche died in 1441 at Santa María la Real de Nieva. Her husband kept the government of Navarre in his own hands rather than yielding it to their son Charles of Viana, the rightful heir. They also had a daughter, Blanche, who married Henry IV of Castile; the marriage was never consummated, and after 13 years he sought and obtained a divorce.
blankenburg-harz: Blankenburg (Harz) is a town and health resort in the district of Harz in Saxony-Anhalt, at the northern foot of the Harz Mountains at a height of about 234 metres. It lies west of Quedlinburg, south of Halberstadt and east of Wernigerode. Above the town, on the hill of Blankenstein, stands Blankenburg Castle, and the Teufelsmauer, or Devil's Wall, a sandstone rock formation, offers views across the plain. The town was largely rebuilt after a fire in 1836.

The first traces of settlement date to the Old Stone Age, and the first recorded mention of Blankenburg goes back to 1123, when Lothair of Supplinburg, Duke of Saxony, installed Poppo, a nephew of Bishop Reinhard of Halberstadt, as count at the castle. In 1180–82 Frederick Barbarossa had Blankenburg devastated because it had pledged sole allegiance to Henry the Lion. After the last count of Regenstein died, the county went in 1599 back to the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

In the 17th century the dukes made it a secondary residence, and it flourished under Duke Louis Rudolf, who was given Blankenburg in 1707 as a paragium. The county was raised to an imperial principality that was ruled independently until 1731, when Louis Rudolf became a duke and it was reunited with Brunswick. The present Little Castle with its terraced and Baroque gardens dates from that time. From 1815 to 1918 the town belonged to the Duchy of Brunswick.

In September 1933 the Brunswick SS commander Jeckeln herded together 140 communists and social democrats in the town, and they were severely beaten, some dying as a result. During the Second World War a subcamp of Buchenwald, later subordinated to Mittelbau-Dora, held some 500 prisoners at forced labour in the factories of Blankenburg-Oesig, and a further subcamp was occupied in February 1945 by inmates of an Auschwitz subcamp. Memorials in the town commemorate them. In 1945 the district was moved from the British to the Soviet zone and later became part of East Germany.

The town's economy rests on tourism and spa and health facilities, and the Little Castle holds the town museum. The physicist Polykarp Kusch, a co-recipient of the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1955, the archaeologist Robert Koldewey and the philosopher Oswald Spengler were born there.
blantyre: Blantyre lies in the Shire Highlands, at the geographical centre of Malawi's Southern Region, and covers an area of 228 km2. The city stands in hilly country at elevations from about 780 to 1,612 metres. Mount Soche, Ndirande mountain, Chiradzulu mountain and Michiru Mountain surround it, and rivers and streams rise in these hills and radiate from the city. The rainy season runs from November to April, and the dry season from May to October.

The mission was founded in 1876 by the Church of Scotland. The site was chosen by the British missionary Henry Henderson, who was joined there on 23 October 1876 by Dr T. T. Macklin and others. Macklin took over the leadership and began building. The first ordained minister, Rev. Duff MacDonald, arrived in 1878. The first missionaries faced local opposition, and three of them were recalled. From 1881 to 1898 the mission was run by David Clement Scott, who built the Church of St Michael and All Angels between 1888 and 1891 with a team of local workmen who had no knowledge of European building techniques. Scott also compiled an Encyclopaedic Dictionary of the Mang'anja Language, later edited by his successor Alexander Hetherwick.

A trading company grew up beside the mission. The Livingstonia Central Africa Trading Company, founded in Glasgow in 1877 and renamed the African Lakes Corporation in 1878, moved in 1881 to Mandala, across the River Mudi. Its Mandala House survives as a National Monument and is the oldest building in Malawi. Blantyre became a British consular station in 1883 and a municipality by 1895, Malawi's oldest. Its commerce began with the colonial trade in ivory, and by the First World War its people included Africans from neighbouring districts and South Asian traders.

Until 1905 the town's growth was confined to three areas within 2 km of each other: the mission, Mandala, and the government and commercial triangle. Limbe began to develop in 1906, after the Shire Highlands Railways Company set up its headquarters and workshops there and the Imperial Tobacco Group built a packaging and grading factory nearby. Indian wholesale and retail shops multiplied, and by 1910 Limbe had surpassed Blantyre. The two towns were merged into one city in 1956.

Blantyre is Malawi's centre of finance and commerce and its second largest city, with 800,264 people at the 2018 census. It is the capital of the Southern Region and of Blantyre District. The Malawi Stock Exchange, opened in November 1996, stands on Victoria Avenue. The city holds eight National Monuments, mostly historic buildings, and the Michiru Mountain Conservation Area lies among its hills.
blekinge: Blekinge is one of the traditional Swedish provinces, on the coast of the Baltic Sea in Götaland, bordering Småland and Scania. It is the second-smallest province by area, after Öland, and the smallest on the mainland. Its name comes from a dialect adjective, bleke, which corresponds to the nautical term for dead calm. The relief is an uneven valley terrain with a scenic archipelago, the bedrock is mostly granite and gneiss, and oak forests characterise its nature. It has warm summers and mild winters by Swedish standards and is sometimes called Sweden's garden.

Evidence of human habitation in western Blekinge dates to about 9700 BCE in the Vesan area, then a small island surrounded by open grassland. A settlement at nearby Ljungaviken, dated to 6500 BCE, contains the remains of at least 50 wooden houses and a buried dog. A survey in 2021 of a pile barrier in the bay of Lyckeby showed that its wood was felled in 1113-14.

Blekinge belonged to Sweden until the early 13th century, when it became part of Denmark; the Danish Census Book is the first secure written evidence of Danish control. With Skåne and Halland it formed Skåneland, the eastern part of the Danish kingdom, where Scanian Law prevailed. As a border province it was often raided and looted by Swedish troops during the Danish-Swedish wars. Sölvesborg was the seat of administration in the west and Kristianopel in the east, and Ronneby (1387), Sölvesborg (1445), Elleholm and Kristianopel had city privileges.

In 1658 Blekinge was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde and has remained Swedish since. Two new towns were built, Karlshamn, chartered in 1664, and Karlskrona, in 1680, to which the populations of Ronneby and Kristianopel were forcibly relocated. Karlskrona has been the principal naval base of Sweden for more than 300 years. The province was granted its arms in 1660, based on a 15th-century seal, with the three crowns of Sweden placed on an oak trunk to mark the change in its status.
blida: Blida lies 190 metres above sea level at the base of the Tell Atlas, on the southern edge of the fertile Mitidja Plain and the right bank of the Oued el Kebir, which flows out of the Chiffa gorge. The stream's abundant water powered large corn mills and several factories and fed the town's fountains and irrigated gardens. Orchards and gardens surround the town, which is known as the city of roses. Its name is a diminutive of the Arabic belda, city. Chréa National Park, one of the largest in the country, lies within Blida, and the nearby Chiffa gorge is one of the few habitats of the endangered Barbary macaque.

No ancient centre preceded the city. It was identified with a medieval town of Mitidja, which was ruined during the campaigns of the Beni Ghania. The present town was founded by Moors, principally Sidi Ahmed El-Kebir, in the 16th century. A mosque was built by order of Khair-ed-din Barbarossa, and under the Turks the town was of some importance. Its gates no longer exist, but their names, such as Bab Er-Rahba and Bab Es-Sebt, are still used as reference points for streets and businesses.

After an earthquake in March 1825 the town was rebuilt on a grid plan, on a site about a mile from the ruins. In 1839 French troops occupied the city and built a military base, an airbase, a communications centre and a military hospital. Life was racially segregated: Muslims were confined to a crowded ghetto, and boarding schools kept separate dormitories. The occupation lasted until Algeria won independence in the Algerian War. Another earthquake damaged the town in 1867.

Blida is the capital of Blida Province, about 45 km south-west of Algiers. The Berbers of the province, the Djebailia, speak Taqbaylit, a Berber language close to the Kabyle varieties spoken east of Algiers. The Stade Mustapha Tchaker, opened in 2002, is the home ground of the Algeria national football team.
bloemfontein: Bloemfontein lies in central South Africa, on the southern edge of the Highveld at an elevation of about 1,400 metres, bordering the semi-arid region of the Karoo. The area is generally flat, with occasional hills, called koppies in Afrikaans, and the vegetation is Highveld grassland. Summers are hot and rainfall comes mainly as short afternoon thunderstorms, while winters are cool and dry with frosty nights. The city is also known as Mangaung in Sesotho, meaning place of cheetahs, and as the city of roses, for its abundance of the flowers and an annual rose festival.

Bloemfontein was historically a settlement of the Orana and the Barolong, and then of Boers. It was officially founded in 1846 as a fort by the British Army major Henry Douglas Warden, as a British outpost in the Transoranje region. That region was occupied by various groups, among them the Orana, Cape Colony Trekboers, the Griqua and the Barolong. The Orange River Sovereignty was proclaimed in 1848 with a British Resident at Bloemfontein, and the Orange Free State, an independent Boer republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers, existed from 1854 to 1902.

On 31 May 1910, exactly eight years after the Boers signed the Peace Treaty of Vereeniging that ended the Anglo-Boer War, South Africa became a Union. Disagreement over where the capital should be ended in a compromise that allowed Bloemfontein to host the Appellate Division and become the Union's judicial capital, and it was also given financial compensation.

Residential segregation in the town began in the 19th century. Ordinance 1 of 1860 decreed that no non-white person, without written permission from the landlord, which was the British government, had the right to occupy urban land in towns that had no municipality. On 3 June 1861 the council marked out separate locations for the black population and for Coloured people, whose inhabitants had to pay a hut tax and a grazing rights tax. This laid the foundation for the residential segregation later planned by the architects of apartheid, which the National Party began to implement after winning the 1948 election.

Bloemfontein is the capital and largest city of the Free State province, with 256,185 residents at the 2011 census within the Mangaung municipality of 747,431. It remains the seat of the Supreme Court of Appeal, formerly the Appellate Division, and the Constitutional Court has been in Johannesburg since 1994. The city has the Anglo-Boer War Museum, the National Women's Monument, the National Museum and the Oliewenhuis Art Museum, as well as Boyden Observatory.
blood-transfusion: Recorded research into blood transfusion began in the 17th century, after William Harvey's experiments on the circulation of the blood, with successful experiments in transfusion between animals. Working at the Royal Society in the 1660s, the physician Richard Lower devised methods of cross-circulation in animals, using closed arteriovenous connections to prevent clotting. In his own account, towards the end of February 1665 he drew blood from a medium-sized dog until its strength was nearly gone, then introduced blood from a larger mastiff fastened alongside it. The animal recovered with no sign of discomfort. Attempts to transfuse animal blood into humans gave variable and often fatal results.

Blood transfusion is the intravenous transfer of blood products into a human or other animal. Except in major trauma, whole blood is rarely used in modern practice, and instead components such as red blood cells, plasma and platelets are transfused. Donated blood is separated by centrifugation into red cells, plasma and platelets, and plasma can be processed further into albumin, clotting factor concentrates and immunoglobulins. Red cells are typically stored at 1 to 6 °C, platelets at 20 to 24 °C with continuous agitation, and plasma frozen at −18 °C or lower.

Only in 1901, when the Austrian Karl Landsteiner discovered three human blood groups, O, A and B, did transfusion gain a scientific basis and become safer. He found that mixing incompatible blood provokes an immune response in which the red cells clump. He won the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine in 1930. George Washington Crile is credited with the first surgery using a direct transfusion, in 1906 at St. Alexis Hospital in Cleveland.

Before a transfusion the recipient's blood is typed for its ABO and Rh status and screened for antibodies. Most acute haemolytic reactions come from clerical errors or mistaken typing. Blood type O negative is compatible with anyone and is kept for emergencies.
blue-division: Francisco Franco took power in the Spanish Civil War, which killed more than 300,000 people, with help from Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. Spain stayed formally neutral in World War II but did not hide its sympathy for the Axis. Franco met Adolf Hitler at Hendaye on 23-24 October 1940, but could not win promises of colonial territory in North Africa.

After the German invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, Foreign Minister Ramón Serrano Suñer proposed a Spanish contribution to what Spanish officials called an anti-communist crusade, and Franco agreed. Germany accepted on 24 June. Recruitment began on 27 June and 18,373 men had volunteered by 2 July. Half the officers and sergeants were professional soldiers, and General Agustín Muñoz Grandes took command.

The volunteers trained at Grafenwöhr in Bavaria and, after taking the Hitler Oath on 31 July 1941, were incorporated in the Wehrmacht as the 250th Division. Marching towards Smolensk, they were rerouted in September to Army Group North and first held a 50-kilometre section of the Volkhov River front near Novgorod. In August 1942 they moved to the southeastern flank of the siege of Leningrad, near Pushkin, Kolpino and Krasny Bor.

In February 1943, at the Battle of Krasny Bor, the division held its ground at heavy cost against a Soviet force seven times larger. Allied pressure then grew on Franco. He ordered withdrawal on 10 October 1943, and on 3 November the government ordered all troops home. Close to 3,000 refused and formed the Blue Legion, which was ordered home in March 1944; the rest joined German units.

As many as 45,000 Spaniards served on the Eastern Front by rotation. The Blue Division and its successors lost 4,954 men killed and 8,700 wounded, and 372 were taken prisoner by the Red Army. Spain and the Soviet Union had no diplomatic relations, so 286 prisoners stayed in captivity until 2 April 1954, when the ship Semiramis brought them to Spain.

Hitler had a medal struck for the division in January 1944, the only German Army component to receive one of its own. A war cemetery in Veliky Novgorod holds 1,900 of its soldiers. A Russian interpreter, Vladimir Kovalevskii, left an account of low discipline and crimes by the volunteers, and Novgorod's churches were damaged and their iconostases burned or taken to Germany.
blue-nile: The Blue Nile rises at Gish Abay in Ethiopia, where it is called the Abay, and flows through Lake Tana and out into a canyon about 400 kilometres long. The canyon, cut in the Ethiopian Highlands to a depth of some 1,500 metres, is a tremendous obstacle to travel between northern and southern Ethiopia. The Blue Nile Falls, called Tis Abay, meaning great smoke, lie at its start. The river then runs about 650 kilometres through Sudan and joins the White Nile at Khartoum. It supplies 80 to 86 percent of the Nile's water in the rainy season, and its floods contributed to the fertility of the Nile Valley and so to the rise of ancient Egypt.

The Egyptian fear that Ethiopia might block the river shaped the long relationship between the two countries. Ethiopia depended on the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria for its metropolitan, and from the 11th century the threat to block the river helped secure the appointment of Egyptian metropolitans, though neither diversion nor large-scale use of the water was ever attempted. Emperor Amda Seyon I first occupied the basin and began spreading Christianity there. Later Solomonic emperors, among them Dawit II, Yeshaq I and Zara Yaqob, used their control of the river as a diplomatic tool and identified it with the biblical Gihon.

The Spanish Jesuit Pedro Páez reached the source on 21 April 1618, and the Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the source of the Nile in 1770. The canyon defeated outsiders' attempts to follow the river, from Frédéric Cailliaud in 1821 to W. W. Macmillan in 1902. In 1968 a team of 60 British and Ethiopian servicemen and scientists, led by John Blashford-Snell at the request of Haile Selassie, made the first full descent from Lake Tana to a point near the Sudanese border.

The Blue Nile is vital to Egypt, which receives over 85 percent of its Nile streamflow from it. Its floods in lower Egypt ended with the completion of the Aswan Dam in 1970. In Sudan the Roseires and Sennar dams supply hydroelectric power and irrigate the Gezira Scheme, noted for its cotton. The river's summer floods carry a great amount of silt, which turns its water dark brown or almost black.
bluefields: Bluefields lies on the central Mosquito Coast. The city stands beside the bay of the same name and consists of 17 neighborhoods, together with the port of Bluefields Bluff, which lies on a peninsula about 8 km away. Because of gradual erosion the peninsula is becoming a true island that closes the Bay of Bluefields on the east side. The climate is a trade-wind tropical rainforest one, with a drier period from February to April and extremely heavy rain for the rest of the year.

From the early seventeenth century European privateers and pirates, particularly those associated with Dutch and English interests, frequented the Mosquitian Shore and used the Bluefields River and nearby bays as harbours and meeting points. The area was already inhabited by several Indigenous nations, including the Kukra, Ulwa, Rama and Miskito. An early description appears in the Minutes of a Committee for Providence Island of 14 June 1637, in which Albertus Blauvelt, mate of the Expectation, reported a good harbour at the river's mouth. The British navy traded here and used the port for naval operations during the Anglo-Spanish War of 1779–1783.

Bluefields rose to regional prominence in 1844, when it was designated the administrative centre of the Kingdom of Mosquitia, which kept its independence and later a protectorate status under Great Britain. The Moravian Church was established in 1848 and founded the first organised schools in the region; among its first pupils was George Augustus Frederic, the future Miskito king. Between the 1860s and 1880s British and American investment made the town a commercial hub for bananas, timber and maritime trade, with a population of Creoles, Miskito, European settlers and other Indigenous communities. Growth slowed after the Nicaraguan occupation of Mosquitia in 1894, when the city became the capital of the Zelaya Department.

Bluefields is the capital of the South Caribbean Coast Autonomous Region of Nicaragua. The port was mined by the United States in 1984 during the Contra War, and the city suffered extensive damage from Hurricane Joan in 1988 before it was rebuilt. It remains a centre of Afro-Caribbean and Indigenous identity and reflects the longstanding traditions of Mosquitia. It has two universities, a campus of URACCAN and the Bluefields Indian and Caribbean University.
bob-hawke: Robert James Lee Hawke was born on 9 December 1929 in Border Town, South Australia, the second child of Arthur Clem Hawke, a Congregationalist minister, and Edith Emily Hawke, a schoolteacher. He was educated at Perth Modern School and the University of Western Australia, graduating in 1952, and then won a Rhodes Scholarship to University College, Oxford, where he wrote a thesis on wage-fixing in Australia. In 1956 he joined the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) as a research officer. He became its advocate in the national wages case, won a fifteen-shilling increase in 1959, and in 1969 was elected ACTU president although he had never held elected office in a union.

Hawke became president of the Labor Party in 1973. In 1980 he stood down from both presidencies and was elected to the House of Representatives for Wills. Three years later he was elected unopposed to replace Bill Hayden as Labor leader and, within five weeks, led it to a landslide victory at the 1983 election. He was sworn in as prime minister on 11 March 1983 and won again in 1984, 1987 and 1990, which made him the most electorally successful prime minister in Labor's history.
