According to 2 Kings 22 and 23, the high priest Hilkiah found the book of the law in the temple in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, and Josiah launched a reform of worship based on it. Many scholars believe it was the Deuteronomic Code. Hosea, in the northern kingdom, refers to the Exodus and a covenant while Isaiah does not, leading scholars to conclude that the traditions behind Deuteronomy have a northern origin.

After Babylon destroyed the Kingdom of Judah in 586 BCE, the Deuteronomistic elite in exile created a history of Israel in the books of Joshua through Kings to show that the disaster was punishment for failing to follow the law. Deuteronomy became its introduction. The mainstream view holds that it was later detached and joined to the four books before it, because Moses was already its central character.
book-of-documents: According to a later tradition, Confucius compiled the Book of Documents as a selection from a much larger group of documents, but the early history of the text is obscure. Writers from Confucius onwards drew on it to illustrate general principles, though several different versions seem to have been in use. It was cited increasingly in works through the 4th century BCE, such as the Mencius, Mozi and Zuo Zhuan. Mencius and Xunzi refused to accept it as genuine in its entirety, in contrast to the reverence of the Han dynasty, when its compilation was attributed to Confucius.

The transmitted text is grouped into four sections: the semi-mythical reign of Yu the Great, and the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties. The Zhou section is over half the text. Most chapters are represented as formal speeches by kings or other important figures, such as announcements, declarations made before battle, and commands to a vassal. A speech is often introduced with the phrase Wáng ruò yuē, which scholars take to mean that the originals were prepared scripts read out by an official on the king's behalf.

The five Zhou announcements have the most archaic language and are considered by most scholars to record speeches of King Cheng of Zhou and of the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao, his uncles, in the late 11th century BCE. They set out the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven, which explains how the virtuous Xia became corrupt and were replaced by the Shang, who in turn were replaced by the Zhou. Most scholars believe the chapters on Yu, the Xia and the early Shang were composed later, some as late as the 4th or 3rd centuries BCE.

Many copies were destroyed in the Qin dynasty's burning of books. Fu Sheng reconstructed 29 chapters from hidden copies at the start of the Han dynasty, known as the Modern Script. A longer Old Script version, with some 16 additional chapters, was said to have been found in a wall of Confucius's house in the reign of Emperor Wu and interpreted by his descendant Kong Anguo, but it was lost by the end of the Han dynasty.

In 317 CE Mei Ze presented to the Eastern Jin court a version of 58 chapters as Kong Anguo's text. It was widely accepted and made the official interpretation by imperial decree in 653. Doubts began in the Song dynasty, and in the 17th century Yan Ruoqu's study convinced most scholars that the added Old Script chapters were fabricated. Bamboo slips from tombs of the state of Chu, dated to around 300 BCE, quote previously unknown passages.
book-of-exodus: The English name comes from the Greek éxodos, meaning departure, the title of the book in the Septuagint. In Hebrew it is called Shemot, Names, after its opening words. Jewish and Christian tradition ascribes the book, and the whole Torah, to Moses, but scholars abandoned that view by the end of the 19th century because of discrepancies and repetitions in the text. Modern scholars see its initial composition as a product of the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BCE, based on earlier written sources and oral traditions, with final revisions in the Persian period. In approximate round dates, the process began around 600 BCE and ended around 400 BCE with the books as unchangeable sacred texts.

The book opens some 400 years after the end of Genesis, when a Pharaoh who does not remember Joseph fears the numerous enslaved Israelites and orders the killing of newborn boys. Moses is saved, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, flees to Midian and encounters God in a burning bush. After ten plagues, the last the death of the Egyptian firstborn, Pharaoh lets the Israelites go, and the sea parts for them.

At Sinai God pronounces the Ten Commandments and the Covenant Code of ritual and civil law, in Exodus 20:22–23:33, which resembles the Laws of Hammurabi in content and structure. The later chapters give instructions for the Tabernacle and the priesthood.

The biblical scholar Carol Meyers calls Exodus arguably the most important book in the Bible, because it presents the defining features of Israel's identity: memories of hardship and escape, a binding covenant with a God who chooses Israel, and guidelines for the life of the community. Its central theme is the Sinaitic covenant, which resembles ancient Middle Eastern treaties but is made between a god and a people rather than between a ruler and a vassal.

Most mainstream scholars do not accept the account as historical, and the consensus is that the Pentateuch does not accurately describe the origins of the Israelites, who seem to have formed in the central highlands of Canaan in the late second millennium BCE. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman argue that archaeology has found no evidence for the Exodus as described. A majority of scholars nonetheless think the story has a historical core, though they disagree about what it was, and the names Moses, Aaron and Phinehas seem to be of Egyptian origin.
book-of-genesis: The name Genesis comes from the Greek for origin, the title of the book in the Septuagint; in Hebrew it is called Bereshit, In the beginning, after its first word. Genesis was written anonymously. Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the whole Pentateuch to Moses, but modern scholars believe it was the work of many authors and editors writing much later. Internal contradictions suggest this, among them two creation narratives.

By the end of the 19th century most scholars held the documentary hypothesis, in which four sources, the Yahwist, the Elohist, the Deuteronomist and the Priestly source, were combined by editors. Since the 1980s revisions have been proposed. Most scholars now agree that Genesis reached its final form after the Babylonian exile. The original manuscripts are lost, and surviving copies vary across the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Genesis falls into the primeval history of chapters 1 to 11 and the ancestral history of chapters 12 to 50. The first includes two creation stories, Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, Cain and Abel, the Flood and the Tower of Babel. God sends the Flood because human sin has corrupted the world, sparing the righteous Noah and his family in an ark, and then makes a covenant with Noah marked by the rainbow.

The second part follows Abraham, who at God's command travels from Ur of the Chaldees to Canaan, then his son Isaac and his grandson Jacob, whose name is changed to Israel. Through Jacob's son Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers and later made second in command in Egypt, the family goes down to Egypt, where the book ends. Scholars generally see a divine promise of offspring, blessing and land as the theme of the patriarchal stories.

Jewish and Christian chronologers added up the spans in its genealogies to calculate the age of the world, and this reckoning underlies the Hebrew and Byzantine calendars. From the 16th to the 19th century scholars in Europe treated Genesis as factual and tried to fit new findings in geology to its account; Johann Jakob Scheuchzer took fossils to be creatures killed in the Flood. This reading lost favour as evidence mounted that the Earth was far older. Its statement that humanity is created in the image of God became a foundational theme within Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
book-of-han: The work developed from a continuation of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, begun by Ban Biao at the start of the Later Han dynasty and usually called Later Traditions. Other scholars of the time, including Liu Xin and Yang Xiong, also wrote continuations. After Ban Biao's death his eldest son Ban Gu was dissatisfied with what his father had completed and began a new history starting with the beginning of the Han dynasty, unlike Sima Qian's, which began with China's earliest rulers of tradition. In this way he initiated the jizhuanti format for dynastic histories that remained the model for the official histories until modern times.

Ban Gu died in prison in 92, and his younger sister Ban Zhao finished the book in 111, 19 years later. She is thought to have written volumes 13 to 20, eight chronological tables, and volume 26, the treatise on astronomy, the latter with the help of Ma Xu.

The finished work has 100 fascicles. It contains annals in 12 volumes, which are emperors' biographies in strict annal form, 8 volumes of chronological tables of important people, 10 volumes of treatises, each on an area of effort of the state, and 70 volumes of biographies. The biographies confine themselves to events that show the exemplary character of the person, and treat two or more people together when they belong to the same class. The last articles describe China's relations with peoples at and beyond the frontiers, including Nanyue, Minyue and Ba.

Where the two histories overlapped, Ban Gu adopted much of Sima Qian's material nearly verbatim, sometimes expanding it. Fascicle 21 describes the Triple Concordance Calendar System developed by Liu Xin.

The Book of Han is the best source, and sometimes the only one, for many topics such as the literature of the period. It is also called the Book of the Former Han to distinguish it from the Book of the Later Han, composed in the fifth century by Fan Ye. It is counted among the Four Histories of the Twenty-Four Histories canon, together with the Records of the Grand Historian, the Records of the Three Kingdoms and the History of the Later Han.

Its treatise on geography, in volume 28, gives the first unambiguous appearance of the people of Japan in written history: "The people of Wo are located across the ocean from Lelang Commandery, are divided into more than one hundred tribes, and come to offer tribute from time to time." The annals and the chapters on Wang Mang were translated into English by Homer H. Dubs.
book-of-jeremiah: The Book of Jeremiah is the second of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Its opening verses name it as the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, a priest from the town of Anatot, to whom the word of God came in the days of King Josiah. His career covered the last years of the kingdom of Judah: Josiah's reforms, Babylon's destruction of Assyria, a brief period in which Egypt made Judah a vassal, and Babylon's defeat of Egypt in 605 BCE, which left Judah a Babylonian vassal. Judah revolted twice more, and the second revolt ended with the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the kingdom.

The book falls roughly into six parts: the core of Jeremiah's message in chapters 1 to 25, biography and encounters with other prophets in 26 to 29, promises of restoration in 30 to 33, the fall of Jerusalem in 34 to 45, oracles against the nations in 46 to 51, and an appendix retelling the Second Book of Kings. Its poetic oracles speak of Israel's unfaithfulness and call for repentance. Jeremiah presents the covenant between God and Israel as conditional, and chapter 31 looks to a new covenant that will not be broken. The book also records sign-acts, such as wearing an ox yoke and buying a field at Anathoth, and shows the prophet taunted, jailed and thrown into a pit.

The book survives in two related versions, the Masoretic Hebrew text and the Greek of the Septuagint, which is about one eighth shorter. Both forms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and most scholars hold that the Hebrew behind the Greek is older. Authentic oracles are probably in the poetic sections of chapters 1 to 25, while the whole has been heavily edited by followers, perhaps including the scribe Baruch, and by later Deuteronomists. Second Temple Judaism attributed to Jeremiah the Book of Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter of Jeremiah. Early Christians based their understanding of Jesus as the bearer of a new covenant on chapter 31.
book-of-joshua: The book is anonymous. The Babylonian Talmud attributed it to Joshua himself, but John Calvin rejected that view, and by the time of Thomas Hobbes it was recognised that the book was written much later than the period it depicts. Scholars now agree that it was composed as part of the Deuteronomistic history, which runs from Deuteronomy to the Books of Kings, first at the court of King Josiah in the late 7th century BCE and extensively revised in the 6th. The earliest parts are probably chapters 2 to 11, the conquest story. The book was not completed until after the fall of Jerusalem to the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 586 BCE.
Fragments of Joshua from the Hasmonean period were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, and the earliest complete Hebrew copy is in the Aleppo Codex of the 10th century CE.

The book tells of Israelite campaigns in central, southern and northern Canaan and the division of the land among the Twelve Tribes. It opens after the death of Moses, with God's commission to Joshua, and ends with Joshua's farewell address and the covenant at Shechem. The conquest runs from the reconnaissance of Jericho and the crossing of the Jordan to the fall of Jericho, Ai, and campaigns in the south and north. The land is the central subject, and obedience to the Law and to the command of herem, the ban on treaties, mercy and intermarriage with the enemy, is a constant theme.

The prevailing scholarly view is that Joshua is not a factual account. Archaeology indicates a gradual, indigenous emergence of Israel from Canaanite society. The 13th-century BCE setting coincides with the Bronze Age Collapse, but with few exceptions, Hazor and Lachish among them, the cities destroyed are not those the Bible associates with Joshua, and Jericho and Ai show little sign of occupation in the Late Bronze Age, though recent excavations at Jericho have questioned this. In the 1930s Martin Noth criticised the book's usefulness for history.

Many scholars read the book as describing what would now be called genocide, and the archaeologist William G. Dever uses that word. Others hold that the label is anachronistic. They explain the killings by cultural norms, since Israel was not the only Iron Age state to practise herem, and by theology, and some take the violent language as hyperbole, comparable to extrabiblical military reports.
book-of-kells: The Book of Kells is one of the latest and finest of the Insular manuscripts made from the late 6th to the early 9th centuries in monasteries of Britain and Ireland, among them the Lindisfarne Gospels and the Book of Armagh. It was created in a Columban monastery in Ireland or Scotland and may have had contributions from several Columban houses. Its fully developed ornament places it in the late 8th or early 9th century. The woad and lichen used for its blue and purple pigments are taken as strong evidence of an origin in modern Scotland.

The Annals of Ulster record that in 1007 the great Gospel of Columkille was stolen from the sacristy of the stone church at Cenannas on account of its wrought shrine. It was recovered months later under a sod, without its gold and jewelled cover.

The manuscript contains the four Gospels in Latin, with prefaces, summaries and canon tables. It now has 340 leaves of calf vellum, or 680 pages. Its text is largely from the Vulgate, with passages from earlier Vetus Latina versions, and is in Insular majuscule by at least three scribes. Its decoration surpasses that of other Insular Gospel books: ten full-page illustrations and pages full of initials, interlace and human and animal forms in purple, red, green and yellow, with no gold or silver leaf. It seems to have stood on the high altar and been used at Mass, with appearance preferred to practicality, and errors were left uncorrected.

The book stayed at Kells until 1654, when Cromwell's cavalry was quartered in the church and the governor sent it to Dublin. Henry Jones, Bishop of Clogher, presented it to Trinity College in 1661. In the 19th century its link with Columba was used to argue Ireland's cultural primacy, and its designs influenced the Celtic Revival and were copied in metalwork, embroidery and pottery. It was rebound in four volumes in 1953, and UNESCO added it to its Memory of the World International Register in 2011.
book-of-mormon: The book was first published in 1830 by Joseph Smith under the title The Book of Mormon: An Account Written by the Hand of Mormon upon Plates Taken from the Plates of Nephi. According to Smith's account and the book's own narrative, it was engraved in otherwise unknown characters on golden plates by ancient prophets. The last of them, Moroni, buried the plates in what is now Manchester, New York.

Smith said that Moroni appeared to him as an angel in 1823, when he was seventeen, and told him of the buried plates, and that in 1827 he was shown their location and instructed to translate them into English. A different view holds that Smith himself composed the book from the material and ideas of his nineteenth-century surroundings, and in the twenty-first century the leading naturalistic explanations take this view.

The Book of Mormon is a compilation of smaller books, most of them named after a main narrator or a prominent figure, running from the First Book of Nephi to the Book of Moroni. Its English imitates the style of the King James Version of the Bible. The narrative begins in Jerusalem around 600 BCE with Lehi and his family, who are led by God from the city shortly before its fall to the Babylonians. They cross the Arabian peninsula and then sail to a promised land, presumably in the Americas. Their community grows and splits into two warring groups, the Nephites and the Lamanites, and this conflict runs through the rest of the narrative.

The pivotal event is the appearance of Jesus Christ in the Americas shortly after his resurrection. The title page gives the book's purpose as the convincing of Jew and Gentile that Jesus is the Christ. Prophets in the book see and preach him long before his birth.

Early followers read the book as confirming and supplementing the Bible, and they drew on its picture of the church in drawing up their own articles. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints counts it among its four standard works and holds it to be the word of God, and it regards the book as both literal history and the keystone of its faith.

Independent archaeological, historical and scientific communities have found little evidence for the civilisations it describes, and they point to a nineteenth-century origin in its language and content. Academics and organisations connected to the movement argue that it is an authentic account of the pre-Columbian Americas. The book has been translated fully or partly into at least 112 languages.
book-of-psalms: The Book of Psalms is an anthology of Hebrew religious hymns, the first book of the Ketuvim, or Writings, in the Tanakh. The composition of the psalms spans at least five centuries, from Psalm 29 in the 10th century BCE to psalms clearly from the post-Exilic period, not earlier than the 5th century BCE. Most originated in the kingdom of Judah and were associated with the Temple in Jerusalem, where they probably served as librettos for worship.

Of the 150 psalms, 116 have superscriptions. The most common names are 'of David' (73 psalms), Asaph (12) and the sons of Korah (11). Modern scholars do not accept Davidic authorship as historical fact and see the attributions as a way of linking writings to well-known figures. Many scholars think the psalms were gathered into one collection in the Second Temple period, and the Dead Sea Scrolls suggest that the content and order of Psalms 90 to 150 were not fixed in the mid-1st century CE.

The book is divided into five sections, each ending with a doxology: Psalms 1 to 41, 42 to 72, 73 to 89, 90 to 106 and 107 to 150. The division was probably made by the final editors to echo the five books of the Torah. Hermann Gunkel's form-critical study sorted the psalms into five main types: hymns, communal laments, royal psalms, individual laments, the most common type, and individual thanksgivings. There are also wisdom psalms, pilgrimage psalms and others.

The poetry rests chiefly on parallelism, in which a second line restates, opposes or amplifies the first. Some psalms echo earlier regional texts, including Ugaritic poetry and the Babylonian Enūma Eliš. The numbering differs, mostly by one, between the Hebrew and the Greek manuscripts. The Septuagint adds a Psalm 151, and some Syriac versions add Psalms 152 to 155.

The psalms were written as songs. More than a third are addressed to a music director, and some headings name instruments or melodies. According to the medieval scholar Saadia Gaon, the Levites originally sang them in the Temple precincts. In later Jewish and Christian tradition they became prayers, for individuals and for congregations alike.

The earliest Christians used them in worship, and the Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and other churches have recited them in cycles over one or more weeks. In the early centuries a candidate for bishop was expected to know the whole Psalter by heart. Muslims believe that David received the Psalms, the Zabur, as a scripture. Composers from Orlando di Lasso and Heinrich Schütz to George Frideric Handel and Felix Mendelssohn have set them to music.
book-of-rites: The Book of Rites is a diverse compilation of texts of uncertain origin and date. Unlike the Rites of Zhou and the Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial, it has no consistent overall structure. Some sections define ritual terms, and others deal with the life and teachings of Confucius. Parts have been traced to earlier works such as the Xunzi and the Lüshi Chunqiu, while other sections are believed to date from the Former Han period. In China the Doubting antiquity movement questioned whether it contains genuine Warring States documents. In 1993 a copy of the Black Robes chapter was found in Tomb 1 of the Guodian tombs in Jingmen, Hubei, sealed around 300 BCE, which reopened the debate over the dating of other chapters.

Many Confucian texts were destroyed in the Burning of the Books in 213 BCE under Qin Shi Huang, but scholars who had memorised or hidden the classics helped to rebuild them in the early Han dynasty. The Book of Rites was said to have been fully recovered, though the Classic of Music could not be recompiled and survives only in fragments, mainly in the Record of Music chapter of this book. According to the Book of Sui, Dai De cut a collection of 214 books to 85 in the 1st century BCE, and his nephew Dai Sheng abridged it to 46. Ma Rong added three more. Later scholarship doubts that account.

Zheng Xuan, a student of Ma Rong, produced an annotated edition of 49 books that became the authoritative version and is still the standard one. It formed the basis of the Right Meaning of the Ritual Records, the imperially sanctioned text and commentary established in 653 CE.

Chapters of the book provided the foundation for the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean. In the Song dynasty Zhu Xi edited these two texts and, with the Analects and Mencius, they became the Four Books. After the Yuan dynasty adopted the Five Classics and the Four Books as orthodox, and the Ming and Qing upheld the choice, they became the standard curriculum for the civil service examinations. From 1313 to 1905 mastery of them was essential for anyone seeking official posts.
book-of-the-later-han: The Hou Hanshu is one of the Twenty-Four Histories. It was compiled by Fan Ye and others in the 5th century, during the Liu Song dynasty, from a number of earlier histories and documents. It covers the Later or Eastern Han, which is separated from the Early or Western Han by the fall of Wang Mang, overthrown in 23 CE by a peasants' revolt known as the Red Eyebrows.

As an orthodox history it is unusual in being completed over two hundred years after the fall of the dynasty it describes. Fan Ye's primary source was the Dongguan Hanji, the Han Records of the Eastern Lodge, which was written during the Han dynasty itself. He also drew on accounts by Sima Qian and Ban Gu and on many other works, among them the Annals of the Later Han by Yuan Hong of the 4th century. Most of these sources did not survive intact. Fan Ye's text was later annotated at least twice, first by the Liang dynasty scholar Liu Zhao and then by a team led by Crown Prince Zhanghuai of the Tang dynasty.

The book belongs with the Records of the Grand Historian, the Book of Han and the Records of the Three Kingdoms among the four early historiographies of the Twenty-Four Histories canon. Its Treatise on the Western Regions rests on a report composed by Ban Yong, presented to Emperor An of Han around 125, which presumably includes notes from his father Ban Chao. Fan Ye says plainly that the new information in this section comes from that report. It forms the 88th chapter, or the 118th in some editions.

The treatise is a key source for the culture and economy of the Western Regions, including the earliest accounts of Daqin, the Roman Empire, and some of the most detailed early reports on India and Central Asia. It records an eclipse followed by a circular halo during the reign of Emperor Guangwu, who took it as a sign that the affairs of Heaven and mankind were upended and proclaimed that he would pardon the sins of the population himself. It also contains references to events after the death of Emperor An, including a brief account of the first official envoys from Rome in 166.
booker-t-washington: Booker was born to Jane, an enslaved woman, on the plantation of James Burroughs near Hale's Ford in Franklin County, Virginia. He never knew his exact birth date, although evidence that emerged after his death indicates 5 April 1856, and he never knew his father, said to be a white man from a neighbouring plantation. He worked in salt furnaces and coal mines in West Virginia, and at 16 made his way east, mostly on foot, to the Hampton Institute, where his entrance exam was to clean a room and where he worked as a janitor to pay his way.

In 1881 Samuel C. Armstrong, the president of Hampton, recommended Washington, then 25, as first leader of the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in Alabama, a teachers' college. It opened on 4 July 1881, and the next year Washington bought a former plantation as its site, where students built their own school and learned trades as well as academic subjects. By his death Tuskegee had more than 100 buildings, about 1,500 students and 200 faculty. He directed millions of dollars from white philanthropists such as Andrew Carnegie and Julius Rosenwald to small rural schools across the South, and founded the National Negro Business League in 1900.

His Atlanta Exhibition address of 1895 was seen as a revolutionary moment, but W. E. B. Du Bois, who had supported him, later called it the Atlanta Compromise, criticising Washington as too accommodating to white interests. Washington urged progress through education and entrepreneurship rather than direct challenges to Jim Crow segregation, though he also secretly supported court challenges to it. His autobiography Up from Slavery, published in 1901, remained the best-selling autobiography by an African American for more than sixty years. In October 1901 he dined at the White House with President Theodore Roosevelt, which drew racist attacks from Southern Democratic politicians.

Washington collapsed in New York in 1915 and asked to die at Tuskegee, where he arrived on 14 November 1915 and died a few hours later, aged 59. After his death he was heavily criticised for accommodating white supremacy, while since the late twentieth century historians have taken a more balanced view. The years from 1880 to 1915 have been called the Age of Booker T. Washington.
bor-serbia: The name of the town comes from the Serbo-Croatian word bor, meaning pine. In 1835 Miloš Obrenović invited August Herder, the son of J. G. Herder, to the region to carry out geological investigations. Later Đorđe Vajfert invested in exploration and sought foreign capital to begin industrial exploitation. He signed a contract with Mirabaud, and the Compagnie française des mines de Bor was established in Paris on 30 September 1903.

Nazi Germany invaded Yugoslavia on 27 March 1941. Führer Directive No. 25 held that possession of the Bor copper mines was very important, since they could supply 50 per cent of Germany's wartime copper requirements. Ownership was seized from the French company and taken over by the Prussian National Bank. Prison camps were quickly established, most of them named after German cities. The largest, called Berlin, stood in Bor itself and housed the headquarters of the Hungarian battalion, with satellite camps within 50 kilometres. In May 1943 there were about 23,000 forced labourers from Serbia among the inmates, not counting the Kapos.

Gerhard Fränk, vice president of Organisation Todt, devised the use of Hungarian Jews to work the mines. His reasoning was that Serbian Jews had already been killed and that Serbians could not be trusted. The plan began in February 1943 and progressed only after the resignation of Vilmos Nagy, Hungary's Minister of Defense, on 8 June 1943. The Hungarian government and Organisation Todt then agreed to send 6,000 labour servicemen to Bor in exchange for a monthly shipment of 100 tons of copper ore, and in June 1944 another 3,250 followed. Most were Jews, with some Jehovah's Witnesses and Seventh-Day Adventists.

As the Axis forces withdrew from Yugoslavia, the labour servicemen were evacuated on death marches to Germany in September and October 1944, guarded by Hungarian soldiers. Many were shot along the way, including 700 to 1,000 killed in a pit at a brickyard in Crvenka on the night of 7 to 8 October. The Jewish Hungarian poet Miklós Radnóti, one of those marched out of Bor, was shot at Abda between 6 and 10 November 1944, and his last poems were found in his raincoat when his body was exhumed from a mass grave.

Bor received urban status in 1947, when its population was 11,000, and became a city in June 2018. It is the administrative centre of the Bor District in eastern Serbia and had 40,845 inhabitants at the 2022 census. It lies by the Kriveljska River, near a reservoir called Bor Lake.
bora-bora: The main island is the remnant of an extinct volcano that was active in the Upper Pliocene, between 3.45 and 3.10 million years ago, and was later partly depressed and strongly eroded. It measures only 8 km from north to south and 5 km from east to west. Mount Otemanu, at 727 metres, is its highest point, and Mount Pahia rises to 661 metres. The bay of Tuuraapuo was the volcano's main crater, and its collapsed south-western edge survives as the islets Toopua and Toopua-iti.

A lagoon surrounds the island and is separated from the sea by a barrier reef with a single opening, the Teavanui Passage, west of the main island. To the east and north the reef carries islets of coral debris and sand, called motu. The main settlement, Vaitape, lies on the western side.

The island's old name in Tahitian, Porapora mai te pora, means created by the gods, often shortened to Porapora, first born. The Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen sighted it in 1722, and he and his crew adopted the form Bora Bora, which has stood on Western maps since. Polynesian settlers had arrived around the 3rd century CE. James Cook sighted the island on 29 July 1769 with the help of the Tahitian navigator Tupaia. The London Missionary Society arrived in 1820, and a Protestant church was founded in 1890. Bora Bora was an independent kingdom until 1888, when France annexed it as a colony and forced its last queen, Teriimaevarua III, to abdicate.

In the Second World War the United States chose Bora Bora as a supply base for the South Pacific. Under Operation Bobcat, nine ships brought 18,000 tonnes of equipment and nearly 7,000 soldiers, who built an oil depot, an airstrip, a seaplane base and defences, including at least eight 7-inch guns served by the 13th Coast Artillery Regiment. The island saw no combat and the American presence went uncontested throughout the war. The base closed officially on 2 June 1946. The airstrip, on Motu Mute, was never enlarged for large aircraft but was French Polynesia's only international airport until Faa'a International Airport opened next to Papeete in 1960.

Bora Bora forms part of the commune of Bora-Bora, which also includes the atoll of Tupai, in the Leeward Islands of the Society Islands of French Polynesia. Its land area is 30.55 km2, and Tahitian and French are the main languages. The economy rests almost wholly on tourism. Hotel Bora Bora opened in 1961, and the first over-water bungalows were built nine years later. The eight American guns remain in the area.
boran: Boran, also spelled Buran, was the daughter of Khosrow II and the Byzantine princess Maria. Her father was overthrown and executed in 628 by his son Kavad II, who had all Boran's brothers and half-brothers killed, including the heir Mardanshah. According to one chronicle, Boran was also Kavad II's wife, an instance of the Zoroastrian practice of close-kin marriage. Kavad II died some months later in an epidemic known as the Plague of Sheroe, and his young son became Ardashir III. The Sasanian civil war of 628 to 632 followed, in which powerful nobles took autonomy, and the Persian (Parsig) and Parthian (Pahlav) noble families renewed their hostility.

The Pahlav leader Farrukh Hormizd began to support Boran, who minted coins in Pahlav areas. On 27 April 630 Shahrbaraz killed Ardashir III and was himself murdered about forty days later by Farrukh Hormizd, who helped Boran take the throne in late June 630. She was the first queen to rule the empire, and her accession probably owed much to her being, with her sister Azarmidokht, the only legitimate heir able to rule. She made Farrukh Hormizd chief minister and worked for stability through just laws, repair of infrastructure, lower taxes and coinage. Her coins were minted in Pars, Khuzestan, Media and Abarshahr, and no objection to her sex is recorded.

She was soon deposed in favour of Shapur-i Shahrvaraz and then Azarmidokht, who had Farrukh Hormizd killed. His son Rostam Farrokhzad took Ctesiphon, had Azarmidokht blinded and killed, and restored Boran in June 631. She gave Rostam overall power, and sent an embassy led by the catholicos Ishoyahb II to Emperor Heraclius, which was well received.

A revolt broke out in Ctesiphon the following year, led by Parsig who disliked Rostam's regency, and Boran was killed, presumably strangled by Piruz Khosrow. Rostam and Piruz Khosrow then agreed to place her nephew Yazdegerd III on the throne, ending the civil war. According to al-Tabari, she reigned sixteen months in all. She was the penultimate Sasanian ruler.

Her coins are the only Sasanian coins with a queen's portrait. They return to her father's design and bear the legend Boran, restorer of the race of Gods, a claim to divine descent not used since Shapur II in the 4th century. She also issued bronze coins, and one gold issue is known.
boris-godunov: Boris Godunov was the son of Feodor Ivanovich Godunov, called Krivoy, the one-eyed, and his wife Stepanida Ivanovna. His career began at the court of Ivan the Terrible. He took part in the Serpeisk campaign of 1570 as an archer of the guard, became an oprichnik the next year, and strengthened his position by marrying Maria Grigorievna Skuratova-Belskaya, daughter of Malyuta Skuratov-Belskiy, head of the oprichniki. In 1580 Ivan chose Boris's sister Irina to marry his son Feodor, and Boris was promoted to boyar.

Ivan IV on his deathbed named a council, including Godunov, to guide his feeble son Feodor I. Boris held the second place in the regency until the death in 1586 of the tsar's uncle Nikita Romanovich, and then had no serious rival. Ivan's young son Dmitry, moved to Uglich, died there in 1591 in suspicious circumstances. A commission headed by Vasili Shuiski reported that the boy had cut his own throat in an epileptic seizure; his mother claimed that Godunov's agents had murdered him, and Godunov's guilt was never established.

As regent he founded towns including Samara, Saratov, Voronezh and Tobolsk, and saw the Russian Orthodox Church receive its patriarchate. A decree of 1597 forbade peasants to move from one landowner to another and led to serfdom in its harshest form.

When Feodor died childless on 7 January 1598, Patriarch Job proposed Boris, who accepted the throne only from a Zemsky Sobor; it elected him unanimously on 21 February, and he was crowned on 1 September. He was the first tsar to bring in foreign teachers on a large scale and to send young Russians abroad to study. In November 1600 he moved against the Romanov clan, tonsuring and exiling Feodor Nikitich Romanov. A famine in 1601–1603 killed hundreds of thousands, and peasants and slaves fled to the southern frontier and the Cossacks.

In the autumn of 1604 a pretender claiming to be the dead Dmitry crossed into Russia from Poland–Lithuania with about 2,000 Polish nobles and some thousands of Cossacks, and the southern towns rose for him. Godunov's government said he was Grigory Otrepyev, an escaped monk. Boris died on 23 April 1605, probably of a stroke, after taking monastic orders under the name Bogolep. His sixteen-year-old son Feodor II was crowned, but the army at Kromy went over to the pretender, and Feodor and his mother were killed on 10 June 1605. Many people took Boris's death as divine punishment. Pushkin's play of 1831 and Mussorgsky's opera dramatise his story.
boris-i-of-bulgaria: Boris was the son and successor of Presian I of Bulgaria. In 852 he sent emissaries to Eastern Francia to confirm the peace of 845. In 854 the Moravian prince Rastislav persuaded him to help against Louis the German, and the campaign was a disaster: Louis invaded Bulgaria, and the Croats also attacked. Peace was restored in 855, but meanwhile a conflict with the Byzantines, begun in 855 or 856, cost him Philippopolis (Plovdiv), the region of Zagora and the ports of the Gulf of Burgas. An invasion of Serbia in 853 or 854, led by his son Vladimir-Rasate, was beaten by Mutimir's army, and Boris then made peace with the Serbs.

Late in 863 the Byzantine emperor Michael III declared war on Bulgaria during a famine and natural disasters. Boris made peace, promising to accept Christianity by the eastern rite in return for territorial concessions in Thrace, and at the start of 864 he was secretly baptised at Pliska with Michael III as godfather, taking the name Michael. Historians give several reasons: diplomacy, the influence of a sister baptised in Constantinople, and the wish to unite the Bulgar warrior aristocracy and the Slavs, who had different beliefs. In the summer of 865 a group of boyars rose in revolt, and Boris suppressed it and executed 52 boyars with their families.

Boris sought an autocephalous church, and in August 866 sent 106 questions to Pope Nicholas I. When Rome refused to name Formosus archbishop, Bulgaria turned back to Constantinople, and at the Fourth Council of Constantinople in 870 its church was made an autocephalous archbishopric. In 886 his governor of Belgrade received the exiled disciples of Cyril and Methodius, and Boris welcomed Clement of Ohrid and Naum of Preslav. They set up centres of teaching and trained Slavonic-speaking priests to replace the Greek clergy, and in 893 the Cyrillic script and Old Bulgarian were declared official.

In 889 Boris abdicated and became a monk. His son Vladimir tried to restore paganism, which brought Boris out of retirement in 893. He defeated Vladimir, had him blinded, and at the Council of Preslav placed his third son Simeon I on the throne. About 895 he emerged again to help Simeon against the Magyars. He died on 2 May 907, and where he was buried is uncertain; it may be near Preslav, near Pliska or at a monastery near Varna. The Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint, the baptiser of Bulgaria and Equal-to-the-Apostles, with a feast on 2 May.
boris-iii-of-bulgaria: Boris was born in Sofia on 30 January 1894, the eldest son of Ferdinand I, Prince of Bulgaria, and Princess Marie Louise of Bourbon-Parma. In 1896 his father had the infant converted from Catholicism to Eastern Orthodoxy to reconcile Bulgaria and Russia, which brought Ferdinand excommunication by Pope Leo XIII. In September 1918 Bulgaria was defeated in the Vardar Offensive, and Ferdinand abdicated in his favour; Boris became tsar on 3 October 1918.

The Treaty of Neuilly of 1919 made Bulgaria cede territory, pay heavy reparations and cut its army. The prime minister Aleksandar Stamboliyski was overthrown in a military coup on 9 June 1923. In April 1925 a bomb at the Saint Nedelya Church in Sofia killed 213 members of the political and military elite, and military reprisals then killed several thousand communists and agrarians. In 1934 the Zveno movement seized power and banned political parties; in 1935 Boris overthrew it and from then ruled as a de facto absolute monarch.

In September 1940, with German support, Bulgaria received Southern Dobrudja from Romania. In January 1941 Boris approved the antisemitic Law for Protection of the Nation, which denied citizenship to Bulgarian Jews. In March 1941 Bulgaria joined the Axis and let German troops use its territory to invade Yugoslavia and Greece, receiving most of Yugoslav Macedonia and Greek Thrace; Boris was called the Unifier. Bulgaria took no part in the invasion of the Soviet Union. In March 1943 Bulgarian authorities deported 11,343 Jews from the occupied territories to Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka.

When Germany pressed for the deportation of Bulgaria's own Jews, a public outcry followed, led by the deputy speaker of parliament, Dimitar Peshev, and Archbishop Stefan. Boris then refused to allow the deportation of Bulgaria's nearly 50,000 Jews, though almost 20,000 were expelled to the countryside.

Boris died of apparent heart failure on 28 August 1943, shortly after returning from a meeting with Hitler. Rumours of assassination spread at once, but there is no evidence that Hitler planned it. His six-year-old son Simeon succeeded him as Simeon II.
boris-pasternak: Boris Leonidovich Pasternak was born in Moscow on 10 February 1890 (29 January in the old style), into a wealthy, assimilated Jewish family. His father, Leonid Pasternak, was a post-Impressionist painter who taught at the Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture, and Architecture; his mother, Rosa Kaufman, was a concert pianist. The family home was visited by Sergei Rachmaninoff, Rainer Maria Rilke and Leo Tolstoy.

Pasternak first studied music at the Moscow Conservatory and composed, and he later went to Germany to study philosophy. In 1912 he met Ida Wissotzkaya in Marburg. Her family, troubled by his poor prospects, persuaded her to refuse his proposal, and he told of the rejection in the poem Marburg, written in 1917.

Pasternak's first book of poems, My Sister, Life, was composed in 1917 and published in Berlin in 1922, and it soon became an important collection in the Russian language. He also became a literary translator, rendering plays by Goethe, Schiller, Pedro Calderón de la Barca and Shakespeare. His translation of the first part of Faust drew an attack in Novy Mir in August 1950, which accused him of distorting Goethe's meanings.

In 1934 Osip Mandelstam recited his epigram on Stalin to him; Mandelstam was arrested that May, and Pasternak appealed to Nikolai Bukharin on his behalf. In 1937 he refused to sign a writers' statement supporting death sentences in the trial of Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and others. During the Second World War he served as a fire warden in Moscow and in 1943 visited soldiers at the front.

Doctor Zhivago, which contains passages from the 1910s and 1920s, was completed in 1955. Novy Mir refused it in 1956 for its rejection of socialist realism, and censors objected to its criticism of Stalinism, collectivisation, the Great Purge and the Gulag. It was first published in Italy in 1957. Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958 and was forced to decline it.

Pasternak died of lung cancer at his dacha in Peredelkino on 30 May 1960. Despite a small notice in the Literary Gazette, handwritten notices of the funeral were posted through the Moscow subway, and thousands of admirers attended despite surveillance. His companion Olga Ivinskaya and her daughter were arrested after his death and accused of dealing with Western publishers; she served four years of an eight-year sentence.

The Soviet state kept criticising him until the 1980s. His son Yevgeny accepted the Nobel Prize on his behalf in 1989, and the house-museum in Peredelkino was founded in 1986. Doctor Zhivago has been part of the main Russian school curriculum since 2003, and David Lean's film of 1965 was unavailable in Russia until perestroika.
boris-yeltsin: Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was born on 1 February 1931 in Butka, a village in the Ural Oblast of the Russian SFSR. His family were ethnic Russians who had lived in the Urals since at least the eighteenth century. In September 1949 he entered the Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk, where he studied industrial and civil engineering, played volleyball and kept out of political organisations, and he then worked in construction. He became a full member of the Communist Party in March 1961, and by December 1965 he was director of the Sverdlovsk House-Building Combine.

In October 1976 Yeltsin became First Secretary of the party committee of Sverdlovsk Oblast, one of the youngest provincial first secretaries in the Russian SFSR. In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev brought him to Moscow. He supported perestroika at first, but later criticised it as too moderate and called for a multi-party democracy. On 10 September 1987 he wrote a letter of resignation from the Politburo, the first person in Soviet history to resign voluntarily from its ranks.

On 29 May 1990 he was elected chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the Russian SFSR, and on 12 July 1990 he resigned from the Communist Party. On 12 June 1991 he won 57 per cent of the vote in the republic's presidential election, becoming the first popularly elected head of state in Russian history. He was instrumental in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991, after which the RSFSR became the Russian Federation. Days later he began radical economic reform, through shock therapy, privatisation and the lifting of price controls.

In 1993 he ordered the dissolution of the Russian parliament, which impeached him. The crisis ended when troops loyal to him stormed the parliament building, and he then introduced a new constitution that expanded the powers of the president. The First Chechen War began in 1994, and he was re-elected in 1996.

Yeltsin resigned by the end of 1999 and was succeeded by Vladimir Putin, whom he had appointed prime minister a few months earlier. He died on 23 April 2007 and was given a state funeral. He has been praised for his part in dismantling the Soviet Union and introducing new freedoms, and criticised for economic mismanagement and abuse of presidential power.
borneo: Borneo is the third-largest island in the world, with an area of 748,168 square kilometres. It lies at the geographic centre of Maritime Southeast Asia, north of Java, west of Sulawesi and east of Sumatra, and the equator divides it roughly in half. It was part of Sundaland, joined to mainland Asia, until sea level rose at the end of the Last Glacial Period. Its rainforest, estimated at around 140 million years old, is among the oldest in the world and shelters many endemic species, including the Bornean orangutan. In Indonesia the island is also called Kalimantan, a name that comes from Pulu K'lemantang, as its people called the island when the Portuguese explorer Jorge de Menezes met them in the sixteenth century.

Archaeological evidence shows that people lived on Borneo for tens of thousands of years. A cave at Lahad Datu in Sabah suggests settlement about 46,000 years ago, and the Trader Cave at Niah in Sarawak has yielded tools and human remains dated between 55,000 and 65,000 years ago. The island is home to hundreds of Indigenous communities, many grouped under the broad term Dayak. Trading settlements were connected to regional maritime networks by the first millennium CE, and Chinese records use the term Bo-ni for Borneo in 977. The Javanese poem Nagarakretagama, written in 1365 at the court of Majapahit, mentions the island as Nusa Tanjungnagara, the island of the Tanjungpura Kingdom.

Empires, kingdoms and sultanates emerged around the coasts. The Sultanate of Brunei held influence over much of coastal Borneo and parts of the southern Philippines at its peak in the 15th century, and the Sultanate of Sulu became a maritime power in north-eastern Borneo. The interior remained politically diverse and was governed largely by local Indigenous systems of authority rather than by a single state. After Malacca fell in 1511, Portuguese merchants traded with Borneo, and from 1530 especially with Brunei, but never tried to conquer it. The British began trading with Sambas in 1609 and the Dutch with Banjar and Martapura in 1644.

Japanese forces occupied most of Borneo from 1941 to 1945. Many coastal people fled to the interior, and many Indigenous and Chinese people were executed after resistance movements such as the Jesselton Revolt.

Borneo is divided among three states. About 73 per cent of the island belongs to Indonesia, as the provinces of Kalimantan, about 26 per cent forms the Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak, and the sultanate of Brunei occupies a small area on the north-west coast. The name Borneo is closely tied to Brunei, since early European travellers recorded variants such as Burnei for the sultanate before the name was applied to the whole island.
bornholm: Bornholm lies in the Baltic Sea east of the rest of Denmark, south of Sweden, north-east of Germany and north of Poland. It is known as the sunshine island for its weather and the rock island for its geology, which is granite except along the southern coast. In Old Norse the island was Borgundarholmr, a name related to words for height and rock, because it rises high from the sea. Its early names include Burgendaland in the 9th century, and some scholars believe the Burgundians took their name from it.

Strategically placed, Bornholm has been fought over for centuries. It has usually been ruled by Denmark but also by Sweden and by Lübeck, to which Frederick I of Denmark pawned it for fifty years from 1525, in payment for its support in his winning the Danish throne. Swedish forces conquered it during the Torstenson War in 1645, but it was returned to Denmark. In 1658 Denmark ceded it to Sweden under the Treaty of Roskilde, along with the rest of Skåneland, Bohuslän and Trøndelag. A revolt broke out the same year and culminated on 8 December 1658, when Villum Clausen shot the Swedish commander Johan Printzensköld. The islanders then handed the island back to the Danish kings.

German forces occupied Denmark on 9 April 1940. On 22 August 1942 a V-1 flying bomb crashed on the island during a test, one of the first signs to British Intelligence of German flying-bomb development. Soviet aircraft bombed the main towns on 7 and 8 May 1945, and Soviet troops landed on 9 May, when the German garrison of about 12,000 surrendered after a short fight. The Soviet forces left on 5 April 1946. Sweden afterwards gave aid to rebuild Rønne and Nexø.

Bornholm is a Danish island, and Rønne is its largest town and seat. With Ertholmene it is the last remaining Danish territory in Skåneland east of Øresund. The ruin of Hammershus at the north-western tip is the largest medieval fortress in northern Europe. The island has 15 medieval churches, four of them round churches, and at Rispebjerg are remains of Neolithic sun temples and Iron Age earthworks. In the early 20th century it drew artists who formed the Bornholm school of painters.
borno-state: Borno borders Yobe to the west, Gombe to the southwest and Adamawa to the south, and its eastern and northern borders form parts of the national frontiers with Cameroon, Niger and Chad. It is the only Nigerian state to border three countries and the second largest by area. Semi-desert Sahelian savanna covers the north, West Sudanian savanna the centre and south, and part of the Mandara Plateau lies in the southeast. The far northeast holds the Nigerian portion of Lake Chad. Kanuri and Shuwa Arabs live throughout the north and centre, and many other groups live elsewhere. About 85 per cent of the people are Muslim.

From the 700s the area lay within the Kanem Empire. In the late 1300s Kanem, after unsuccessful wars, moved west and became the Bornu Empire, which ruled the wider area for about 500 years. The Fulani jihad of the early 1800s weakened Bornu, and much of the south was taken into the Adamawa Emirate under the Sokoto Caliphate. About eighty years later the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquered the empire, and he ruled until French forces killed him at the Battle of Kousséri in 1900. The British, French and Germans then divided the lands, and in 1902 the British incorporated Borno into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate and in 1907 set up a new capital at Maiduguri.

Nigeria became independent in 1960. Borno was part of the Northern Region until 1967, when the area became part of the North-Eastern State. Borno State was formed on 3 February 1976, with ten other states, from the breakup of that state. Local government reform in 1976 reduced the power of the emirs, and by 1979 their jurisdiction covered only cultural and traditional affairs. In 1991 a group of local government areas in the west formed the new Yobe State.

Maiduguri is the capital and a major regional centre of trade and services. The state has 27 local government areas and emirate councils, among them Borno, Bama, Dikwa and Biu, which advise on cultural and traditional matters. Its economy has relied on livestock and crops, and it holds deposits of kaolin, clay, trona and iron ore. Higher institutions include the University of Maiduguri. Since 2009 it has been the centre of the Boko Haram insurgency.
borobudur: Borobudur stands in Magelang Regency in Central Java, about 40 kilometres northwest of Yogyakarta, between the twin volcanoes Sindoro-Sumbing and Merbabu-Merapi and the Progo and Elo rivers. Scholars following de Casparis conclude that the Sanjaya and Sailendra dynasties shared power in central Java for a century and a half, with alternating succession traced from 732 until 882, and that many Hindu and Buddhist monuments rose around the Kedu Plain in that period. Evidence suggests that Borobudur was built in the 8th century and later abandoned.

Its abandonment remains a mystery, and it is not known when pilgrimage ceased. Some sources name the period between 928 and 1006, when King Mpu Sindok moved the capital of the Mataram kingdom to East Java after volcanic eruptions. A poet of the Majapahit era mentions the vihara in Budur in the Nagarakretagama, written around 1365.

Borobudur is built as a single large stupa and, seen from above, takes the form of a giant tantric Buddhist mandala representing Buddhist cosmology. Its square foundation measures about 118 metres on each side, and it has nine platforms, the lower six square and the upper three circular, topped by a central dome. About 55,000 cubic metres of andesite were laid without mortar and joined by knobs, indentations and dovetails, and the reliefs were carved in place after the building was complete.

Pilgrims climb through stairways and corridors lined with 1,460 narrative relief panels. Reliefs on the hidden base illustrate the law of karma, others tell the life of Prince Siddhartha from the Lalitavistara, the Jataka stories of the Buddha's earlier lives, and Sudhana's search for truth. The temple holds 432 Buddha statues in niches on the square platforms, and 72 more sit inside perforated stupas on the circular platforms.

Under British administration from 1811 to 1816, Stamford Raffles was told in 1814 of a big monument deep in the jungle near the village of Bumisegoro. He sent the Dutch engineer Hermann Cornelius, who with 200 men cut down trees, burned vegetation and dug away the earth, though he could not uncover all the galleries. Raffles did not visit the site himself but is credited with bringing it to the world's attention. In 1885 Jan Willem IJzerman found that the base enclosed a hidden foot, and a commission formed in 1900 proposed protection. A major renovation funded by UNESCO took place in 1973.
borte: Few facts are known about Börte's early life, and what is known comes largely from the Secret History of the Mongols, the oldest surviving literary work in the Mongolian language. She was born around 1161 into the Olkhonud of the Khongirad, a people friendly to the Borjigin, the tribe of Temüjin. Her parents were Dei-Sechen and Chotan.

When Temüjin was nine, his father Yesügei met Dei-Sechen on a journey to find a bride. Dei-Sechen described a dream that he took as a good omen, and Yesügei accepted Börte, then ten, as Temüjin's future wife, with Temüjin to stay with her family. On the way home Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars and died, and Temüjin returned to his family. In 1178, after seven years apart, he went back to Börte and married her.

Soon after the marriage the Three Merkit attacked the camp on the Burgi Escarpment. Temüjin's family escaped on horses, but Börte was left behind and was captured. The raid was said to be revenge for the earlier abduction of Temüjin's mother, Hö'elün, from the Merkit. Temüjin sought help from Ong Qan, who had received Börte's dowry, a black sable coat, and after about eight months they attacked the Merkit and recovered her. The Secret History tells how she recognised his voice and ran to him.

Börte brought independent wealth from her dowry and shared the management of the camp's people, animals and economy with Hö'elün. Her nine children, four sons and five daughters, were central to Temüjin's rule: the daughters married allies, and the sons took part in his conquests. She advised him to break with the military leader Jamuqa, and she was named Grand Empress after he became Genghis Khan. While he campaigned she stayed behind and helped his brother Temüge govern the homeland, holding her own court and much of the Kherlen River.

Doubts about the true father of her eldest son Jochi, who was born after her captivity, led to quarrels between Jochi and his brother Chagatai. Genghis Khan denied them and claimed Jochi as his son, but he chose neither of them as his successor. Ögedei was selected instead, and Jochi's descendants founded the Golden Horde.
Börte died in 1230, after her husband. She was revered by the Mongols as a mother figure, a standing helped by the orphans she adopted and raised as her own, including Qutqu Noyan and Buda Noyan.
boshin-war: After two centuries of isolation, the Perry Expedition of 1854 opened Japan to world trade. The unequal treaties brought dissent against the Tokugawa shogunate, which became the radical sonnō jōi movement, meaning revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians. The shogun sought French help for training and weapons from 1865. Chōshū defeated the shogunate in the summer of 1866 and had formed a secret alliance with Satsuma. In late 1866 the shogun Tokugawa Iemochi and Emperor Kōmei died, and Tokugawa Yoshinobu and Emperor Meiji succeeded them. Yoshinobu resigned his authority to the emperor in 1867, on a proposal from the daimyō of Tosa, which ended the shogunate.

On 27 January 1868 shogunate forces attacked Chōshū and Satsuma at the Battle of Toba–Fushimi, near Kyoto. The imperial side was outnumbered three to one but fully modernized. An imperial banner was given to them on the second day, and daimyō who had been faithful to the shogun began to defect. Saigō Takamori led the imperial forces east and surrounded Edo in May, and Katsu Kaishū negotiated its surrender. A northern coalition of domains, including Sendai and Aizu, kept fighting until Aizuwakamatsu was attacked in October.

Enomoto Takeaki fled to Hokkaido with the remnants of the navy and founded the Republic of Ezo, Japan's only republic. It won no international recognition, and the Battle of Hakodate ended the last holdout.

About 8,200 men were killed. The emperor's residence moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, at the end of 1868, the domains became prefectures in 1871, and the samurai class was abolished, which brought some into new careers and left many in poverty. Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa held most key government posts for decades. Tokugawa loyalists were shown clemency through Saigō Takamori's persistence. The victors gave up expelling foreigners in favour of modernization. The war has been called a bloodless revolution, but conflict between western samurai and modernizers led to the Satsuma Rebellion nine years later.
bosniaks: Slavs settled the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the sixth century, during the Migration Period, as small tribal units of the Slavic group the Byzantines called the Sclaveni. The first mention of a Bosnian entity, in the De Administrando Imperio of about 960, calls Bosnia a small land belonging to Byzantium, a geographical rather than a national entity. By the 12th century Bosnia had become independent of Hungarian overlordship under Kulin Ban, who ruled from 1180 to 1204.

Bosnia lay between Catholic and Orthodox areas, with rugged terrain and poor communications, and it developed its own church, the Bosnian Church, which both Rome and Constantinople condemned as heretical. Hungary invaded Bosnia between 1235 and 1241 but withdrew. Scholars disagree on whether the Bosnian Church was dualist; John Fine stresses evidence that it kept basic Catholic theology.

After the Ottoman conquest of the Kingdom of Bosnia in 1463 a distinct community of Bosnian Muslims began to form as the local Slavic population embraced Islam. Mass conversion came in the 1480s in central Bosnia and later elsewhere, at its fullest in the 16th century. At its height Muslims were up to three-fourths of the population, but wars and plagues later reduced them, since they lived in densely populated towns and had to serve in Ottoman campaigns. In the late 17th and early 18th centuries around 130,000 Muslim refugees arrived from Ottoman lands lost in Hungary, Slavonia, Croatia and Dalmatia.

Under Ottoman rule life was structured along religious lines, and the term Bosniak was mainly a territorial designation. Austria-Hungary promoted a non-confessional unitary Bosniak identity, but only a small circle of Muslim notables favoured it, among them Mehmed Kapetanović. In the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes Bosnian Muslims were not acknowledged as a distinct ethnic group. In the Bosnian War they were subjected to ethnic cleansing and genocide, and hundreds of thousands fled. The Dayton Agreement recognises Bosniaks as one of the three constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Most Bosniaks speak the Bosnian language, a variety of Serbo-Croatian mutually intelligible with Croatian and Serbian, with more loanwords from Ottoman Turkish, Arabic and Persian. They are traditionally and predominantly Sunni Muslim, and Sufi orders such as the Naqshbandiyya and Qadiriyya have played a significant role. Traditional culture includes the melancholic folk songs called sevdalinka. Their traditional symbol is a coat of arms with six golden lilies, derived from that of the medieval Kingdom of Bosnia.
bosnian-war: The war arose from the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The League of Communists of Yugoslavia had lost its ideological force at the end of the Cold War, and ethnic nationalism had revived in the 1980s after violence in Kosovo. After Slovenia and Croatia seceded in 1991, the multi-ethnic Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, inhabited mainly by Muslim Bosniaks (44%), Orthodox Serbs (32.5%) and Catholic Croats (17%), held a referendum on independence on 29 February 1992. Bosnian Serb representatives boycotted it and rejected the result, having already proclaimed their own Serb republic on 9 January 1992.

The war is commonly dated from 6 April 1992, when the new republic was internationally recognised. Bosnian Serb forces led by Radovan Karadžić, supported by the government of Slobodan Milošević in Serbia and supplied by the Yugoslav People's Army, seized about 70% of the country in a campaign marked by widespread ethnic cleansing. Serb forces began shelling Sarajevo on 6 April. Croat forces formed the Croatian Defence Council on 8 April, and tensions between Croats and Bosniaks led to the Croat-Bosniak War in early 1993.

In 1994 the Washington Agreement created the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and allied Bosniaks and Croats against the Republika Srpska. After the Srebrenica and Markale massacres, NATO's Operation Deliberate Force in 1995 targeted the Serb army and proved key in ending the war. The Dayton Accords were initialled on 21 November 1995.

Estimates of the dead range widely, from 25,000 to 329,000, depending on who is counted. A database published in Sarajevo in 2007 names at least 97,207 people killed or missing, and over 2.2 million people were displaced. An estimated 12,000 to 50,000 women were raped, mostly Bosniak women and mainly by Serb forces. The killing of over 8,000 Bosniak males at Srebrenica in July 1995 by Serb forces is the only incident in Europe since the Second World War recognised as a genocide. In 2007 the International Court of Justice found that Serbia had failed to prevent it.
bosphorus: The Bosporus is a strait in Turkey, straddled by the city of Istanbul, which connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and forms one of the continental boundaries between Asia and Europe. Between its limits it is 31 km long, with a minimum width of 700 m between Kandilli Point and Aşiyan, and its depth in midstream varies from 13 to 110 m. Together with the Dardanelles it forms the Turkish Straits, and it is the world's narrowest strait used for international navigation. The name comes from the Greek Bosporos, folk-etymologised as cattle passage, after the myth of Io, who was turned into a cow and wandered until she crossed it.

As part of the only passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, the Bosporus has always been of commercial and military importance. In the 5th century BCE Athens depended on grain from the Black Sea ports and kept alliances with cities that controlled the straits, such as Byzantium. The Persian king Darius I crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of connected boats while marching against the Scythian horsemen.

In preparation for the conquest of Constantinople the Ottomans built the Anadoluhisarı in 1393 and the Rumelihisarı in 1451 on either side of the strait. The final 53-day campaign ended on 29 May 1453 and transferred control of the Bosporus to the Ottomans, who made Constantinople their capital. Control of the straits was an objective in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 and in the Allied attack at Gallipoli in 1915. The Montreux Convention of 20 July 1936 treats the strait as an international shipping lane while allowing Turkey to restrict the naval traffic of states without a Black Sea coast.

Most of the shores are heavily settled, as Istanbul extends inland from both banks. They were once lined with small fishing villages, whose names often keep the suffix köy, village, as in Ortaköy and Arnavutköy. The strait has 620 waterfront houses, yalı, from the Ottoman period, and Ottoman palaces such as Dolmabahçe and Beylerbeyi stand on or near it. Three bridges, a highway tunnel and a railway tunnel link the two banks.
boston: Boston stands on the Shawmut Peninsula, beside Boston Harbor, an arm of Massachusetts Bay. Its highest point is Bellevue Hill, at 330 feet above sea level. Since independence the city has expanded well beyond the original peninsula by filling in land and annexing neighbouring towns. Boston Common, near Beacon Hill, is part of the Emerald Necklace, a string of parks designed by Frederick Law Olmsted.

Before European colonisation the surrounding region was inhabited by the Massachusett people, who built small seasonal communities there. When settlers led by John Winthrop arrived in 1630 they found the Shawmut Peninsula nearly empty of Native people, most of whom had died of diseases brought by earlier settlers and traders.

The first European to live there was William Blaxton, an Anglican cleric educated at the University of Cambridge. He invited Isaac Johnson, a leader of the Puritans, to cross from the failing colony of Charlestown and share the peninsula, and in September 1630 the Puritans made the crossing. Johnson, in one of his last acts before his death on 30 September 1630, named the settlement after his hometown of Boston, Lincolnshire. Puritan ethics and their focus on education shaped the early city, and Boston Latin School, the first public school in America, was founded in 1635.

Boston was home to several seminal events of the American Revolution: the Boston Massacre of 1770, the Boston Tea Party of 1773, the Battle of Bunker Hill in 1775 and the Siege of Boston from 1775 to 1776. After independence it became an important port and manufacturing centre as well as a centre of education and culture, and it has been called the Athens of America for its literary culture. Its firsts include Boston Common in 1634, the oldest public park in the United States, and the Tremont Street subway of 1897, the first subway system.

Boston is the capital and most populous city of Massachusetts and a cultural and financial centre of New England. The Boston Red Sox play at Fenway Park, built in 1912, which is the oldest stadium in active use among the four major American professional sports leagues.
boston-tea-party: The protest arose from two problems facing the British Empire: the financial difficulties of the East India Company and a dispute over how far Parliament's authority extended over colonies that elected no members to it. The Townshend Revenue Act of 1767 laid new taxes, which colonists met with protests and boycotts. Meanwhile the company, burdened by taxes, by smuggled Dutch tea that undersold it and by the Bengal famine of 1769 to 1773, amassed a large unsold surplus. Parliament passed the Tea Act on 10 May 1773 to help it.

The Act in fact lowered the price of legally imported tea, but Samuel Adams considered the British tea monopoly equal to a tax, and others saw a threat to colonial rights. In every colony except Massachusetts, protesters forced the consignees to resign or the tea to go back to England.

In Boston, Governor Thomas Hutchinson held his ground and persuaded the consignees, two of them his sons, not to give way. When the Dartmouth arrived in late November, thousands met on 29 November 1773 at the Old South Meeting House. British law gave the ship twenty days to unload and pay the duties before the cargo could be confiscated. Hutchinson refused to let it leave, and two more ships, the Eleanor and the Beaver, arrived.

On 16 December, the last day of the deadline, some 5,000 to 7,000 people gathered at Old South. After a report that Hutchinson had again refused, Samuel Adams announced that the meeting could do nothing further to save the country. That evening a large group, some dressed as Mohawk warriors and armed with axes, boarded the three vessels at Griffin's Wharf and over three hours emptied all the chests into the harbour, destroying 92,616 pounds of tea, which the East India Company valued at £9,659.

Britain regarded the act as treason. In 1774 Parliament passed the Intolerable Acts, which, among other measures, ended local self-government in Massachusetts and closed Boston's port. The other colonies answered by convening the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia, which coordinated resistance in the Continental Association of October 1774. The Battles of Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775 began the Revolutionary War. The name Boston Tea Party gained currency only in the early 19th century; the event had been called the Destruction of the Tea.
botswana: Botswana has a total area of 581,730 square kilometres and is topographically flat, with approximately 70% of its territory part of the Kalahari Desert. It borders South Africa, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The terrain consists of sandy soils, rocky hill ranges and grasslands, and the climate is generally semi-arid, with highly seasonal rainfall. The north and east receive more rain than the dry southwest, and much of the population lives in the southeast.

In the northwest the Okavango River spreads across the Kalahari in a vast inland delta of channels, lagoons, islands and seasonal wetlands, rather than flowing to the sea. The Chobe River in the north forms part of the border with Namibia.

Stone tools in present-day Botswana date back two million years, and the ancestors of the Khoe and the San lived in the region 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Rock art dates back approximately 30,000 years. Around 2,000 years ago people introduced cattle, sheep, pottery and agriculture. Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into the region between 2,000 and 1,500 years ago: the Kalanga arrived around 200 CE and the ancestors of the Tswana around 400 CE, bringing iron and copper tools and establishing permanent settlements. Trade expanded from the seventh century, and the Toutswe people, the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and later Great Zimbabwe became important regional powers, with cattle and gold playing major economic roles.

From the fifteenth to the eighteenth century Tswana and Kalanga peoples formed new political communities. Tswana society was organised into merafe, governed by chiefs called dikgosi. The Difaqane of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century caused widespread warfare and migration, and by the 1840s many states had been re-established and were governed through the kgotla, a traditional community council. Missionaries arrived in 1816, followed by British traders and explorers, and David Livingstone established a mission in 1845. The discovery of the Tati Goldfields in 1868 led to a gold rush and the growth of Francistown. In 1885 the British declared the protectorate of Bechuanaland, which became independent on 30 September 1966.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city. Botswana is a parliamentary republic, and its government draws on both the Westminster system and the tribal governments of the Tswana. English is the official language and Setswana is widely spoken. The Tswana make up about 79% of the population, the Kalanga about 11% and the San about 3%. Botswana is a member of the Southern African Development Community, the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations.
boudica: Boudica was the consort of Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, a tribe living in what is now Norfolk and parts of neighbouring counties. The Iceni had revolted against the Romans in 47 and afterwards kept their independence. Prasutagus ruled as a nominally independent ally of Rome and had two daughters with Boudica. In his will he made both the daughters and the emperor Nero his heirs. The name may be an honorific title, and the name she bore for most of her life is unknown.

Accounts of the revolt come from Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio. Dio wrote the longest, about 140 years after her death, and his text survives only in an epitome by the 11th-century monk John Xiphilinus. His details are often fictitious, and the speeches both Tacitus and Dio give her were never recorded.

When Prasutagus died, the Romans ignored his will and absorbed the kingdom into the province of Britannia. Tacitus tells of pillaging and of the flogging of Boudica and rape of her daughters. Dio mentions none of this and gives other causes, among them the recall of loans by Seneca. The Iceni and the Trinovantes raised an army reported at 120,000 men and attacked Camulodunum, a colony for retired soldiers. The Legio IX Hispana tried to relieve the town and was overwhelmed.

The governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus reached Londinium before the rebels but, outnumbered, abandoned it, and they burned it. They also sacked Verulamium. Modern estimates put the dead at 70,000 to 80,000 Romans and Britons.

Suetonius gathered nearly 10,000 men and took a stand in a narrow pass with a wood behind. His javelins, wedge formation and cavalry crushed the larger British army. Tacitus says that Boudica poisoned herself, while Dio says she fell ill and died and was given a lavish burial. The crisis made Nero consider withdrawing from Britain, but the victory confirmed Roman control of the province. Interest in Boudica revived in the English Renaissance and brought her fame in the Victorian era.
bougainville-island: Bougainville is the main island of the Autonomous Region of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, with a land area of 9,384 square kilometres. Its highest point is Mount Balbi, at 2,715 metres. Buka Island lies to the north across a narrow strait, and the Shortland Islands of the independent Solomon Islands lie less than 9 kilometres to the south. The island has several volcanoes, of which Bagana in the north-central part is conspicuously active, and is largely covered by rainforest. Most people are Christian, and Tok Pisin and English are the languages of government, alongside many local languages from Austronesian and North and South Bougainville families.

During the last ice age Bougainville was part of a single landmass, Greater Bougainville. The earliest evidence of settlement is at Kilu Cave on Buka, from between 26,700 and 18,100 BCE, left by Melanesian people likely related to modern Papuans and Indigenous Australians. Austronesian settlers arrived in the 2nd millennium BCE with pigs, chickens, dogs and obsidian tools. The French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville reached the island in 1768 and named it after himself. Whaling ships called for provisions from 1822 to 1881. Germany annexed it into German New Guinea in 1899, and missionaries arrived in 1902. Australia occupied it in the First World War and held it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920.

Japan invaded in 1942, and Allied forces began the Bougainville campaign in 1943. On 18 April 1943 the Japanese admiral Isoroku Yamamoto died there when his plane was shot down. Japanese garrisons held out until 1945, and Australia resumed control. When Papua New Guinea became independent in September 1975, Bougainville declared itself the Republic of the North Solomons, but it was absorbed into the new state.

Copper on the island had been under development since 1972, and the Panguna deposit is estimated at a billion tonnes of ore and 12 million ounces of gold. The mine, run by a Rio Tinto-owned operation, caused heavy environmental damage and was shut down in a revolt against it.
