The Bougainville Civil War of 1988 to 1998 claimed over 15,000 lives, and a blockade by Papua New Guinea left the islanders without medical supplies and caused many deaths. Peace talks brokered by New Zealand began in 1997, and a peace agreement of 2001 promised a referendum on independence.

In the referendum of November and December 2019, 98.31 per cent of voters chose independence from Papua New Guinea, on a turnout of 87.38 per cent. The result was not contested, but the referendum was not binding on the national government, and talks between the two governments followed. Bougainville is the largest island of the Solomon Islands chain although it belongs politically to Papua New Guinea.
boulogne-sur-mer: Boulogne-sur-Mer stands on the English Channel at the mouth of the river Liane, in the department of Pas-de-Calais, on the Côte d'Opale. The French name derives from the Latin Bononia, also the Roman name of Bologna in Italy. Both are thought to come from native Celtic place-names, with bona possibly meaning foundation, citadel or granary. The epithet sur-Mer, on sea, distinguishes the city from Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris.

The foundation of Gesoriacum is credited to the Celtic Boii. A tall lighthouse, the Tour d'Ordre, was built there around 39 CE on the order of Caligula, possibly in preparation for an invasion of Britain, and fell into the sea through coastal erosion in 1644. From Claudius's invasion in 43 the town was the major port linking the empire with Britain and the chief base of the Roman navy's British fleet until its admiral Carausius rebelled in 286. The junior emperor Constantius Chlorus besieged it by land and sea in 293, and its name changed to Bononia by 310.

In the Middle Ages Boulogne was capital of an eponymous county founded in the mid-9th century. Count Eustace II helped William the Conqueror conquer England, and his wife founded the church that became Notre-Dame cathedral, a pilgrimage site from the 12th century. The English occupied the town several times during the Hundred Years War, and again from 1544 to 1550, when France bought it back for 400,000 crowns. In 1805 Napoleon gathered the Grande Armée there for a planned invasion of Britain. The railway to Paris, completed in 1848, made it a bathing resort for wealthy Parisians.

Boulogne was one of the three base ports most used by Commonwealth armies on the Western Front in the First World War. Allied bombing on 15 June 1944 completely destroyed the harbour and surrounding area, and Canadian troops liberated the town in September 1944. It is France's largest fishing port, specialising in herring, and its 12th-century belfry is a World Heritage Site.
bourges: Bourges stands in central France where the Auron flows into the Yèvre, in the region of Centre-Val de Loire. Its name derives either from the Bituriges, its original inhabitants, or from a Germanic word burg, meaning a hill or village. The Celts called it Avaricon and Latin speakers Avaricum. In the fourth century BCE, and still in Caesar's time, the area around it was the centre of a Gallic confederacy.

In 52 BCE the Gauls adopted a scorched-earth policy to deny Caesar's forces supplies, but the inhabitants of Avaricum persuaded the council not to burn their town. Its marshes, a river that nearly encircled it and a strong southern wall spared it for a time. Caesar's forces nevertheless captured and destroyed it, killing all but 800 of its inhabitants. Rome rebuilt it with a monumental gate, aqueducts, baths and an amphitheatre, and the Roman town grew larger than the medieval one. Saint Ursinus, of the third century, is considered its first bishop.

In the 8th century Bourges lay on the northern edge of the Duchy of Aquitaine and was the first town to face Frankish attacks across the Loire. Charles Martel captured it in 731, and Duke Odo the Great retook it. Pepin the Short destroyed much of it in a siege in 762. It was capital of the Viscounty of Bourges until 1101 and of the Duchy of Berry from 1360. Charles VII sought refuge there in the 1420s, and his son Louis XI was born there in 1423. In 1438 Charles issued the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges. A fire in 1487 destroyed a third of the town, and its economic decline began.

Bourges is the capital of the department of Cher and was capital of the former province of Berry. Its Gothic cathedral, built from 1195 to 1255 and one of the earliest examples of High Gothic, was added to the World Heritage list in 1992. The 15th-century Palais Jacques Cœur and a sixty-five-hectare district of half-timbered houses also survive. From the 1860s the town became an important centre of artillery production, after Napoleon III moved the École de pyrotechnie militaire there from Metz.
boxer-rebellion: After the First Sino-Japanese War, villagers in North China feared the growth of foreign spheres of influence and resented Christian missionaries, who ignored local customs and used their power to protect their followers in court. Shandong, where the Righteous and Harmonious Fists arose, had long been troubled by social unrest, religious sects and martial societies. In 1897 and 1898 drought and floods forced farmers into the cities, and the movement blamed these disasters on foreign and Christian influence. American missionaries probably first called its members Boxers, because of the martial arts they practised. Their main rite was a spiritual possession with whirling swords and incantations, and they claimed invulnerability to cannon, rifle shot and blade.

From 1899 the movement spread across Shandong and the North China Plain, destroying foreign property such as railways and attacking or murdering Chinese Christians and missionaries. In January 1900 Empress Dowager Cixi, with a majority of conservatives at court, issued edicts in its defence. In the spring it moved north towards Beijing, burning churches and intimidating officials. Diplomats, missionaries, soldiers and some Chinese Christians took refuge in the Legation Quarter, which the Boxers besieged.

On 17 June 1900 the Eight-Nation Alliance, of American, Austro-Hungarian, British, French, German, Italian, Japanese and Russian troops, stormed the Dagu Forts at Tianjin. On 21 June Cixi issued a decree that was in effect a declaration of war on the powers. Officials were divided, and those in the southern provinces ignored the order to fight. The Alliance defeated the Imperial Army at Tianjin and reached Beijing on 14 August, ending the 55-day siege of the Legations.

Looting of the capital and countryside followed, together with summary executions of suspected Boxers. The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 required the execution of officials who had supported the movement, allowed foreign troops to be stationed in Beijing and imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver, more than the government's annual tax revenue, to be paid over 39 years to the eight nations. The Qing dynasty's handling of the rebellion further weakened its credibility and its control over China. It led to the Late Qing reforms and, to a greater extent, to the Xinhai Revolution.
boyaca-department: Boyacá lies almost entirely within the mountains of the Eastern Cordillera, although its western end reaches the Magdalena River at Puerto Boyacá. It covers 23,189 square kilometres and borders Santander and Norte de Santander to the north, Arauca and Casanare to the east, Cundinamarca to the south and Antioquia to the west. The Cordillera rises to 5,380 metres in the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, and the department also holds high plateaux, a small part of the Middle Magdalena valley and a part of the eastern Llanos. The Altiplano Cundiboyacense, shared with Cundinamarca, is densely populated. The name comes from the Chibcha word Bojacá, which means near the cacique or region of the royal mantle.

Before the Spanish arrival the territory belonged to the Muisca. Under the chiefdom of the zaque of Hunza they lived mainly by agriculture and by mining gold and emeralds. The Spaniard Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada conquered the northern Muisca, whose last zaque was Aquiminzaque, shared out the land in encomiendas and made the indigenous people work for him. In 1539 the conquistador Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded Tunja on sites where the indigenous people had earlier had villages, and Tunja became one of the main political and economic centres of the Viceroyalty of New Granada.

In the war of independence the region was a battleground between royalist armies and patriot armies led by Simón Bolívar. The Battle of the Vargas Swamp was fought on 25 July 1819, and the decisive Battle of Boyacá at the Puente de Boyacá on 7 August 1819; the patriots won both. Gran Colombia created a Boyacá Department in 1824. After the Granadine Confederation was formed in 1858 the territory became the Sovereign State of Boyacá, one of the original nine states of the United States of Colombia. Civil wars, among them the war of 1860–1862 and the Thousand Days War, and changing constitutions, including that of 1886, then reshaped it until it took its present form as a department.

Boyacá is one of the thirty-two departments of Colombia, with Tunja as its capital. It is divided into 13 provinces and two special districts, with 123 municipalities. Many rivers rise there, the most important being the Chicamocha and the Arauca, and it has several lakes, among them Lake Tota, Lake Sochagota and Lake Fúquene. El Cocuy and Pisba National Parks lie in the north-east. The department is known as the Land of Freedom because of the battles of 1819, and it has three universities, among them the Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia.
boyana-church: The church was built in three stages: in the late 10th or early 11th century, in the mid-13th century and in the mid-19th century. The oldest part, the eastern church, is a small one-apse cross-vaulted church with built-in cruciform supports. The second section adjoins it and was commissioned by Sebastocrator Kaloyan and his wife Desislava. It is a two-floor tomb-church, with a ground-floor family sepulchre under a semi-cylindrical vault, with two arcosolia on the north and south walls, and an upper-floor family chapel identical in design to the eastern church. The western section was built with donations from the local community.

A patron's inscription in Middle Bulgarian, dated to indiction 7 of the year 6767 (1259), records that the temple of Saint Nicholas and the martyr Panteleimon was raised with Kaloyan's funds and care. It calls him cousin of the Tsar and grandson of Stephen, King of Serbia, and says the church was decorated under the Bulgarian Tsar Constantine Asen.

Fragments of an earlier layer of frescoes, from the 11th and 12th centuries, survive on the lower apse, the north wall, the upper west wall and the south vault. The second layer was painted over it by a team of unknown artists, who decorated both floors of Kaloyan's building. In all, 89 scenes with 240 human images cover the walls.

In the oldest section, Christ Pantocrator fills the dome, angels the drum below it and the four Evangelists the pendentives. The narthex holds eighteen scenes from the life of Saint Nicholas, which include details of contemporary life: in the Miracle at Sea, the ship and the sailors' hats recall the Venetian fleet.

The frescoes were restored and cleaned in 1912–1915 by an Austrian and a Bulgarian specialist, and again in 1934 and 1944. The church was closed to the public in 1954 for conservation and partly reopened in 2006. Under the National Historical Museum it fully reopened on 2 October 2008.

The name Boyana Master stands for the unknown team, trained in the Turnovo School of Painting, and many experts hold that the frescoes mattered for the development of medieval Bulgarian and European painting. During restoration in 2006–2008 an inscription reading 'I, Vasiliy inscribed' was found under plaster. The museum's director took it for the painter's name, while other historians think an assistant could equally have left it.
boyar: The title boila was held by Bulgar aristocrats, mostly regional governors and noble warriors, in the First Bulgarian Empire (681-1018). Byzantine documents render its plural as boilades; in the 10th-century protocol of Emperor Constantine VII the Bulgarian nobles are called boliades. According to Max Vasmer, the older Slavic form bolyarin was borrowed into Old Church Slavonic from the Danubian Bulgar language, which was Turkic. In the Second Bulgarian Empire the title was bolyar, a hereditary rank divided into great and minor boyars.

In Kievan Rus' from the 9th to the 13th century boyars wielded power through their military support of the princes, though their standing came to depend on service to the state and on a family history of service. In Novgorod and Pskov they formed a kind of republic that limited the princes' power until Moscow conquered both. After the Mongol invasion the boyars of modern Belarus and Ukraine were absorbed into the Lithuanian and Polish nobility; in Galicia they were given the rights of the szlachta from 1430.

Until the 16th century a boyar in Moscow did not have to be Russian or Orthodox, and some came from Lithuania or the Nogais. Ivan IV became grand prince in 1533 at the age of three, and boyar factions competed for the regency. In 1565 he divided the realm in two and in his private part began the oprichnina terror, which crushed boyar opposition. After the Rurik dynasty ended with the death of Fedor, the boyar Boris Godunov tried to proclaim himself tsar, but several boyar factions refused to recognise him.

In Moldavia and Wallachia the boyar class emerged from the chiefs of rural communities, who made their judicial and administrative functions hereditary. The social order ran from boyar to mazil, then the răzeș or yeoman, and finally the rumân or serf. Being a boyar meant owning land, having serfs and holding a military or administrative office, a boierie, which only the prince could grant. Land was hereditary, and the prince could take it away only for grave reasons such as treason. Boyars ranked in three states, and only those of the first state could grow a beard.
boyoma-falls: The falls consist of seven cataracts, each no more than 5 metres high, that extend over more than 100 kilometres along a curve of the Lualaba River between the river port towns of Ubundu and Kisangani, also known as Boyoma, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Together they have a total drop of 61 metres. The two major cataracts are the first below Ubundu, which forms a narrow and crooked stream that is hardly accessible, and the last, which can be seen and visited from Kisangani. At the bottom of the rapids the Lualaba is known as the Congo River. A portage railway of 1 metre gauge bypasses the rapids and connects Kisangani with Ubundu.

The last of the seven cataracts is also known as the Wagenia Falls, after the local Wagenya fishermen, who developed a special technique for fishing in the river. They build systems of wooden tripods across the rapids, fixed in holes carved in the rock by the current. These tripods anchor large baskets that are lowered into the rapids to trap fish. The method is very selective, since the baskets are big and only large fish are caught.

The falls were formerly named after Henry Morton Stanley, who explored the region and noted the technique of the Wagenya. He described how the people, taking advantage of the rocks, fixed upright heavy poles, 6 inches in diameter, to which they attached enormous fish-baskets by means of rattan-cane cable. He counted probably sixty or seventy baskets laid in the river on each side every day, and noted that out of half a dozen baskets twenty-eight large fish were collected.
bp: In May 1908 British geologists found a large amount of oil at Masjed Soleyman in Khuzestan Province in south-western Persia, the first commercially significant oil find in the Middle East. William Knox D'Arcy had obtained, by contract with Ali-Qoli Khan Bakhtiari, permission to explore for oil there. On 14 April 1909 the Anglo-Persian Oil Company was incorporated as a subsidiary of the Burmah Oil Company, and some of its shares were sold to the public. Lord Strathcona became its first chairman and a minority shareholder. The discovery led to the growth of a petrochemical industry and of industries that depended on oil.

In 1954 the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company became the British Petroleum Company. After the 1953 Iranian coup d'état, Iranian Oil Participants Ltd was founded in London in October 1954 to bring Iranian oil back to the international market, and British Petroleum was a founding member with a 40 per cent stake. The consortium agreed to share profits with Iran equally, but not to open its books to Iranian auditors or to admit Iranians to its board. Since 1951 the company has published a Statistical Review of World Energy each year.

The British government sold 80 million shares in 1979 as part of the privatisations of the Thatcher years, reducing its holding to 46 per cent. On 19 October 1987 Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher authorised the sale of its remaining 31 per cent for £7.5 billion. Under the chief executive John Browne the company grew by acquisition: it merged with Amoco in December 1998 to become BP Amoco, and bought Atlantic Richfield and Burmah Castrol in 2000. In 2001 it adopted the name BP and replaced its Green Shield logo with the Helios sunflower symbol, with the slogan Beyond Petroleum.

BP is a vertically integrated company, active in exploration and production, refining, marketing and trading, with its headquarters in London. Its accidents have shaped its public record. In December 1965 Sea Gem, Britain's first oil rig, capsized and 13 crew members were killed. A refinery explosion at Texas City in 2005 killed 15 workers.

The worst was the Deepwater Horizon disaster in the Gulf of Mexico. The rig exploded on 20 April 2010, killing 11 people, and the well was capped on 15 July 2010 after about 4.9 million barrels of oil had leaked, the largest accidental release of oil into marine waters. The company's costs came to more than 65 billion dollars. In 1997 BP had left the Global Climate Coalition, and in 2002 Browne declared that global warming was real; critics have argued that its actions did not match its stated aims.
brac: Brač has an area of 396 square kilometres and is the third largest island in the Adriatic. It is almost 40 km wide from east to west and about 14 km from north to south, and the Brač Channel, 5 to 13 km wide, separates it from the mainland. Vidova gora, at 780 m, is the highest point of the Adriatic islands. The island is mostly limestone, formed in the Cretaceous about 100 million years ago; it became an island only within the last 12,000 years. Its Greek name was Elaphousa, apparently from the word for stag, and the Latin name was Brattia.

The Kopačina cave near Donji Humac holds finds dated to the 12th millennium BCE, among the oldest traces of human habitation in Dalmatia. In the 2nd millennium BCE the Illyrians arrived and replaced the earlier population. Brač came under Roman rule with the provinces of Illyricum and Dalmatia in 32-27 BCE. The writer Vladimir Nazor called it an island without history, for neither Illyrians, Greeks nor Romans founded a large settlement on it. In the ninth century the Narentines, a South Slavic people, held the island, which with neighbouring islands was called Maronia.

In 1000 the Venetian doge Pietro II Orseolo set out to pacify the Narentines, and Venice conquered Brač that year. Hungarian kings held the island in the 1180s and again after the Treaty of Zadar of 1358. On 1 April 1278 Venice agreed to a plea from Brač and Hvar for protection from pirates. Venice reconquered the island in August 1420 and ruled until 1797, when the Habsburg monarchy annexed most of its territory. The Black Death struck in 1425-1427 and 1434-1436, reducing the population from 6,000 to 2,000.

The island is part of Split-Dalmatia County, with a city, Supetar, and seven municipalities. Its population fell from about 40,000 early in the 20th century to about 13,000 at its end, mainly through emigration to Latin America, New Zealand and Australia. The white limestone, quarried for millennia, was used in Diocletian's Palace in Split, and the island's olive oil has a protected designation of origin.
bracara-augusta: The site lies in the heart of Minho, in a transitional region between east and west, between mountains, forests, valleys and plains. Human occupation there dates back thousands of years, with vestiges of monumental structures from the Megalithic era. During the Iron Age the Castro culture extended into the northwest, and the Bracari occupied high ground in fortified settlements called castrum. The region became the domain of the Callaici Bracarii, a Celtic tribe who occupied what is now northern Portugal, Galicia and Asturias.

The Romans began their conquest of the region around 136 BCE and finished it, by conquering the northern regions, in the reign of Augustus. The civitas was founded in 16 BCE and, in the administrative reorganization of the new acquisitions, Bracara was rededicated to the emperor and took the name Bracara Augusta. The city developed greatly during the 1st century and reached its maximum extent around the 2nd. Towards the end of the 3rd century Diocletian promoted it to a capital within the newly founded Roman province of Gallaecia. The poet Ausonius described it as prosperous in the 4th century.

Between 402 and 470 the Suebi conquered the area. In 410 they established a kingdom in the northwest of Iberia, founded by Hermeric and lasting over 150 years, with Bracara as its capital. The old Roman amphitheatre was converted into a fortress. In 455 the Visigothic king Theodoric II sacked the city, destroying many historical and archaeological records, while the Suebi king Rechiar escaped, wounded, to Porto. A list of dioceses and parishes of Braga made in 570 still exists, and by about 584 the Visigoths took permanent control of Gallaecia.

The site is the city of Braga in northwestern Portugal, capital of the district of Braga and of the historical Minho Province. It hosts the oldest Portuguese archdiocese, the Archdiocese of Braga, and is the seat of the Primacy of the Spains. In the Middle Ages it was a main centre of Christianity in Iberia. Archbishop Paio Mendes was a contributor to the recognition of Portugal as an independent kingdom under Afonso I Henriques in 1179, and the city was later handed to the Church's direct control, giving it the nickname Paiz Bracarense. The medieval castle in the city centre was destroyed in 1905.
brahma: The origins of the term brahmā are uncertain, partly because several related words occur in Vedic literature, such as Brahman for the Ultimate Reality and Brāhmaṇa for priest. Brahman is a genderless, abstract metaphysical concept, while Brahmā is a masculine god, and some scholars suggest the god may have emerged as a visible icon of the impersonal principle. A distinct god named Brahma is evidenced in late Vedic texts, and he is frequently identified with Prajapati. One of the earliest mentions of Brahma with Vishnu and Shiva is in the Maitrayaniya Upanishad, probably composed around the late 1st millennium BCE, which links Brahma to the quality called rajas.

In the Puranas Brahma is a secondary creator who creates all forms in the universe but not the primordial universe itself, and his activity depends on a higher god or goddess. Vishnu-focused Puranas say he was born from a lotus emerging from Vishnu's navel. In the Brahmanda Purana there was only an eternal ocean, from which a golden egg called Hiranyagarbha emerged, and Brahma came into being within it. He creates but neither preserves nor destroys, and like all deities he is mortal. His wife is the goddess Sarasvati.

Brahma is traditionally depicted with four faces, each facing a cardinal direction and credited with creating one of the four Vedas, and four arms holding symbols of knowledge and creation. He often has a white beard and sits on a lotus with a swan, the hamsa, as his mount.

In the post-Vedic period Brahma was a prominent god, and a sect of him existed from the 2nd to the 6th century CE. By the 7th century he had lost importance. Historians point to the rise of Shaivism and Vaishnavism and attacks by Buddhists, Jains and followers of Shiva and Vishnu. Today he does not enjoy popular worship, and few temples are dedicated to him in India, the most prominent being the Brahma Temple at Pushkar. His shrines are also found outside India: at Angkor Wat, at Prambanan in Java, and at the Erawan Shrine in Bangkok. The name Burma derives from Brahma.
brahmanas: The Brahmanas are Vedic works attached to the Samhitas, the hymns and mantras, of the Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas. Each Veda has one or more Brahmanas of its own, and each is generally associated with a particular shakha, or Vedic school. The word is loosely translated as explanations of sacred knowledge or doctrine, and according to Sayana a Brahmana has two parts: vidhi, directions for rites, and arthavada, explanatory remarks. The oldest is dated to about 900 BCE and the most recent to around 700 BCE, though the dating is controversial, since the texts were probably recorded only after several centuries of oral transmission.

The Brahmanas are noted for their instructions on the proper performance of rituals and for explaining the symbolism of sacred words and ritual actions. They insist on exact pronunciation, metre and pitch, with coordinated movement of the hands and fingers. The Shatapatha Brahmana, for example, states that verbal perfection made a mantra infallible, while one mistake made it powerless. Scholars suggest that this care preserved the Vedas in an age without writing, when students memorised them and passed them on by recitation.

The texts also record legends and discuss scientific matters of the Vedic period, including observational astronomy and, in relation to altar construction, geometry. The Rigveda has the Aitareya and Kausitaki Brahmanas, the Samaveda the Panchavimsha, or Tandya, Brahmana, which includes the Vratyastoma, a ceremony by which people of non-Aryan stock could be admitted into the Aryan family. The Shatapatha belongs to the White Yajurveda, the Taittiriya to the Black Yajurveda, and the Gopatha to the Atharvaveda. Some Brahmanas also contain mystical and philosophical material that forms the Aranyakas and Upanishads.

Fewer than twenty Brahmanas survive. Most are lost, and the grammarian Panini and Patanjali's Mahabhasya imply that each Veda once had a much larger number. Panini also distinguishes old Brahmanas, taught before Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa set out the Vedic recensions, from new ones expounded by his disciples. The grammarian Yaska's Nirukta, a work on the etymology and interpretation of the Vedas, refers to several of them.

In the 14th century, King Bukka asked his preceptor and minister Madhavacharya to write a commentary on the Vedas so that common people could understand the mantras. Madhavacharya entrusted the task to his younger brother Sayana, who wrote commentaries on the Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads.
brahmaputra: The Brahmaputra is a trans-boundary river that flows through south-western China, north-eastern India and Bangladesh. It is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibetan, the Brahmaputra in Assam, the Siang or Dihang in the Mishmi language and the Jamuna in Bangladesh. It rises on the Angsi Glacier near Mount Kailash. For nearly 1,100 km it runs east between the main range of the Himalayas and the Kailas Range, then breaks through the Himalayas in great gorges and enters Arunachal Pradesh near the village of Gelling.

It flows south-west through the Assam Valley and then south through Bangladesh, merges with the Ganges in the delta, and as the Meghna reaches the Bay of Bengal. It is a classic braided river, prone to channel migration, and one of the few rivers in the world with a tidal bore. It floods catastrophically in spring when Himalayan snow melts, and it is navigable for most of its length.

The upper course of the river was long unknown, and its identity with the Yarlung Tsangpo was established only by exploration in 1884–1886. Brahmaputra means son of Brahma in Sanskrit, a rare male name among the rivers of the Indian subcontinent, and the lower reaches are sacred to Hindus. The early Greek accounts of Curtius and Strabo give its name as Dyardanes and Oidanes.

Its lower course in Bangladesh once ran through the Jamalpur and Mymensingh districts, and some water still flows through that channel, now called the Old Brahmaputra. When and why the main flow moved to the Jamuna channel is debated: one account ties it to an earthquake and the uplift of the Madhupur tract, another to the heavy flooding of the Tista.

The river's delta is home to 130 million people, who depend on the annual flood to bring moisture and fresh sediment to the soils. Two of the three seasonal rice varieties, aus and aman, cannot survive without the floodwater, and fish caught on the floodplain are a main source of protein for many rural people. The Sadiya to Dhubri stretch of 891 km in Assam is National Waterway 2.
brahmi-script: Early theories derived Brahmi from Egyptian hieroglyphs on a pictographic model, but these have lost credence as purely imaginative and speculative. Many scholars link it to Semitic scripts, particularly Aramaic, which was the bureaucratic language of the Achaemenid empire and lay close to the Indian subcontinent. Georg Bühler connected it to Phoenician and proposed an early 8th century BCE borrowing. A difficulty is that Aramaic is also the accepted source of the Kharoṣṭhī script, which looks very different, and why two such scripts arose from it is unexplained.

Other scholars, among them John Marshall and G. R. Hunter, saw similarities with the undeciphered Indus script. Kenneth Norman proposed that Brahmi was devised over a longer period before Ashoka, citing sherds from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka dated to perhaps two centuries earlier, though those finds are controversial.

Brahmi is an abugida: vowels are attached to consonant signs by diacritical marks. It changed relatively little from the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE to the early Gupta period in the 4th century CE. Sometime afterwards the ability to read it was lost. Its name is a feminine Sanskrit word meaning of Brahma. The Lalitavistara Sūtra lists 64 scripts with Brahmi first. The earliest full inscriptions are in Prakrit, from the 3rd to 1st centuries BCE, and the earliest in Sanskrit date from the 1st century BCE.

The Edicts of Ashoka were written in Brahmi and, in the northwest, sometimes in Kharoshthi. Both scripts had died out by about the 4th century CE, so the edicts could not be read when scholars began to study them in the 19th century. James Prinsep, secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, deciphered Brahmi in a series of articles in the Society's journal in the 1830s, building on the work of Christian Lassen, Edwin Norris, H. H. Wilson and Alexander Cunningham.
From the 6th century CE the script diversified into local variants, the Brahmic family. One survey found 198 scripts that ultimately derive from it, used across South and Southeast Asia.
braila: Before the 14th century a small village stood on the site, probably of fishermen and small merchants. It fell to the Mongols in the invasion of 1241. The origin of the name is unknown and thought to be a personal name. The first certain mention is a privilege from Vladislav I of Wallachia exempting German merchants of Brașov from customs duties on the road to the Danube through Braylan. After the fall of Vicina, Brăila became the main harbour of Wallachia and gained town status around 1400. Foreign merchants had to unload their goods there.

In 1462 the fleet of Mehmed the Conqueror, 25 triremes and 150 other ships, burned it to the ground, and the Moldavians under Stephen the Great destroyed it in a campaign against the Wallachian prince Radu the Fair. Bogdan III of Moldavia burned it again in 1512, yet it recovered each time as the gateway for Levantine goods into Wallachia. Around 1538 to 1540 it passed to the Ottoman Empire, which built a stone stronghold there. Michael the Brave of Wallachia held it briefly in 1595 and 1596.

A Wallachian-Russian army conquered it in 1711 during the Pruth River Campaign, and the siege of 1828 preceded its award to Wallachia by the Treaty of Adrianople in 1829. In the 19th century it was one of the three most important Danube ports of Wallachia, and its prosperity peaked at the end of that century and the start of the next.

Brăila is the capital of Brăila County in Muntenia, eastern Romania, and a port on the Danube accessible to small and medium-sized oceangoing ships, with large grain-handling and warehousing facilities. Streets radiating from the port are crossed by concentric streets that follow the geometry of the old Ottoman fortifications. Landmarks include the Greek Church of 1863 to 1872 and the Church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel, a former mosque and the oldest church in the city.
braille: Braille was based on a tactile code now known as night writing, developed by Charles Barbier, in which sets of 12 embossed dots encoded 36 sounds. Louis Braille found three defects in it: the symbols stood for sounds, not letters, so the code could not render spelling; the 12-dot symbols did not fit beneath the pad of the reading finger; and there were no symbols for numerals or punctuation.

His solution was a cell of six dots with a specific pattern for each letter of the alphabet, with numerals and punctuation added. He developed it in 1824 and published it in 1829, later with musical notation. The second revision, published in 1837, was the first binary form of writing developed in the modern era.

A braille cell has six raised dots in two columns of three, numbered one to six. There are 64 possible combinations, including no dots at all for a space. In the original French system the patterns followed the order of the French alphabet of the time, and the first ten letters, a to j, use the upper four dot positions and also stand for the digits 1 to 9 and 0. Braille is an independent writing system for blind readers, and the mappings vary from language to language. English braille has an uncontracted level and a contracted level that uses abbreviations to save space. Extended to eight dots, the cell can encode every printable ASCII character.

Braille can be written by hand with a slate and stylus, each dot made from the back of the page in mirror image, or on a braille typewriter. The first typewriter to gain general acceptance was invented by Frank Haven Hall of the Illinois School for the Blind and presented in 1892. Henry Stainsby developed his Brailler in 1903, and in 1951 David Abraham of the Perkins School for the Blind produced the Perkins Brailler. Braille is read on embossed paper and on refreshable displays whose pins rise and fall to form the symbols. World Braille Day is observed on 4 January, to commemorate Louis Braille's birth, and the United Nations has recognised it since 2019.
brandenburg: Brandenburg lies in northeastern Germany and surrounds Berlin. It borders Poland and the states of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Saxony, and the Oder forms part of its eastern border. Its main rivers are the Spree and the Havel. The name comes from the town of Brandenburg an der Havel, and its origin is unclear: it is thought to derive from the Slavic branyi, marshy, or the Germanic branda, fire. In the extinct local language Polabian the town was called Branibor.

By the 7th century Slavic peoples are believed to have settled the area, the two principal groups being the Hevelli in the west and the Sprevane in the east. From the early 10th century Henry the Fowler and his successors conquered territory up to the Oder, and in 948 Emperor Otto I established margraves over the pagan Slavs there. A great uprising of the Wends drove the imperial forces out in 983. In 1134 Emperor Lothar III granted the Northern March to Albert the Bear, who inherited the town of Brandenburg and the lands of the Hevelli from Pribislav in 1150 and proclaimed himself ruler of the new Margraviate of Brandenburg.

The Ascanian line ended in 1320, and from 1323 to 1415 Brandenburg was under the Wittelsbachs of Bavaria, under whom its margrave gained the status of prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1415 Emperor Sigismund granted the Electorate to the House of Hohenzollern, which ruled until the end of the First World War and made Berlin its capital. Brandenburg converted to Protestantism in 1539, and the Hohenzollerns acquired the Duchy of Prussia in 1618, forming Brandenburg-Prussia.

The Great Elector, Frederick William, rebuilt and consolidated the state after the Thirty Years' War, and in 1701 his son took the title King in Prussia as Frederick I. Brandenburg remained the core of the Kingdom of Prussia and, from 1815 to 1947, was a province of Prussia. After the Second World War the lands east of the Oder–Neisse line were ceded to Poland. East Germany dissolved the state in 1952, and it was re-established in the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.

Brandenburg is a landlocked state of Germany with Potsdam as its capital and about 2.5 million residents. Other major towns are Cottbus, Brandenburg an der Havel and Frankfurt (Oder). In the southeast, part of the historical Lower Lusatia has two official languages, German and Lower Sorbian. A proposal to unify Berlin and Brandenburg was rejected in a referendum in 1996, and the two states still cooperate on many matters.
brandenburg-an-der-havel: Brandenburg an der Havel lies on the banks of the River Havel, which is navigable here as a European Waterway. The name combines two Slavic words, braniti, to protect or defend, and bor, forest or wood. The town gave its name to the medieval Bishopric of Brandenburg, the Margraviate of Brandenburg and the present German state, and it was the original nucleus of the realms of Brandenburg and Prussia. It was capital of the Margraviate until Berlin replaced it in 1417.

Brenna was a Slavic fort, conquered in 929 after the Battle of Lenzen by King Henry the Fowler of Saxony, and first mentioned in documents then as Brennaburg. At the Magdeburg Assembly of Princes in 948 the bishoprics of Brandenburg and Havelburg were established under the control of Otto I. A major Slavic uprising in 983 returned the area east of the Elbe to Slavic chiefs of the Hevelli until the middle of the 12th century. The last of them, Pribislav, died in 1150.

His widow Petrissa enabled Albert I of Brandenburg to take over Brenna. Jaksa of Kopanica drove him out, and he returned in 1157 after a long siege, by agreement and with a joint German and Slav garrison, and styled himself Margrave of Brandenburg. By 1160 nobles, burghers and peasants from the Harz, the Netherlands, the Rhineland and Westphalia were settling the Elbe, Havel and Spree basin. The foundation stone of a cathedral was laid on the cathedral island in 1165, and it was consecrated five years later. In 1314–1315 the Old and New Towns joined the Hanseatic League. Plundering and destruction in the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) led the court to leave. The two towns merged in 1715.

In the late 19th century the town became an industrial centre, making steel, toys and bicycles under brands such as Brennabor. In 1933–1934 one of the first Nazi concentration camps stood here. The Brandenburg-Görden Prison later became a euthanasia centre where the Nazis murdered people with psychiatric disorders, including children, in Action T4, and it was one of the first places where they experimented with killing by gas. Heavy bombing, partly because of the Arado aircraft factory, destroyed 70 percent of the city by 1945.

The Dominsel, the cathedral island, is its historic heart, with the Cathedral of St Peter and Paul, begun in the Romanesque style in 1165 and completed as a Gothic cathedral in the 14th century; the Wagner organ of 1725 is one of the best-known Baroque organs in Germany. Other sights are the brick Gothic Katharinenkirche of 1401, the Old Town Hall with its statue of the knight Roland of 1474, and parts of the medieval wall with four watchtowers.
brandenburg-prussia: The Margraviate of Brandenburg had been the seat of the main branch of the Hohenzollerns, prince-electors in the Holy Roman Empire, since 1415. In 1525 the Treaty of Krakow created the Duchy of Prussia through partial secularization of the State of the Teutonic Order, a vassal of the Kingdom of Poland governed by Duke Albert of Prussia, of a cadet branch of the Hohenzollerns. In 1563 the Brandenburg branch was granted the right of succession by the Polish crown, and it secured the duchy when the Prussian line died out in the male line in 1618. Intermarriage had also brought the lower Rhenish principalities of Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg after the Treaty of Xanten in 1614.

The Thirty Years' War was especially devastating. The elector George William, who ruled from 1619 to 1640, was forced by Wallenstein's army to join the Catholic-Imperial camp in 1627, and later by Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden to grant Sweden transit rights. Protestant and Catholic armies swept the land back and forth. In Brandenburg the war destroyed 60 towns, 48 castles and about 5,000 villages, and an average of 50 per cent of the population died. By the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 Brandenburg gained Minden and Halberstadt and the succession in Farther Pomerania.

Frederick William, known as the Great Elector, ruled from 1640 to 1688. Convinced by the war that the state needed a standing army financed independently of the estates, he won the consent of the estates in a landtag decree of 26 July 1653. During the Second Northern War the Treaty of Labiau in November 1656 conceded him full sovereignty in Ducal Prussia, confirmed by the Treaty of Bromberg in 1657. He won the Battle of Fehrbellin in 1675 and welcomed settlers from across Europe: the Edict of Potsdam attracted more than 15,000 Huguenots. He also founded a navy and, through Benjamin Raule, a colony called Großfriedrichsburg on the Guinea coast and one at Arguin.

In 1701 Frederick III, Elector of Brandenburg, succeeded in raising himself to King in Prussia. This was possible because the Duchy of Prussia lay outside the Holy Roman Empire, and the Habsburgs and other European royals approved as they formed alliances for the War of the Spanish Succession and the Great Northern War. From then on the Hohenzollern domains were called the Kingdom of Prussia. Legally the personal union of Brandenburg and Prussia lasted until the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, but after 1701 Brandenburg was in practice treated as part of the kingdom. Frederick and his successors went on to centralize and expand the state.
braniewo: Braniewo lies on the Pasłęka River about 5 km from the Vistula Lagoon, some 35 km north-east of Elbląg and 55 km south-west of Kaliningrad. The Polish border with the Kaliningrad Oblast is 6 km to the north. The German geographer Johann Friedrich Goldbeck derived the older name Brunsberg from Bruno von Schauenburg, bishop of Olomouc, who accompanied King Ottokar II of Bohemia on the crusade of the Teutonic Knights against the Old Prussians in 1254 and 1267. Another suggestion, Brusebergue, camp of the Prussians, is not documented.

In 1243 the Teutonic Order gave the settlement and the surrounding region of Warmia to the newly created Bishopric of Warmia, and the bishop built his cathedral there. The town received privileges on the model of Lübeck in 1254, was destroyed and depopulated in 1261 during the second Prussian Uprising, and was rebuilt in a new place in 1273 with colonists from Lübeck. Bishop Heinrich Fleming (1278–1300) moved the chapter to Frauenburg, now Frombork. A Franciscan abbey followed in 1296 and a new town in 1342. As a member of the Hanseatic League until 1608 the town traded with England, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands and Livonia.

In 1440 it was a founding member of the Prussian Confederation against Teutonic rule, and in 1454 King Casimir IV Jagiellon incorporated the territory into Poland. The Teutonic Knights renounced their claims in the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. After 1525 many residents turned Lutheran, but in 1526 the town was returned to Prince-Bishop Mauritius Ferber and Warmia stayed predominantly Catholic. Prince-Bishop Stanislaus Hosius brought in the Jesuits and founded the Collegium Hosianum, and a priestly seminary was added in 1564. Among its students were Andrew Bobola and the Latin poet Maciej Kazimierz Sarbiewski. The Swedes looted its library, which held works of Nicolaus Copernicus, in 1626.

Prussia annexed Braunsberg in 1772 in the First Partition of Poland and made it part of East Prussia. The Jesuit college became the State Academy of Braunsberg in 1912, and before the Second World War the town had more than 21,000 inhabitants. Soviet troops captured it on 20 March 1945; about 80 percent of the town was destroyed, and it was handed to Polish authorities on 7 July. Polish settlers, many from eastern Poland annexed by the Soviet Union, repopulated it.

Braniewo is the capital of Braniewo County in the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship, with 16,907 inhabitants in 2021, and the second largest town in Warmia after Olsztyn. The Gothic St Catherine Church, built in 1346 and destroyed in 1945, was rebuilt after 1979 and declared a Basilica Minor in 2001. Local brewing dates back to the 16th century.
brasilia: Brasília sits at an elevation of 1,000 metres on the Brazilian Highlands in the Central-West region of Brazil. Paranoá Lake, a large artificial lake, was built to increase the available water and to maintain the region's humidity. The name comes from the Latin translation of Brazil, suggested for the country's capital in 1821 by José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva.

Brazil's first capital was Salvador, and in 1763 Rio de Janeiro became the capital and remained so until 1960. Resources tended to be concentrated in the southeast, and most of the population lived near the Atlantic coast. A geographically central capital would be more regionally neutral. The idea of moving the capital was conceived in 1827 by José Bonifácio, an adviser to Emperor Pedro I, who presented a plan to the General Assembly for a new city called Brasília, to the west of the heavily populated southeastern corridor. It was to stand upstream on the São Francisco River rather than in the region of Goiás chosen later. The bill was not enacted because Pedro I dissolved the Assembly.

According to a legend, the Italian saint Don Bosco dreamed in 1883 of a futuristic city that roughly fitted Brasília's location, and many references to him, including a church parish, are found in the city today. After the Proclamation of the Republic, the third article of the 1891 Constitution stated that the Union would own, in the central plateau, an area of 14,400 square kilometres, to be demarcated to establish the future federal capital.

The city was developed in 1956 by Lúcio Costa, Oscar Niemeyer and Joaquim Cardozo, in a scheme to move the capital from Rio de Janeiro to a more central location chosen through a committee, with Roberto Burle Marx as landscape architect. President Juscelino Kubitschek founded it on 21 April 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Brasília is the capital of Brazil and of the Federal District, and all three branches of the federal government sit there. It is laid out in the shape of an airplane: the fuselage is the Monumental Axis, a pair of wide avenues flanking a large park, and the cockpit is the Praça dos Três Poderes. Its white modern architecture is by Oscar Niemeyer. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist architecture and urban planning. It is an administrative region rather than a municipality, and the Federal District is divided into 35 administrative regions.
bratislava: Bratislava lies in southwestern Slovakia at the foot of the Little Carpathians, on both banks of the Danube and the left bank of the Morava. It is on the border of Slovakia, Austria and Hungary, the only national capital with land borders with two other sovereign states, and only 60 kilometres from Vienna. The Danube, along which the city developed, was for centuries the chief transportation route.

The first known permanent settlement began with the Linear Pottery Culture around 5000 BCE. About 200 BCE the Celtic Boii tribe founded the first significant settlement, a fortified town known as the Bratislava oppidum, and established a mint that produced gold and silver coins known as biatecs. From the 1st to the 4th century CE the area fell under Roman influence as part of the Danubian Limes, a border defence system. The Romans introduced grape growing.

The Slavs arrived from the east between the 5th and 6th centuries. In response to attacks by the Avars, local Slavic tribes rebelled and established Samo's Empire (623-658), the first known Slavic political entity. In the 9th century the castles at Bratislava (Brezalauspurk) and Devín (Dowina) were important centres of the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia. The medieval settlement Brezalauspurc, meaning Braslav's castle, was first mentioned in 907, but its actual location is under scholarly debate. The name Pozsony first appears in 1002.

From 1536 to 1783 the city was the coronation site, legislative centre and capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, and eleven Hungarian kings and eight queens were crowned in St Martin's Cathedral. Most Hungarian parliament assemblies were held there from the 17th century until the Hungarian Reform Era. The Diet used the University Library building, erected in 1756, from 1802 to 1848, and much significant legislation of the Reform Era, such as the abolition of serfdom and the foundation of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, was enacted there.

Bratislava is the capital and largest city of Slovakia and the seat of the president, parliament and government. The Old Town holds most historical buildings, among them the Town Hall, built in the 14th and 15th centuries, and Michael's Gate, the only gate preserved from the medieval fortifications. The Grassalkovich Palace, built around 1760, is the president's residence. Its history was shaped by Austrians, Bulgarians, Croats, Czechs, Germans, Hungarians, Jews and Slovaks.
braunfels: Braunfels lies in the Lahn-Dill-Kreis in Hesse, on the German Timber-Frame Road. The climatic spa stands about 100 metres above the Lahn valley, 9 km south-west of Wetzlar and 28 km north-east of Limburg an der Lahn. Besides the main town, the municipality includes the villages of Altenkirchen, Bonbaden, Neukirchen, Philippstein and Tiefenbach, which joined it in 1972. Bonbaden was first documented in 772, making it one of the oldest inhabited places in the district.

The town and the seat of the district were first mentioned in 1246, and Braunfels has had town rights since 1607. The castle grew from one built in the 13th century by the Counts of Nassau, and from about 1260 it served as the residence of the noble family of Solms-Braunfels. After the Rhenish League of Towns destroyed Solms Castle in 1384, Braunfels Castle became the seat of the Counts of Solms.

The castle was altered many times in its history of more than 750 years. A fire in 1679 destroyed much of both town and castle. The castle was rebuilt as a Baroque residence, and the town was given a regular marketplace, which still lies in front of the town wall. Beginning in 1880 the castle was remodelled in neo-Gothic style to plans by the builder Edwin Oppler, which gave it its present appearance.

Braunfels Castle holds works by Dutch masters, including van Eyck, and by the Hessian Tischbein family of painters, as well as parts of the Altenberg Altar and Saint Elizabeth's ring. The town has a Princely Family Museum, a local history museum in a former mill and the ruins of Burg Philippstein. Among its people are Amalia of Solms-Braunfels, wife of Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, and Karl of Solms-Braunfels, founder of New Braunfels, Texas, with which the town is partnered.
brazil: Brazil covers 8,515,767 square kilometres, nearly half of the land area of South America (47.7%), and borders every South American country except Ecuador and Chile. Its Atlantic coastline is 7,491 kilometres long. The country contains most of the Amazon basin, with the world's largest river system and most extensive tropical forest, together with wetlands, savannas, plateaus and low mountains. It is the only country that both the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn cross, and it spans four time zones. Most of its territory is tropical, with equatorial rainforest in the north, semiarid land in the northeast and temperate forest in the south.

Human remains found at Pedro Leopoldo, in Minas Gerais, show habitation going back at least 11,000 years, and the earliest pottery found in the Western Hemisphere, near Santarém, was dated to over 8,000 years ago. The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó from 400 to 1400 CE. When the Portuguese arrived, the territory had an estimated Indigenous population of 7 million people, mostly semi-nomadic, among them the Tupis, Guaranis and Gês.

The land was claimed for Portugal on 22 April 1500 by the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral, after the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494. São Vicente was founded in 1532, and in 1534 King John III of Portugal divided the territory into fifteen private captaincies. The system failed, and in 1549 the king created the Governorate General of Brazil at Salvador. In the first two centuries Indigenous and European groups lived in constant war, forming opportunistic alliances.

Brazil became a united kingdom with Portugal in 1815, after the Portuguese court moved to Rio de Janeiro. Prince Pedro of Braganza declared independence in 1822 and founded the Empire of Brazil after a war with Portugal. The constitution of 1824 set up a bicameral legislature, and slavery was gradually abolished until its final abolition in 1888. A military coup in 1889 made the country a presidential republic. A revolution in 1930 brought Getúlio Vargas to power, and his self-coup of 1937 began the authoritarian Estado Novo. Democracy returned after 1945, a military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, and the present constitution dates from 1988.

Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District, which holds the capital, Brasília; São Paulo is the most populous city. The 2022 census counted 203 million people, and 45.3% described themselves as Pardo, 43.5% as White, 10.2% as Black and 0.6% as Indigenous. Its culture derives mainly from Portuguese culture, shaped also by African, Indigenous and other European traditions and by Italians, Germans, Japanese, Jewish and Arab immigrants in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
brazilian-empire: Portugal claimed the territory of Brazil on 22 April 1500, when Pedro Álvares Cabral landed on its coast. In 1808 Napoleon's army invaded Portugal and forced the royal House of Braganza into exile. The Prince regent, later King John VI, established his government in Rio de Janeiro, which became the seat of the Portuguese Empire. When John VI returned to Portugal he left his eldest son Pedro to rule the Kingdom of Brazil as regent. On 7 September 1822 Pedro declared Brazil independent and, after a war against his father's kingdom, was acclaimed Emperor Pedro I on 12 October.

Pedro I clashed with a sizeable parliamentary faction over the role of the monarch. The unsuccessful Cisplatine War ended in 1828 with the secession of Cisplatina, later Uruguay. He also became king of Portugal in 1826, and, unable to handle both countries, abdicated the Brazilian throne on 7 April 1831 and left for Europe. His five-year-old son Pedro II succeeded under a weak regency, and the lack of a ruling monarch to arbitrate led to regional civil wars. By 1846 Pedro II had matured and taken control, and he called the conservatives to form a government in 1848.

From the 1850s Brazil enjoyed stability and prosperity, with railways, the electric telegraph and steamship lines. The Brazilian victories in the Platine War, the Uruguayan War and the Paraguayan War, which ended in 1870, marked a golden age. Slavery was restricted by successive laws and abolished by the Golden Law, signed by Princess Isabel on 13 May 1888. Its end ended the belief of the ultraconservatives, backed by powerful coffee farmers, in the crown's neutrality, and they shifted to republicanism. Historians attribute the main responsibility for the fall of the monarchy to Pedro II, who grew indifferent to its fate. After a 58-year reign he was overthrown in a military coup on 15 November 1889.

The Constitution of 1824 created legislative, moderating, executive and judicial branches. The emperor headed the moderating and executive branches but had few ways of imposing his will on the General Assembly, apart from dissolving it. Catholicism was the state religion, and the emperor controlled church affairs. Slaves made up 29 per cent of the population in 1823 and fewer than 5 per cent by 1887. By 1889 Brazil had 9,200 km of railway track. Noble titles were not hereditary, except for the imperial family.
brazilian-national-anthem: From the proclamation of independence in 1822 until the abdication of Pedro I in 1831, the national anthem was one composed by Pedro I himself, which remains an official patriotic song as the Independence Anthem. After the abdication its popularity fell, and Francisco Manuel da Silva presented his own composition. The date on which he wrote the music is disputed: some historians place it in 1822, others in early 1823, and others hold that it was written in 1831. The music is a patriotic march reminiscent of Gioachino Rossini. The date of its first public performance, 13 April 1831, is now the Day of the Brazilian National Anthem.

The music was first given words by the appeals judge Ovídio Saraiva de Carvalho e Silva, as a hymn commemorating Pedro I's abdication, known as the April 7 Hymn. Those words were thought poor and offensive to the Portuguese and fell out of use, but by 1837 the melody was played without words at all public ceremonies. A new text of 1841 was also abandoned, and Pedro II ordered that the music be played without lyrics whenever he appeared in public.

After the Proclamation of the Republic in 1889 a contest chose a new anthem by Leopoldo Miguez, but after protests Deodoro da Fonseca confirmed Francisco Manuel da Silva's music as the national anthem by a decree of 20 January 1890.

For three decades of the republic the anthem had no official words, and several texts were adopted in different states. The lyrics of Joaquim Osório Duque Estrada, first proposed in 1909, were adapted and made official by a decree of President Epitácio Pessoa on 6 September 1922, during the centennial of independence. The government bought the rights to the text. The lyrics have been described as Parnassian in style and Romantic in content.
brazzaville: Brazzaville lies on the north bank of the Congo River just below Pool Malebo, about 506 km inland from the Atlantic Ocean and at an altitude of 317 m. Directly across the river stands Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and this is the only place in the world where two national capitals developed on opposite banks of a river within sight of each other. Downriver the Congo has numerous rapids, called Livingstone Falls, which prevent navigation from the Atlantic to the city. The name honours the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, born in Italy, who became a French citizen in 1874.

Before colonial rule the site held two trading centres, Mfwa and Mpila, which belonged to the Tio Kingdom. Brazza officially founded the settlement on 10 September 1880, on the existing Bateke settlement of Ncuna. The Tio king Iloo I signed a treaty of protection that placed his lands under French authority, and from October 1880 until May 1882 a small force led by Sergeant Malamine Camara occupied the site to keep it out of Belgian hands. The Berlin Conference of 1884 confirmed French control. The city became the capital of the French Congo in 1904 and remained capital when French Equatorial Africa was formed in 1910 as a federation that included Gabon, the Central African Republic and Chad.

The Congo-Ocean Railway, opened in 1934, linked Brazzaville with the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire and bypassed the rapids; its construction cost the lives of more than 17,000 Africans. During World War II the city served as the capital of Free France. In 1944 it hosted a meeting of French resistance leaders and representatives of France's African colonies, whose Brazzaville Declaration tried to redefine the relationship between France and its colonies.

Brazzaville is the capital and largest city of the Republic of the Congo, with a population of about 2.15 million at the 2023 census. It is both a department and a commune, divided into nine arrondissements. Its port receives raw materials such as rubber, wood and agricultural products, which are sent on to Pointe-Noire for export, and the World Health Organization has its regional office for Africa there. The Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza Mausoleum and the Poto-Poto School of Painting are among its landmarks, and UNESCO named it a City of Music in 2013.
breda: Breda lies in the southern Netherlands, equidistant from Rotterdam and Antwerp. The name derives from brede Aa, the wide Aa, and refers to the confluence of the rivers Mark and Aa. As a fortified city it was of strategic military and political significance. Although a direct fiefdom of the Holy Roman Emperor, the city obtained a municipal charter, and its acquisition through marriage by the House of Nassau placed it at the centre of political and social life in the Low Countries.

In the 11th century Breda was a direct fief of the Holy Roman Emperor, and its earliest known lord was Henry of Brunesheim, who held it from 1080 to 1125. The first mention of Breda in the historical record dates from 1125, when Engelbertus van Breda witnessed a document. The city obtained a municipal charter in 1252, which gave it the right to build fortifications, and it built brick walls and Roman-style gates.

Its acquisition by the House of Orange-Nassau made it a residence city, and the presence of the family attracted other nobles, who built palaces in the old quarters. The most impressive, built by the Italian architect Thomas Vincidor de Bologna for the first Dutch prince, was the first Renaissance-style palace north of the Alps. In the 15th century a great church in Brabantine Gothic style was built, with a tower 97 metres high, called the Grote Kerk or the Church of Our Lady. In 1534 Henry III of Nassau-Breda rebuilt the modest medieval fortifications in impressive style.

During the Cromwellian Commonwealth and Protectorate the exiled Charles II of England stayed in Breda for a little over a month, thanks to the nearness of his sister Mary, Princess Royal and Princess of Orange. His Declaration of Breda of 1660 announced his conditions for accepting the crown of England. The Treaty of Breda, signed on 31 July 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War. Between 1746 and 1748 Breda hosted the Congress of Breda, talks between Britain and France that led to the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

Breda is a city and municipality in the province of North Brabant, the tenth largest in the Netherlands. Historically its economy was mainly industrial and it was a centre of the food and drink industry, with companies such as Hero, Van Melle, De Faam and Kwatta. It also housed the largest brewery in the Netherlands, Oranjeboom. Since 1970 it has become a city of education and students.
bregenz: Bregenz lies on the east and southeast shores of Lake Constance, the third-largest freshwater lake in Central Europe, between Switzerland to the west and Germany to the northwest, with the large forests of the Bregenzerwald to the east. It stands on a plateau falling in a series of terraces to the lake at the foot of the Pfänder mountain. It is a junction of the arterial roads from the Rhine valley to the German Alpine foothills, and cruise ships run on the lake. Vorarlberg, of which it is the capital, is the westernmost state of Austria.

The first settlements date from about 1500 BCE. Strabo mentions the Brigantii as a Celtic sub-tribe of this region of the Alps, and in the 5th century BCE the Celts settled at Brigantion, one of their most heavily fortified places. After a series of battles in 15 BCE the Romans conquered it and it became a Roman camp, and around 50 CE it was made a municipality, Brigantium. It was the seat of the Roman admiralty for Lake Constance and had a theatre. The Alemanni destroyed it in 259/60 and settled the area around 450. Saint Columbanus and Saint Gall worked there as missionaries from 610 to 612.

From 917 the castle was the residence of the Udalrichinger, the ruling dynasty of Vorarlberg, who called themselves Counts of Bregenz; the house died out around 1150. Around 1170 Hugo of Tübingen, called Montfort, founded a town settlement, first documented in 1249. The city was sold to the Habsburgs in 1451 and again in 1523 and stayed under Austrian rule, apart from a brief occupation by Swedish forces under Carl Gustaf Wrangel in the 30 Years' War, until the 19th century. The Swedes destroyed the fortress of Hohenbregenz on the Gebhardsberg in 1647. Bregenz was under Bavarian rule from 1805 to 1814, and since 1726 it has been the main seat of Austrian administration in Vorarlberg.

The harbour on Lake Constance was built from 1842 to 1850, Austrian ship service began in 1884, and railway services have existed since 1872. The Allies bombed the town in 1945, destroying 72 houses, and French troops set up the military government in April and May of that year. The Bregenz Festival, with the Vienna Symphony Orchestra, began in 1946 and is held every summer, with a stage floating on the lake. The upper town keeps remains of its walls, the old town hall of 1662 and Martin's Tower, originally built by the Romans, whose Baroque steeple is the largest bulb-shaped one in Central Europe. The Kunsthaus Bregenz, a modern art museum, was built from 1991 to 1997.
bremen: Bremen is the largest city on the River Weser, about 60 kilometres upstream from its mouth into the North Sea at Bremerhaven, and is completely surrounded by the state of Lower Saxony. The oldest part of the Altstadt, the Old Town, is an oval bounded by the Weser and by the Wallgraben, the former moats of the medieval city walls. It begins at the Marktplatz and ends at the Schnoor quarter.

The city traces its origins to a settlement of the early Middle Ages and became the seat of a bishopric in 787. In the High Middle Ages it grew into a trading centre and joined the Hanseatic League in the 13th century. For most of its 1,200-year history Bremen was an independent city within the Holy Roman Empire, governed by merchants and guilds.

To confirm its independence it had to contend, until the Reformation, with the temporal power of the Church, and after the Thirty Years' War with Sweden, which ruled the surrounding Duchy of Bremen-Verden. George I Louis, Elector of Hannover and from 1714 King of Great Britain and Ireland, acquired Bremen-Verden in 1715 and recognised Bremen as a free city in 1720. The city was captured in 1806, annexed by France in 1810 and regained independence in 1815.

In the late 19th century Prussia drew Bremen into the German Empire. With its new anchorage and wharves at Bremerhaven it became the principal port of embarkation for German and central European emigrants to the Americas. The Norddeutscher Lloyd, founded there in 1857, became one of the world's leading shipping companies. After the First World War Bremen was briefly a Soviet republic, and it lost its autonomy under the Hitler regime. Almost two thirds of the city's fabric was destroyed in the Second World War. Its autonomy was restored, and it became one of the founding states of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Bremen is the capital and most populous city of the state of the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen, which consists of the city and Bremerhaven, with about 586,000 inhabitants. Its Town Hall, built between 1405 and 1410 in Gothic style with a Renaissance façade of 1609–12, and the Bremen Roland, a statue of 1404, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in July 2004. St Peter's Cathedral dates from the 13th century and the Liebfrauenkirche, the oldest church in the town, from the 11th. The city is also known for the Brothers Grimm fairy tale of the Town Musicians of Bremen.
bremerhaven: Bremerhaven lies on the east bank of the Weser estuary in northern Germany, and the River Geeste flows through it before reaching the Weser. Neighbouring villages such as Lehe existed by the 12th century, and Geestendorf is mentioned in documents of the ninth century, on small islands in a swampy estuary. In 1381 Bremen established de facto rule over the lower Weser, including Lehe, later called Bremerlehe. Swedish troops of Bremen-Verden captured it in 1653, and Bremen ceded it in the peace of November 1654 that followed the First Bremian War. In 1672 colonists tried unsuccessfully to build a castle there, Carlsburg, to control shipping bound for Bremen.

In 1827 Bremen, under Bürgermeister Johann Smidt, bought the territory at the Weser's mouth from the Kingdom of Hanover. Bremen sought it to keep its share of overseas trade, which silting of the river threatened. Bremerhaven was founded as a second harbour 50 km downstream, and trade with North America and emigration made it grow quickly. In 1848 it became the home port of the German Confederation's navy under Karl Rudolf Brommy. Hanover founded a rival town, Geestemünde, in 1845. In 1924 Geestemünde and Lehe united as Wesermünde, and in 1939 Bremerhaven, apart from its overseas port, was joined to it.

As a North Sea base of the Kriegsmarine, the city lost 79% of its buildings in Allied bombing, and the raid of 18 September 1944 left the inner city largely destroyed. Key parts of the port were deliberately spared. After the war Wesermünde was an enclave run by the United States within the British zone. In 1947 it became part of the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen and took the name Bremerhaven.

Bremerhaven is a city in its own right and also part of the two-city state of Bremen. It remains one of the busiest ports in Germany, with a large container terminal and Europe's largest car transshipment centre. Its centre was largely rebuilt after the war. The German Emigration Center and the German Maritime Museum, designed by Hans Scharoun, record its seafaring past, and the Alfred Wegener Institute, a national research institute for maritime and climate science, is based there.
bremervorde: Bremervörde lies on the Oste river in the north of the district of Rotenburg in Lower Saxony. It stands near the centre of the triangle formed by the Weser and the Elbe, roughly equidistant from Hamburg, Bremen and Cuxhaven. By 1111 the Saxon Duke Lothair of Supplinburg, later king of the Holy Roman Empire, had built the castle called Vörde at a ford of the Oste. The ford was important for the Oxen Way, an ancient trackway connecting Jutland with Westphalia.

Its position between the Elbe and the Weser made the place a matter of conflict for centuries. It came under Henry the Lion and then, in 1219, under the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen, for which it served as capital, with the archbishop's residence and seat of government. The Bremian Estates usually met elsewhere, and the cathedral chapter sat in the city of Bremen. Maurice of Oldenburg ruled the archbishopric from Vörde as administrator from 1345, and in 1362 he gave up after the castle was besieged by troops of Archbishop Albert II's brothers.

Later archbishops and administrators founded a hospital, extended the castle and built a chancery in 1608, which has housed a museum since 1960. The capital role gave the town the name Bremervörde from the mid-17th century. In 1648 the archbishopric became the Duchy of Bremen under the Swedish Crown, which moved the capital to Stade. The Danish-Norwegian king Frederick III bombed his former residence in 1657, and in 1682 the damaged castle and its church, a burial place of many archbishops, were demolished. The duchy passed to the House of Hanover after the Great Northern War and was abolished in 1823.

Bremervörde is a town in Lower Saxony. The Bachmann Museum, housed in the old chancery, covers regional archaeology, geology and history. The town is the end point of the Deutsche Fährstraße, a route connecting places between Bremervörde and Kiel that are linked with the history of ferries and river crossings.
bren-light-machine-gun: At the close of the First World War in 1918 the British Army had two main automatic weapons, the Vickers medium machine gun and the Lewis light machine gun. The Vickers was heavy and needed a supply of water to keep it firing, which tended to confine it to static defence and indirect fire support. The Lewis was lighter but prone to frequent stoppages, and its barrel could not be changed in the field, so sustained firing overheated it until it stopped altogether.

The Bren was a licensed version of the Czechoslovak ZGB 33, itself a modified version of the ZB vz. 26 that British Army officials tested in a firearms competition in the 1930s. Its designer was Václav Holek. The later Bren featured a distinctive top-mounted curved box magazine, a conical flash hider and a quick-change barrel. The first Bren guns were built at the Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield in September 1937.

In the British and Commonwealth armies the Bren was generally issued on a scale of one per rifle section. Each Universal Carrier of an infantry battalion's carrier platoon carried one, and the 66-man Assault Troop of the British Commandos had four on its nominal establishment. Seeking more firepower at section level, the army aimed at one Bren to every four private soldiers. Later it served in the Korean War, the Malayan Emergency, the Mau Mau Uprising and the Indonesia–Malaysia confrontation, where it was preferred to the heavier belt-fed L7 general-purpose machine gun.

Although the gun was well liked, each cost £40, and only 2,300 of the 30,000 Bren guns issued to the British Expeditionary Force came back to the United Kingdom after the defeat of France. The Mark II, approved in September 1940, simplified the sights, bipod and butt and cut the cost by 20 to 25 per cent. The Mark III, standardised in July 1944 and weighing 8.8 kg, was lightened for jungle warfare.

Enfield produced 220,000 Mark I guns. John Inglis and Company of Canada began production in 1940 and by the end of the war had made 186,000 of all variants, among them 43,000 in 7.92×57mm Mauser for the Chinese National Revolutionary Army. In the 1950s many Brens were re-barrelled for the 7.62×51mm NATO cartridge and fielded from 1955 as the L4, which stayed in British service into the 1990s.

The belt-fed L7 replaced the Bren as the section weapon, and in the 1980s the L86 Light Support Weapon supplemented it, leaving the Bren only as a pintle mount on some vehicles. Its last operational deployment with the British Army, on a limited scale, was in the Gulf War of 1991. Indian Ordnance Factories made a version until 2012.
brendan-the-navigator: Brendan was born in Tralee, in County Kerry, among the Altraige, a clan centred on Tralee Bay, to parents called Finnlug and Cara. Tradition places his birth on the north side of the bay. He was baptised at Tubrid, near Ardfert, by Erc of Slane. For five years he was educated and fostered by Saint Íte of Killeedy, called the Brigid of Munster, and at six he was sent to Jarlath's monastery school at Tuam.

He is counted among the Twelve Apostles of Ireland, said to have been taught by Finnian of Clonard. At 26 he was ordained a priest by Erc. His feast day is 16 May for Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox Christians.

Brendan founded a number of monasteries. His first voyage took him to the Aran Islands, where he founded one, and to Hinba in Argyll, where he is said to have met Columcille. The same voyage is said to have taken him on to Wales and Brittany. Between 512 and 530 he built monastic cells at Ardfert and at Shanakeel, at the foot of Mount Brandon.

Later he travelled to Wales and Iona. Returning to Ireland, he founded a monastery at Annaghdown, where he spent the rest of his life, and a convent there for his sister Briga. He also established the bishopric of Ardfert and founded a monastery at Inis-da-druim, now Coney Island, around 550.

Brendan is known chiefly for the Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis, a Latin narrative of the ninth century whose earliest surviving version dates from about 900. In it Brendan hears of the Promised Land of the Saints from Saint Barinthus and sets out in a hide-covered boat with a company of monks. They travel for seven years among islands, including a giant fish, Jasconius, which they mistake for an island, before they are admitted to the Promised Land and return to Ireland.

The Navigatio belongs to the Irish genre of the immram, a tale of seafaring adventures, and shares features with the Voyage of Máel Dúin. More than 100 manuscripts survive across Europe. An Anglo-Norman version, probably made around 1121 by a cleric called Benedeit, is the earliest surviving narrative text of Anglo-Norman literature. There is no reliable evidence that Brendan reached Greenland or the Americas, but medieval maps showed a Saint Brendan's Island in the Atlantic.
brenner-pass: The Brenner Pass, in German Brennerpass and in Italian Passo del Brennero, is a mountain pass that forms the border between Italy and Austria. It is one of the major passes of the Eastern Alps and has the lowest altitude among the Alpine passes of the area. A railway and a motorway cross it, linking Bolzano to the south with Innsbruck to the north. The name appears first in 1328, as ob dem Prenner, meaning above the Prenner, after a nearby farm. Older theories linking it to the Breuni or to the Gaulish chieftain Brennus are now considered unlikely.

The pass was in frequent use in prehistoric times, and the Romans regularised it. It was not the first Roman road across the Alps: the Via Claudia Augusta, completed in 46 to 47, linked Verona with Augusta Vindelicorum, now Augsburg, by way of the Reschen Pass. A Roman road over the Brenner itself did not exist until the 2nd century. The Alamanni crossed the pass southward in 268 and were stopped that November at the Battle of Lake Benacus. The Romans held it until the end of their empire in the 5th century.

In the High Middle Ages the pass lay on the Via Imperii, the imperial road linking the Kingdom of Germany with the Italian March of Verona. From the 12th century the Counts of Tyrol controlled it within the Holy Roman Empire, and Emperor Frederick Barbarossa often used it on his expeditions into Italy. A carriage road was laid out in 1777 at the behest of Empress Maria Theresa. The Brenner Railway, completed in stages from 1853 to 1867, was the first trans-Alpine railway without a major tunnel; Austria lost Lombardy and Venetia to Italy in 1859 and 1866.

After the First World War the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 1919 gave Italy the Trentino and South Tyrol, and the border was set at the pass.
