The river Senne, now almost completely covered, cuts the city from east to west, and the Sonian Forest rises on its southeastern side. The most common theory derives the name from the Old Dutch Bruocsella, meaning a settlement in the marsh. Saint Vindicianus, Bishop of Cambrai, made the first recorded reference to the place, as Brosella, in 695, when it was still a hamlet.

Lambert I, Count of Louvain, gained the County of Brussels around 1000 by marriage. The town stood on the Senne on an important trade route between Bruges, Ghent and Cologne, and became a commercial centre specialised in the textile trade. It grew to about 30,000 people, and the marshes were drained. In 1183 the Counts of Leuven became Dukes of Brabant, whose duchy was part of the Holy Roman Empire. After Charles the Bold of Burgundy died in 1477, his daughter Mary of Burgundy, born in Brussels, married Maximilian I, bringing the Low Countries under Habsburg rule, and Brussels flourished as the capital of the Burgundian Netherlands.

The Belgian Revolution began in Brussels in 1830 after a performance of Auber's opera La Muette de Portici at the Royal Theatre of La Monnaie. The city became the capital of the new nation, and Leopold I, the first King of the Belgians, took the throne on 21 July 1831. From 1871 many Paris Communards found asylum there, and Victor Hugo and Karl Marx were among earlier exiles. French gradually replaced Dutch as the main language. Brussels hosted world's fairs in 1910, 1935 and 1958.

The Brussels-Capital Region, formed on 18 June 1989 after a constitutional reform, is one of Belgium's three federated regions and an officially bilingual enclave within Flanders, with a population of over 1.2 million. The Belgian Constitution names the City of Brussels as the capital. Brussels is the de facto capital of the European Union and hosts NATO's headquarters. Its landmarks include the Grand-Place, Manneken Pis and the Atomium.
bryggen: Bryggen, meaning the dock, is also known as Tyskebryggen, the German dock. It is a series of Hanseatic commercial buildings on the eastern side of the Vågen harbour in Bergen. In the Middle Ages the area took in all the buildings between the sea and the road called Øvregaten, from Holmen in the north to Vågsbunnen in the south, and according to the sagas the city of Bergen was founded within it. One of the earliest pier constructions has been dated to around 1100.

In the 14th century a Kontor of the Hanseatic League was established at Bryggen. As Bergen developed into an important trading centre the wharfs were improved and the merchants of the Hanseatic League gradually took over the buildings. The warehouses stored goods, particularly stockfish from northern Norway and cereal from Europe. The Kontor's operations ended in 1754, when all the properties passed to Norwegian citizens.

Since most of Bergen's houses were wooden, the city suffered many fires. After one in 1702 damaged the Hanseatic buildings they were rebuilt, and about a quarter of what stands today dates from after that fire. Parts of Bryggen burned again in 1955. A thirteen-year archaeological excavation followed and revealed the everyday runic inscriptions known as the Bryggen inscriptions. The Bryggen museum was built in 1976 on part of the cleared site.

UNESCO listed Bryggen as a World Heritage Site in 1979 under criterion (iii), as a quarter of Hanseatic merchants that illustrates the use of space and dates back to the 14th century. Its notable houses include Bellgården, Svensgården, Enhjørningsgården, Bredsgården, Bugården and Engelgården, and the oldest and tallest building in the area is St Mary's Church. Bryggens Museum and the Hanseatic Museum are among those found there.
brzeg: Brzeg lies in Silesia, in the Opole Voivodeship of Poland, on the left bank of the Oder, between Opole to the east and Wrocław to the north-west. It stands on the Brzeg Plain, part of the Silesian Lowlands, whose fertile soil allowed early agriculture. The Latin name was Alta Ripa and the German Brieg; the name is derived from the Polish word brzeg, meaning shore, and older documents call it the city on the high banks of the Oder. Settlement in the area goes back to the Mesolithic, with the earliest signs between 8000 and 4200 BCE.

Around 990 Silesia was incorporated into the Poland of Mieszko I. Brzeg was first mentioned in 1234 as a trading and fishing settlement, and in 1248 the Silesian duke Henry III the White granted it Magdeburg town rights. It was fortified by the late 13th century. From the early 14th to the late 17th century it was ruled by the Piast dynasty as fiefs of the Bohemian Crown within the Holy Roman Empire, and in the 16th century it had a collegiate school and a municipal school, merged and then split again in 1529 and 1534. The Piast Gimnasium was founded in 1569.

Jews settled in Brieg about 1324 and lent money to the dukes. They were persecuted in the 14th century, an outbreak occurring in 1362, driven out in 1401, allowed to return in 1423 and expelled from the duchies of Brieg and Liegnitz in 1453 after the preaching of the Franciscan John Capistrano. After the Silesian Wars the town passed to Prussia, and it was part of Germany from 1871 to 1945. French forces captured it in 1807 and Napoleon's army pulled down its fortifications. In the census of 1905 it had 27,486 inhabitants, of whom 93% spoke German. After World War II, the German population was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement, and Poles resettled from the Kresy took their place.

Brzeg is the capital of Brzeg County and had 34,778 inhabitants in December 2021. Its old castle, referred to as the Silesian Wawel, houses the Muzeum Piastów Śląskich, and the Renaissance town hall stands on the market square among thirteenth-century townhouses. St. Nicholas's Church is Gothic, and the Odrzańska Gate survives from the old fortifications in a park that replaced them. Industry includes agricultural machinery, electric engines, sugar and confectionery.
bubastis: Bubastis, known in Egyptian as Per-Bast, the House of Bast, lay along the Nile in the Delta region of Lower Egypt and was the capital of its own nome, Am-Khent, the 18th of Lower Egypt. It stood on the Pelusiac branch of the Nile near the entrance to the Wadi Tumilat, which made it a hub for trade and for expeditions to the Sinai and the Levant. Its ruins are in the suburbs of the modern city of Zagazig. It is often identified with the biblical Pi-Beseth. The settlement began at the end of the 4th millennium BCE.

The cult of Bastet is known from the reign of Hotepsekhemwy in the Second Dynasty. In the Fourth Dynasty a governor's palace was built, and in the Sixth Dynasty there were two temples for the royal Ka of Teti and Pepi I. Middle Kingdom kings, among them Amenemhat I and Senusret III, contributed to the sanctuary, and in the Twelfth Dynasty a large palace for the governors was built. Ramesses II expanded the Temple of Bastet, and much of its red granite bears his cartouches; a colossal statue of his daughter-wife Meritamun is among the site's finds.

The city became a royal residence after Shoshenq I became pharaoh in 943 BCE and founded the Twenty-second Dynasty, and it was at its height under that dynasty and the 23rd. Near the city Necho II began, but never finished, the Canal of the Pharaohs between the Nile and the Red Sea. It declined after the conquest by Cambyses II in 525 BCE, when its walls were dismantled. Three Christian bishops of Bubastis are known from the 4th and 5th centuries.

Bastet was at first shown as a lioness and later became associated with the cat, and the tombs at Bubastis were the principal depository in Egypt of cat mummies. Greeks identified her with Artemis, and her oracle grew in popularity after Greek settlers came to the Delta. Herodotus called her festival the most joyous of the Egyptian calendar, with barges of pilgrims singing and playing music down the Nile, and said that as many as hundreds of thousands of pilgrims had attended; he also described the temple as surrounded by two canals and lined with trees.
Excavations include the discovery of the tomb of the vizier Iuty in 1964, a well preserved copy of the Decree of Canopus in 2004, and the German-Egyptian Tell Basta Project since 2008.
bucharest: Bucharest stands on the banks of the Dâmbovița River, which flows into the Argeș, a tributary of the Danube. Several lakes, the largest being Herăstrău, Floreasca, Tei and Colentina, lie across the northern parts of the city along the Colentina River. In the centre a small artificial lake is surrounded by the Cișmigiu Gardens, opened in 1847 to plans by the German architect Carl F. W. Meyer and long frequented by poets and writers.

The origin of the name București is unverified. Tradition links the founding with a man named Bucur, variously a prince, an outlaw, a fisherman, a shepherd or a hunter, and connects the name with the Romanian word bucurie, 'joy'. The Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi claimed it came from a certain Abu-Kariș, and an early 19th-century book derived it from a beech forest, Bukovie.

Bucharest was first mentioned in 1459 as the 'Citadel of București', when it was the residence of the ruler of Wallachia, Vlad the Impaler. The Old Princely Court was built by Mircea Ciobanul in the mid-16th century, and the city became the summer residence of the court. It competed with Târgoviște for the status of capital, as the Ottoman Empire, the suzerain power, increased the importance of southern Muntenia. After 1698, beginning with the reign of Constantin Brâncoveanu, it was the permanent seat of the Wallachian court. Natural disasters partly destroyed it several times in the following two centuries.

From the 18th century the Ottomans appointed Greek Christian administrators, the Phanariotes, to run the town, and their rule ended after the Wallachian uprising of 1821 led by Tudor Vladimirescu. Bucharest became the capital of the Romanian United Principalities in 1862 and boomed after the founding of the Romanian Kingdom in 1881, when it became known for cosmopolitan life and eclectic architecture and was nicknamed the Paris of the East. It was severely damaged in the Second World War. Its population grew rapidly from the late 19th century until the war, and again under Nicolae Ceaușescu from 1965 to 1989, when a massive urbanization campaign drew migrants from rural areas; it first reached one million in the 1940s.

Bucharest is the capital and largest city of Romania. It has a unique administrative status, being the only municipal area that is not part of a county, though its population of 1,716,961 at the 2021 census is larger than that of any county. Among its landmarks is the Palace of the Parliament, built in the 1980s under Ceaușescu and the largest parliament building in the world.
buchenwald-concentration-camp: The Schutzstaffel established Buchenwald at the beginning of July 1937 on the north slope of the Ettersberg, a hill in Thuringia. The proposed name Ettersberg was thought inappropriate because the hill was associated with Goethe, who had lived in Weimar, so the camp was named for the beech forest. The Holocaust researcher James E. Young wrote that SS leaders chose the site precisely to erase the cultural legacy of the area. The camp was designed for 8,000 prisoners, and nearby clay deposits could be made into bricks by forced labour. The first prisoners arrived on 15 July 1937. The main gate bore the motto Jedem das Seine, designed by the prisoner and Bauhaus architect Franz Ehrlich.

Many of the first internees were actual or suspected communists. Later prisoners came from all over Europe and the Soviet Union and included Jews, Poles and other Slavs, Roma, the disabled, political prisoners and prisoners of war. Karl-Otto Koch was commandant from 1 August 1937 to July 1941. From 1942 the SS used prisoner labour for armaments production, renting prisoners to private firms at 4 to 6 Reichsmarks a day, and conditions in the subcamps were worse than in the main camp.

Prisoners were deliberately kept starving, and many were worked to death. Others were shot or hanged or died in medical experiments; in 1942 and 1943, 729 inmates were used in typhus vaccine trials, and 154 died. At least 1,000 Soviet prisoners of war were shot in the back of the neck in 1941-42. The total of 56,545 deaths out of 280,000 prisoners includes 33,462 recorded by the SS, 8,483 shootings, an estimated 1,100 hangings and an estimated 13,500 deaths in evacuation transports.

On 8 April 1945 two prisoners, Gwidon Damazyn and Konstantin Ivanovich Leonov, sent a radio message to the American Third Army, which answered that it was rushing to their aid. American troops reached the camp on 11 April, and Edward R. Murrow broadcast his report on 12 April. From August 1945 to 1 March 1950 the Soviet authorities held former Nazis and anti-communist dissidents there as NKVD special camp Nr. 2 and destroyed much of the site on its closure. Today the site is a memorial with a museum, managed by the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation.
buckeburg: Bückeburg is a town in Lower Saxony, Germany, on the border with North Rhine Westphalia. It lies in the district of Schaumburg, close to the northern slopes of the Weserbergland ridge, and has a population of 21,030. Houses began to gather around the castle about 1365, and a city wall protected the town in the 17th century. In the 19th century it was connected to the Minden and Hanover Railway and housed a synagogue.

Bückeburg was the capital of the tiny principality of Schaumburg-Lippe until the German Revolution of 1918 to 1919. Schaumburg-Lippe then continued as an independent German state, a Free State, until 1946. The princely family surrendered political power in 1918 but still owns the palace and lives there.

The Town Church of Bückeburg was one of the first Lutheran churches built after the Reformation. It is known for its pulpit and especially for its ornately decorated bronze-cast font by the Dutch artist Adriaen de Vries. The court drew writers and musicians in the 18th century. The composer Johann Christoph Friedrich Bach, a son of J. S. Bach, worked at the court from before 1751 until his death in 1795, first as a harpsichordist and from 1759 as Konzertmeister, or director, of the court orchestra. He is buried in the churchyard of the town church. The poet Johann Gottfried Herder was the court's superintendent and chief preacher from 1771, and Bach set several of his texts.

Bückeburg was later a British garrison town, with residents who worked at the British Military Hospital in Rinteln or at the Prince Rupert School there. The number of British military residents fell significantly in the late 1990s, when the hospital closed.

Bückeburg Palace, whose history spans 700 years, with the most important contributions from the 16th, 17th and 19th centuries, was the residence of the Princes of Schaumburg-Lippe. Part of it is open to the public and it houses significant works of art and a notable library. The Princely Mausoleum in the palace grounds, built in 1915 in Neo-Romanic style and resembling the Roman Pantheon, is described as the world's largest private sepulchre still in use, and its cupola has a gold mosaic. The town is also home to a helicopter museum with 40 actual helicopters.
buda: Buda is the part of Budapest that lies on the western bank of the Danube. Historically the name referred only to the royal walled city on Castle Hill, which Béla IV constructed between 1247 and 1249 and which is now called the Várnegyed, or Castle Quarter. The name is also used loosely for the city's I, II, III, XI, XII and XXII districts, which include medieval Óbuda and cover a third of the city's area. A medieval legend derives the name from Bleda, called Buda in Hungarian, the brother of the Hunnic ruler Attila; an alternative derivation takes it from Aquincum, meaning place of water.

The fortress and palace that Béla IV built in 1247 were the nucleus around which the town grew, and in 1361 it became the capital of Hungary, which it remained until 1873. In 1432 Bertrandon de la Broquière wrote that Buda was governed by Germans in police and commerce, and noted a significant Jewish population. Buda had a German majority in the 15th century, though the royal treasury recorded a Hungarian majority in 1495.

From 1541 to 1686 Buda was part of Ottoman-ruled central Hungary and the capital of the province of Budin; by the middle of the 17th century it had a Muslim majority, largely through an influx of Balkan Muslims. In 1686, two years after an unsuccessful siege, a Holy League army of over 74,000 men from many European countries reconquered the city. Bourgeois families from southern Germany then moved into the almost deserted city, and Hungarians slowly became the majority during the 19th century. In 1873 Buda was united with Pest and Óbuda to form Budapest.

Buda's landmarks include the Royal Palace, Matthias Church, the Citadella, the Gellért Baths, the Buda Hills and Sándor Palace, the residence of the President of Hungary. Jadwiga of Poland, the first female monarch of the Kingdom of Poland, was born there around 1373.
budapest: Budapest stands on the River Danube, at the centre of the Pannonian Basin, on an ancient route linking the hills of Transdanubia with the Great Plain. The names Buda and Pest are of obscure origin. Buda was probably the name of the first constable of the fortress built on Castle Hill in the 11th century, or derives from a personal name of Turkic origin, Bod or Bud, meaning 'twig'. Before the unification of 1873 the towns together were sometimes called Pest-Buda. In colloquial Hungarian, Buda means the districts west of the Danube, including the former Óbuda, and Pest those to the east. The city is now divided into 23 districts.

The first settlement on the territory of Budapest was built by Celts before 1 CE and was later occupied by the Romans. The Roman settlement of Aquincum became the main city of Pannonia Inferior in 106 CE. It began as a military settlement, around which a city gradually rose, and its site corresponds to the Óbuda district. The Romans built roads, amphitheatres, baths and houses with heated floors. The area east of the Danube was outside the Roman Empire and remained Germanic and Sarmatian in character.

After the foundation of Hungary in the late 9th century the area was pillaged by the Mongols in 1241. It became the royal seat in 1361, and under Matthias Corvinus Buda was by the 15th century one of the European centres of Renaissance culture. The siege of Buda in 1541 was followed by nearly 150 years of Ottoman rule, and after the reconquest of Buda in 1686 the region entered an age of prosperity. The city was the focal point of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, the Battle of Budapest in 1945 and the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. In 1896 it opened the first underground transit line on the European continent, now the M1 Millennium Underground.

Budapest is the seat of the Hungarian national government, and the National Assembly sits in the neo-Gothic Hungarian Parliament, the largest building in the country. The historic centre along the Danube, with Buda Castle and the 13th-century Matthias Church, is a World Heritage Site, as are the Castle Hill, the Danube embankments and Andrássy út. Other landmarks include the State Opera House, St Stephen's Basilica, which displays the Holy Right Hand of Hungary's first king, and the Roman remains of the Aquincum Museum. The city has been a spa destination since Roman times, with more than 100 medicinal geothermal springs.
buddhas-of-bamiyan: Bamiyan lies on the Silk Road in the Hindu Kush, about 130 kilometres north-west of Kabul at an elevation of 2,500 metres. Since the 2nd century CE it had been a Buddhist religious site under the Kushans, a thriving centre of religion, philosophy and art. Monks lived as hermits in small caves cut into the cliffs, many decorating them with statues and frescoes in the culture of Gandhara. The two Buddhas were carved possibly around the 6th century, when the Hephthalites ruled the region as principalities.

The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited the site on 30 April 630. He described Bamyan as a flourishing Buddhist centre with more than ten monasteries and more than a thousand monks, and noted that both figures were decorated with gold and fine jewels.

The Buddhas were technically reliefs, since each merged at the back into the cliff wall. The smaller, 38 metres tall, was called Shah Mama, Queen Mother, and the larger, 55 metres tall, Salsal. The main bodies were hewn from the sandstone cliff, and the details were modelled in mud mixed with straw and coated with stucco, which was painted to enhance the faces, hands and folds of the robes. The larger statue was painted carmine red and the smaller in several colours. The sculptures show a later stage of the blended Greco-Buddhist style of Gandhara.

Numerous caves around the Buddhas were decorated with wall paintings. The ceiling above the smaller Buddha showed a solar deity in a golden chariot drawn by four horses, derived from the Iranian god Mithra as revered in Sogdia. The paintings combine Buddhist art, Gupta art from India, and influences from the Sasanian and Byzantine empires.

Bamiyan passed to Muslim rule in 770 and finally, in 977, under Turkic Ghaznavid rule. In 1221 Genghis Khan invaded the valley, wiping out most of its population, but left the Buddhas undamaged. In the 17th century the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb briefly ordered artillery used against the carvings, which survived without major harm. In July 1999 Mullah Omar decreed that the statues be preserved.

On 26 February 2001 Omar ordered the destruction of all statues in Afghanistan, and in March 2001 the Taliban destroyed both Buddhas, a decision justified by the Taliban as being in accordance with Islamic law. International and local opinion condemned it. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003 as an outstanding expression of Gandharan Buddhism. The outlines of the Buddhas remain recognisable in their niches.
buddhism: Buddhism is based on teachings attributed to the Buddha, a wandering ascetic and religious teacher who lived in South Asia in the 6th or 5th century BCE, the 5th century being the best estimate. The accounts of his life in the early texts are inconsistent. They give his family name as Gautama and place his birth at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal. Legends make his father a king named Suddhodana, but scholars such as Richard Gombrich doubt this, since the evidence suggests he came from the Shakya community, governed by a small oligarchy or council.

The roots of the religion lie in the intellectual ferment of Iron Age India around the middle of the first millennium BCE, the period of the Upanishads and the rise of the Śramaṇa movements, which included Buddhism and Jainism.

According to tradition, the Buddha taught a path that leads to release from dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness, by reaching nirvana, the extinguishing of the passions. He regarded it as a Middle Way between extreme asceticism and sensory indulgence. The Four Noble Truths hold that everything is impermanent, yet people crave and cling to impermanent things, which is dukkha, and that the Noble Eightfold Path leads out of the cycle of rebirth. Taking the Three Refuges, in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, is the traditional first step in most schools.

The Buddha's words were first passed on orally, and the first canonical texts were probably written down in Sri Lanka about 400 years after his death. Scholars generally recognise two surviving branches, Theravāda and Mahāyāna. Theravada holds the Pali Canon as its only authority, and Mahayana, with roots in the 1st century BCE, also honours later literature and stresses the Bodhisattva ideal of working for the liberation of all beings. Vajrayāna, which includes esoteric tantric techniques, may be seen as a separate branch or part of Mahayana.

Buddhism spread gradually through much of Asia along the Silk Road and reached the West in the 19th century. Until the early second millennium it was widely practised in the Indian subcontinent before declining there. Learning centres such as Nalanda and Vikramashila preserved classical Indian disciplines, including grammar, astronomy and medicine, and taught foreign students from across Asia. The religion influenced the cultures of Asia deeply, in philosophy, art, architecture and festivals, and shaped the development of Hinduism, Taoism and Confucianism.
budingen: Büdingen lies in the south of the Wetterau below the Vogelsberg hills, at about 160 metres, 15 km north-west of Gelnhausen and about 40 km east of Frankfurt am Main. It stands in a wet and swampy valley, so the castle and old town rest on centuries-old oak planks laid across vertical beech piles. The water level has to be kept high enough that no air reaches these foundations. Its heavily fortified medieval town wall and half-timbered houses are what it is mainly known for.

The wooden church of Saint Remigius was built around 700 by an unknown lord, and a floor was added about 1050. A document of 847 names a Büdingen, though it is unclear which place of that name is meant. The House of Büdingen is first mentioned in 1131, and became Burggrafen of Gelnhausen in 1155. The town is officially mentioned in 1206, and the ruling house died out with Gerlach II before 1247. On 26 July 1330 Emperor Louis IV granted market-town status. In 1353 Burggraf Heinrich II gave the townspeople freedom and some independence in return for defending the town, which led to the founding of the Marksmen's Society, still one of the oldest rifle associations in Germany.

Since 1442 the masters of Büdingen have been counts of Isenburg-Büdingen. After a local war, Count Ludwig II built a new defensive wall with 22 towers around the old stronghold between 1480 and 1510. It is nearly complete and is among the most important medieval fortifications in Germany. The town became Protestant in 1521, later Calvinist. As many as 114 people were victims of witch hunting in 1633 and 1634, though prosecutions began in 1567. In 1634, during the Thirty Years' War, Imperial troops took the town from its Swedish occupiers.

Count Wolfgang Ernst founded the Latin School in 1601, today the Wolfgang-Ernst-Gymnasium. In 1712 Count Ernst Casimir I issued an edict of tolerance allowing religious dissenters to settle, and by 1724 a suburb at the Lower Gate, or Jerusalem Gate, housed Huguenots, Waldensians and other separatists. After the Congress of Vienna Büdingen passed in 1816 to Hesse-Darmstadt. The town became a garrison in 1936, and United States troops were stationed there from 1945 until 2007.

Since 1972 the municipality has included sixteen formerly independent villages, and the district of Büdingen was dissolved the same year, when Büdingen and the district of Friedberg formed the Wetteraukreis.
buea: Buea lies in Fako Division on the eastern slopes of Mount Cameroon. It has a subtropical highland climate that closely borders on a tropical rainforest climate, with an average high of about 21.1 °C and an average low of about 16.1 °C, the hottest month being February and the coldest August. The built-up area includes many villages and neighbourhoods such as Muea, Molyko, Great Soppo and the settlements named for their distance in miles along the road, Mile 14 to Mile 18. Tea growing is an important local industry, especially at Tole.

According to local tradition Buea was founded by a hunter who came from the Bomboko side of the mountain and named the new-found land in amazement a Bue, meaning literally a son of bué. A king resisted German troops during the invasion, and the resistance remains popular folklore. Its people were originally mainly Bakweri. Buea was the colonial capital of German Kamerun, and the German colonial administration there was temporarily suspended during the eruption of Mount Cameroon, which lasted from 28 April until June 1909.

The palatial former residence of the German governor Jesko von Puttkamer survives among a handful of colonial-era buildings, though some German buildings suffer from age and lack of maintenance. Buea was later the capital of the Southern Cameroons from 1949 until 1961 and then of West Cameroon, until 1972, when Ahmadou Ahidjo abolished the Federation of Cameroon.

Buea is the capital of the Southwest Region of Cameroon. It hosts the University of Buea, Cameroon's first anglophone university, and several other institutions of higher learning, among them one of Cameroon's three Catholic universities. The town has an annex of the National Archives of Cameroon. Its economy draws on the students who come to study there, and tech hubs such as ActivSpaces, launched in 2009, have grown up around the university. Mount Cameroon is a popular attraction for visitors. The nearest major port and international airport are at Douala.
buenos-aires: Buenos Aires lies on the southwest shore of the Río de la Plata, which is called the world's widest river, in the pampa region. Several districts, among them Puerto Madero and the main port, were built on land reclaimed along the river. The area was once crossed by streams and lagoons. As floods damaged the city's infrastructure in 1908, many streams were channelled, and from 1919 most were enclosed. The Maldonado was tubed in 1954 and now runs below Juan B. Justo Avenue. The city is laid out on a rectangular grid of square blocks, 110 metres long, called manzanas.

The name comes from Santa Maria de los Buenos Aires, Holy Mary of the Good Winds. Spanish sailors, especially Andalusians, invoked the Virgin of the Buen Ayre, named after Our Lady of Bonaria in Cagliari, Sardinia. Juan Díaz de Solís was the first European to reach the Río de la Plata, in 1516, and was killed in an attack by the Charrúa. Pedro de Mendoza founded the city on 2 February 1536, in what is now the San Telmo district.

Attacks by indigenous people forced the settlers away, and the site was abandoned in 1541 or 1542. A second and permanent settlement was established on 11 June 1580 by Juan de Garay, who came down the Paraná River from Asunción. He named it Santísima Trinidad, and its port became the Puerto de Santa María de los Buenos Aires. Later rule is grouped as Habsburg Spain to 1700, Bourbon Spain to 1808, the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata from 1810 and the Argentine Confederation from 1831. The State of Buenos Aires existed from 1852 to 1861.

In 1880, after the Argentine Civil War, the city was federalised and split from Buenos Aires Province, and its limits grew to include Belgrano and Flores. Since the 19th century the city and country have received millions of immigrants from many parts of the world. The Parque Tres de Febrero was inaugurated on 11 November 1875, and the Botanical Gardens on 7 September 1898, both later work of the French Argentine urbanist Carlos Thays.

Buenos Aires is the capital and largest city of Argentina. A constitutional amendment of 1994 gave it autonomy, hence its formal name, the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, and its citizens elected their first chief of government in 1996. The city proper had 2,891,082 residents at the 2010 census, with 13,147,638 in Greater Buenos Aires. It is home to the Teatro Colón, an opera house, and to the Avenida 9 de Julio, 140 metres wide. The city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2005 as a City of Design.
bugis: The Bugis, or To Ugi, are an Austronesian people and the most numerous of the three major ethnolinguistic groups of South Sulawesi, with the Makassarese and the Torajans. The earliest inhabitants of South Sulawesi were hunter-gatherers of the Toalean culture. Austronesian ancestors of the Bugis settled on Sulawesi around 2500 BCE, and linguistic evidence points to immigration from Taiwan and possible ultimate ancestry in South China. Their homeland is the area around Lake Tempe and Lake Sidenreng in the Walannae Depression, where they probably settled in the mid- to late second millennium BCE. The lakes and hills allowed wet rice, shifting cultivation, hunting and gathering.

Between 1200 and 1600 the political landscape of lowland South Sulawesi changed radically, partly through trade and contact with the Maritime Silk Road. Most states were small chiefdoms whose ruling class dominated the export of rare commodities. In the 1500s Luwu was the major political force in the Bugis heartland. In 1544 the Portuguese trader Antonio de Paiva, who had been sailing between Sulawesi and Malacca since 1542, baptized La Putebulu, Datu of Suppa', and his family, followed by the king of Siang. Later the Makassarese state of Gowa expanded northward and absorbed many Bugis states, while the Kingdom of Bone expanded southward. A war between Bone and Gowa broke out in 1562. The Bugis converted from animism to Islam in 1605.

The balance of power was upset from the end of the seventeenth century by dynastic disputes and by the fall of Makassar. Makassar had been a crucial starting point for Bugis who sought wealth in the western archipelago, since the Dutch restricted their access to the eastern spice islands, and Bugis emigration became a major feature of the archipelago's history.

Customs are based on the concept of Pangadereng, which consists of Ade' (custom), Rapang (jurisprudence), Bicara (judiciary) and Warik (social system); after Islamisation Syara' (Syariah) was added. An ethical code of Siri' na Pacce, shame and compassion, is shared with the Makassarese, Mandarese and Torajans. The Lontara script, which traces its origin to the Kawi script, was used for contracts, trade laws, treaties, maps and journals, on palm-leaf manuscripts and in books, and its influence spread to Flores and Sumbawa. Most Bugis speak the Bugis language, which belongs to the South Sulawesi language group, as well as Indonesian. The Bugis number around six million, less than 2.5 per cent of the population of Indonesia.
bujumbura: Bujumbura stands on the north-eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika, the second deepest lake in the world after Lake Baikal. The city lies at the mouth of the Ruzizi River and of the smaller Mutimbuzi, Ntahangwa, Muha and Kanyosha rivers. Its climate is tropical savanna, with a wet season from October to April. Because it is near the equator, temperatures vary little through the year, and the moderate altitude keeps them lower than might be expected, with highs around 29 degrees and lows around 19.

Bujumbura grew from a small village after it became a military post in German East Africa. After the First World War it was made the administrative centre and de facto capital of the Belgian League of Nations mandate of Ruanda-Urundi, and its name was changed from Usumbura to Bujumbura on Burundi's independence in 1962. The Belgian colonial period left a mark on the city centre, whose buildings of the first half of the 20th century include elements of Modernism and Art Deco, many still visible in the historical centre.

Since independence Bujumbura has been the scene of repeated fighting between the country's two main ethnic groups. During the Burundian Civil War of the 1990s, Hutu militias opposed the Tutsi-dominated Burundi Army, and the battles destroyed hospitals, administrative buildings, the University of Burundi and other schools in the city, severely crippling the local economy.

Bujumbura is the largest city and main port of Burundi, its economic capital and, until 2019, its political capital. Parliament voted on 16 January 2019 to return the political capital's status to Gitega, leaving Bujumbura as the centre of commerce.

The Port of Bujumbura is the largest on Lake Tanganyika. Burundi depends on its neighbours for access to the ocean, and about 80 per cent of its external trade travels by the lake and then by road or rail through Tanzania, Congo or Zambia. The port ships most of the country's chief export, coffee, as well as cotton and tin ore. Nearby sights include Rusizi National Park and the Livingstone-Stanley Monument at Mugere, which marks where David Livingstone and Henry Morton Stanley visited 14 days after their first meeting at Ujiji in Tanzania.
bukhara: Bukhara stands in Transoxiana, west of Samarkand, and was one of the most prosperous cities of the region because of its position on the Silk Road. The exact name of the city in ancient times is unknown; the whole oasis was called Bukhara, and the name probably passed to the city only in the tenth century. Some scholars derive it from the Sanskrit vihāra, a Buddhist monastery, while others derive it from a Sogdian word for monasteries meaning place of good fortune. The History of Bukhara by Narshakhi, completed in 943–944, lists its other names, among them the copper city and the city of merchants.

The first Islamic account relates that the Arab invader Ubaidullah bin Ziad found Bukhara a Buddhist country, with monasteries, ruled by a queen regent acting for her son. By 850 it was the capital of the Samanid Empire and the birthplace of the scholar Imam Bukhari. The Samanids revived Persian culture far from Baghdad, and the poet Rudaki, called the father of Persian poetry, was born and raised in Bukhara. In its golden age the city was a major intellectual centre of the Islamic world, known for its many libraries. At the start of the 11th century it passed to the Turkic Kara-Khanid Khanate, whose rulers built the Kalyan Minaret and the Magok-i-Attari Mosque.

Genghis Khan besieged Bukhara for 15 days in 1220, and the city was completely destroyed. It recovered under the Timurids, and in the 16th century it became the capital of the Uzbek Khanate. Its influence in the wider Islamic world began to diminish after the arrival of the Uzbeks. For several centuries Bukhara and Khiva were major centres of the slave trade. Bukhara was the home of Sheikh Baha' al-Din Naqshband, a central figure in the development of the Naqshbandi Sufi order. The Mir-i-Arab Madrasah was built in 1535–1536.

Bukhara was the last capital of the Emirate of Bukhara. In 1920 Red Army troops under Mikhail Frunze attacked the city. The Emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, fled on 31 August, and on 2 September, after four days of fighting, the emir's citadel, the Ark, was destroyed. The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic existed from 1920 to 1924, when the city was integrated into the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic.

Bukhara is a city of Uzbekistan and the capital of Bukhara Region. Its historic centre, with numerous mosques and madrasas, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the city has about 140 architectural monuments. They include the Ark fortress, the Ismail Samani mausoleum of the 9th or 10th century and the Kalyan Minaret, a brick tower 45.6 metres high. The Kalyan Mosque, arguably completed in 1514, can hold twelve thousand people.
bukoba: Bukoba lies on the south-western shore of Lake Victoria in the north-west of Tanzania, only one degree south of the Equator, in a region bordering Uganda. It is a flat, compact town surrounded by hills, with a white sandy beach and a large market. It has an upland tropical monsoon climate, milder than most of that type because of its altitude, with a mean temperature in every month of between 18 °C and 22 °C and two rainy seasons. Bukoba is the capital of the Kagera region and the seat of Bukoba Urban District.

Emin Pasha founded Bukoba in 1890 as the first German military station on Lake Victoria, in the territory of the Lesser Kyamutwara kingdom. Its king, Mukotani, was hospitable to the Germans and directed them against his rivals, Kayoza of Bugabo and Mutatembwa of Kiziba. After unrest in neighbouring Uganda the town received fleeing Catholic missionaries in February 1892. It developed into a port through which grain, hides and ivory passed. The Germans built a fort in 1901, and by 1914 Bukoba had one of three transmission stations in German East Africa, with Dar es Salaam and Mwanza.

Riots broke out during the Maji Maji Rebellion of 1905–1907 and were quickly suppressed; in the reprisals King Ntare of the Karagwe Kingdom was hanged on a tree in Bukoba. In the East African campaign of the First World War the British sacked the town on 2 June 1915 and raided it again on 21–23 June, with widespread pillaging and rape reported. German East Africa passed to British control after the war. On 18 October 1978, in the opening actions of the Uganda–Tanzania War, Ugandan MiG aircraft bombed Bukoba, causing panic but little destruction, and civilians fled the town.

Bukoba had a population of 144,938 at the 2022 census. Its port, about three kilometres from the centre, is the second-largest Tanzanian port on Lake Victoria after those of Mwanza, and a passenger service links it to Mwanza. The town also has an airport with flights to Mwanza and Dar es Salaam, and roads lead to Uganda's Rakai District. Kaitaba Stadium holds 15,000 people, and the football club Kagera Sugar plays in the Tanzanian Premier League.
bukovina: Bukovina lies on the northern slopes of the central Eastern Carpathians and the adjoining plains, at the crossroads of Central and Eastern Europe. Bukovina proper covers 10,442 square kilometres. Its name first appears in a document of the Voivode of Moldavia Roman I Mușat of 30 March 1392 and comes from the Slavic word buk, beech tree; the German name Buchenland and the Romanian Țara Fagilor both mean land of beech trees. The region was long inhabited by Romanians in the south and Ukrainians in the north, and it was known for its ethnic variety.

Traces of settlement go back to the Paleolithic, and the Trypillian culture, Scythians, Dacians and Getae followed, with Goths appearing by the 4th century and Slavic people in the 5th and 6th. From the late 10th century Bukovina became part of Kievan Rus', and then of the Principality of Galicia-Volhynia. In the 14th century it passed to Hungary and became part of the Principality of Moldavia; the voivode Dragoș is named as the founder of Moldavia, whose name comes from the Moldova River in Bukovina. Suceava, in the south, was its capital from the late 14th century to the mid-16th century.

In 1497 Stephen III of Moldavia defeated an army of King John I Albert of Poland at the Battle of the Cosmin Forest, and in 1514 Moldavia became a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. Under Stephen the Great and his successors the painted monasteries of Moldovița, Sucevița, Putna, Humor and Voroneț were built.

After the Russo-Ottoman Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 21 July 1774, the Habsburg monarchy occupied the region in October 1774, and the Convention of Pera of 7 May 1775 ceded it. It was a district of the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria until it became the Duchy of Bukovina in 1849. The first census to record ethnicity, in 1851, counted 380,826 people, 48.5% of them Romanians and 38.1% Ukrainians. Russian armies occupied Czernowitz three times in the First World War, and after Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918 the Romanian army took the province, against Ukrainian protest. In 1930 it had 839,500 inhabitants, 43% Romanian, 28% Ukrainian, 11% Jewish and 9% German.

After the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact the Soviet Union demanded Bukovina from Romania on 26 June 1940, and Romania ceded the northern part, including Cernăuți, on 28 June. Romania held the north again from 1941 as an ally of Nazi Germany, but the Soviet army retook it in 1944.

Northern Bukovina is now the Chernivtsi Oblast of Ukraine, and southern Bukovina is part of Suceava County in Romania. Several of the painted monasteries are World Heritage Sites, among the painted churches of northern Moldavia.
bulacan: Bulacan lies in the southern portion of the fertile plains of Central Luzon, immediately north of Metro Manila and on the north-eastern shore of Manila Bay. It covers 2,796.10 square kilometres and is drained by the Angat and Pampanga rivers. The Sierra Madre forms its eastern highlands, where the highest point, Mount Oriod, rises to 1,206 metres. The province takes its name from the town of Bulakan, derived from the Tagalog word bulak, meaning cotton, because of the abundance of cotton plants growing there.

After the defeat of the Macabebe and Hagonoy forces under Bambalito at the Battle of Bangkusay on 3 June 1571, Martín de Goiti moved north, reaching Lubao in September 1571 and Malolos and Calumpit on 14 November 1571. Adelantado Miguel Lopez de Legazpi made Calumpit and Malolos an encomienda entrusted to Sargento Juan Moron and Don Marcos de Herrera. Research by historians of the Center for Bulacan Studies and others shows that Bulacan was identified as a visita of Tondo in 1578, and the province's founding is dated 15 August 1578. Bulacan was natively Kapampangan when the Spaniards arrived, but it became predominantly Tagalog after many Tagalog refugees from Manila and northern Cavite fled there when the British invaded Manila.

In 1899 the Barasoain Church in Malolos was the birthplace of the First Philippine Republic, sometimes described as the first constitutional democracy in Asia. The Americans held the country's first municipal election at Baliwag on 6 May 1899, and under American rule Malolos housed the seat of government, with the Casa Real as the provincial governor's seat from 1900 to 1930. The Japanese army occupied Bulacan in 1942 and made the Casa Real its headquarters, and combined Filipino and American forces and guerrillas liberated it in 1945. After the war the province was caught up in the Hukbalahap Rebellion. On 7 November 1975 Presidential Decree 824 removed the municipality of Valenzuela from Bulacan to form the National Capital Region.

The capital is the city of Malolos. Bulacan has 20 municipalities and four cities, one of which, San Jose del Monte, is the largest. The 2024 census counted 3,876,806 people. Tagalog is the predominant language, and some inhabitants speak Kapampangan. The Alta Kabulowan, or Dumagat people, the first inhabitants of Bulacan, live in San Miguel, Doña Remedios Trinidad, Norzagaray and San Jose del Monte. Malolos is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Malolos.
bulawayo: Bulawayo is the largest city of Zimbabwe's Matabeleland region. It covers 546 square kilometres in the west of the country along the Matsheumhlope River, and most of its people belong to the Ndebele, with minorities of Shona and others. The city lies close to Matobo National Park and the Khami World Heritage Site.

The settlement began as a kraal of the Ndebele king Mzilikazi, who led his people north from Kwazulu. His son Lobengula succeeded him in the 1860s and ruled from Bulawayo until 1893. The name comes from the Ndebele word bulala and is translated as the one to be killed. Many European powers coveted the town, and Britain used Cecil Rhodes and the Chartered Company to avoid alarming its rivals. Lobengula once described Britain as a chameleon and himself as the fly.

In the First Matabele War of 1893, troops of the British South Africa Company invaded and forced Lobengula to leave, after he had blown up munitions and set the town on fire. On 4 November 1893 Leander Starr Jameson declared Bulawayo a settlement under company rule, and Rhodes ordered it founded on the ruins of the royal kraal, where State House now stands. During the Second Matabele War the town was besieged from March 1896. Settlers sheltered in a laager, and more than 10,000 Ndebele warriors gathered but never mounted a significant attack. Relief forces arrived in late May 1896.

Bulawayo became a municipality in 1897 and a city in 1943. By the late 1930s it was no longer the country's largest city, as activity shifted east towards Salisbury, but after the Second World War it grew again as an industrial centre.

Bulawayo is Zimbabwe's second largest city, and a hub of the national rail network and headquarters of the National Railways of Zimbabwe. Its wide central streets were designed so that ox-drawn carts could turn in them. The National University of Science and Technology and the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe are in the city, which is nicknamed the City of Kings.
bulgaria: Bulgaria covers 110,994 square kilometres in the east of the Balkans, south of the Danube and west of the Black Sea, with a coastline of 354 kilometres. Its main topographical features are the Danubian Plain, the Balkan Mountains, the Upper Thracian Plain and the Rila-Rhodope massif. The Balkan Mountains run from west to east through the middle of the country, and Musala, at 2,925 metres, is the highest point in both Bulgaria and the Balkans. Plains occupy about a third of the territory and plateaux and hills 41%. The climate is varied and changeable because the country lies at the meeting point of Mediterranean, Oceanic and Continental air masses.

Neanderthal remains of around 150,000 years ago are among the earliest traces of human activity, and the Karanovo culture arose c. 6,500 BCE. The Varna culture is credited with the invention of goldworking and produced the oldest golden jewellery in the world, over 6,000 years old. The Thracians appeared on the Balkan Peninsula before the 12th century BCE, and after the defeat of the second Persian invasion in 479 BCE most of the tribes united under king Teres to form the Odrysian kingdom.
Philip II of Macedon vassalised it in 341 BCE, and it became a Roman province in 45 CE. In the 6th century the Slavs entered the Balkans and assimilated the Thracians.

The Bulgars, led by Asparuh, permanently invaded the Balkans in the late 7th century and established the First Bulgarian Empire, recognised by the Byzantine Empire in 681. It dominated most of the Balkans and influenced Slavic cultures through the Cyrillic script, which the Preslav Literary School developed. It lasted until the early 11th century, when the Byzantine emperor Basil II conquered and dismantled it.

A revolt in 1185 established the Second Bulgarian Empire, which reached its apex under Ivan Asen II (1218–1241), and in 1396 the empire, weakened by wars and feudal strife, fell under Ottoman rule for nearly five centuries.

The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 resulted in the third and current Bulgarian state, which declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1908. Many ethnic Bulgarians were left outside its borders, which stoked irredentist sentiment, conflicts with neighbours and alliances with Germany in both world wars.

In 1946 Bulgaria came under the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc as a socialist state, and the Communist Party gave up its monopoly on power after the revolutions of 1989. It has been a parliamentary republic of 28 provinces since the constitution of 1991, and a member of the European Union and NATO.
bulgarians: Bulgarians derive their name from the Bulgars. The name is not fully understood and is difficult to trace back before the 4th century CE; it may come from a Proto-Turkic word meaning to mix or stir. Among the main elements that formed the Bulgarians are the Thracians, a native ancient Balkan people, and the early Slavs, who migrated into the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries CE and imposed their language and culture on the local Thracian, Roman and Greek communities.

The question of ethnogenesis has been contested since the 19th century. Suggested proportions of Thracian, Bulgar and Slavic ancestry have shifted with the political situation: the Communist government encouraged the study of the Thracians in the 1970s, while some nationalist writers have reinterpreted the Danubian Bulgars as a numerous people rather than a limited group of Turkic horsemen.

Bulgaria was founded in 681 as a Slav-Bulgar state. A symbiosis took place between the numerically weak Bulgars and the numerous Slavic tribes who accepted the common name Bulgarians. After the adoption of Orthodox Christianity in 864 it became one of the cultural centres of Slavic Europe, and its position was consolidated by the invention of the Cyrillic script in its capital Preslav at the eve of the 10th century.

The development of Old Church Slavonic literacy in the 10th century prevented the assimilation of the South Slavs into neighbouring cultures and stimulated a Bulgarian national identity. Ottoman rule lasted from 1396 to 1878. During the Russo-Turkish Wars of 1806–1812 and 1828–1829 Bulgarian emigrants formed the Bulgarian Countrymen's Army and joined the Russian army, hoping for liberation. Under the Ottoman Empire a struggle began for schools and liturgy in Bulgarian and for an independent church organisation, which flared up in several dioceses in the 1820s.

Most Bulgarians live in Bulgaria, and there are historical communities in North Macedonia, Ukraine, Moldova, Serbia, Albania, Romania, Hungary and Greece. Bulgarians speak a South Slavic language mutually intelligible with Macedonian. It shares some developments with Romanian, Albanian and Greek, and was influenced by Greek and Turkish.

Most Bulgarians are at least nominally members of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church, founded in 870 and autocephalous since 927. It was abolished during Ottoman rule, revived in 1873 as the Bulgarian Exarchate and soon raised again to a patriarchate.
bulgars: The Bulgars were Turkic semi-nomadic warrior tribes of the Pontic-Caspian steppe and the Volga region. Their original homeland is unclear, but is believed to lie in Kazakhstan and the North Caucasian steppes. Some scholars propose that they were a branch of the Huns or absorbed them, a question still debated. Because of the lack of definitive evidence, modern scholarship explains their origin as ethnogenesis, in which warrior elites ruled a variety of groups that adopted a shared name. The first clear mention of the Bulgars is from 480, when they were allies of the Byzantine Emperor Zeno against the Ostrogoths.

After the Western Turkic Khaganate declined in the middle of the 7th century, the Bulgars revolted against the Avars under Kubrat, around 635, and founded Old Great Bulgaria. It proved a loose tribal union, and a rivalry with the Khazars ended in Khazar victory in 668. The union broke up. Some Bulgars stayed in the Pontic steppe as Khazar vassals, and others, led by Kotrag, moved to the middle Volga and founded Volga Bulgaria with Bolghar as capital.

Asparukh, a third son of Kubrat according to Nikephoros I, crossed the Danube and in 681 conquered Scythia Minor, establishing the First Bulgarian Empire, where the Bulgars became a political and military elite. They merged with the Byzantine populations and Slavic tribes there and were in time Slavicized, becoming one of the ancestors of modern Bulgarians. The Volga Bulgars accepted Islam in 922, repelled the first Mongol attacks in 1223 and were subdued by the Mongols in 1237.

The Bulgars shared the culture of the nomadic horsemen of Central Asia, moving seasonally in search of pasture while trading with settled societies, from whom they learned blacksmithing, pottery and carpentry. In the Balkans they quickly adopted the sedentary life of the Slavs. The Danubian Bulgars had a clan and military system of inner and outer tribes under a ruling clan, whose ruler's title was khan.

Little is known of their religion, but it is believed to have been monotheistic, centred on the Turkic sky deity Tengri, known to them as Tangra. Their elite spoke a Turkic language of the Oghur branch, the only surviving member of which is Chuvash. The Volga Tatars, Bashkirs and Chuvash are said to descend from the Volga Bulgars.
bulguksa: The temple's records state that a small temple stood on the site under King Beopheung in 528. The Samguk Yusa records that the present temple was built under King Gyeongdeok in 751, begun by the chief minister Kim Daeseong to pacify the spirits of his parents. After Kim's death the Silla royal court completed it in 774 and gave it its name, Bulguksa, the Temple of the Buddha Land. The wooden buildings were burned to the ground during the Imjin wars. Reconstruction began after 1604, with about forty renovations until 1805, and a major restoration between 1969 and 1973 brought the complex to its present form. The stone structures are preserved from the original Silla construction.

Bulguksa stands on Tohamsan in Gyeongju and is a head temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. A double staircase and bridge leads to the Jahamun gate: the upper Cheongungyo, or Blue Cloud Bridge, has sixteen steps and the lower Baegungyo, or White Cloud Bridge, eighteen, 34 in all, matching the 34 steps to enlightenment. The semicircular arch beneath is the oldest of its kind in Korea. The bridges were probably built in 750 in the reign of King Gyeongdeok.

Two pagodas stand before the main hall, Daeungjeon, which enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha. Seokgatap is 8.2 metres tall, a traditional Korean-style pagoda with simple lines. Dabotap is 10.4 metres tall, dedicated to the Many Treasures Buddha of the Lotus Sutra and known for its ornate structure; its image appears on the South Korean 10 won coin. The complex also holds gilt-bronze seated statues of Vairocana and of Amitabha, which stylistic evidence dates to around the 8th and 9th centuries.

The temple is regarded as a masterpiece of the golden age of Buddhist art in the Silla kingdom. It contains six National Treasures, among them the two pagodas, the bridges and the two gilt-bronze statues, and in 1995 Bulguksa and the nearby Seokguram Grotto were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. In 1966 a version of the Dharani sutra, dated between 704 and 751 and printed on a mulberry paper scroll 630 centimetres long, was found there; it is among the earliest woodblock prints in the world. Hyun Jin-geon wrote a historical novel on the building of the two pagodas, the basis of the 1957 film Shadowless Pagoda.
bundesrat-germany: The Bundesrat's predecessor was the Federal Convention, or diet, of the German Confederation of 1815 to 1866, which consisted of representatives of the member states and was chaired by the Austrian representative. The term Bundesrath appeared in a proposed reform act of 1863. When the North German Confederation was founded on 1 July 1867, its Bundesrath, expressly modelled on the old diet, served as one legislative body beside the elected Reichstag. It kept its name when the Confederation became the German Empire in 1871.

The imperial Bundesrat could initiate legislation, and every bill of the Reichstag, the budget included, needed its consent. With the Emperor's agreement it could dissolve the Reichstag, which made it in theory the more powerful body. Its delegates were usually high-ranking civil servants, and the chancellor chaired it without being a member.

In the revolution of 1918 the Council of People's Representatives limited the Bundesrat to administrative functions. Under the Weimar Constitution of 11 August 1919 it was replaced by the Reichsrat, which could no longer initiate legislation and could only veto bills, a veto the Reichstag could overrule only by a two-thirds majority. A law of 14 February 1934 abolished the Reichsrat.

After the Second World War the chamber was re-established under the Basic Law as the Bundesrat, and it held its first session on 7 September 1949. In power it stands between the strong imperial Bundesrat and the weak Reichsrat. It has the right of legislative initiative and an absolute veto over bills that directly affect the states; other vetoes the Bundestag can overrule. It met in the Bundeshaus in Bonn, in a wing built for it, and moved to the former Prussian House of Lords in Berlin in 2000, a year after the Bundestag, keeping Bonn as a second seat.

The Bundesrat is not elected and is not a parliamentary chamber. It is an assembly of delegations from the sixteen state governments, usually the minister-president and cabinet ministers, bound to act according to their government's agreements. Each state casts its votes together, and none has fewer than three or more than six, in a degressive proportion to population, so that smaller states have more votes than strict proportion would give them. The presidency rotates annually among the minister-presidents.

It cannot amend a bill. An approval bill, which directly affects the states, needs a majority of all possible votes, while an objection bill becomes law unless the Bundesrat objects within 14 days. A mediation committee of equal numbers from both chambers negotiates when the two disagree. The Bundesrat also elects half the judges of the Federal Constitutional Court with the Bundestag and holds powers in a legislative emergency.
burao: The Somali word burco describes open, elevated land with soft, rich soil, and the Burao area is considered fertile. The city began in the late 18th century as a well, called Ceel-Gooni, used by nomads of the surrounding area. A town grew around it, and because of the water along the dry valley it became a small inland market linking the port of Berbera with the interior and offering trading facilities to the region's nomadic population.

For much of the 19th century Burao was the capital of the Habr Yunis Sultanate, ruled at different times by Sultan Nur Ahmed Aman, Sultan Awad Deria and Sultan Madar Hersi. The explorer Frank Linsly James, a guest of Sultan Awad Deria in 1884, described a display by Habr Yunis horsemen in the bed of the Togdheer River. British forces burned the settlement to the ground in 1900, and the modern town was re-established in 1910. The Dervish movement was founded at Burao in 1899, when Mohammed Abdullah Hassan and his followers assembled there with other clans and declared open hostility to the British.

In 1922 the people of Burao rose against a heavy tax. In the disturbances Captain Allan Gibb, the district commissioner, was shot dead, and aircraft of the Royal Air Force, requested from Aden, bombed the town with incendiaries and burned the settlement to the ground; the British afterwards abandoned the tax policy. In July 1945 the religious leader Sheikh Bashir led a rebellion of Habr Je'lo tribesmen that began with an attack on Burao's prison; he was killed in the mountains of Bur Dhab, and a secondary school in Burao bears his name. In the 1950s the expanding livestock trade, with animals exported to Saudi Arabia, made Burao the second largest city of the protectorate.

In May 1988 the Somali National Movement captured Burao in about two hours, and the Somali army replied with heavy artillery, tanks and aerial bombardment. Reports describe killings of civilians, and the city was razed and most of its inhabitants fled to Ethiopia. In May 1991 a Central Committee of the movement met at Burao and agreed to revoke the union with the Somali Democratic Republic, forming the Republic of Somaliland, with Abdirahman Ahmed Ali Tuur elected to govern for two years.

Burao is the capital of the Togdheer region and the second largest city of Somaliland. Its main residents are the Habr Je'lo, Habr Yonis, Isamusa and Arap, all subdivisions of the Isaaq clan-family. The city is divided into four wards: Mohamed Ali, Farah Omar, Lihle and Sheikh Bashir.
burdur: Burdur stands on the shore of Lake Burdur in south-western Turkey. Habitation in the surrounding province goes back to 6500 BCE, and the earliest sign of settlement in the city itself dates to the Early Bronze Age. In antiquity the area belonged to the region of Pisidia. The city may have changed its location several times: the ancient town of Limnombria lay closer to the lake, and in the Byzantine period the city existed as Polydorion, from which the present name derives.

The urban history of Burdur is generally held to begin with the Turkish settlement that followed the Seljuq victory at Manzikert in 1071. Turks became the majority of the population after 1211, and the first settlement was moved uphill away from the lake because of malaria. Kilij Arslan II, the Seljuq sultan of Rum, imposed his rule in 1177, and the town was captured by the Mongol Empire in 1260. Trade through Antalya made it a commercial stop for tragacanth, wine, wax, wood and tar.

In 1300 the Hamidids under Dündar Bey took Burdur and built its Grand Mosque, around which the town developed. The Ilkhanate captured it in 1324, and Dündar Bey's son recovered it in 1328. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1330 and described a town of orchards and farms with a castle near the mosque and a guild of ahis controlling commerce and production. The Ottoman sultan Bayezid I took Burdur in 1391, and in 1478 it had four quarters, three Muslim and one Christian.

A small Greek population lived in the city until the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey, and an abandoned Greek church there has been turned into a museum with a large dinosaur fossil. Burdur has about 95 thousand inhabitants and is home to Mehmet Akif Ersoy University.
burebista: The area between the Danube, Tisza and Dniester rivers, roughly modern Romania, became home to Thracian peoples including the Getae and the Dacians around the 7th and 6th centuries BCE. The Getae lived in the lower Danube basin and traded with the Greek cities of the Black Sea coast, while the Dacians lived along the southern Carpathian Mountains, whose isolation helped them survive. From the 4th century to the middle of the 2nd century BCE La Tène Celts influenced them, introducing the potter's wheel, better metalworking and probably coinage. Before Burebista, Dacia had a succession of kings, among them Dromichaetes, Oroles and Rubobostes. Only a few ancient sources on Burebista survive, including Strabo, Jordanes and inscriptions from Balchik and Nesebar.

The date of his accession is debated among scholars. Burebista was the first king to unify the Dacian tribes, with the support of the religious establishment, and his realm was probably a weakly centralised state with a military organisation like that of the Hellenistic kingdoms; archaeologists disagree about how centralised it was. In the Orăștie Mountains he built stone hill forts at Costești, Blidaru, Piatra Roșie and Bănița, which show Greek military architecture.

He destroyed the Boii and Taurisci in the middle Danube early in his campaigns, then the Bastarnae, and probably conquered the Scordisci, and he raided Thrace, Roman Macedonia and Illyria. From about 55 BCE he took the Greek cities of the Black Sea coast, among them Olbia, Tyras, Histria, Tomis, Callatis, Odessos, Messembria, Apollonia and Dionysopolis.

An inscription of 48 BCE calls Akornion of Dionysopolis his friend and says he was sent to Pompey to seek the title king of kings for Burebista. In the Roman civil war Burebista backed Pompey, which made him an enemy of Julius Caesar, who planned a campaign against him. His force may have numbered up to 200,000 men, though it is disputed whether this was an army or all able-bodied men.

Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE, and Burebista was killed at about the same time in a plot by the Dacian aristocracy, who saw a centralised state as a threat to their privileges. His kingdom broke up. It was divided into four parts under the religious elite, and by the time of Augustus into five. Dacia was united again by Decebalus and ended as an independent kingdom after Trajan's conquest in 106 CE.

In the 1960s statues of Burebista and Decebalus were put up in Romania, and in 1980 the government marked the 2,050th anniversary of his state, a commemoration that the Ceaușescu regime used to legitimise its own rule. Historians have described the nationalist claim that Burebista's descendants are the true ancestors of the Romanians as an imaginary history.
burgenland: From the fourth century BCE the area was dominated by Celts, and in the first century CE it became part of the Roman Empire, in the province of Pannonia. The Ostrogoths settled there in 380, and later it belonged in turn to the Huns, the Lombards, the Avars and the Frankish Empire. It remained the western frontier of the medieval Kingdom of Hungary until the sixteenth century. Most of its people were German-speaking, apart from Hungarian border guards, and in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries German Protestant refugees came, fleeing the suppression of the Reformation in Austrian lands.

According to the census of 1910, 74 per cent of the inhabitants spoke German, 15 per cent Croatian and 9 per cent Hungarian. The treaties of Saint Germain and Trianon assigned German West Hungary to Austria, and the Federal Constitutional Act of 25 January 1921 gave it the name Burgenland. When Austrian officials arrived on 28 August 1921, Hungarian irregulars under Pál Prónay prevented them. The Venice Protocol, mediated by Italy, ended the crisis: Hungary disarmed the irregulars in return for a plebiscite held in December in Sopron and eight villages, whose voters chose Hungary. The rest went to Austria, and its parliament chose Eisenstadt as capital in 1925.

Burgenland is the easternmost and least populous state of Austria, 166 km long from north to south and as little as 5 km wide at Sieggraben. Lake Neusiedl, Austria's largest lake, lies in the north, shared with Hungary. After the Anschluss in 1938 the state was dissolved; it was re-established on 1 October 1945 in the Soviet occupation zone, which ended in 1955. On 27 July 1989 the foreign ministers of Austria and Hungary cut the Iron Curtain at Klingenbach.
burgos: Burgos lies in the north of the Iberian Peninsula, near the confluence of the Arlanzón and the Vena rivers and at the edge of the central plateau, at an elevation of 865 metres. Early humans occupied sites around Burgos as early as 800,000 years ago, and the nearby site of Atapuerca, 20 kilometres to the east, has yielded fossils and stone tools of the earliest known hominids in western Europe. When the Romans took possession the site had been a Celtic city. The name Burgos probably reflects the Visigothic word for walled villages, from the Gothic baurgs.

After the Visigoths drove back the Suebi in the 5th century and the Berbers briefly held Castile in the 8th, Alfonso III of Asturias conquered the area about the middle of the 9th century and built castles, from which Castile took its name, the land of castles. Diego Rodríguez Porcelos gathered the inhabitants of the surrounding country into one fortified village in 884, and the city began to be called Caput Castellae, Head of Castile. In the 11th century it became an archdiocesan see and capital of the Kingdom of Castile. It was a major stop for pilgrims on the French Way to Santiago de Compostela and a centre of trade, attracting a large foreign merchant population that joined the city oligarchy.

In the 13th and 14th centuries Burgos was a favourite seat of the kings of León and Castile and a favoured burial site. Royal charters of 1255 and 1266 relieved from taxes those citizens who owned horses and could arm themselves. In 1285 Sancho IV added a body called the jurado to the town council, and on 9 June 1345 Alfonso XI established direct royal rule through the Regimiento of sixteen appointed men. In 1574 Pope Gregory XIII made the bishopric a metropolitan archbishopric at the request of Philip II. During the Peninsular War Wellington withdrew from the siege of Burgos, and the castle was destroyed by the French in 1813.

Burgos is the capital of its province in Castile and León and its second most populated city. Construction of its Gothic cathedral began in 1221 and spanned mainly the 13th to 15th centuries; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and holds the remains of El Cid and his wife Doña Jimena. The city also has the monastery of Las Huelgas, founded in 1180 by Alfonso VIII, and the Carthusian monastery of Miraflores, with the tombs of Juan II and Queen Isabella of Portugal. The Museum of Human Evolution, opened in 2010, draws on the Atapuerca site. The University of Burgos was established in 1994.
burgtheater: The original Burgtheater was set up in a tennis court, called a ball house at the time, which Ferdinand I had built in 1540 in the lower pleasure garden of the Hofburg after the older ball house burned down in 1525. The theatre opened on 14 March 1741 at the wish of Empress Maria Theresa, who wanted a theatre beside her palace. Its first building adjoined the Hofburg at Michaelerplatz, opposite St Michael's Church. Before 1776 the theatre was leased from the state, and after the bankruptcy of its curator the state under Joseph II took over its operation in 1776. Joseph II called it the German National Theatre that year.

Three of Mozart's operas had their premieres there: Die Entführung aus dem Serail in 1782, Le nozze di Figaro in 1786 and Così fan tutte in 1790. So did his Piano Concerto No. 24 in 1786 and Beethoven's First Symphony on 2 April 1800.

The old house gave exceptional acoustics but was too small for its audience. A description of 1884 said the auditorium could hardly hold half of those who wished to enter. The last performance there, in October 1888, was Goethe's Iphigenie auf Tauris. The theatre moved on 14 October 1888 to a new building on the Ringstraße designed by Gottfried Semper and Karl Freiherr von Hasenauer, whose interiors were decorated with frescoes by Gustav Klimt, Ernst Klimt and Franz von Matsch showing theatrical history. A bombing raid on 12 March 1945 largely destroyed it, and a fire of unknown origin damaged it further a month later. It was rebuilt between 1953 and 1955.

Until 1918 it was known as the K.K. Hofburgtheater, and the Viennese call it die Burg. Its company created a traditional style of speech and performance, and the Burgtheater German was groundbreaking for German-language theatre. The house kept a strongly traditional stage until the late 1960s. From the early 1970s it became a venue for some of Europe's most important directors and designers, and under Claus Peymann it staged the first performances of plays by Thomas Bernhard, Elfriede Jelinek, Peter Handke, Peter Turrini and George Tabori. Its ensemble has about 120 members.
burgundians: The Burgundians are one of the disappearing and reappearing tribes listed by the historian Peter Heather, which appear in Roman records in one place and reappear much later in another. The earliest named by Greco-Roman writers lived near the Vistula in present-day Poland between the first and third centuries; Pliny the Elder lists the Burgodiones among the Vandili. Roman panegyrics report that in the late third century they suffered devastating defeats by the Gepids and Goths, which may have driven some of them west. They later appear near the Main, and in the fourth century they became Roman allies against the Alemanni. Early in the fifth century, in a period of wider crisis, the Gibichung-led Burgundians crossed the Rhine and settled within the empire.

The Rhine kingdom, probably near Worms, was destroyed in 436 when the Romans and their Hun allies killed many Burgundians together with their king Gundahar. His death became a central theme in medieval Germanic heroic legend, including the Nibelungenlied, where he is Günther. The Gallic Chronicle of 452 records that in 443 Sapaudia was given to the remainder of the Burgundians, to be divided with the native inhabitants; the territory included Geneva, and later Lyon became the capital. Ian N. Wood believes that a true Burgundian kingdom emerged only between 474 and 494.

After about 480 Gundobad became principal king, sharing power with his brothers. Civil war broke out in 500 when Godegisel allied with Clovis I of the Franks and defeated Gundobad; with Visigothic support Gundobad regained control in 501. Gundobad died in 516 and left the throne to his Catholic son Sigismund. The Frankish empire incorporated the kingdom in 534.

The Burgundians left several legal codes, which are among the fullest evidence for how the early successor states legislated. Gundobad published edicts concerning relations between Burgundians and Roman citizens, and a Roman law, the Lex Romana Burgundionum. Little is known of their language beyond some names and a few words in legal texts, but it was Germanic. The court at Geneva and Lyon had an Arian faction, which held sway over some kings, including Gundobad, but several women of the royal family were Catholics, and Clovis is said to have been converted by his Burgundian wife.
burgundy: Burgundy is named for the Burgundians, an East Germanic people who moved west beyond the Rhine in the late Roman period. Gallic Celts, above all the Aedui, were the first recorded inhabitants, and the Roman Empire absorbed them after the Battle of Alesia. In the 4th century the Burgundians settled in the western Alps and founded a kingdom, which the Franks conquered in 532. In 843 the Treaty of Verdun divided the old Burgundian lands, and the north-western part went to the West Frankish Kingdom. From the early 10th century it was organised as the Duchy of Burgundy, and from 1004 the House of Burgundy, a cadet branch of the French royal House of Capet, ruled it.

Burgundy was home to some of the most important churches and monasteries of the medieval West. Cluny, founded in 910, influenced Europe for centuries, and the first Cistercian abbey was founded at Cîteaux in 1098. Bernard of Clairvaux's influence helped spread hundreds of Cistercian abbeys across Europe in the following century. During the Hundred Years' War King John II of France gave the duchy to his youngest son, Philip the Bold, and it became a rival to the crown. Philip the Good acquired Namur, Hainaut, Brabant and Holland.

The Valois-Burgundian State held fiefs from the western Alps to the North Sea, and its dukes were among the wealthiest princes in Europe, sometimes called Grand Dukes of the West. At the Battle of Nancy in 1477 the last duke, Charles the Bold, was killed. The French crown annexed the duchy, which became a province in 1482, while the Low Countries possessions passed to his daughter Mary and her Habsburg descendants. The division of the Burgundian inheritance marked the beginning of a long French-Habsburg rivalry.

The province of Burgundy lasted until 1790, when the departments replaced it. Burgundy now means the area of the departments of Côte-d'Or, Saône-et-Loire, Yonne and Nièvre, with Dijon as its capital. It was an administrative region from 1982 to 2015 and merged with Franche-Comté in 2016. The abbeys of Fontenay and Vézelay are World Heritage Sites, and Vézelay is still a starting point for pilgrimages to Santiago de Compostela. Cluny was almost entirely destroyed during the French Revolution. The region is also known for Burgundy wine.
burhanpur: Burhanpur lies on the north bank of the Tapti River. It was a town of some importance under the Rashtrakuta dynasty, from 753 to 982, but came to prominence in the medieval period. Malik Nasir Khan, the Faruqi sultan of Khandesh, founded the city at the urging of Shaikh Zainuddin and named it after the Sufi saint Burhan-ud-Din. It became the capital of the Khandesh sultanate. Miran Adil Khan II, who reigned from 1457 to 1501, built a citadel and palaces and made it a major centre of trade and textile production.

In 1601 Akbar annexed the sultanate, and Burhanpur became the capital of Khandesh subah, one of the new top-level provinces of the Mughal Empire. Its governor Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan built a new water supply and several gardens. In 1609 Jahangir appointed his second son Parviz governor of the Deccan provinces, and the prince made Burhanpur his headquarters.

Shah Jahan spent considerable time in Burhanpur and added to the Shahi Qila, and many surviving monuments date from his rule. Tradition says his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in the palace's royal bath while giving birth to her fourteenth child and was buried there for six months before her body was moved to the Taj Mahal.
