The Maratha Peshwa Bajirao took the town in the 1720s, and in 1818 the Marathas handed it to the British. Burhanpur remains known for textiles and is the largest centre of the power-loom industry in Madhya Pradesh. The Shahi Qila is mostly in ruins. The Jama Masjid was begun under the Faruqi dynasty and completed under Akbar.
burhanuddin-rabbani: Burhanuddin Rabbani was born on 20 September 1940 in the village of Yaftal, in the Fayzabad District of Badakhshan, the son of Muhammed Yousuf. He was a Tajik. He studied Islamic Law and Theology at Kabul University, graduating in 1963, and was hired there as a professor. In 1966 he went to Al-Azhar University in Cairo, where he formed close ties with the leadership of the Muslim Brotherhood. He was one of the first Afghans to translate the works of Sayyid Qutb into Persian, and he spoke six languages.

In 1972 a council of fifteen chose Rabbani as head of Jamiat-e Islami, a party composed mainly of Tajiks. In the spring of 1974 police came to Kabul University to arrest him; his students prevented it and he escaped to Pakistan, where he established the party. When the Soviets intervened in 1979, he helped lead Jamiat-e Islami in resistance to the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan regime.

His forces were the first mujahideen elements to enter Kabul in 1992, when that regime fell, and he took over as president under the Peshawar Accords. His rule was limited, because the country was fractured by civil war. He fled after the Taliban took Kabul in 1996, and his government in exile remained the internationally recognised one while controlling about a tenth of the country. He served briefly as president again from 13 November to 22 December 2001, when Hamid Karzai was chosen as interim leader at Bonn.

Rabbani later headed the High Peace Council, formed in 2010 to start talks with the Taliban. He was killed on 20 September 2011, his 71st birthday, by a suicide bomber who came to his home in Kabul posing as a Taliban envoy. The Afghan parliament suggested the title Martyr of Peace for him.
burj-khalifa: The tower was designed as the centrepiece of Downtown Dubai, a large mixed-use development of 30,000 homes, nine hotels, the Dubai Mall and an artificial lake. The decision to build it was reportedly based on the government's wish to diversify from an oil-based economy to one based on services and tourism.

Skidmore, Owings and Merrill of Chicago did the architecture and engineering, with Adrian Smith as chief architect and Bill Baker as chief structural engineer. The primary contractor was Samsung C&T of South Korea. Excavation began in January 2004, and the exterior was completed on 1 October 2009. The developer, Emaar Properties, had financial problems during the Great Recession, and the president of the United Arab Emirates, Khalifa bin Zayed, organised federal support. Mohammed bin Rashid, Ruler of Dubai, changed the name from Burj Dubai to Burj Khalifa at the inauguration.

The roof height, excluding the antenna but including a 242.6 metre spire, is 828 metres. The primary structure is reinforced concrete, and some of the structural steel was salvaged from the demolished Palace of the Republic in East Berlin. The design draws on the Islamic architecture of the region, such as the Great Mosque of Samarra, and its Y-shaped floor plan was designed to optimise residential and hotel space. It uses the bundled tube design of the Willis Tower, invented by Fazlur Rahman Khan, so that proportionally only half the steel of the Empire State Building was needed. It has 57 elevators and 8 escalators.

During construction the tower passed one record after another. In July 2007 it surpassed Taipei 101 as the tallest building, and in September 2007 it passed the CN Tower as the tallest freestanding structure. In April 2008, at 629 metres, it passed the KVLY-TV mast to become the tallest human-made structure. It opened on 4 January 2010, though much of the interior was unfinished, and the last major planned facility opened on 23 January 2011. Its records include the most floors, 163, and the world's longest elevator travel distance, 504 metres. Above the 80th floor, residents wait two extra minutes to break their Ramadan fast, since the sun stays visible longer at height.
burkina-faso: Burkina Faso covers 274,223 square kilometres. Most of the country is a peneplain, a gently undulating landscape with a few isolated hills that are the last vestiges of a Precambrian massif. The southwest is a sandstone massif, bordered by cliffs up to 150 metres high, where the highest peak, Ténakourou, rises to 749 metres. The country owed its former name, Upper Volta, to three rivers, the Black Volta (Mouhoun), the White Volta (Nakambé) and the Red Volta (Nazinon). Only the Black Volta and the Komoé flow year-round, and water shortages are often a problem in the north.

The northwest was populated by hunter-gatherers from about 14,000 BCE to 5,000 BCE, and agricultural settlements were established between 3600 and 2600 BCE. The oldest evidence of iron smelting in Burkina Faso dates from 800 to 700 BCE and forms part of the Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy World Heritage Site. The Bura culture existed in the southeast from the 3rd to the 13th century CE.

From medieval times until the end of the 19th century the central region was ruled by the Mossi, descendants of Dagomba warriors from present-day Ghana who mixed with Mandé and other local peoples in the 11th century. They established separate kingdoms, among them Tenkodogo, Yatenga, Zandoma and Ouagadougou, and defended their territory, beliefs and social structure against attempts at conquest and conversion from Muslims to the northwest.

The Tarikh al-Sudan reports that a Mossi ruler took control of Timbuktu between 1328 and 1338, during the reign of Mansa Musa, and the Tarikh al-fattash describes conflicts between the 15th-century Mossi king Komdao and the Songhay ruler Sonni Ali. The Mossi were defeated at the Battle of Kobi in 1483. The French colonised the area in 1896 as part of French West Africa, and it became fully independent in 1960 as the Republic of Upper Volta. On 4 August 1984 President Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso.

Ouagadougou is the capital and largest city. The name joins Burkina, from Mooré, meaning upright, with Faso, from Dyula, meaning fatherland. The country is a semi-presidential republic and a member of the United Nations. About half the population is Mossi, whose kingdom is led by the Mogho Naba, whose court is in Ouagadougou. There are more than 60 indigenous languages, and Mooré is spoken by more than half the population. Most people are Muslim, with Christian and animist minorities. Literature rests on oral tradition, and Ouagadougou hosts the International Art and Craft Fair, one of the most important African handicraft fairs.
burlington-new-jersey: Burlington stands on the banks of the Delaware River in Burlington County, New Jersey, and is a suburb of Philadelphia within the Philadelphia metropolitan area. The Burlington-Bristol Bridge crosses the river to Bristol in Pennsylvania. The city takes its name, as does the county, from the town of Bridlington in England, of which Burlington was a district. It was first incorporated on 24 October 1693 and reincorporated by royal charter on 7 May 1733. After independence the State of New Jersey incorporated it on 21 December 1784.

The council of West Jersey Proprietors purchased roughly 30 miles of riverfront land from the Lenape in 1676. English settlers, primarily Quakers, founded Burlington on part of that land in 1677. In 1702 West Jersey and East Jersey were combined into a single Crown Colony. The Quakers formally established their congregation in 1678 and met in private homes until Francis Collings built a hexagonal brick meeting house between 1683 and 1687. The Lenape chief King Ockanickon, a loyal friend of the English settlers, was buried in the cemetery in 1681. The present meeting house on High Street dates from 1783.

The Anglican congregation, founded in 1702 by George Keith and John Talbot, built Old St Mary's, the oldest church in Burlington and New Jersey. In 1837 Bishop George Washington Doane founded St Mary's Hall, the first Episcopal boarding school offering a classical education for girls and the first such school in New Jersey. About 1845 the druggist and Quaker abolitionist William Allinson converted the building at 301 High Street into a pharmacy and a centre of anti-slavery activity; local tradition holds that fugitive slaves hid in tunnels beneath it on the Underground Railroad. In 1796 the county seat moved to Mount Holly Township, a more central location.

The city has 9,743 inhabitants at the 2020 census. Its waterfront park was developed through urban renewal and flood control projects in the late 1960s and 1970s. Burlington has two historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the Burlington Historic District and the adjacent High Street Historic District, and New St Mary's Church, designed by Richard Upjohn and begun in 1846, is a National Historic Landmark.
burushaski: Burushaski is a language isolate spoken by the Burusho people, native to northern Gilgit-Baltistan in Pakistan, and its name in the language means our language. About 120,000 speakers live in Pakistan, in the Hunza, Nagar and northern Gilgit districts, the Yasin Valley and the Ishkoman Valley, and a few hundred in Srinagar in India. Because the two regions where it is spoken are separated by Hunza Valley areas where the Indo-Aryan language Shina is spoken, it is generally believed to have been spoken over a much wider area in the past.

The Hunza and Nagar varieties differ only slightly, but the Yasin variety, also called Werchikwar, is much more divergent, and is sometimes considered a distinct language. Its speakers are bilingual in Khowar. The variety spoken in India has been influenced by Kashmiri, Hindi and Urdu.

Burushaski is an ergative language with a generally subject-object-verb word order. Nouns fall into four classes: male human beings, gods and spirits; female human beings and spirits; animals and countable things; and abstract concepts, fluids and uncountable things. Some words belong to two classes with different meanings, so that báalt means apple when countable and apple tree when uncountable. Words for parts of the body and kinship terms always carry a pronominal prefix, so that one cannot say mother or arm, only my arm or your mother.

The number system is vigesimal, based on twenty, so that 40 is twice twenty and 60 is three times twenty. The verb is very rich in forms: it has three basic stems, and a finite verb can take up to four prefixes and six suffixes in a system of eleven possible positions. Prefixes can mark whether an action was willing or unwilling, as in the difference between he dived and he sank.

Attempts to link Burushaski with other language families have not been accepted by a majority of linguists. Proposals include the North Caucasian, Kartvelian and Yeniseian languages, a wide Dené-Caucasian grouping, and a relationship with Indo-European. Roger Blench noted in 2008 that the supposed evidence rests on vocabulary that may be better explained by language contact, and that almost all Burushaski farming vocabulary appears to be borrowed from Dardic, Tibeto-Burman and North Caucasian languages.

Burushaski has been predominantly a spoken language. Allamah Nasiruddin Nasir Hunzai wrote poetry in it in the 1940s and devised an alphabet derived from Urdu, adding letters for sounds Urdu lacks, and Ghulamuddin Ghulam Hunzai wrote in a modified Arabic script. Hermann Berger created a Latin-based orthography favoured by researchers. A three-volume Burushaski-Urdu Dictionary was compiled in 2006, 2009 and 2013 at the University of Karachi. Tibetan sources record a Bru zha language of the Gilgit valley that appears to have been Burushaski, but no manuscripts in it are known to survive.
bury-st-edmunds: Bury St Edmunds lies in the middle of an undulating part of East Anglia known as the East Anglian Heights, with land to east and west rising above 100 metres, though parts of the town are as low as 30 metres where the Rivers Lark and Linnet pass through it. Excavation on its outskirts in the 2010s found evidence of Bronze Age activity and Roman coins of the first and second centuries. Its name is connected with the word borough, and the second part honours Edmund, King of the East Angles, called Edmund the Martyr, who was killed by the Vikings in 869. In the Anglo-Saxon period the town was called Bedricesweord or Bedericesworth.

The town was originally called Beodericsworth and was laid out on a grid pattern by Abbot Baldwin around 1080. Its Christian heritage dates from the founding of the abbey in 1020, and Edmund's shrine made it an important place of pilgrimage. Henry I granted the borough a charter, now lost, and the abbey controlled the borough until its dissolution in 1539. The townspeople sacked the abbey in the 14th century, and it was largely destroyed in the 16th century at the Dissolution of the Monasteries. James I issued a new charter in 1606 confirming the borough's ancient rights. The town stayed prosperous through the 17th and 18th centuries and declined relatively with the Industrial Revolution.

Its population had reached 12,538 by 1841. A permanent military presence began with the Militia Barracks of 1857 and Gibraltar Barracks of 1878. Zeppelin bombs fell on the town in 1915 and 1916, and in the second raid seven civilians were killed. The British Sugar factory, the town's largest landmark, was built in 1925, and the Theatre Royal, designed by William Wilkins, dates from 1819 and is the only surviving Regency theatre in the country.

Bury St Edmunds is a market town and civil parish in the West Suffolk district, with a built-up area of 41,280 people at the 2021 census. It is the seat of the Diocese of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich, with its cathedral at St Edmundsbury Cathedral, and the remains of the abbey stand in gardens in the centre. Brewing and sugar processing are industries, and the town is the cultural and retail centre for West Suffolk.
bushehr: Bushehr is a port city on the Persian Gulf and the capital of Bushehr province. It lies about 300 km from Shiraz and 600 km from Basra. The origin of the name is uncertain. The popular derivation from Abū Šahr, father of the city, is unlikely, and the name may be an abbreviation of Bokht-Ardashir, meaning Ardashir has given, though this lacks conclusive evidence. Several supposed early mentions, including the first by an Arab geographer in 1225, have been disputed as possibly referring to Reishahr, a harbour 10 km to the south where archaeology points to a much older settlement.

In 1734 Nader Shah made Bushehr the headquarters of the Persian Gulf fleet he wished to create, and for a massive warship had heavy timber brought from the forests of Mazandaran, 1,000 km away. Its shell drew the notice of European travellers for the next 50 years. Nader's naval plans ended when he was murdered in 1747, but Bushehr continued as a prominent port for at least 150 years. The Dutch East India Company kept a trading post there from 1737 to 1753, and in 1763 its Arab ruler, Sheikh Nasr Al-Madhkur, allowed the British East India Company to build a base and residency there, with a monopoly on importing woollen goods.

Bushehr replaced Bandar Abbas as Iran's most important commercial port when the political and economic centre moved to Shiraz under the Zand ruler Karim Khan Zand, who reigned from 1751 to 1779. In the 19th century the site offered few advantages: it was exposed to pirates, European ships had to anchor about four kilometres offshore because the water was shallow, the well water was salty, and the summer heat and humidity were unbearable. British forces occupied the town in the Anglo-Persian War, and it surrendered in December 1856.

The 2016 census counted 223,504 people in the city. It is hot and semi-arid. A nuclear power plant stands about twelve kilometres away; work by a Bonn firm began under a contract of 1975 and stopped in 1979, and the plant was later completed in cooperation with Russia and began supplying electricity in September 2011.
bushido: Bushido is a samurai moral code concerning attitudes, behaviour and lifestyle. Its origins date to the Kamakura period (1185 to 1333), but the code was formalised in the Edo period (1603 to 1868). The word is rarely attested in pre-modern literature and first appears in the Kōyō Gunkan of about 1616, a military chronicle of the Takeda clan. The ideas it formalised appeared as unwritten customs in the 12th century under the shogun Minamoto Yoritomo, and a Way of the Bow and the Horse existed from that century. During the Muromachi period (1336 to 1573) the way of the warrior was refined by adding Zen meditation, painting, the tea ceremony and poetry, including the death poem written before battle.

Bushido was never a single code that every samurai had to follow. Interpretations varied by clan, by individual and by era. Sengoku bushido put honour, warfare, weapon mastery and valour first. Samurai were as practical on the battlefield as other warriors, sometimes retreated from unwinnable battles, and did not seek an honourable death, which was honourable only in the service of a daimyo and while furthering his cause.

Japan then enjoyed two and a half centuries of relative peace under the Tokugawa Shogunate, and bushido was refined from a focus on valour in battle to one on moral integrity. Miyamoto Musashi (1584 to 1645) and Yamamoto Tsunetomo (1659 to 1719) wrote at length about their interpretations. Influences included Zen Buddhism, Shinto and Confucianism.

The Meiji restoration abolished the samurai class in the 1870s. Bushido of the Meiji era stressed loyalty to the emperor and self-sacrifice more than many Tokugawa interpretations did. Nitobe Inazō's book Bushido: The Soul of Japan made it known abroad, though scholars regard the morals he described as romanticised. In Shōwa Japan before and during the Second World War bushido was used for militarism, to present war as purifying and death as a duty. In the Taishō period it was advocated as the way of the merchant, and it is still invoked in business and martial arts.
busseto: Busseto is a comune in the province of Parma, in Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy, about 8 kilometres south of Cremona in Lombardy. It has about 6,763 inhabitants. Its name appears as Buxetum in the first written sources of the early twelfth century, and may derive either from buxus, the box shrub, or from a word for a fenced pen for oxen.

The history of Busseto is well documented back to the 10th century. For almost five hundred years it was the capital of the Stato Pallavicino, which eventually became part of the Duchy of Parma. La Rocca, the fortress at the centre of the town, stands on the site of a stronghold founded in the eleventh century by Adalberto Pallavicini, a member of the family.

In the first half of the thirteenth century the fortress was laid out afresh with a moat and a drawbridge facing the square. Later damage destroyed the drawbridge and parts of the walls, and in 1857 the architect Pier Luigi Montecchini rebuilt most of it in neo-Gothic style. It keeps its thirteenth-century keep and main tower.

La Rocca is now the municipal palace and contains the Teatro Verdi, a small theatre of 300 seats built by the municipality without the composer's prior approval, although Giuseppe Verdi gave money towards its completion. The National Giuseppe Verdi Museum is housed in the Renaissance Villa Pallavicino and was opened on 10 October 2009.

Verdi was born in the nearby village of Le Roncole in 1813 and moved to Busseto in 1824. The town preserves Casa Barezzi, the home of his patron and later father-in-law Antonio Barezzi, where Verdi gave his first public performance in 1830. He bought Palazzo Orlandi in 1845 and lived there with Giuseppina Strepponi from 1849 to 1851, composing Luisa Miller, Stiffelio and Rigoletto. His villa at Sant'Agata nearby became his main home after 1851.
buton-island: Buton, also written Butung, Boeton or Button, covers roughly 4,727 square kilometres, about the size of Madura. Its largest town is Baubau, where the Wolio and Cia-Cia languages are spoken. Major nearby islands include Wawonii to the north, Muna and Kabaena to the west and Siumpu to the south-west, while the Tukangbesi Islands lie just to the east and Batuatas Island to the south. The Bouton Passage, as it was known before independence, was an important point for navigation in the northern Flores Sea. The island is largely covered by rainforest and is one of only two habitats of the anoa, a type of buffalo.

In the precolonial era the island, then usually known as Butung, lay within the sphere of influence of Ternate. Especially in the sixteenth century Buton served as an important secondary regional centre within the Ternaten empire, controlling regional trade and collecting tribute to be sent to Ternate. The Sultanate of Buton ruled over the island until the 20th century. Sultan Murhum, the first Islamic monarch on the island, is remembered in the name of Murhum Harbor in Baubau.

The languages spoken on Buton include Wolio, Cia-Cia, several dialects of Muna, Tukang Besi, Kumbewaha, Lasalimu, Kamaru, Pancana, Busoa, Taloki, Kulisusu and Kioko, and Indonesian is widely used and taught in schools. In 2009 the Cia-Cia in Baubau began to use the Korean Hangul alphabet for their language, with textbooks made by a linguistic society in Seoul, and it continues to be taught in schools in that script.

The island has a massive reserve of natural asphalt and several other minerals. Administratively it is divided among five second-level units: Baubau City, Buton Regency, part of South Buton Regency, North Buton Regency and part of Muna Regency.
buyid-dynasty: The Buyids descended from Panah-Khusrow, a Zoroastrian from Daylam. His son Buya, a fisherman from Lahijan, converted to Islam, and Buya's three sons, Ali, Hasan and Ahmad, founded the dynasty. The Buyids claimed royal descent from the Sasanian king Bahram V. Ali ibn Buya served the Daylamite warlord Makan ibn Kaki and then Mardavij, founder of the Ziyarid dynasty, who granted him Karaj in 932. When Mardavij planned to have him killed, the brothers fled with 400 Daylamite followers to Fars, won Arrajan and defeated the Abbasid general Yaqut for control of the province. Ali then took its capital, Shiraz.

Mardavij's assassination in 935 threw the Ziyarid lands into chaos. Ali and Ahmad conquered Khuzistan, while Hasan took Isfahan and in 943 Ray, so gaining all of Jibal. In 945 Ahmad entered Iraq and seized Baghdad. The Abbasid court submitted to him as the real ruler, and the Buyids built a palace just north of the caliph's, while the caliph, left with no vizier, became a figurehead. The brothers took the honorific titles Imad al-Dawla, Rukn al-Dawla and Mu'izz al-Dawla. Kerman fell in 967, Oman in 967, the Jazira in 979, Tabaristan in 980 and Gorgan in 981.

Fanna Khusraw, Adud al-Dawla, who ruled from 949 to 983, took the dynasty to its height. After his death his sons fought each other, local dynasties became independent in parts of the realm and the confederation slowly broke up. In 1029 Mahmud of Ghazna deposed the Buyid ruler at Ray, who had asked for help against his own Daylami troops. In 1055 the Seljuk leader Tughril occupied Baghdad and ousted the last Buyid ruler there, and the dynasty's rule ended in 1062.

The Buyids formed a confederation of three principalities, in Fars, Jibal and Iraq, in which land was divided among the sons and each amir enjoyed a high degree of autonomy. The senior amir had formal precedence but little control outside his own lands. Their army began with Daylamite foot soldiers and added Turks to the cavalry, and the two groups often quarrelled. Soldiers were paid by iqtas, rights to a share of a province's tax revenue. The Buyids revived Sasanian titles and carved inscriptions at Persepolis, but used Arabic as the language of their realm and patronised Arabic poets and historians, among them al-Mutanabbi at Adud al-Dawla's court in Shiraz.

Initially Zaydi Shi'a, they became Twelver Shi'a, patronised Twelver scholars and built at the shrines of Kadhimiya, but they kept the Sunni Abbasid caliphs as figureheads and were known as tolerant of the Sunni majority. Their realm included many Zoroastrians and Christians. They restored the Baduriya dam, and Adud al-Dawla built the Band-e Amir dam near Shiraz, a hospital in Baghdad and a mausoleum at the burial place of Ali.
buyuk-menderes-river: The Büyük Menderes, meaning Great Meander, rises in a spring near Dinar, in west central Turkey, and flows through the Büyük Menderes graben to Lake Işıklı. It passes the Adıgüzel and Cindere dams and the towns of Nazilli, Aydın and Söke before it drains into the Aegean Sea close to the ancient Ionian city of Miletus. Its sinuous course gave its name to the common term meander, for the characteristic bends of rivers.

In antiquity the Maeander, from the Greek Maíandros, was a well-known river of Caria in Asia Minor. It appears first in the Catalog of Trojans in Homer's Iliad, together with Miletus and Mycale. Its sources were placed near Celaenae in Phrygia, now Dinar, where it gushed forth in a park of Cyrus. Ancient writers differed over whether it shared its sources with the river Marsyas, which Xenophon says rose in a royal palace, and some said it flowed from a lake on Mount Aulocrene. William Martin Leake reconciled the accounts by suggesting that both rivers have their origin in the lake above Celaenae but issue from different parts of the mountain.

The river was so well known for its windings that its classical name became proverbial. Its whole course runs south-west on the south of the range of Mount Messogis. South of Tripolis it receives the Lycus and becomes a river of some importance. Near Carura it passes from Phrygia into Caria and winds through the Maeandrian plain, to reach the Gulf of Icaros between the Greek cities of Priene and Myus, opposite Miletus and only 10 stadia from it. Its tributaries include the Orgyas, Marsyas, Cludrus, Lethaeus and Gaeson in the north and the Obrimas, Lycus and Harpasus in the south.

The Maeander is deep but not broad, so that in many places its depth equals its breadth and only small craft can navigate it. It often overflows its banks, and the mud deposited at its mouth pushed the coast 20 or 30 stadia, about 4 to 6 kilometres, further into the sea and joined several small islands to the mainland. Its river god, also called Meander, was one of the sons of Oceanus and Tethys, and a legend told of an underground link between the Maeander and the Alpheus River in Elis.
byblos: Byblos lies on the coast of Lebanon about 42 kilometres north of Beirut. It is believed to have been first settled between 8800 and 7000 BCE and continuously inhabited since 5000 BCE. Urbanisation is thought to have begun in the third millennium BCE, making it one of the oldest cities in the world. The name appears as kbnj in Egyptian records going back to the pharaoh Sneferu and as Gebal in Phoenician inscriptions, and it seems to mean Well of the God. Because the city imported papyrus from Egypt, byblos came to mean papyrus in Greek, and the English word Bible ultimately derives from it.

In the Early Bronze Age Byblos developed from a fishermen's village around a shrine at a natural spring into a town with a temple compound. It was a wealthy ally of Egypt for many centuries. About 1350 BCE the Amarna letters include 60 letters from Rib-Hadda and his successor Ili-Rapih, rulers of Byblos, mostly Rib-Hadda's pleas to Akhenaten for military help. When the New Kingdom collapsed in the 11th century BCE, Byblos became the foremost city of Phoenicia. Five royal inscriptions of about 1150–950 BCE, among them the Ahiram sarcophagus, show a Phoenician alphabet of twenty-two characters.

Sibittibaal of Byblos became tributary to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 BCE, and under the Achaemenid Empire Byblos was one of four Phoenician vassal kingdoms. Alexander the Great brought Hellenistic rule in 332 BCE. In the Greco-Roman period it was a centre of the cult of Adonis, and a theatre was built in the 3rd century. Prosperity returned with the First Crusade in 1098.

As Gibelet the city belonged to the Crusader County of Tripoli, and the Genoese Embriaco family held it as a hereditary lordship. Saladin took the town in 1187 and Baibars conquered it in 1266, but the Embriacos kept it until around 1300. The Ottoman Empire ruled it from 1516 until 1918, and it was under the French Mandate from 1920 until 1943.

Byblos is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its archaeological site includes the L-shaped temple of about 2700 BCE, the Temple of the Obelisks, the royal necropolis with the tomb of King Ahiram, the Roman theatre and the Crusader castle of the 12th century. A medieval wall surrounds the old town.
byelorussian-ssr: Before the First World War the lands of modern Belarus belonged to the Russian Empire, which had gained them in the Partitions of Poland. After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918 the Belarusian Democratic Republic was proclaimed under German occupation. As German troops left, the Bolsheviks advanced west, took Minsk on 10 December 1918, and set up the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia. It was merged with the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, a union that ceased to exist in the Polish–Soviet War.

The Red Army broke the Polish front in 1920 and retook Minsk on 11 July, and the republic was re-founded on 31 July 1920. The Treaty of Riga of February 1921 divided the country: almost half, Western Belarus, went to Poland, and the rest was the Soviet republic, with 52,400 square kilometres and 1.544 million people. It became one of the four founding members of the Soviet Union in December 1922.

The 1930s marked the peak of Soviet repressions in Belarus. By incomplete calculations about 600,000 people fell victim to them between 1917 and 1953, and over 250,000 Belarusians were deported as kulaks or their families. In September 1939, after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union incorporated the territories known as West Belarus into the republic.

Nazi Germany occupied Belarus in the summer of 1941. It deported some 380,000 people for forced labour and killed hundreds of thousands of civilians. About 800,000 Belarusian Jews, about 90 percent of the Jewish population, were killed in the Holocaust, and more than 600 villages such as Khatyn were totally annihilated. Over 2,000,000 people, almost a quarter of the population, died during the three years of occupation.

After the war the republic became a founding member of the United Nations, with its own seat beside the Soviet Union and the Ukrainian SSR. Its Supreme Soviet declared sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and independence on 25 August 1991, and on 19 September the republic was renamed the Republic of Belarus.

Until 1990 the republic was a one-party state governed by the Communist Party of Byelorussia, a branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Minsk was its capital and largest city, and the official languages were Belarusian and Russian. Most of its 10 million people in 1989 were Belarusians, with significant minorities of Russians, Poles, Ukrainians and Jews. It was one of the more developed Soviet republics, with advanced manufacturing and agriculture.
bytom: Bytom lies in Upper Silesia, 7 km northwest of Katowice. Its bedrock holds coal and iron ore from the Carboniferous period, and in the Bytom basin triassic rocks carry ore, zinc and lead reserves. The city's coat of arms shows a miner mining coal on one half and a yellow eagle on a blue field, the symbol of Upper Silesia, on the other.

The town is first recorded as Bitom in 1136, when it was part of the medieval Kingdom of Poland. Excavations show a fortified settlement, probably founded by Bolesław I the Brave in the early 11th century. It profited from its place on trade routes linking Kraków with Silesia and Hungary with Moravia and Greater Poland. The first church of the Virgin Mary was built in 1231, and the Mongols raided the town in 1259. The duchy lay under the overlordship of the Kingdom of Bohemia from 1289 and lasted until 1498, when it was reunited with the Duchy of Opole.

The town came under the Habsburg monarchy in 1526, and in 1742 it became part of the Kingdom of Prussia during the Silesian Wars. In 1683 King John III Sobieski visited on his way to the Battle of Vienna. After 1871, in the German Empire, the city grew and industrialised rapidly. According to the Prussian census of 1905 it had 60,273 inhabitants, of whom 59% spoke German, 38% Polish and 3% both.

Bytom was a main centre of Polish organisation in Upper Silesia. The newspaper Dziennik Górnośląski appeared from 1848, and Polish societies were harassed by the Prussian authorities. In the plebiscite of 1921, 74.7% of the votes in the city were for Germany and 25.3% for Poland. The synagogue was burned on 9 and 10 November 1938, and the Red Army captured the city in January 1945.

Bytom is a city in the Silesian Voivodeship of southern Poland. It is the home of the Silesian Opera and the Upper Silesian Museum, and it holds part of the Tarnowskie Góry Lead-Silver-Zinc Mine and its Underground Water Management System, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
byzantine-iconoclasm: By the sixth century Christian worship included a belief in the intercession of saints and the use of relics and holy images. Iconoclasm drew on the biblical commandment against graven images, which iconoclasts read as forbidding the making and veneration of icons. Traditional explanations point to Islamic prohibitions of images, but newer studies find that the spread of iconoclasm did not depend on distance from the Arab frontier. A large submarine volcanic eruption in the Aegean in the summer of 726 was probably a precursor, and many, probably including Emperor Leo III the Isaurian, took it as divine judgment on the use of images.

The classic account says that between 726 and 730 Leo III ordered an image of Christ over the Chalke Gate of the Great Palace removed and replaced with a cross, and that some of those assigned to the task were killed by iconodules. He apparently forbade the veneration of images in an edict of 730, which did not apply to the emperor's image or the cross. Germanos I, the iconophile Patriarch of Constantinople, resigned or was deposed.

Leo's son Constantine V, who ruled from 741 to 775, was personally committed to the ban and in 754 summoned the Council of Hieria, where 338 bishops declared the painting of holy figures blasphemous. Neither Orthodox nor Catholic tradition now accepts its claim to be the Seventh Ecumenical Council, since no patriarch or representative of one was present. Leo V the Armenian began a second period in 815, after Byzantine defeats by the Bulgarian khan Krum, and a synod in Hagia Sophia in 815 made iconoclasm official again.

John of Damascus, who lived in Muslim territory, and Theodore the Studite, abbot of the Stoudios monastery, were the chief opponents of iconoclasm. John held that he worshipped the creator of matter, not matter, and the iconophiles argued that the incarnation allowed Christ to be depicted. The period greatly reduced the Byzantine art that survives from before it.

The Papacy supported images throughout. Pope Gregory III excommunicated iconoclasts, and in 754 the emperor seized papal properties in Sicily, Calabria and Illyria, while Pope Stephen II made an alliance with the Frankish Kingdom. The controversy ended the so-called Byzantine Papacy and widened the gap between Byzantine and Carolingian traditions.
byzantion: The origin of the name is unknown. It has been suggested to be Thracian, perhaps from the personal name Byzas, which means he-goat. Greek legend names Byzas as the leader of the Megarian colonists and founder of the city. The city was mainly a trading city because it stood at the only entrance to the Black Sea, and it later conquered Chalcedon across the Bosphorus. Its position, surrounded by water on almost all sides, made it highly defensible.

Tradition says Byzas of Megara founded the city after sailing northeast across the Aegean. The date is usually given as 667 BCE on the authority of Herodotus. Constantine the Great favoured that dating and marked the city's 1,000th anniversary between 333 and 334. The Persian Empire took the city at the time of Darius I's Scythian campaign in 513 BCE. In the Peloponnesian War Sparta took it in 411 BCE to cut off grain supplies to Athens, and the Athenians retook it in 408 BCE.

After the city sided with Pescennius Niger against Septimius Severus, Roman forces besieged it and badly damaged it in 196 CE. Severus rebuilt it, and it soon regained its prosperity. In 330 CE Constantine I refounded it as an imperial residence modelled on Rome, known as Nova Roma and later as Constantinople. For centuries it was the capital of the Byzantine Empire. The Ottoman Turks conquered it on 29 May 1453.

The name Byzantium was used for the Eastern Roman Empire as a whole only from 1555, when the historian Hieronymus Wolf introduced it. Its inhabitants continued to call their state the empire of the Romans. From the 9th century the names Byzantius and Byzantinus were applied to the empire's gold coinage, which gave the English words besant, byzant and bezant.
